exhibits.title: Five Guided Layer Ablations
exhibits.action: Predict the adversary outcome, apply each named layer change, and compare the channel result across five chained experiments.
exhibits.outcome: The fluent-speaker, obscurity-only, unauthenticated peer, repeated key and nonce, and per-message ratchet cases expose the load-bearing protections.
exhibits.limits: The browser requires the separately built WebAssembly package; the ratchet is symmetric and does not promise post-compromise security.

exhibits.title: Two Transfer Challenges
exhibits.action: Configure the switches to defend named adversaries without forward secrecy, then find a minimal two-time-pad configuration.
exhibits.outcome: A per-condition checklist scores defenses and minimality and offers an explanatory answer after the attempt.

exhibits.title: Transmission and Layer Controls
exhibits.action: Edit two messages, choose a KEM backend and AEAD suite, toggle the layers and fault, or select a preset.
exhibits.outcome: The channel reruns and reports the adversary recovery and intended recipient delivery for the chosen configuration.
exhibits.limits: The weak transport layer is intentionally illustrative; KEM options depend on the compiled WASM features.

exhibits.title: Named Adversaries and Metadata
exhibits.action: Inspect computed A1–A5 defenses and the metadata list as layer settings change.
exhibits.outcome: The panel separates plaintext recovery today from key compromise and harvest-now-decrypt-later, and lists leaks unaffected by switches.

exhibits.title: Wire Frames and Handshake
exhibits.action: Compare the two wire frames, focus hexdump fields, and open transcript and key internals.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect parsed frame boundaries, key comparison, authenticated handshake sequence, and intended recipient result.

exhibits.title: Terms and Navajo Code-Talker Context
exhibits.action: Read inline glossary definitions and the historical account of the codebook and Joe Kieyoomia.
exhibits.outcome: Distinguish the codebook layer from linguistic obscurity and locate the historical analogy and its limits.
exhibits.section: Why this stack, and whose it was

exhibits.title: Six Layer Captions with Live Demonstrations
exhibits.action: Open each layer’s Job, Adversary, consequence, 1942 and modern captions, then press Show me to apply its demonstration configuration.
exhibits.outcome: The module supplies one tested configuration and expected verdict per key-agreement, AEAD, transport, authentication, ratchet and nonce-fault layer.
exhibits.limits: Transport is framing and padding rather than a confidentiality guarantee; the symmetric ratchet does not heal after compromise.

exhibits.title: Ciphertext XOR and Bounded Crib Recovery
exhibits.action: Disable the ratchet and repeat the AEAD nonce, then inspect the known first message, recovered second-message bytes and crib-length boundary.
exhibits.outcome: The shared key and nonce yield equal keystream segments; the XOR cancels the stream only over the overlapping known-plaintext length.
exhibits.limits: The panel appears only for the KeystreamReuse verdict; repeating a nonce under a fresh ratchet key does not create this two-time pad.

exhibits.title: Guided accumulator story
exhibits.action: Step through the revocation scenario and reset it.
exhibits.outcome: The guided path applies each change to the same accumulator state as the main exhibits.
exhibits.limits: The 512-bit modulus and known factorization are teaching parameters.

exhibits.title: Revocation without the list
exhibits.section: The point: revocation without the list
exhibits.action: Fetch a certificate proof, revoke or un-revoke it, and check the cached proof against the changing digest.
exhibits.outcome: Shows an absence proof becoming stale, a new membership proof, and measured proof bytes beside CRL and Merkle alternatives.
exhibits.limits: A scenario with an illustrative CA size; not a deployed revocation service.

exhibits.title: Constant-size accumulator digest
exhibits.section: The exponent grows. The digest does not.
exhibits.action: Step prime representatives into the exponent and add larger crowds.
exhibits.outcome: Displays a growing product alongside a modulus-bounded digest, measuring actual modular exponentiation and byte sizes.
exhibits.limits: The digest is bounded by the chosen 512-bit toy modulus; this does not claim 512-bit security.

exhibits.title: Membership witness and verifier
exhibits.section: Membership proof — “I am in the set”
exhibits.action: Select a member, build and verify its witness, or request one for an absent label.
exhibits.outcome: Compares w^e mod N to the published digest digit by digit; the honest witness builder refuses absent elements.
exhibits.limits: Membership is not zero knowledge; a witness can expose set relationships.

exhibits.title: Non-membership witness and verifier
exhibits.section: Non-membership proof — “I am NOT in the set”
exhibits.action: Choose an absent label, solve the Bézout identity, build its witness and verify; try a present label.
exhibits.outcome: Shows a·u+b·x=1 and checks A^a·d^x mod N equals g; a present element cannot satisfy the coprimality requirement.
exhibits.limits: Proofs are built over small teaching parameters with a known factorization.

exhibits.title: Witnesses after set changes
exhibits.section: A living set — and the witnesses that go stale
exhibits.action: Mint held membership and absence witnesses, add or remove elements, update witnesses from public data, and compare deletion methods.
exhibits.outcome: Shows changed digests, failed stale proofs, repaired witnesses and full-recompute versus trapdoor deletion.
exhibits.limits: The shortcut deletion uses the factorization intentionally known to this page; real setups must protect or avoid that trapdoor.

exhibits.title: RSA accumulator and Merkle tree
exhibits.action: Choose deployment size, parameter assumptions and update load; compare measured proofs for the current set and scaling projections.
exhibits.outcome: Shows constant-size accumulator witnesses versus logarithmic Merkle paths and tradeoffs around trusted setup and update load.
exhibits.limits: Scaling for very large sets uses checked formulas, while the displayed current set runs both structures; projections are not benchmarks.

exhibits.title: Adversarial witness attempts
exhibits.action: Select one of ten attacks, predict acceptance and run against the ordinary verifier.
exhibits.outcome: Shows eight rejected attempts and two accepted violations when the input contract or setup assumption is removed.
exhibits.limits: Accepted contrived cases deliberately bypass contract or assumption; they do not imply a valid production accumulator can be forged.

exhibits.title: Generate safe-prime parameters
exhibits.section: The parameters — and who holds the keys to them
exhibits.action: Generate fresh safe primes at selected toy bit lengths or restore shipped parameters.
exhibits.outcome: Recomputes digest and witnesses, exposes p and q, and explains why a known factorization invalidates a production setup.
exhibits.limits: 256–512-bit choices are insecure toy sizes; the page intentionally knows p and q.

exhibits.title: Adaptor signature relation
exhibits.action: Run or step through locking, pre-signing, completion and extraction; try a wrong secret.
exhibits.outcome: The pre-signature fails ordinary BIP-340 verification, the adapted signature verifies, and extraction recovers the adaptor secret from the pair.

exhibits.title: Atomic swap event ledger
exhibits.action: Advance the swap one event at a time and toggle cheating or skipped pre-verification.
exhibits.outcome: See the modeled ledger settlements and how Bob can extract the right secret yet fail to claim the other payment after accepting a pre-signature for the wrong adaptor point.
exhibits.limits: Ledgers and timelocks are deterministic teaching state machines; there is no blockchain, script, mempool or fee model.

exhibits.title: PTLC multi-hop settlement
exhibits.action: Settle the routed payment hop by hop and vary corruption or blinding.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect per-hop adaptor points and whether downstream extraction supplies the upstream settlement secret.
exhibits.limits: Real pre-signature arithmetic is embedded in a modeled route; channel state, fees, network and onion routing are outside the lab.

exhibits.title: Nonce reuse and point substitution
exhibits.action: Trigger the repeated nonce attack or inspect a pre-signature made for the wrong point.
exhibits.outcome: A forged signature on an untouched message is accepted by the BIP-340 verifier; pre-verifying against the intended point detects substitution.

exhibits.title: Published vector verification
exhibits.action: Run the vector table through pre-sign, pre-verify, adapt, verify and extract where signable.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect reproduced acceptance or rejection and extraction checks, including negative verify-only rows.

exhibits.title: Real and modeled adaptor-signature boundaries
exhibits.action: Open the Honesty tab and inspect the real, modeled and absent features and threat assumptions.
exhibits.outcome: Separate real BIP-340/adaptor computations from ledger, timelock and routing state machines, and identify constructions the lab does not implement.

exhibits.title: AEGIS-256 Encrypt, Decrypt, and Tamper
exhibits.action: Generate a key and nonce, encrypt a message with associated data, decrypt, then flip a ciphertext or tag bit.
exhibits.outcome: Shows ciphertext and tag, then reports authentication failure for modified inputs.
exhibits.limits: Educational TypeScript implementation, not a production library.

exhibits.title: AEGIS State Machine
exhibits.action: Initialize, absorb an associated-data block, encrypt a plaintext block, and finalize step by step.
exhibits.outcome: Displays the six-block state and the transitions that produce ciphertext and an authentication tag.

exhibits.title: One AES Round Under the Hood
exhibits.action: Step through the AES round used by the state machine.
exhibits.outcome: Exposes SubBytes, ShiftRows, MixColumns, and key mixing as a teaching trace.
exhibits.section: Open the black box: watch one AES round mix

exhibits.title: Initialization Avalanche
exhibits.action: Flip one nonce bit and trace the 16 setup updates.
exhibits.outcome: Charts how changed state bits spread across the six blocks.
exhibits.section: Avalanche: what the 16 setup updates buy

exhibits.title: AEGIS Nonce Reuse
exhibits.action: Encrypt two messages under the same key and nonce and compare against fresh nonces.
exhibits.outcome: Exposes recoverable sibling plaintext blocks under reuse and contrasts with fresh-nonce outputs.
exhibits.limits: The demonstration targets the guaranteed leakage in its constructed messages, not every consequence of reuse.

exhibits.title: Random Nonce Collision Explorer
exhibits.action: Change the message count and compare nonce sizes.
exhibits.outcome: Computes collision probability using the birthday bound.
exhibits.section: How long are random nonces safe? The birthday bound, live

exhibits.title: AEGIS and AES-GCM Benchmark
exhibits.action: Run browser throughput trials of AEGIS-256 and WebCrypto AES-GCM.
exhibits.outcome: Reports measured speeds on the current device and contextualizes differences.
exhibits.limits: Browser timings depend on device and implementation; they are not universal performance rankings.

exhibits.title: AEGIS, GCM, and ChaCha20-Poly1305 Tradeoffs
exhibits.action: Read the comparison table and AEGIS family variants.
exhibits.outcome: Contrasts key and nonce lengths, hardware throughput context, nonce discipline, standardization, and state or SIMD rate among family members.
exhibits.limits: The table’s throughput statements are qualitative; the separate local benchmark is implementation and device dependent.

exhibits.title: AEGIS Family and Deployment Boundary
exhibits.action: Read the final family comparison and deployment context.
exhibits.outcome: Separates AEGIS-128L, AEGIS-256, and wide SIMD variants by state, rate, key, and nonce size while situating the demo’s variant.
exhibits.limits: The adjacent 2026 RFC and draft status statements are pinned to this source, not a live standardization check.

exhibits.title: One ciphertext, two keys
exhibits.action: Replay the published two-key fixture, switch tag lengths, and compare constructed, identical and tampered associated data.
exhibits.outcome: Actual state traces converge for the constructed contexts; both keys authenticate the same ciphertext, while the negative controls reject the second context.
exhibits.limits: Known attacker-chosen key and associated-data contexts; no unknown-key recovery or fixed-key authentication forgery.

exhibits.title: Bytes are polynomials
exhibits.action: Enter two hex bytes and compute their XOR, xtime, finite-field product and extended-Euclid inverse.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect the polynomial steps and AES field reduction; zero has no multiplicative inverse.
exhibits.limits: Single-byte teaching arithmetic, not a constant-time cryptographic implementation.

exhibits.title: Build the S-box
exhibits.action: Construct all S-box entries and toggle the deliberately affine-only table.
exhibits.outcome: Compare computed inversion-plus-affine S-box entries with the standard and inspect how removing inversion changes the mapping.
exhibits.limits: The affine-only variant deliberately removes an essential nonlinear step.

exhibits.title: Move and mix
exhibits.action: Step ShiftRows and MixColumns on the state grid for the selected key and block.
exhibits.outcome: See byte locations, column mixing and structural dependencies as the state changes.
exhibits.limits: Structural dependency does not ensure a visible difference on every chosen input.

exhibits.title: Expand the key
exhibits.action: Choose AES-128, AES-192 or AES-256, inspect expanded words and step through the schedule.
exhibits.outcome: Trace RotWord, SubWord and round constants, including the extra AES-256 SubWord case.
exhibits.limits: A deterministic preset or seeded teaching generator is not secret-key generation.

exhibits.title: The whole cipher
exhibits.action: Step a complete encryption layer by layer and run the WebCrypto cross-check.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect intermediate round states and ciphertext; AES-128/256 are cross-checked against WebCrypto and AES-192 against pinned FIPS vectors.
exhibits.limits: Hand-built inspectable AES is not constant-time or production encryption; the WebCrypto check uses the first CBC block.

exhibits.title: Reverse the cipher
exhibits.action: Decrypt using correct InvCipher or deliberately select forward round keys or forward MixColumns.
exhibits.outcome: The correct inverse restores the block; each wrong operation leaves an invalid but full-length output.
exhibits.limits: This steps InvCipher; EqInvCipher is described but not implemented.

exhibits.title: Remove a layer, run the break
exhibits.section: Remove a layer, run the break
exhibits.action: Remove SubBytes, inversion, ShiftRows or MixColumns from the AES-128 data path, run the matching attack and compare with full AES controls.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect attack recoveries, matrices or codebooks, avalanche diagnostics and fresh held-out verification; partial codebook coverage is marked unknown.
exhibits.limits: Attacks apply to deliberately broken AES-128 variants, not practical key recovery against full AES; key schedule retains the real S-box.

exhibits.title: Inject a fault, recover the key
exhibits.section: Inject a fault, recover the key
exhibits.action: Inject known-location round-9 byte faults into AES-128, compare correct and faulty ciphertexts, then intersect last-round-key candidates.
exhibits.outcome: Two faults per affected quartet isolate round key 10; reversing the key schedule and a held-out encryption independently verify the recovered master key.
exhibits.limits: Logical known-location single-byte fault model; not physical injection, not arbitrary ciphertext corruption, and the recomputation comparison is not a universal defense.

exhibits.title: Keep only accepted outputs, recover a byte
exhibits.section: Keep only accepted outputs, recover a byte
exhibits.action: Choose a first-round S-box bit, fault model and output policy; execute correct and faulted AES-128 trials, then rank all 256 first-key-byte guesses from the inputs selected by observable output handling.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect real-AES fault witnesses, a separately labeled analytic census and seeded finite-sample ranks; a secret-independent null and hidden-selection case remove the modeled signal, while an exact clean-reference oracle restores selection.
exhibits.limits: Chosen-input one-byte logical model with a declared profiled landing rate; the census is analytic rather than sampled evidence, and the deterministic teaching infection is not timing-oblivious, hardened, universal or the cited circuit defense.

exhibits.title: ECB: Repeated Blocks
exhibits.action: Encrypt repeating text or an uploaded image with ECB.
exhibits.outcome: Compare ciphertext blocks and an image view that preserves repeated-block structure; decrypting one tampered ciphertext block illustrates absent authentication.
exhibits.limits: Educational mode implementation; ECB has no integrity check and is inappropriate for multi-block secret data.

exhibits.title: CBC: Chaining, IVs and Bit Flips
exhibits.action: Encrypt with CBC, test IV reuse or the targeted bit-flip puzzle, then decrypt with correct and modified inputs.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect chained blocks and how IV reuse reveals shared prefixes or ciphertext modification changes decrypted bytes without an integrity guarantee.
exhibits.limits: CBC alone provides confidentiality, not authenticity; the padding-oracle attack is covered in a separate lab.

exhibits.title: GCM Nonce-Reuse Forgery
exhibits.action: Edit two one-block plaintexts and a forged target, then run reused-nonce recovery and the fresh-nonce control.
exhibits.outcome: Display recovered GHASH subkey H, recovered tag mask, forged ciphertext and tag, and whether WebCrypto AES-GCM accepts the forged message.
exhibits.limits: The worked algebra uses two equal-length single-block ciphertexts with empty AAD; it does not recover the AES encryption key, and the fresh-nonce control should reject.

exhibits.title: GCM Authenticated Encryption
exhibits.action: Enter plaintext and AAD, select a tag length, encrypt and try wrong AAD, wrong nonce or a flipped ciphertext bit.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect ciphertext and tag; WebCrypto rejects decryption after unauthenticated changes.
exhibits.limits: Correct use requires unique nonces per key; a shorter tag reduces forgery resistance and may require specific message-length and usage limits.

exhibits.title: Padding Oracle Attack
exhibits.action: Enter a secret plaintext, set up a CBC padding oracle, and run byte-wise attack queries.
exhibits.outcome: Watch padding-validity queries and recovered plaintext bytes with a query counter.
exhibits.limits: The laboratory intentionally exposes a padding-validity signal; it is not inherent to every CBC deployment.

exhibits.title: Same plaintext, all seven modes
exhibits.action: Enter repeated-block plaintext and click “Encrypt under all 7 modes.”
exhibits.outcome: Compare seven ciphertext block grids for ECB, CBC, CTR, OFB, CFB, GCM and CCM; repeated ECB blocks are marked.
exhibits.limits: A side-by-side block grid illustrates one property; it is not a comprehensive security proof. CBC, CTR, OFB and CFB remain confidentiality-only; GCM and CCM include authentication.

exhibits.title: CTR Keystream and Nonce Reuse
exhibits.action: Encrypt two messages with AES-CTR, inspect counter blocks, decrypt, and deliberately repeat a nonce.
exhibits.outcome: The reused keystream cancels under ciphertext XOR so known first plaintext recovers overlapping second plaintext.
exhibits.limits: CTR alone does not authenticate ciphertext; unique counter blocks are required.

exhibits.title: OFB Keystream, Access Cost, and Bit Flip
exhibits.action: Precompute OFB stream, encrypt, compare an uncached random-access block with CTR, then reuse an IV or flip a ciphertext bit.
exhibits.outcome: The lab shows sequential feedback, overlapping keystream exposure under IV reuse, and one-bit malleability without a tag.
exhibits.limits: AES evaluation counts are logical mode operations; the WebCrypto CBC wrapper computes a discarded padding block.

exhibits.title: CFB Feedback and Error Propagation
exhibits.action: Encrypt under CFB-8 or CFB-128, flip a bit, delete a byte or aligned block, reuse an IV, or rewrite a known block.
exhibits.outcome: Traces show ciphertext feedback, resynchronization conditions, chosen-block malleability and overlap leakage.
exhibits.limits: This is SP 800-38A CFB, not OpenPGP resynchronization; it supplies confidentiality only.

exhibits.title: Zero-IV CFB-8 Weak-Key Search
exhibits.action: Search or cancel a bounded random-key experiment with all-zero IV and plaintext.
exhibits.outcome: A key with first AES_K(0) byte equal to zero preserves the zero register, illustrating the structural condition behind a Zerologon-style weakness.
exhibits.section: Deliberately broken: the zero-IV CFB-8 property behind Zerologon
exhibits.limits: The search is capped at 4,096 teaching keys and does not emulate Netlogon or measure compromise time.

exhibits.title: CCM Authenticated Encryption
exhibits.action: Enter plaintext and AAD, encrypt under AES-CCM, inspect CBC-MAC and CTR framing, then tamper and decrypt.
exhibits.outcome: The receiver rejects modified inputs; comparison with GCM highlights different AEAD constructions and nonce discipline.

exhibits.title: AES Mode Decision Guide
exhibits.action: Read the recommended mode choices and risk boundaries for general applications, constrained devices, legacy CBC and ECB.
exhibits.outcome: The guide groups GCM and CCM as authenticated modes and warns that CBC without a MAC, ECB patterns, and unauthenticated stream modes have different failure modes.

exhibits.title: Step through the colour mixing analogy
exhibits.action: Advance the colour mixing picture one stage at a time.
exhibits.outcome: The picture shows private starting colours and public mixtures arriving at a shared colour.
exhibits.limits: An analogy; colour mixing is not X25519 mathematics.

exhibits.title: Run a fresh X25519 exchange
exhibits.action: Run the exchange and open the full working.
exhibits.outcome: Compare separately computed 32-byte secrets and public values; published RFC 7748 vectors and all-zero checks appear.
exhibits.limits: Two roles are simulated locally; no peer authentication, key derivation, or secure messaging protocol.

exhibits.title: Compare a guessed private value against the exchange
exhibits.action: Run an exchange, inspect the public transcript, then roll or enter a private-value candidate.
exhibits.outcome: A real X25519 computation compares the candidate-derived secret to the actual secret and reports whether it was recovered.
exhibits.limits: Only guessing Alice’s private input is modeled; a revealed private input is a leak rather than a transcript-only attack.
exhibits.section: Everything, and it is not enough

exhibits.title: Let a stranger answer instead
exhibits.action: Run a fresh exchange with an unverified stranger answering Alice.
exhibits.outcome: The two sides agree on bytes and the displayed checks pass despite Alice having no assurance that the peer is Bob.
exhibits.limits: This separate example demonstrates the identity gap; it does not run a full man-in-the-middle protocol attack.

exhibits.title: Three Cellular Keystream Families
exhibits.action: Enter a 128-bit key, COUNT, bearer, direction, and byte length, then generate SNOW 3G, AES-CTR, and ZUC keystreams.
exhibits.outcome: Side-by-side hexadecimal outputs and known-answer indicators show each family under the same tuple.
exhibits.limits: The interface caps output at 256 bytes and covers confidentiality generators, not full cellular negotiation or integrity.

exhibits.title: Internal State Clock
exhibits.action: Choose SNOW 3G, AES-CTR, or ZUC and step backward or forward through the captured input, transform, and output stages.
exhibits.outcome: A mechanism diagram follows the live generator trace and exposes bit-order notes.

exhibits.title: Reused Radio Tuple Recovery
exhibits.action: Choose a family and two messages, reuse the key, COUNT, bearer, and direction tuple, then run the attack.
exhibits.outcome: The two ciphertexts, their XOR, and recovered second message demonstrate keystream cancellation.
exhibits.section: Reuse the tuple. Recover the message.

exhibits.title: 256-Bit Cellular Family Mapping
exhibits.action: Inspect the successor-family table and illustrative encrypt-then-MAC control-flow sketch.
exhibits.outcome: Labels map SNOW, AES, and ZUC families to named confidentiality, integrity, and combined-mode profiles.
exhibits.limits: The successor mapping is metadata only; the lab does not generate 256-bit output or verify these modes with known-answer tests.

exhibits.title: Authenticated exchange
exhibits.action: Step through AKE1 using certificates, an encrypted session key and signed nonce and ciphertext.
exhibits.outcome: Displays peer checks, key agreement and a bound application channel.
exhibits.limits: Keys and toy CA live only in memory; the network and attacker are scripted.

exhibits.title: Remove one AKE protection
exhibits.section: 2 · Remove one field, run its attack
exhibits.action: Select V1–V6, run honest peers and attack, then restore the field and replay.
exhibits.outcome: Exposes key exposure, replay or identity misbinding from unsigned ciphertext, nonce, target identity or unauthenticated CTR variants.
exhibits.limits: Each rung is a distinct scripted insecure definition; not a general protocol model checker.

exhibits.title: Long-term key leakage
exhibits.action: Record protected messages under AKE1 and signed ephemeral AKE2eg, then leak P’s long-term or ephemeral key.
exhibits.outcome: Compares post-compromise decryption: AKE1 recorded traffic is exposed by long-term-key leakage, while the ephemeral exchange has a different boundary.
exhibits.limits: Demonstration retains session material in memory for the scripted leak; no persistent or real network threat model.

exhibits.title: Passive and active identity views
exhibits.action: Compare AKE2eg and AKE4eg passive observer views, then probe as a fake responder.
exhibits.outcome: Shows certificates visible in AKE2eg and encrypted inside AKE4eg; an active fake cannot deliver Q’s valid certificate and signature.
exhibits.limits: The active probe is one scripted experiment, not a universal identity-hiding proof.

exhibits.title: Real and fabricated transcript
exhibits.section: 5 · Could Q have made this alone?
exhibits.action: Compare a real AKE5 transcript with one fabricated by Q, beside signed AKE4eg.
exhibits.outcome: Q-made AKE5 messages satisfy the local consistency checks, illustrating honest-Q deniability.
exhibits.limits: The stronger P-deniability simulator and proof are explicitly outside this page.

exhibits.title: Ascon sponge and permutation
exhibits.action: Apply p12, step a round or a layer, then walk initialization, AD absorption, plaintext encryption and tag finalization.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect live 320-bit state and verify that the staged ciphertext and tag match the Ascon encryption API.

exhibits.title: Live Ascon-AEAD128
exhibits.action: Enter a key, nonce, associated data and plaintext, then encrypt, decrypt or tamper with ciphertext.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect ciphertext and tag; modified data fails authenticated decryption.
exhibits.limits: Classroom keys may appear in shareable lesson URLs; never use real keys there.

exhibits.title: Break It Yourself: nonce reuse
exhibits.action: Encrypt two chosen messages under one repeated nonce and compare with fresh nonces.
exhibits.outcome: Compare ciphertext and plaintext XOR and recover the leaked message prefix; Ascon duplex feedback makes the displayed recovery diverge after the first differing block.

exhibits.title: Ascon-Hash256 avalanche
exhibits.action: Hash user text and flip a bit for the avalanche test.
exhibits.outcome: Compare the two computed digests and their changed bits.

exhibits.title: Ascon-XOF128 variable output
exhibits.action: Choose XOF input and length, then compare the output with Ascon-Hash256.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect a computed variable-length XOF output and the fixed-length hash contrast.
exhibits.section: Ascon-XOF128 — A Hash With a Volume Knob

exhibits.title: Local AEAD and hash benchmark
exhibits.action: Run the benchmark on this machine.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect local throughput for Ascon-AEAD128 and Ascon-Hash256 in JavaScript beside native WebCrypto AES-256-GCM and SHA-256.
exhibits.limits: Browser timing reflects this BigInt teaching build against native browser cryptography on the current machine; it does not measure constrained hardware.

exhibits.title: Constrained-device AEAD property table
exhibits.action: Read the Ascon, AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 comparison table.
exhibits.outcome: Compare listed key/state sizes, implementation considerations, standards and target devices as descriptive properties.
exhibits.limits: The table’s size, power and side-channel claims are narrative estimates, not measurements from the browser benchmark.

exhibits.title: Ascon exhibit self-check
exhibits.action: Answer five questions, check responses and follow each explanation back to its exhibit.
exhibits.outcome: See a score and per-question feedback on the already demonstrated Ascon concepts.

exhibits.title: Ascon five-bit S-box microscope
exhibits.action: Select a bit column of the live state or toggle five input bits manually.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect five computed output bits from the cipher’s bitsliced S-box and see how one vertical state column transforms.

exhibits.title: One-bit Ascon permutation avalanche
exhibits.action: Select or randomize one state bit, plant the difference, step one round or run all twelve.
exhibits.outcome: Compare two live 320-bit permutation states and count the changed bits after each round.
exhibits.section: The Avalanche — One Bit Becomes Half the State

exhibits.title: Ascon embedded-device scenario
exhibits.action: Inspect a smart-water-meter scenario and its resource and implementation comparison.
exhibits.outcome: See why the page positions Ascon for small devices with limited memory and no AES hardware.
exhibits.limits: The displayed memory, code-size, power and side-channel assertions are illustrative text, not measurements by this lab.

exhibits.title: Measured Boot and PCR Extension
exhibits.action: Step a boot chain, edit measured bytes, and watch PCR extensions.
exhibits.outcome: Displays hashes and the changing PCR register bank for each stage.
exhibits.limits: The TPM is modelled in software; no hardware boundary is enforced.

exhibits.title: Quote and Evidence Appraisal
exhibits.action: Request a fresh quote and appraise the signed TPMS_ATTEST against policy and reference measurements.
exhibits.outcome: Shows signature, nonce, PCR and event-log checks, along with an EAT representation.
exhibits.limits: The TPM and trust anchors are software fixtures; EAT is not COSE_Sign1 wrapped.

exhibits.title: Restricted Signing and Magic Value
exhibits.action: Toggle the attestation-key restricted attribute and the quote magic bytes before signing external data.
exhibits.outcome: Shows when signing is refused and whether an externally crafted quote-shaped payload can verify.
exhibits.limits: Validation tickets and TPM policy are modelled without a hardware TPM.

exhibits.title: Tampering, Replay, and Wrong Machine
exhibits.action: Edit a bootloader measurement or choose quote replay and wrong-machine scenarios.
exhibits.outcome: Compares rejection checks and divergence from expected PCR values.

exhibits.title: After-Boot Runtime Compromise
exhibits.action: Load a runtime component after the last measured boot event and re-quote.
exhibits.outcome: Shows a clean static boot quote alongside a compromised runtime state omitted from quoted PCRs.
concepts: time of check versus time of use
exhibits.limits: This fixture does not quote runtime measurement PCR 10.

exhibits.title: Attestation Key and Trust Anchor
exhibits.action: Select stolen-key, software-key, endorsement-enrollment, or hostile-anchor cases.
exhibits.outcome: Separates a valid signature from trustworthy hardware provenance and correct anchor policy.
exhibits.limits: Certificate chain assertions are modelled rather than encoded and chain-verified.

exhibits.title: Remote Attestation Verifier Failure Taxonomy
exhibits.action: Read each laboratory failure code beside the verifier condition and corresponding field terminology.
exhibits.outcome: Distinguishes mismatched PCR values, stale nonce, untrusted or uncertified keys, bad signature, missing reference, and algorithm or magic failures.
exhibits.section: Every failure code this verifier can report
exhibits.limits: Code names are local teaching vocabulary, not standardized TPM or RATS error codes.

exhibits.title: Direct Anonymous Attestation Membership and Controlled Linkability
exhibits.action: Compare stable attestation-key identity with CDL Pi_DAA+ issuer membership, then exercise same and different basenames, issuer rotation with re-Join, credential corruption, and private-key rogue-list state.
exhibits.outcome: Current-run Setup, Join, BBS+ credential, Sign, Verify, Link, rotation and private-key rogue-list computations derive the displayed pseudonyms and acceptance or rejection results.
exhibits.limits: This is a zero-application-attribute, named-basename-only Type-3 BLS12-381 adaptation of CDL Pi_DAA+, not a TPM/ISO ECDAA profile or hardware implementation. The authenticated Join channel and unique-TPM admission rule are external, bsn=bottom and signature revocation are omitted, JavaScript arithmetic is variable-time, and anonymous provenance does not establish runtime integrity.

exhibits.title: Compose a policy and seal a record under it
exhibits.section: Compose a policy and seal a record under it
exhibits.action: Edit threshold gates and attributes or select a preset, then seal a chosen record.
exhibits.outcome: The browser builds a FAME ciphertext-policy encapsulation under BLS12-381 and protects the record with derived AES-256-GCM key and policy AAD.
exhibits.limits: A teaching browser implementation; editing a policy requires resealing, and pairings in JavaScript do not provide timing protection.

exhibits.title: The tree becomes a matrix
exhibits.action: Change a tree to include repeated attributes and threshold gates, then inspect the one-use row-label transform and matrix.
exhibits.outcome: The UI displays the monotone span program, injective labels, key-copy cost and reconstruction target vector.
exhibits.limits: General k-of-n gates can produce nontrivial field coefficients; the dynamic copy registry can make older issued keys stale.

exhibits.title: Issue keys, then try to open the record
exhibits.section: Issue keys, then try to open the record
exhibits.action: Issue or re-issue attribute keys and attempt to decrypt the sealed record as each person.
exhibits.outcome: Satisfied policies open the record; denied attempts show the missing row or gate and a named failure reason.
exhibits.limits: The scheme enforces the selected policy, which may itself be inappropriate; key material stays in the browser tab.

exhibits.title: Threshold gates and the Lagrange step
exhibits.section: Threshold gates and the Lagrange step
exhibits.action: Set a threshold such as 2 of 3 and choose whose key to reconstruct with.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect Lagrange coefficients and the linear combination of held rows, including whether it reaches the target vector.
exhibits.limits: This displays the algebra for the chosen policy and holders, not a security proof.

exhibits.title: Collusion: pool two keys and watch it fail anyway
exhibits.section: Collusion: pool two keys and watch it fail anyway
exhibits.action: Choose two holders whose union covers a policy, splice their key material and try decryption.
exhibits.outcome: The policy rows may cover the matrix, but mismatched key blinding leaves a wrong group value and AES-GCM rejects the record.
exhibits.limits: One splicing attempt demonstrates the mechanism, not a proof of FAME security; FAME itself supplies no collusion-detection verdict.

exhibits.title: The authority can read everything
exhibits.action: Mint an authority key satisfying the policy, then decrypt with it.
exhibits.outcome: The authority obtains a qualifying key through KeyGen and opens the sealed record.
exhibits.limits: The master secret itself is not passed directly to the Decrypt function; trust in the issuer is required. This is the original single-authority FAME route; RW15 later splits namespaces, but each issuer can still mint its own attributes.

exhibits.title: There is no revocation
exhibits.action: Revoke a holder in the UI, seal a new record and try the old key.
exhibits.outcome: A previously issued qualifying key still opens the new ciphertext, showing that list removal does not revoke cryptographic access.
exhibits.limits: The original FAME route itself has no cryptographic revocation. Exhibit 11 separately executes bounded application-layer epoch gating and owner-assisted DEK rewrap; it does not turn native FAME into a revocable-ABE construction.

exhibits.title: Failure codes
exhibits.action: Inspect the original FAME workflow's table of named success, refusal and internal outcome codes.
exhibits.outcome: The reference explains which condition each code reports and which invariant should never appear as a user verdict.
exhibits.limits: A UI failure code is diagnostic, not a cryptographic security proof. This table covers exhibits 1–8 only; FABESA, RW15 and epoch lessons define their own outcome codes beside their results.

exhibits.title: Hide attribute values with bounded FABESA CP-A2BE
exhibits.section: Hide attribute values with bounded FABESA CP-A2BE
exhibits.action: Compare World A and World B's public views, select a key and ciphertext condition, then run bounded candidate opening or the candidate-cap fixture.
exhibits.outcome: The ciphertext policy exposes names, structure, matrix and dimensions; ciphertext/public-key group encodings and lengths are visible; the selected key exposes its names; and the page derives candidate count from that policy and key. Attribute values and record plaintext remain hidden; a matching hidden-value key opens through AES-GCM tag acceptance while negative and over-bound cases reject or refuse.
exhibits.limits: Only attribute values are hidden; names, structure, dimensions and lengths remain public. The profile permits one value per public name and no repeated policy names; it does not implement §3.4's multi-use extension. Candidate/tag recognition is a bounded teaching adaptation and does not transfer the paper's theorem or provide production hardening.

exhibits.title: Combine independent issuers with RW15
exhibits.action: Run the same-GID opening, bypass the normal interface for the raw cross-GID pool, then compromise Hospital and mint its attribute for a new GID.
exhibits.outcome: Hospital and Board use independent authority secrets. Components issued to one byte-exact canonical GID open the two-authority policy; a raw pool from two GIDs satisfies the LSSS labels but recovers the wrong target-group element and fails the record tag; exposing Hospital's secret breaks a Hospital-only branch while Board remains required.
exhibits.limits: The cited RW15 theorem is static random-oracle q-DPBDHE2 security with statically declared corrupt authorities under its challenge restriction. The page tests a narrower exposed-authority-secret case and assumes authenticated, byte-identical GIDs across issuers; it does not establish rogue-key, adaptive-corruption, directory, CCA, policy-privacy, sender-authentication, side-channel or production security.

exhibits.title: Advance an epoch and account for revocation work
exhibits.section: Advance an epoch and account for revocation work
exhibits.action: Run the complete lifecycle: seal once, advance the epoch, withhold a revoked holder's new key, test retained and current snapshots, compare rollback with and without trusted state, rewrap the header, and inspect escrow and measured work.
exhibits.outcome: A fresh complete business-plus-epoch FAME key opens current data while the revoked holder receives none; retained old material still opens the old snapshot. A separately trusted checkpoint detects an old header, owner-assisted rewrap changes the access header without changing payload ciphertext, and the page exposes both escrow paths and counters from the executed run.
exhibits.limits: This owner-assisted per-record application adaptation is not RW15, revocable ABE, revocable-storage ABE, self-updatable encryption or public ciphertext update. It assumes authenticated issuer state and key delivery, cannot erase retained keys, ciphertexts or plaintext, and detects rollback only against separately trusted current state; no combined theorem or scalable bulk-revocation claim is made.

exhibits.title: Flip a bit and compare hash outputs
exhibits.action: Choose SHA-256, SHA3-256, or BLAKE3; change the input bit and optionally sweep every bit.
exhibits.outcome: Display two digests, changed output-bit count, and a distribution across input-bit flips.
exhibits.limits: Observed output changes are samples; approximately half changed bits is a statistical expectation, not a guarantee per input.

exhibits.title: Forge a prefix-MAC through SHA-256 length extension
exhibits.action: Edit a known message and appended text, guess or sweep secret length, then test a forged SHA-256 prefix MAC.
exhibits.outcome: Shows glue padding, continued digest, and server verification; only a correct secret-length guess validates.
exhibits.limits: Applies to the deliberately insecure SHA-256(secret ∥ message) construction, not to arbitrary SHA-256 use or HMAC.

exhibits.title: Test the same continuation against HMAC-SHA256
exhibits.action: Set message, extension, and guessed secret length, then inspect the HMAC continuation attempt.
exhibits.outcome: A forged prefix-MAC style continuation fails HMAC verification while a genuine HMAC can verify.
exhibits.limits: This contrasts one attack path and does not establish every property of HMAC.

exhibits.title: Compare hash constructions and run a local benchmark
exhibits.action: Inspect the SHA-256, SHA3-256, and BLAKE3 comparison and run the 1 MB browser benchmark.
exhibits.outcome: Shows construction differences and measured local processing times.
exhibits.limits: Benchmark results reflect browser and implementation paths and are not universal algorithm speed rankings.

exhibits.title: Trace hash primitives into other cryptographic systems
exhibits.section: Where hashes live in the portfolio
exhibits.action: Read the cross-demo examples.
exhibits.outcome: Connects HMAC authentication, HKDF key derivation, hash-based signatures and commitments to the hash lessons.
exhibits.limits: Static cross-demo context; no additional cryptographic operation.

exhibits.title: Run BB84 with or without intercept-resend Eve
exhibits.action: Choose photon count, noise and QBER threshold, then run without Eve and with a full intercept-resend Eve; inspect the animated photon sample and sifting table.
exhibits.outcome: The classical model displays sent, sifted and sacrificed counts and observed QBER; an ideal noiseless full-interception run tends toward 25% QBER, while sample results vary.
exhibits.limits: No photons or quantum states are produced. This models one Eve strategy and does not calculate a finite-key secrecy proof or guarantee detecting every eavesdropper.

exhibits.title: Estimate errors and decide whether to abort
exhibits.action: Adjust channel noise or the QBER threshold and repeat; inspect the sacrificed-bit error count and decision gauge.
exhibits.outcome: The run aborts at or above the chosen threshold and discards the key, including when noise alone causes excess disturbance; below it the demonstration continues.
exhibits.limits: The threshold is a teaching control, not a derived security bound. Alice and Bob see disturbance, not its cause.

exhibits.title: Hash retained bits and try AES-GCM
exhibits.action: After an accepted simulated exchange, inspect Alice's and Bob's separately SHA-256-derived keys and encrypt a message using Alice's key.
exhibits.outcome: AES-GCM decryption with Bob's key succeeds when the retained bits agree and rejects when residual bit disagreements produce a different key.
exhibits.limits: The cryptographic hash and AEAD run for real on bits generated by a classical BB84 simulation; the main run omits reconciliation and privacy amplification. Hashing does not create secrecy or prove Eve's knowledge is small.

exhibits.title: Try public reconciliation and conditional extraction
exhibits.action: Supply a hypothetical conditional min-entropy lower bound after an accepted run and press Try post-processing.
exhibits.outcome: The teaching model publishes Hamming syndromes and a 16-bit verification tag, attempts one correction per seven-bit block, subtracts public leakage and a margin from the assumed entropy budget, then may apply a public-seeded Toeplitz extractor or output zero bits.
exhibits.limits: The supplied entropy bound is not inferred from QBER. The model is not a finite-key QKD proof, and its extracted bits are not used for the main AES-256 key.

exhibits.title: Compare receipt-first and early-basis schedules
exhibits.action: Choose Bob confirms receipt first or Alice reveals bases too early and compare the exact four-state enumeration under the specified Eve.
exhibits.outcome: With Eve permitted to store each qubit until an early basis announcement, the modeled Eve learns the sifted bits without induced QBER; receipt-first forces a basis choice before the announcement and reveals the usual full-intercept disturbance.
exhibits.limits: This exact enumeration is for a deliberately specified attack and timing assumption, not a general proof that receipt-first alone secures QKD.

exhibits.title: BB84 Threat and Deployment Boundaries
exhibits.action: Read security analysis, real-world limitations, and deployed-network context.
exhibits.outcome: The section distinguishes a modeled intercept-resend signal from source, detector, authentication, finite-key, and hardware limits.
exhibits.limits: The browser is an idealized simulation and SHA-256 of residual bits is not a proven privacy-amplification extractor.

exhibits.title: bcrypt Anatomy and Key Schedule
exhibits.action: Inspect an annotated generated bcrypt hash and run the Eksblowfish schedule at a chosen cost.
exhibits.outcome: The version, cost, salt, and digest are identified while a real worker hash drives the staged cost display.

exhibits.title: bcrypt 72-Byte Password Boundary
exhibits.action: Enter two long passwords and hash the first, then verify the second against it.
exhibits.outcome: Byte counts and the bcrypt comparison show when differing suffixes after byte 72 still match.

exhibits.title: bcrypt Hash Generator
exhibits.action: Enter a password, set cost factor, and generate a new bcrypt hash.
exhibits.outcome: The resulting salt and hash anatomy and measured computation time appear with relative cost.
exhibits.limits: The UI permits costs 4 through 14; timings depend on this browser and device.

exhibits.title: Cost Factor Timing Benchmark
exhibits.action: Run hashes at several costs and inspect the bar chart and cracking estimates.
exhibits.outcome: Worker measurements illustrate cost scaling; estimates extrapolate from local timing.
exhibits.limits: Cracking estimates are illustrative extrapolations from local browser measurements.

exhibits.title: Verification and Timing Comparison
exhibits.action: Verify a password against a bcrypt hash and run the naive versus fixed-work timing visualization.
exhibits.outcome: The result reports a real bcrypt match; the timing view contrasts early-exit comparison with constant-work comparison.
exhibits.limits: The timing panel has measured-histogram and simulated modes; simulated bars are illustrative, not a measured network attack.

exhibits.title: Password Hashing Alternatives
exhibits.action: Read the algorithm table and run a local bcrypt versus PBKDF2 timing race.
exhibits.outcome: The table contrasts MD5, SHA-256, PBKDF2, bcrypt, scrypt, and Argon2id; the race reports worker bcryptjs and WebCrypto PBKDF2 times.
exhibits.limits: The timing comparison crosses JavaScript bcrypt and native WebCrypto PBKDF2 and does not rank equal-security settings.

exhibits.title: Three Password Database Breaches
exhibits.action: Breach plaintext records, look up unsalted MD5 digests in a precomputed table, and attack salted bcrypt hashes at costs 4, 8, or 12.
exhibits.outcome: The displays expose plaintext immediately, recover only wordlist-covered MD5 passwords, and run genuine bcrypt comparisons with progress and time budget.
exhibits.limits: The password database and wordlist are small teaching fixtures; incomplete dictionary recovery is not proof that a real account is safe.

exhibits.title: Lock a secret to a round
exhibits.section: Lock a secret to a future round
exhibits.action: Enter a message and future round, lock it, then try an early open and a genuine but wrong-round signature.
exhibits.outcome: The same decryptor refuses before the target and opens once its round signature is available.
exhibits.limits: Pairing and envelope encryption are real; beacon ticking is an in-page simulation with a known secret.

exhibits.title: Unchained versus chained beacon
exhibits.action: Pause or fast-forward rounds, verify signatures, and switch between unchained and chained identities.
exhibits.outcome: Shows valid BLS pairing checks and that a chained future identity depends on unpublished earlier signatures.
exhibits.limits: Round progression is an in-tab clock, not drand network consensus.

exhibits.title: Step through timelock encryption
exhibits.section: The mechanism, one step at a time
exhibits.action: Step through IBE setup, target identity, pairing mask, signature release and decryption; open an independent reference ciphertext.
exhibits.outcome: Displays sender and recipient pairing values and the Fujisaki–Okamoto consistency check.
exhibits.limits: This implements the IBE layer and a reference vector, not the age file container or an external live beacon.

exhibits.title: Three models under hardware speedup
exhibits.section: Three models under a faster adversary
exhibits.action: Change attacker speed, delay, audience and beacon availability to compare puzzle, VDF and beacon lock.
exhibits.outcome: Chart and table show compute-bound openings accelerating with hardware, while beacon lock depends on signature release and availability.
exhibits.limits: The comparison models timings and assumptions; it does not execute a VDF or time-lock puzzle.

exhibits.title: Halt the beacon
exhibits.action: Halt the simulated beacon while ciphertexts await a future round.
exhibits.outcome: Pending messages become stranded because no future signature is produced.
exhibits.limits: Resetting the in-page beacon rescues items; a real halted beacon may be permanently unavailable.

exhibits.title: Attack the real decryptor
exhibits.action: Try nine wrong-signature, altered-ciphertext and operator-compromise paths on a separate locked message.
exhibits.outcome: The decryptor rejects ordinary early-opening attempts; an operator signing early succeeds and violates the timing assumption.
exhibits.limits: The attacker’s ability to induce an early operator signature is intentionally granted for one scenario.

exhibits.title: Differential trace
exhibits.action: Enter two byte plaintexts and step through their paired cipher traces.
exhibits.outcome: Follow XOR differences across toy cipher layers.
exhibits.limits: The trace uses an educational small-state cipher.

exhibits.title: Live differential attack
exhibits.action: Set input and target differences, collect chosen plaintext pairs and run a last-round attack or pair-count sweep.
exhibits.outcome: See ranked key candidates, bias distribution and whether the recovered last-round key separates from noise.
exhibits.limits: The attack targets a toy cipher; statistical outcomes depend on chosen differences and pair count.

exhibits.title: FEAL-4 attack walkthrough
exhibits.action: Encrypt a block, collect controlled pairs, run the attack, inspect oracle queries and test recovery on fresh ciphertext.
exhibits.outcome: View four-round peel stages and whether recovered material predicts previously unseen blocks.

exhibits.title: PRESENT-80 full cipher
exhibits.action: Provide an 80-bit key and block, trace S-box and bit permutation layers, step key schedule and encrypt all 31 rounds.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect the computed round states and run a 2^16 key-register unwind from a known final-round key and pair.
exhibits.limits: The active-S-box observation is pair-specific and does not prove a bound across every characteristic.

exhibits.title: S-box difference table
exhibits.action: Switch weak and strong boxes and inspect the difference distribution table; select a cell for the attack.
exhibits.outcome: Compare differential counts and how a box choice changes the toy attack surface.

exhibits.title: Differential cryptanalysis timeline
exhibits.action: Select milestones from DES design through Biham and Shamir, Coppersmith and Serpent.
exhibits.outcome: Read the changing historical narrative and distinguish public discovery from earlier classified design knowledge.

exhibits.title: Serpent differential-resistance comparison
exhibits.action: Inspect DES, AES and Serpent S-box difference counts, denominators and round counts.
exhibits.outcome: Compare design margins while reading the warning that S-box bounds and added rounds do not prove whole-cipher immunity.
exhibits.section: Why Serpent Survived: Defense Against Differential Cryptanalysis

exhibits.title: Reduced-round ChaCha research context
exhibits.action: Read the linked reduced-round differential-linear attack context.
exhibits.outcome: Distinguish paper cost estimates on 6, 7 and 7.5 rounds from the full 20-round ChaCha20 path; this page does not execute that attack.

exhibits.title: Parity and QC-MDPC Primer
exhibits.action: Encode a small parity-check example and explore a circulant row.
exhibits.outcome: Shows how a parity rule detects an error and how one row generates a quasi-cyclic block.
exhibits.limits: Small examples precede the reduced BIKE simulation.

exhibits.title: BIKE Key Generation
exhibits.action: Generate a key pair with the simulation parameters.
exhibits.outcome: Displays sparse private structure, dense public representation, and comparative key sizes.
exhibits.limits: Runs at r=587 rather than the full BIKE Level 1 parameter set.

exhibits.title: Encapsulation and BGF Decoding
exhibits.action: Encapsulate a secret, decapsulate, then step or play through decoder iterations.
exhibits.outcome: Shows syndrome reduction and whether the recovered error yields the same shared secret.
exhibits.limits: Reduced parameters permit visible decoding failures and do not provide production security.

exhibits.title: Decoder Failure Rate Lab
exhibits.action: Choose an error weight and run repeated planted-error decoding trials.
exhibits.outcome: Plots measured failure rates and checks exact error recovery, including over multiple fresh keys.
exhibits.limits: The measured reduced-parameter failure rate is not the specification-level failure rate.

exhibits.title: BIKE Secret to AES-GCM
exhibits.action: Encrypt a message using a BIKE-derived secret as an AES-256-GCM key.
exhibits.outcome: Shows authenticated message encryption and decryption following the KEM.
exhibits.limits: The BIKE component still uses reduced demonstration parameters.

exhibits.title: BIKE versus ML-KEM
exhibits.action: Compare specification key and ciphertext sizes and assumption families.
exhibits.outcome: Displays tabular and visual differences without running the compared full-parameter KEMs.
exhibits.limits: Full-parameter figures are specifications, not timings measured by this simulation.

exhibits.title: Code-Based Assumption Diversity
exhibits.action: Read why a code-based KEM can diversify a lattice-based migration and what failure-rate tradeoff BIKE carries.
exhibits.outcome: Relates QC-MDPC syndrome decoding to ML-KEM module-LWE and contrasts BIKE, HQC, and McEliece roles.
exhibits.limits: The panel is historical and explanatory; its standardization/deployment statements should not be treated as live recommendations.

exhibits.title: LPN and Syndrome-Decoding Assumption
exhibits.action: Open the deeper hardness disclosure after the QC-MDPC circulant visualization.
exhibits.outcome: Connects sparse-error recovery from a public syndrome with the code-based assumption underlying the BIKE KEM.
exhibits.limits: This panel states an assumption and uses a reduced toy code; it is not a hardness proof or full-parameter security estimate.

exhibits.title: Physical Faults Outside the FO Check
exhibits.action: Read the physical-fault scope note adjacent to the KEM comparison.
exhibits.outcome: Separates fault injection elsewhere in decapsulation from ciphertext tampering and from mathematical attacks on QC-MDPC.
exhibits.limits: The cited laser-fault result is described under its hardware conditions; this browser lab does not reproduce it.

exhibits.title: Lock, sign, and verify
exhibits.action: Generate or enter a secp256k1 key and transaction value, select valid, wrong-key, forged-signature, tampered-transaction or edge-case spend scenarios, and open the byte inspectors.
exhibits.outcome: View the P2PKH lock, unlocking data, address, sighash preimage, DER signature and HASH160 pipeline; the scenarios expose why each spend passes or fails.
exhibits.limits: A focused single-signature legacy P2PKH teaching engine, not a consensus node; Taproot, multisig and timelocks are context only.

exhibits.title: Run the script on the stack
exhibits.section: Run the script on the stack
exhibits.action: Step forward or backward, auto-run, scrub the timeline or jump to a script token for each scenario.
exhibits.outcome: The shared stack shows each opcode consumption and result, a final pass or fail verdict, and a comparison matrix for all scenarios.
exhibits.limits: Only the implemented subset of Bitcoin Script and the selected legacy spending forms are executed.

exhibits.title: Generate a key and derive two Bitcoin addresses
exhibits.action: Generate a private key and follow secp256k1 public key, HASH160, P2PKH and P2WPKH derivations.
exhibits.outcome: Shows key and address encodings, copyable values, and QR renderings for both address formats.
exhibits.limits: Locally generated teaching keys and QR codes must not receive real funds.

exhibits.title: Generate a BIP-39 mnemonic and BIP-32 master key
exhibits.action: Generate a mnemonic, inspect entropy and checksum encoding, derive seed and master key.
exhibits.outcome: Displays words, checksum bits, seed material, and the root of a deterministic wallet tree.
exhibits.limits: The interface exposes secret material; never enter a real wallet phrase.

exhibits.title: Corrupt or validate a seed phrase
exhibits.action: Flip an entropy bit, substitute a final word, search a change the checksum misses, or validate an entered phrase.
exhibits.outcome: Shows how BIP-39 checksum detects some changes yet can accept a changed valid phrase.
exhibits.limits: Checksum validity is not proof of ownership, authenticity, or correct wallet destination.

exhibits.title: Walk a derivation path to receive addresses
exhibits.action: Edit derivation path and receive index and inspect the first five derived addresses.
exhibits.outcome: Compares deterministic child keys and addresses, including legacy and SegWit encodings.
exhibits.limits: The displayed bc1 encoding from a BIP-44 legacy subtree is valid but not the standard native SegWit purpose path.

exhibits.title: Confirm the written mnemonic order
exhibits.action: Generate a phrase, start the drill and select shuffled words in their original order.
exhibits.outcome: A mistaken position is marked so a bad backup can be caught during setup.
exhibits.limits: Local rehearsal; a phrase held only in memory is not a backup.

exhibits.title: Derive five receive addresses from one seed
exhibits.action: Generate a mnemonic and inspect indices zero through four of the receive path.
exhibits.outcome: Table derives P2PKH and P2WPKH encodings for each child key; purpose note distinguishes legacy subtree from standard wallet discovery.
exhibits.limits: Both address columns are intentionally from a legacy BIP-44 subtree; a standard SegWit wallet scans another purpose subtree.

exhibits.title: Recompute wallet specification vectors
exhibits.action: Inspect automatic checks of private-key-one P2PKH, BIP-39 seed and BIP-32 extended keys.
exhibits.outcome: Full computed values are compared to published constants and receive match or mismatch badges.
exhibits.limits: Passing vectors tests only the listed cases; not an audit.

exhibits.title: Explain WIF, hardened derivation and watch-only keys
exhibits.action: Read concept cards and glossary terms.
exhibits.outcome: Distinguishes WIF from new secrets, hardened versus normal paths, xpub visibility and address checksum typo detection.
exhibits.limits: Concept cards only; path derivation is shown separately.

exhibits.title: Review custody and seed-handling limits
exhibits.action: Read self-custody and backup guidance cards.
exhibits.outcome: Explains that each leaked key layer can spend descendants and a checksum cannot verify destination ownership.
exhibits.limits: Educational browser lab; generated keys should not receive funds.

exhibits.title: Encrypted ClientHello Overview
exhibits.action: Read the ECH protection boundary and relation to the imported HPKE lab.
exhibits.outcome: The explanation identifies the inner destination, public outer name, and what the encrypted handshake does not hide.

exhibits.title: Observer ClientHello Comparison
exhibits.action: Send ordinary and ECH ClientHellos and compare the observer-visible field views.
exhibits.outcome: The observer sees the clear SNI without ECH and the public outer name and encrypted payload with ECH.

exhibits.title: Outer AAD Swap Attack
exhibits.action: Build and seal ECH, then rewrite the outer SNI while keeping its ciphertext.
exhibits.outcome: Real HPKE decryption rejects the swapped outer because the ClientHelloOuter is bound as associated data.
exhibits.section: Inner and outer — why the whole outer is the AAD

exhibits.title: ECHConfig DNS Bootstrap
exhibits.action: Look up the HTTPS record with plaintext or encrypted DNS selected.
exhibits.outcome: The modeled observer view shows when ECHConfig lookup leaks the intended hostname before the TLS handshake.
exhibits.section: The bootstrap problem — where the key comes from
exhibits.limits: DNS lookup and observer trace are modeled locally, not live DNS traffic.

exhibits.title: Substituted ECHConfig
exhibits.action: Run an attack in which the client accepts an attacker-provided ECHConfig.
exhibits.outcome: The real seal succeeds to the attack key, demonstrating that encryption alone cannot authenticate configuration delivery.
exhibits.section: Whose key did you encrypt to?
exhibits.limits: The substituted configuration is a controlled fixture; the panel does not emulate browser trust policy.

exhibits.title: ECH GREASE Wire Comparison
exhibits.action: Put a real ECH client and a GREASE client on the wire and inspect server handling.
exhibits.outcome: Their outer shapes obscure client ECH support while only the real payload can decrypt.
exhibits.section: GREASE — everyone sends ECH, even those who can’t

exhibits.title: Tampered and Stale Configuration Retry
exhibits.action: Flip a public-key bit or use a rotated ECH key, then retry using the server-provided retry_configs.
exhibits.outcome: Initial server decryption fails and the authenticated retry path can recover with a fresh configuration.

exhibits.title: ECH Deployment Boundaries
exhibits.action: Read protocol fallback, DNS-delivery, and enterprise-policy caveats.
exhibits.outcome: The panel distinguishes ECH rejection and authentication failure from untrusted configuration stripping.
exhibits.limits: This text explains protocol requirements and does not test browser fallback behavior.

exhibits.title: Encrypted addition through the Oracle
exhibits.action: Choose two uint8 values, generate client keys, encrypt and transmit, ask the Oracle to add ciphertexts, then decrypt locally.
exhibits.outcome: Shows ciphertext fingerprints and an earned comparison of decrypted and plaintext sums modulo 256.
exhibits.limits: Oracle is a demonstration server and may be offline; the client alone has the decryption key. Values must not be sensitive.

exhibits.title: Fresh ciphertext for the same values
exhibits.action: Re-encrypt identical inputs with fresh randomness and compare Oracle-side fingerprints.
exhibits.outcome: Different ciphertext digests represent the same plaintext values.
exhibits.limits: Fingerprints reveal byte differences, not cryptographic security of the server.

exhibits.title: Plaintext and ciphertext worlds
exhibits.action: Inspect synchronized computation tracks and the noise and bootstrapping diagram after an Oracle response.
exhibits.outcome: Relates Enc(a) plus Enc(b) to modular sum and illustrates noise reset qualitatively.
exhibits.limits: The visual noise strip is explanatory; it is not an instrument reading the TFHE ciphertext noise.

exhibits.title: Local toy multiply and noise budget
exhibits.section: LOCAL MULTIPLY BENCH — SPEND THE NOISE BUDGET YOURSELF
exhibits.action: Chain toy encrypted additions or multiplications and inspect each decrypted answer, ciphertext size and noise bound.
exhibits.outcome: Shows when lack of bootstrapping removes correctness guarantee, with observed wrap and possible errors.
exhibits.limits: A tiny unsigned base-256 model with a 48-bit secret; insecure and distinct from TFHE, without bootstrapping.

exhibits.title: Oblivious HTTP knowledge split
exhibits.action: Choose GET or POST and an AEAD, run the exchange, and advance the request and response steps.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect which party can see client identity versus request content as HPKE and relay forwarding operate.
exhibits.limits: The relay and gateway run in one browser session rather than separate network services.

exhibits.title: Colluding relay and gateway
exhibits.action: Toggle collusion after an exchange.
exhibits.outcome: Joined logs associate the relay identity column with the gateway request column.

exhibits.title: Traffic correlation without collusion
exhibits.action: Simulate four concurrent clients, then join observations by size or timing.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect possible cross-party matches made without exchanging cryptographic keys.

exhibits.title: OHTTP tamper and key leakage
exhibits.action: Try a generated wrong key, tamper with a forwarded byte or supply the gateway private key.
exhibits.outcome: Compare decryption failure and authenticated tamper rejection with successful decryption by a holder of the gateway key.

exhibits.title: OHTTP honest scoping
exhibits.action: Read the real-versus-modeled panel and scope guard.
exhibits.outcome: Distinguish local HPKE/BHTTP operations from simulated network metadata, and identify content, timing, size and non-collusion privacy limits.
exhibits.section: Honest scoping — what this lab does and does not show

exhibits.title: Request and response OHTTP key schedules
exhibits.action: Run an exchange and inspect the live request HPKE values beside the response Export and HKDF values.
exhibits.outcome: Compare independently derived client and gateway response AEAD keys and nonces byte for byte.

exhibits.title: OHTTP, VPN, Tor and IT-PIR assumptions
exhibits.action: Read the comparison table for identity, request visibility, trust and cost.
exhibits.outcome: Contrast organizational non-collusion in OHTTP with the distinct assumptions and costs of the other privacy architectures.
exhibits.limits: VPN, Tor and IT-PIR are described for comparison; this browser lab does not implement them.
exhibits.section: Where this sits: OHTTP vs VPN vs Tor vs IT-PIR

exhibits.title: Named split-knowledge deployments
exhibits.action: Inspect the page’s iCloud Private Relay, Firefox and Privacy Pass examples.
exhibits.outcome: See different settings in which identity and request visibility may be separated, with each example labeled as context.
exhibits.limits: The named services are contextual examples and are not connected or implemented here.

exhibits.title: Blind RSA Protocol
exhibits.action: Blind a message, have the signer sign, unblind, verify, then tamper and re-verify.
exhibits.outcome: Shows signer and requester views and verifies the unblinded signature.
exhibits.limits: The bare-hash textbook form is malleable; a toy-number mode is also provided.

exhibits.title: RFC 9474 Blind RSA
exhibits.action: Prepare and blind a PSS-encoded message, blind-sign, finalize, and verify natively.
exhibits.outcome: Demonstrates an RSA-PSS compatible result and rejects a tampered signature.
exhibits.limits: The issuer applies raw RSA to client-chosen blinded values; production deployment requires protocol safeguards.

exhibits.title: Chaum E-Cash
exhibits.action: Issue a blind-signed coin, spend it, attempt reuse, and try a forged coin.
exhibits.outcome: Shows merchant acceptance, double-spend rejection, and forged-signature rejection.

exhibits.title: Anonymous Voting
exhibits.action: Issue a blind-signed ballot token, submit a vote, and test a forged token.
exhibits.outcome: Shows authority-issued eligibility and ballot verification without exposing the issuance link in the display.

exhibits.title: Anonymous Credentials
exhibits.action: Issue and present an over-18 credential, then attempt a forged claim.
exhibits.outcome: Compares valid presentation and rejected attribute forgery.
exhibits.limits: This narrow over-18 token demonstration is not a general selective-disclosure system.

exhibits.title: Textbook Blind Schnorr
exhibits.action: Run a blind Schnorr flow over Ed25519 and tamper with its signature scalar.
exhibits.outcome: Shows verification and rejection, while explaining the concurrent-issuance weakness of this textbook construction.
exhibits.limits: The displayed textbook protocol is vulnerable under concurrent issuance.

exhibits.title: Blind RSA and EC Timing
exhibits.action: Run a timing comparison for RSA and elliptic-curve blind-signature flows.
exhibits.outcome: Displays local timings and contrasts key/signature sizes and protocol caveats.
exhibits.limits: The Schnorr column uses the vulnerable textbook protocol; timings are device-dependent.

exhibits.title: Blind Schnorr Concurrent-Issuance Limit
exhibits.action: Read the ROS assumption and concurrent-session attack alongside the single-session blind Schnorr run.
exhibits.outcome: Explains why a valid one-session signature does not establish one-more unforgeability for the textbook protocol under many concurrent requests.
exhibits.section: The assumption behind the Schnorr column — and why it does not hold
exhibits.limits: The full ROS attack is cited and discussed, not executed here; the signature flow is one session.

exhibits.title: Blind RSA Raw-Oracle Attack Model
exhibits.action: Read the delayed-target attack note and compare it to the stated one-more-RSA proof model.
exhibits.outcome: Distinguishes temporary raw signing-oracle exposure from ordinary RSA-PSS signing, and demonstrated 1024-bit attack from larger-key extrapolation.
exhibits.limits: The full-scale attack is not run; the research note describes a separate model and extrapolated larger key estimates.

exhibits.title: Concurrent Blind Schnorr Research Variants
exhibits.action: Read the comparison with Schnorr² and Okamoto-Schnorr² after the ROS caveat.
exhibits.outcome: Distinguishes conditional concurrent one-more-unforgeability proofs for different two-commitment protocols from the vulnerable textbook single-session protocol run in the lab.
exhibits.section: Research update: different protocols can support concurrent issuance
exhibits.limits: The two research variants are described, not implemented or standardized by this demo.

exhibits.title: Randomized and Deterministic Blind RSA
exhibits.action: Choose the randomized SHA-384 PSS variant or deterministic PSSZERO, then inspect prefix, salt, blind-sign and ordinary PSS verification.
exhibits.outcome: Contrasts a 32-byte requester prefix and 48-byte salt with no prefix or salt, while showing both variants retain blind issuance and compatible signature verification.
exhibits.limits: The browser signs under a local teaching issuer; it does not run a deployed Privacy Pass service.

exhibits.title: TL;DR
exhibits.action: Read the attack summary and start the guided tour.
exhibits.outcome: The introduction separates paper-measured leakage claims from the toy descent and names the candidate score as the central mechanism.
exhibits.limits: The page reconstructs a published result; the introductory paper numbers are not produced by the toy.

exhibits.title: Live readout
exhibits.action: Watch the live statistics update during the selected toy descent.
exhibits.outcome: The panel shows seed, relation count, bit-flip noise, search tier, violated-relation score and status.
exhibits.limits: All numbers in this readout belong to the toy engine, not the cited paper run.

exhibits.title: Watch the descent
exhibits.action: Adjust leaked relations, bit-flip noise and seed; predict, play or step a multi-tier hill-climb and optionally overlay alternate starts.
exhibits.outcome: The toy candidate score descends toward its hidden 8-coordinate key under suitable settings and may stall at high noise.
exhibits.limits: An illustrative n=8 model with one-sided constraints; this does not recover a real ML-DSA key or match the paper scale.

exhibits.title: Inside one relation
exhibits.action: Advance through leaked relations, change the heatmap axes and choose a new starting cell or random start.
exhibits.outcome: The relation microscope shows predicted and observed bits; the score landscape projects candidate, true key and optimization path.
exhibits.limits: The two-dimensional heatmap is a projection of the toy score, not a full real-key landscape.

exhibits.title: How reliable is the toy?
exhibits.action: Run 10, 25 or 50 independent toy trials at the selected relation count and noise.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect recovery rate and a histogram of steps for successful trials.
exhibits.limits: The observed rate is for the toy distribution and chosen sample size, not a measured ML-DSA attack success rate.

exhibits.title: Toy vs. paper — the honesty bridge
exhibits.section: Toy vs. paper — the honesty bridge
exhibits.action: Compare the live toy with a parameter-set replay and visualizations of the cited paper measurements.
exhibits.outcome: Displays distinct toy and paper dimensions, relation counts and noise ceilings, and paper table values without running the paper-scale attack.
exhibits.limits: Paper-scale replay is static reported data; the cited PDF and per-setting counts are subject to its published source, not live computation.

exhibits.title: Noise explorer
exhibits.action: Inspect repeated toy recovery runs across leak-bit noise rates next to the paper-reported tolerance.
exhibits.outcome: The chart marks the toy ceiling and illustrates its divergence from a paper-measured 45% figure.
exhibits.limits: The paper reference and live toy use different models; equal noise rates do not imply equal attack behavior.

exhibits.title: How one leaked bit breaks the silence
exhibits.section: How one leaked bit breaks the silence
exhibits.action: Read the leakage mechanism, no-leakage contrast, implications, defenses, misconceptions and self-check.
exhibits.outcome: Explains how many correlated bits can guide a score-based search, and why no leakage and noisy leakage lead to different outcomes.
exhibits.limits: Narrative examples and assessment are explanatory; they do not establish real-world exploitability for an arbitrary implementation.

exhibits.title: Parameters & sources
exhibits.action: Inspect the provenance table, toy settings and reproducibility snippet.
exhibits.outcome: The page labels transcribed paper figures and the live toy parameters separately and provides a way to verify its figures.
exhibits.limits: A transcribed table is not independent replication of paper-scale key recovery.

exhibits.title: Known gaps (honest by construction)
exhibits.action: Read the listed differences between the toy and the published attack.
exhibits.outcome: The limitations distinguish toy dimension and optimizer, transcription rather than reproduction, and the cost of the preliminary noisy result.
exhibits.limits: The listed paper noise result has a narrower parameter scope and a larger leak requirement than the exact setting.

exhibits.title: Generate and verify a 64-bit range proof
exhibits.action: Choose a value, generate its commitment and range proof, then verify using reference or single-MSM checks.
exhibits.outcome: Displays a Pedersen commitment, proof data, verification verdicts, and timing.
exhibits.limits: Demonstration implements a fixed 64-bit proof, not a production deployment with transaction binding.

exhibits.title: Prove several values with one aggregated Bulletproof
exhibits.action: Choose a count and run a true aggregate for the largest power of two at or below it.
exhibits.outcome: Both verifiers check one proof; UI compares its byte length and timings against multiple 672-byte single proofs.
exhibits.limits: Educational, unaudited TypeScript cryptography; count snaps down to power of two.

exhibits.title: Compare theoretical and batched proof sizes
exhibits.action: Adjust the values slider and inspect the size bars.
exhibits.outcome: Shows estimated true aggregate, batched single-proof, and naive Schnorr costs as count changes.
exhibits.limits: True aggregate and Schnorr bar estimates are formulas; live aggregate execution is separate.

exhibits.title: Replay proof against a different commitment
exhibits.action: Generate a valid proof and try to verify it against a new commitment.
exhibits.outcome: The verifier rejects because the transcript proof is bound to its original commitment.
exhibits.limits: Educational local demonstration; no network replay.

exhibits.title: Modify t-hat and reverify
exhibits.action: Tamper with the current proof scalar and invoke both verifiers.
exhibits.outcome: Both verifier variants report rejection of the modified proof.
exhibits.limits: One illustrative field mutation, not a complete adversarial security test.

exhibits.title: Serialize and verify an imported proof
exhibits.action: Export proof and commitment hex, paste them back or into another browser, and verify.
exhibits.outcome: Deserialized proof is verified without original prover state.
exhibits.limits: Unaudited implementation; imported hex is local only.

exhibits.title: Reproduce proof bytes using a seed
exhibits.action: Apply a string seed or restore crypto.getRandomValues, then generate proofs.
exhibits.outcome: Seeded mode makes proof bytes reproducible for teaching.
