exhibits.limits: Deterministic RNG is for tests and teaching; unsafe for protecting real commitments.

exhibits.title: Benchmark prover and two verifier implementations
exhibits.action: Run single and aggregated cases at counts one, two, four and eight.
exhibits.outcome: Table reports byte sizes and measured local prove, reference verify and MSM verify times.
exhibits.limits: Browser timings depend on device and runtime; not a general benchmark.

exhibits.title: Read ordered append and challenge events
exhibits.action: Generate a proof and inspect ordered transcript events.
exhibits.outcome: Shows prover and verifier Fiat-Shamir state transitions underlying noninteractive challenge generation.
exhibits.limits: Unaudited teaching implementation, no independent transcript security audit.

exhibits.title: Inspect serialized proof bytes and challenge scalars
exhibits.action: Generate a proof and inspect component lengths, six IPA rounds, sampled hex, challenge values and timings.
exhibits.outcome: Accounts for the range proof representation and Fiat-Shamir challenge fields.
exhibits.limits: Wall-clock performance depends on browser and device.

exhibits.title: Evaluate verifier polynomial identity on proof points
exhibits.action: Open the equation ramp after proving and compare left and right point expressions.
exhibits.outcome: A live field-and-point calculation confirms the first Bulletproof verifier identity for the current commitment.
exhibits.limits: Shows one displayed equation and conceptual second equation; full verification is a separate control.

exhibits.title: Build scalar vectors from secret bits and challenges
exhibits.action: Generate a proof and inspect first entries of bit vector and derived l/r vectors.
exhibits.outcome: Shows how bit constraints are folded into one scalar inner product for the proof.
exhibits.limits: Displays first eight entries and constant terms; full blinding terms are not shown.

exhibits.title: Watch six inner-product folding rounds
exhibits.action: Generate a proof and follow real L/R point pairs from vector length 64 down to one.
exhibits.outcome: Demonstrates logarithmic payload versus sending both 64-entry vectors.
exhibits.limits: Visualization of a local proof, not an audited protocol implementation.

exhibits.title: Test a commitment outside the 64-bit range
exhibits.action: Select two-to-the-64 or negative one and attempt to prove the committed value.
exhibits.outcome: The prover can only prove a truncated in-range witness tied to a different commitment, so verification against the original fails.
exhibits.limits: Illustrative cheating strategy; does not enumerate all possible adversaries.

exhibits.title: Perform the Five-Card AND Gate
exhibits.action: Choose Alice and Bob bits, arrange their commitments with the dealer card, cut the row, reveal it, and read the answer.
exhibits.outcome: Spade adjacency computes the AND gate while the guided six-step explanation shows how the row was constructed.
exhibits.limits: It models an honest physical dealer and valid card placement.

exhibits.title: Exhaustive Cyclic-Cut Correctness
exhibits.action: Change the starting row and try every cut, then inspect the full ten-row partition and truth table.
exhibits.outcome: Rows rotate only within the adjacent or separated spade orbit, preserving the output for all cuts.

exhibits.title: Revealed-Row Privacy Table
exhibits.action: Inspect exact probabilities of each revealed row for all input pairs under a uniform cut.
exhibits.outcome: Equal conditional distributions for input pairs with the same output show that cards add no information beyond the AND answer.
exhibits.limits: The claim assumes uniform cuts, no peeking or marked backs, and honest bit encoding.

exhibits.title: Break Privacy with a Biased Dealer
exhibits.action: Adjust five cut probabilities, use presets, and play the revealed-row guessing game.
exhibits.outcome: Exact arithmetic and empirical rounds show how a random but nonuniform cut can leak Alice’s bit.
exhibits.limits: The arithmetic is exact over this toy state space; the game samples rounds and excludes peeking, marked cards, and dishonest input placement.

exhibits.title: Cards Against Circuits
exhibits.action: Vary adversary work and security parameter, then inspect the chart and practical comparison table.
exhibits.outcome: The physical card gate and computational garbled-circuit assumptions are compared across scale and security.
exhibits.limits: The card protocol computes one two-party AND gate under trusted physical handling; the chart is an illustrative comparison, not a running garbled circuit.

exhibits.title: Encrypt and decrypt
exhibits.action: Enter text and a 256-bit key and 96-bit nonce, then encrypt, copy ciphertext and decrypt.
exhibits.outcome: Shows plaintext XOR keystream bytes and recovered text.
exhibits.limits: ChaCha20 here provides confidentiality only; no Poly1305 tag or tamper detection.

exhibits.title: Keystream and nonce change
exhibits.action: Generate a 64-byte block, regenerate a nonce or flip one nonce bit.
exhibits.outcome: Compares keystream grids and changed bytes after a nonce change.
exhibits.limits: An avalanche display is an example, not a proof of security or an authentication property.

exhibits.title: ChaCha20 quarter-round stepper
exhibits.action: Initialize a block and step or play through quarter-round operations.
exhibits.outcome: Displays the 4×4 state and add-rotate-XOR updates across 20 rounds.
exhibits.limits: The stepper traces one block; it does not expose a practical attack on full ChaCha20.

exhibits.title: Two-message nonce reuse
exhibits.action: Encrypt two messages under one key and nonce, then guess a crib in one message.
exhibits.outcome: Shows ciphertext XOR cancelling the repeated keystream and recovers corresponding guessed bytes of the other message.
exhibits.limits: The plaintext recovery requires a correct guess and aligned bytes; it is not automatic full decryption.

exhibits.title: Reduced-round research trace
exhibits.action: Select a reduced prefix and step its public-input round function trace.
exhibits.outcome: Shows intermediate state without changing the full-round cipher playground.
exhibits.limits: It does not implement the cited bit-puncturing attack, attack-cost measurement or fractional-round cipher.

exhibits.title: ChaCha20 design and safety notes
exhibits.action: Open comparison, state-matrix and safe-usage tabs.
exhibits.outcome: Explains ARX design, 4×4 state layout and key/nonce safety rules.
exhibits.limits: These tabs explain design constraints; they are not experiments or security proofs.

exhibits.title: Build a path versus validate it
exhibits.action: Follow candidate chain construction and validation.
exhibits.outcome: See that an apparently connected certificate path may fail policy checks even when signatures verify.

exhibits.title: Certificate validator puzzle
exhibits.action: Choose a leaf-to-root path and a failing check across staged certificate scenarios.
exhibits.outcome: The lab validates the proposed chain and compares the ruling with the actual failing check.

exhibits.title: Same chain, different roots
exhibits.action: Compare candidate paths under different trust stores.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect how trust anchor selection changes path validation results.

exhibits.title: Certificate inspector
exhibits.action: Select a certificate and inspect fields, extensions and DER bytes.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect the encoded certificate evidence used in chain checks.

exhibits.title: Bring your own chain
exhibits.action: Paste PEM certificates, choose a hostname and EKU, then validate the chain.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect the constructed path or detailed validation failure from supplied certificates.

exhibits.title: Certificate path validation scope
exhibits.action: Read the scope card after the certificate workbench.
exhibits.outcome: Separate path validation from TLS handshakes, Certificate Transparency, live revocation, parser fuzzing and issuance.

exhibits.title: Masked Comparison Leakage Replay
exhibits.action: Select masking order, noise, and a target bit, then run synthetic leakage traces.
exhibits.outcome: Plots correlation and estimated trace effort, with a resolved bit of a live ML-KEM shared secret.
exhibits.limits: Trace leakage and effort are synthetic; they do not measure a physical implementation.

exhibits.title: Imperfect Decapsulation-Failure Oracle
exhibits.action: Adjust oracle error and availability, then run the adaptive recovery replay.
exhibits.outcome: Charts recovered fraction, confidence, and queries under a noisy or intermittent simulated oracle.
exhibits.limits: The replay models a reduced inference mechanism, not a measured attack on a device.

exhibits.title: NTT and CRT RNR Blinding
exhibits.action: Compare seeded unblinded and blinded runs under matched noise, optionally injecting a fault.
exhibits.outcome: Shows correlation curves and branch outcomes including integrity abort under the modelled fault.
exhibits.limits: Synthetic leakage and fault branches demonstrate direction, not device-level efficacy.

exhibits.title: FO Re-encryption Mirror and Implementation Leakage
exhibits.action: Open the concept primer and trace why a defensive ciphertext comparison can become a leakage point.
exhibits.outcome: Connects ML-KEM decapsulation, masked comparison leakage, noisy failure signals, and NTT/CRT blinding as two attacks and one defense.
exhibits.limits: The primer maps research mechanisms; the three replay panels use synthetic traces or modeled faults.

exhibits.title: ML-KEM Decapsulation and Implicit Rejection
exhibits.action: Open the normal-flow primer and trace ciphertext decryption, deterministic re-encryption, comparison, and accept-or-reject selection.
exhibits.outcome: Maps each replay to the comparison, failure signal, or arithmetic stage of the Fujisaki–Okamoto flow.
exhibits.section: What is ML-KEM decapsulation? — the normal flow all three cards perturb
exhibits.limits: Pipeline is a primer; complete end-to-end KEM implementation is delegated to a sibling lab.

exhibits.title: Incomplete FO Comparison Case Studies
exhibits.action: Read the research update on unchecked ciphertext tails and an unverified v coordinate.
exhibits.outcome: Contrasts affected implementation comparisons and deliberately faulty simulations with correctly comparing every ciphertext byte.
exhibits.section: Research update: a comparison that skips the tail
exhibits.limits: Neither this primer nor the three replays recovers a key using the reported attack; statements are pinned to cited preprints and stated conditions.

exhibits.title: One Masked Comparison Trace
exhibits.action: Run masked leakage and inspect a resolved ML-KEM bit split into random shares, each share’s noisy leak, their product, and accumulating correlation.
exhibits.outcome: Shows how a higher-order distinguisher combines share leakage and why additional shares only raise trace cost in the presence of enough noise.
exhibits.limits: The secret bit comes from real ML-KEM; per-share leakage and trace-effort estimates are seeded synthetic models, not device measurements.

exhibits.title: Tanner Graph Repairs a Noisy Guess
exhibits.action: Step through six-bit variable and parity-check nodes as two checks correct a wrong channel reading.
exhibits.outcome: Displays sum-product belief propagation used by the imperfect-oracle replay to fuse unreliable bit evidence with parity constraints.
exhibits.section: How parity checks repair a wrong guess (belief propagation)
exhibits.limits: The six-bit demonstration shares the model decoder; it does not recover a hardware ML-KEM key.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 1: Encrypt a Number, Compute on It, Get It Back
exhibits.section: Exhibit 1: Encrypt a Number, Compute on It, Get It Back
exhibits.action: Enter a decimal number and encrypt then decrypt it using the toy-parameter CKKS engine.
exhibits.outcome: Compare the decoded result with the input and observe approximation from encoding and ciphertext noise.
exhibits.limits: The actual ciphertext operations use n=8 and insecure toy moduli; the demonstration offers no production security.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 2: Encode, Encrypt, Add, Decrypt
exhibits.action: Encode four slots, encrypt vectors A and B, add ciphertexts, decrypt, switch coefficient view and tamper with a coefficient.
exhibits.outcome: See ciphertext components and approximate slot-wise sums, and how coefficient modification moves decoded output.
exhibits.limits: Homomorphic computation does not provide ciphertext integrity; the tiny parameters are only for teaching.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 3: Homomorphic Multiplication and Rescaling
exhibits.action: Encrypt two vectors, multiply ciphertexts, rescale and decrypt while observing scale, level and degree.
exhibits.outcome: The modulus chain and precision displays change as multiplication grows scale and rescaling consumes a level.
exhibits.limits: Small fixed parameters and limited depth; coefficients are illustrative, and this implementation is unaudited.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 4: Encrypted Neural Network Inference
exhibits.action: Adjust four inputs, run plaintext inference, then encrypt inputs, evaluate a polynomial network and decrypt.
exhibits.outcome: Compare approximate encrypted output with plaintext, including a visual of where the polynomial differs from ReLU.
exhibits.limits: The model is a small teaching network; polynomial activation approximates ReLU and toy CKKS is not secure.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 5: Precision, Scale, and Error Accumulation
exhibits.section: Exhibit 5: Precision, Scale, and Error Accumulation
exhibits.action: Reset a CKKS encryption of pi and repeatedly add 0.125 or multiply by 1.1.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect the operation log, relative error and remaining correct digits as the computation accumulates error.
exhibits.limits: Precision behavior depends on this toy modulus chain and chosen operations.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 6: The FHE Trilogy — Choosing the Right Scheme
exhibits.section: Exhibit 6: The FHE Trilogy — Choosing the Right Scheme
exhibits.action: Compare CKKS with BFV and TFHE and read the threat model and validity-bit caveat.
exhibits.outcome: The scheme guide distinguishes approximate arithmetic, exact integer arithmetic and bit-level operations, and names what the lab does not protect.
exhibits.limits: A selection guide and threat-model explanation; it does not execute BFV or TFHE.

exhibits.title: Compute modular wraparound and zero divisors
exhibits.action: Enter operands and modulus; run addition or multiplication examples.
exhibits.outcome: Shows exact reduced residues, clock or strip visual, and a nonzero zero-divisor example.
exhibits.limits: Small-number arithmetic lesson with input limits and no production cryptography.

exhibits.title: Find an inverse with extended Euclid
exhibits.action: Enter a and n and step through Euclid divisions.
exhibits.outcome: Shows Bézout coefficients, gcd, and an inverse only when the gcd is one.
exhibits.limits: Exact arithmetic within the lab’s supported modulus range.

exhibits.title: Count units and evaluate Euler phi
exhibits.action: Enter a modulus and compare direct unit enumeration with factorization-based phi.
exhibits.outcome: Displays coprime residues and the totient count from two methods where supported.
exhibits.limits: Direct counting has a tighter bound than factorization and is unavailable for large supported inputs.

exhibits.title: Watch powers return to one or enter a nonunit cycle
exhibits.action: Enter base and modulus or choose a precondition-breaking example.
exhibits.outcome: Plots the power walk and reports order and Euler-theorem relation for units.
exhibits.limits: Euler theorem applies to units; a nonunit need not return to one.

exhibits.title: Compare generators and toy Diffie-Hellman spaces
exhibits.action: Choose prime p, base g, and exponents; compare order-two, prime-order subgroup, and whole-group examples.
exhibits.outcome: Shows subgroup order, shared secret, search space and guess count.
exhibits.limits: Small public teaching exponents and primes are not secure Diffie-Hellman parameters.

exhibits.title: Recombine two or three congruences
exhibits.action: Enter two or three congruences and test compatible or incompatible shared factors.
exhibits.outcome: Displays a combined solution modulo the least common multiple or reports no solution.
exhibits.limits: The example range is bounded; noncoprime moduli require compatibility, not automatic product modulus.

exhibits.title: Montgomery REDC, Encoded Chaining and Fixed Work
exhibits.action: Choose two integers, an odd modulus N and a power-of-two radix R greater than N; encode through REDC, inspect one encoded product and a product-and-square chain, then run the fixed 4,096-operation ordinary/Montgomery comparison.
exhibits.outcome: For N = 17 and R = 32, the panel derives N′ = 15, R² mod N = 4, low-word cancellation and decoded product 15; it keeps (a·b)²·a encoded to result 12, while N = 9 and R = 16 expose raw candidate 9 and the required 9 − 9 final subtraction. Setup, ordinary-loop, Montgomery-loop and final-decode measurements remain separate, and both fixed schedules agree.
exhibits.limits: This is a bounded TypeScript BigInt power-of-two specialization for odd N at most 10^12 and a supplied power-of-two R greater than N. The single Worker timings include validation and trace-object work and establish neither a general performance result nor constant-time behavior; JavaScript BigInt is not constant-time. This is teaching code, not production cryptography, and Montgomery multiplication is distinct from the Montgomery ladder.

exhibits.title: Published Collision Pair and Byte Difference
exhibits.action: Select the SHAttered SHA-1 PDFs or an MD5 identical-prefix or chosen-prefix pair.
exhibits.outcome: The file evidence, byte differences, whole-file minimap, and optional PDF preview establish that the two inputs are genuinely distinct.

exhibits.title: Verify Broken-Hash Collision
exhibits.action: Hash both files with the pair’s broken hash and inspect their digests.
exhibits.outcome: The browser recomputes the same MD5 or SHA-1 digest for different files and shows the published provenance.
exhibits.limits: This verifies bundled published collision pairs; it does not search for a new collision.

exhibits.title: Identical-Prefix Versus Chosen-Prefix
exhibits.action: Inspect the pair’s prefix structure and the two collision models.
exhibits.outcome: The explainer separates a shared starting prefix from attacker-selected distinct prefixes and links the source.

exhibits.title: Internal Chaining-State Convergence
exhibits.action: Read a block-by-block state trace for both files.
exhibits.outcome: The crafted blocks show different intermediate states converging to the same chaining value for the broken hash.
exhibits.section: 5 · Inside the hash: states forced to converge

exhibits.title: Modern Digest Contrast
exhibits.action: Hash the exact same two files with SHA-256 and SHA3-256.
exhibits.outcome: Their resulting digests differ, locating the observed collision in the broken function rather than in hashing generally.
exhibits.limits: No practical full-round SHA-256 or SHA3-256 collision is demonstrated.

exhibits.title: Verification Ledger and Export
exhibits.action: Inspect the verification ledger, copy the proof, or download its JSON.
exhibits.outcome: The artifact records computed equality, file difference, and vector status for independent inspection.

exhibits.title: One-Bit Tamper Control
exhibits.action: Select a file, byte, and bit to flip, then rehash or reset.
exhibits.outcome: The changed digest breaks the published collision and distinguishes collision construction from universal digest equality.

exhibits.title: Mint a Common-Suffix Collision
exhibits.action: Append chosen equal bytes to both files, or choose a mismatched-suffix control, and recompute.
exhibits.outcome: The precondition check and measured digests show when a new, equal-length collision survives a common suffix.
exhibits.limits: This extends an existing published pair; it is not a new collision search or secret-prefix length-extension forgery.

exhibits.title: Reduced-Round SHA-2 Research Pair
exhibits.action: Switch between 36-step compression and wrong-round controls or flip a message bit.
exhibits.outcome: The supplied research pair matches under its 36-step convention while full standard SHA-256 digests differ.
exhibits.limits: This verifies a supplied reduced-round pair without padding; it does not reproduce the attack search or break standard full SHA-256.

exhibits.title: Commit, open, and try to cheat
exhibits.action: Commit a message with a fresh salt, then open the published SHA-256 commitment honestly or with a changed message.
exhibits.outcome: The verifier accepts a matching opening and rejects the changed opening, with the commitment and comparison shown.
exhibits.limits: One failed tampering attempt illustrates binding; it is not a proof that collisions cannot be found.
exhibits.section: Exhibit 1 — Commit, Open, and Try to Cheat

exhibits.title: Binding, quantified
exhibits.action: Run a batch of 3,000 alternative-opening trials against a fixed SHA-256 commitment.
exhibits.outcome: The collision-search result and an order-of-magnitude meter compare attempts with a generic 2^128 collision-work benchmark.
exhibits.limits: The button actually searches alternatives against one fixed commitment, a harder fixed-target trial; the generic 2^128 benchmark is for unrestricted birthday collisions. The finite trial cannot establish binding.

exhibits.title: Hiding and how it breaks
exhibits.action: Sample salted commitments to 0 and 1, toggle a computationally unbounded attacker, then build an unblinded SHA-256(message) and run a small dictionary attack.
exhibits.outcome: One sampled digest-bit frequency chart, conditional hash-versus-Pedersen hiding explanation, and a candidate recovery verdict show what salt contributes.
exhibits.limits: A single sampled output bit cannot prove indistinguishability; the unbounded-attacker toggle is explanatory, while Pedersen's guarantee assumes a uniform secret scalar.

exhibits.title: Pedersen commitments and additive homomorphism
exhibits.action: Commit and open one numeric message, then add commitments to two messages without opening either first.
exhibits.outcome: Live P-256 point checks validate openings and the homomorphic sum; an SVG shows a schematic tip-to-tail analogy.
exhibits.limits: Actual point arithmetic uses P-256; SVG placement is schematic. The teaching hash-to-point derivation is not an RFC 9380 production suite and code is unaudited.

exhibits.title: Sealed-bid auction
exhibits.action: Set three bids, publish their salted commitments, then reveal and verify all openings.
exhibits.outcome: The sealed table opens and displays the verified winning bid.
exhibits.limits: All participants are assumed to reveal; production auctions require deadlines and non-reveal rules.

exhibits.title: Coin flip and selective abort
exhibits.action: Commit Bob's bit, choose Alice's bit, then open honestly, attempt a changed bit, or selectively withhold an unfavorable opening.
exhibits.outcome: XOR results, rejected changes, aborted rounds, and a four-case table show that binding does not prevent selective abort bias.
exhibits.limits: This is a toy two-party workflow; a real protocol needs abort handling.
exhibits.section: Coin flip: a committed bit can still be withheld

exhibits.title: Where Commitments Appear and Scope
exhibits.action: Read the application map and the source and limits notes.
exhibits.outcome: Examples connect VSS share checks, threshold nonce commitments, Fiat–Shamir transcript binding, input consistency, and polynomial commitments.

exhibits.title: Ciphertext length probe
exhibits.action: Enter a guessed synthetic token and measure the ciphertext size produced by real gzip followed by AES-GCM.
exhibits.outcome: Reports the measured ciphertext byte count, including the 16-byte authentication tag, while the real decrypt-and-authenticate check remains valid.
exhibits.limits: Synthetic local response; no TLS/network probe or general secret recovery.

exhibits.title: Compare equal-length guesses and mitigations
exhibits.action: Compare four equal-length candidates under shared gzip, separate gzip dictionaries, or disabled compression.
exhibits.outcome: A matching reflection may compress shorter in a shared context; splitting contexts removes the cross-string signal in this setup while authentication still passes.
exhibits.limits: Shorter is not guaranteed to mean correct; compressor ties, response variation and padding can alter observations. Separate contexts do not hide length generally.

exhibits.title: What passed, and what failed?
exhibits.action: Run a probe or comparison, then inspect the authentication result, length verdict, negative claim and scope disclosure.
exhibits.outcome: Actual AES-GCM decrypt-and-authenticate results and measured ciphertext lengths drive the verdict: shared compression can expose a size difference without breaking AES, while one sample or tied lengths remain inconclusive.
exhibits.limits: The page observes synthetic local ciphertext lengths, not HTTP or TLS records, network noise or arbitrary secret recovery; equal lengths do not prove secrecy.

exhibits.title: Ordinary public signature
exhibits.action: Generate Alice’s signing key, sign a statement and let Bob and Dave verify the same public evidence; change the words.
exhibits.outcome: Both public verifiers can independently check the signature, and a changed message is rejected.

exhibits.title: Designated confirmer exchange
exhibits.action: Seal a fictional statement, select Alice or Carol and ask for a commitment before Bob chooses a fresh challenge and checks the response.
exhibits.outcome: The live verifier checks confirmation equations for the signed claim; the candidate inequality branch is separately labeled experimental.
exhibits.limits: Experimental Type-3 adaptation; full-scheme security and non-transferability are not established.

exhibits.title: Forged recording versus live challenge
exhibits.action: Let Eve fabricate a recorded proof for changed words, then issue a different challenge to the fixed commitment and response.
exhibits.outcome: The recorded equations pass under Eve’s chosen challenge while the same answer fails Bob’s later challenge.
exhibits.limits: The comparison illustrates transcript simulation but does not prove malicious-verifier or concurrent-session guarantees.
exhibits.section: A passing recording. A failing live answer.

exhibits.title: Candidate affirmative inequality proof
exhibits.action: Alter Alice’s signed claim, request the separate inequality commitment, choose a fresh challenge and verify the response.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect candidate inequality equations as affirmative evidence for invalidity, distinct from a refusal or failed confirmation.
exhibits.limits: The inequality proof is an experimental Type-3 reconstruction; complete DCS security and malicious-verifier guarantees are unproved.

exhibits.title: Designated confirmer research evidence desk
exhibits.action: Open the research view and inspect formal field-model claims, independent checks, open obligations and a public transcript export.
exhibits.outcome: Distinguish what was implemented or checked from full-protocol and privacy claims that remain open.
exhibits.limits: The abstract field model and independent sample verifier do not establish security of the complete browser protocol.
exhibits.section: Inspect the claim. Reproduce the check.

exhibits.title: Symbolic confirmer protocol and message-order attack
exhibits.action: Generate toy signer and confirmer keys, issue a symbolic object, ask either role for a proof and try Eve’s challenge-first trick.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect five equation checks and see the same forged response fail under Bob’s different challenge.
exhibits.limits: Public toy exponents expose secrets; the symbolic model offers no secrecy or zero knowledge and does not implement disavowal.
exhibits.section: Can Carol prove Alice signed it?

exhibits.title: One-message designated-verifier proof
exhibits.action: Create a registered verifier key, ask the selected signer or confirmer to prove with the branch witness, make a second accepted proof with the verifier secret, forge an accepted false-statement transcript, and compare both with the separate public-equation proof.
exhibits.outcome: One verification algorithm accepts both permitted designated-proof origins. The exact randomness bijection makes their true-statement transcript distributions identical, while the verifier-secret path also accepts for a false statement; the public comparison instead exposes equations any reader can recompute.
exhibits.limits: This adapts the paper's section 5 construction to the lab's Type-3 confirmation relation and implements Definition 1 only. It is not the generic Cramer–Damgård–Schoenmakers OR composition, a strong designated-verifier protocol, a designated-verifier signature or a completed designated-confirmer signature. The lab supplies no section 5 security theorem, and the public comparison has no lab-supplied proof-of-knowledge, soundness or unforgeability theorem.
exhibits.section: A proof addressed to one verifier.

exhibits.title: Sealed Transcript Baseline
exhibits.action: Inspect a clean tool exchange, then relabel a segment or edit its body after sealing.
exhibits.outcome: Shows host chain and tool signature checks passing on the clean turn and failing on altered metadata or bytes.
exhibits.limits: The agent response is scripted, not a model invocation.

exhibits.title: Injection in Tool, Runtime, and Persisted State
exhibits.action: Switch among acts 2 through 4 and inspect signed lower-trust content alongside the scripted agent response.
exhibits.outcome: Shows that authentic content can still contain instructions the agent should not obey.
exhibits.limits: The mock agent illustrates specific failure paths; it does not predict arbitrary models.

exhibits.title: Transcript Splice and Replay
exhibits.action: Select the splice/replay act and inspect the session-bound transcript checks.
exhibits.outcome: Shows that valid content can be misplaced and that binding position and session matters.

exhibits.title: Tool Signature and Host Seal
exhibits.action: Flip a tool signature or simulate a compromised host minting a system tag.
exhibits.outcome: Separates the source signature from the host seal and reports which trust assertion each change affects.
exhibits.limits: The compromised-host branch assumes the adversary has host sealing authority.

exhibits.title: Chain and Session Binding
exhibits.action: Swap or drop transcript segments, corrupt a previous link, or claim a different protocol version.
exhibits.outcome: Shows shape, order, and version checks fail in distinct ways.

exhibits.title: Honest Tool Hostile Payload versus Malicious Tool
exhibits.action: Select a genuine retrieval of hostile content and a compromised tool holding the expected signing key.
exhibits.outcome: Shows verification can pass while the scripted agent takes the attacker-desired action.
exhibits.limits: Passing provenance and integrity checks does not establish content safety or tool intent.

exhibits.title: Full Lab Envelope and Canonical Encoding
exhibits.action: Switch to Full lab and inspect each segment’s sealed fields, chain hash, encoded leaf bytes, and raw transcript.
exhibits.outcome: Shows the length-prefixed encoding and which values are covered by the leaf hash versus checked as the previous-chain mirror.
exhibits.limits: The fixture uses published fixed teaching keys, and the agent response is a deterministic script rather than a model measurement.

exhibits.title: Runtime Error as Authenticated Hostile Context
exhibits.action: Open the runtime-result act and relabel its traceback as system or tool output.
exhibits.outcome: Shows an honestly sealed runtime error carrying a hostile instruction while role relabeling fails verification.
exhibits.limits: Agent compliance is a deterministic scripted policy, not a real model outcome.

exhibits.title: Persisted State Reintroduced as Authority
exhibits.action: Open the persisted-state act, inspect the sealed scratchpad, then relabel or edit it after sealing.
exhibits.outcome: Shows content carried over a turn boundary and reread as agent notes with valid provenance, while byte edits and role changes fail.
exhibits.limits: The state is a fixture; no external agent memory or live model is involved.

exhibits.title: Expected Signing Key Held by a Hostile Tool
exhibits.action: Open the malicious-tool act and inspect the signed invoice response and verification verdict.
exhibits.outcome: Shows that a pinned key can truthfully authenticate bytes from a compromised tool without proving the tool’s intent or supply-chain integrity.
exhibits.limits: All-green verification and compromised-agent verdict are generated against a deterministic scripted agent.

exhibits.title: Algorithm comparison panels
exhibits.action: Generate bytes and reseed HMAC-DRBG, ChaCha20-DRBG and the Dual_EC-style model side by side.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect output bytes, bit heatmaps and reseed counters for three implemented generators.
exhibits.limits: Dual_EC uses real P-256 math with a chosen demo Q; its request lifecycle omits the final P update and simplifies seeding and reseeding.

exhibits.title: Statistical Tests (SP 800-22)
exhibits.action: Generate output for each algorithm, then run four sample statistical tests.
exhibits.outcome: Compare p-values and pass or fail labels across the three samples, including a backdoored generator that may pass.
exhibits.limits: Four tests on a sample cannot certify cryptographic security or standard conformance; repeat without new Generate or Reseed reuses the same state snapshot.

exhibits.title: TRIGGER ATTACK
exhibits.action: Generate Dual_EC-model output, trigger recovery using the demo P and Q relationship, then click Generate to confirm the precomputed prediction.
exhibits.outcome: The attack theater shows state candidates and predicted future output, with a matching next-click result or failure after reseeding.
exhibits.limits: A chosen demo trapdoor is known to this page; this does not demonstrate knowledge of the historical published Q secret. Model lifecycle and output framing differ from NIST Dual_EC_DRBG.

exhibits.title: Known Answer Test Results
exhibits.action: Open KAT to run HMAC-DRBG known-answer vectors and ABOUT to inspect generator and model boundaries.
exhibits.outcome: The modal reports vector matches; the scope panel explains real curve arithmetic, demo Q, seeding and request simplifications.
exhibits.limits: KAT results check specific HMAC-DRBG vectors; they do not validate the security of the Dual_EC model or other deployments.

exhibits.title: Encode a message in DNS queries
exhibits.action: Edit hidden text and DNS label, request, cover-traffic, jitter, loss, and cache controls; switch between sender and defender views.
exhibits.outcome: Simulated queries, decoded text, loss, and detector evidence respond to selected controls.
exhibits.limits: Synthetic browser model; no DNS queries or actual exfiltration are sent.

exhibits.title: Encode bits in packet timing
exhibits.action: Adjust short and long delays, jitter, loss, and decoder threshold.
exhibits.outcome: The simulated arrival gaps, decoded bits, confidence, and distribution show signal degradation.
exhibits.limits: Generated events and timings are a model, not live network measurements.

exhibits.title: Alter a network header carrier
exhibits.action: Choose a carrier field and middlebox actions, then compare normal and revealed covert views.
exhibits.outcome: Shows encoded header fields and how normalization or rewriting affects recovery.
exhibits.limits: Packet displays are synthetic and do not write traffic to a network.

exhibits.title: Hide message bits in a carrier image
exhibits.action: Use the sample image or a local upload and change hidden message and image controls.
exhibits.outcome: Compares simulated embedded pixels, capacity, and detector observations.
exhibits.limits: Local image processing is a teaching model; perceptual invisibility and detector failure are not guaranteed.

exhibits.title: Test how a warden changes channel capacity
exhibits.action: Toggle warden actions across simulated carriers.
exhibits.outcome: Shows closed, residual, rate-limited, surviving and out-of-path classifications.
exhibits.limits: Outcome categories use model thresholds and do not certify a real deployment.

exhibits.title: Follow hidden text through carrier representations
exhibits.action: Edit the global hidden message and inspect text, bytes, bits, and carrier previews.
exhibits.outcome: The same bits appear as different observable traffic or media properties.
exhibits.limits: Preview is illustrative; no transmission occurs.

exhibits.title: Encode bits in ICMP echo data or identifier
exhibits.action: Choose echo data or Identifier low bit; vary chunking, cover pings, loss, payload clamping, and NAT rewriting.
exhibits.outcome: Simulated echoes decode differently as intermediaries normalize data or rewrite identifiers; defender sees echo statistics.
exhibits.limits: Seeded browser simulation; no network traffic or hardware measurements.

exhibits.title: Encode bits in order of event pairs
exhibits.action: Adjust network reordering while observing event-pair order and decoded bits.
exhibits.outcome: A reversed pair can flip a bit; pair-frequency structure supplies a defensive clue.
exhibits.limits: Seeded browser simulation; no network traffic or hardware measurements.

exhibits.title: Rank permutations of HTTP headers as message symbols
exhibits.action: Change normal cover requests and toggle a proxy that re-sorts headers.
exhibits.outcome: The receiver ranks valid header permutations; normalization disrupts order and the defender sees order fingerprints.
exhibits.limits: Seeded browser simulation; no network traffic or hardware measurements.

exhibits.title: Hide symbols in protocol transitions
exhibits.action: Vary host cover traffic, flow loss and egress blocks while reading transition sequences.
exhibits.outcome: The receiver follows a shared state machine; losing or blocking flows disrupts decoding and a peer transition matrix exposes structure.
exhibits.limits: Seeded browser simulation; no network traffic or hardware measurements.

exhibits.title: Infer routing bits from library transfer records
exhibits.action: Toggle daily-aggregate data minimization and reveal routing bits in a synthetic item-transfer log.
exhibits.outcome: Detailed records permit decoding while aggregation cuts the unintended inference channel.
exhibits.limits: Synthetic records; no actual patron data is used.

exhibits.title: Decode a message from modelled LED brightness
exhibits.action: Adjust lit and dark levels, ambient noise, drift, sampling, blink period, and threshold.
exhibits.outcome: Recovered bits, confidence, measured versus predicted error and luminance distributions change.
exhibits.limits: Synthetic optical model; no physical transmitter or sensor.

exhibits.title: Decode a message from modelled cache probe latency
exhibits.action: Select a probe protocol and vary hit/miss cycles, jitter, eviction, repetitions, and threshold.
exhibits.outcome: The model displays recovered bits, error, confidence and latency histograms as co-tenant noise changes.
exhibits.limits: Abstract cache simulator; no real cache probes.

exhibits.title: Inspect anomaly indicators across channels
exhibits.action: Select a channel and compare overview scores with per-channel statistics.
exhibits.outcome: Synthetic traffic reveals channel-specific indicators such as DNS characters, timing histograms, pair structure and header-order fingerprints.
exhibits.limits: Indicators on seeded synthetic cases are not operational detection probabilities.

exhibits.title: Classify unseen traffic before ground truth is revealed
exhibits.action: Generate seeded case sets, name a tell and make clean, suspicious or covert calls.
exhibits.outcome: Reveal panels score caught covert cases, misses and false alarms, making tradeoffs explicit.
exhibits.limits: Six synthetic cases per set; not field validation.

exhibits.title: Read ROC and confusion results for hand-built detectors
exhibits.action: Compare deterministic clean and covert sweeps across detectors and thresholds.
exhibits.outcome: ROC, AUC, confusion matrices, false positives and misses show how threshold choices affect each statistic.
exhibits.limits: Synthetic benchmark and chosen distributions; anomaly score is not probability.

exhibits.title: Compare fitted timing detector to hand-built detector under shift
exhibits.action: Inspect train, held-out and shifted case AUC plus fitted feature weights.
exhibits.outcome: A fitted model can change ranking performance when clean pollers and narrow-separation covert channels shift the distribution.
exhibits.limits: Small synthetic datasets; no deployment accuracy claim.

exhibits.title: Compare capacity, noise and indicators across carriers
exhibits.action: Read the nine-column channel comparison table.
exhibits.outcome: Carrier, storage/timing type, illustrative capacity, reliability, noise, breakage and indicators sit side by side.
exhibits.limits: Illustrative qualitative comparison, not measured production throughput.

exhibits.title: Map channels to hiding patterns and scope exclusions
exhibits.action: Read eleven-pattern taxonomy and built versus concept-only carrier cards.
exhibits.outcome: The atlas distinguishes network PDU patterns from excluded payload carriers and non-network media.
exhibits.limits: Some carriers are descriptions only; no operational tools.

exhibits.title: Map documented cases to carriers and detectors
exhibits.action: Read five source-linked incidents and their named modeled statistics.
exhibits.outcome: The cases separate deliberate covert signaling from side-channel leakage and unintended inference.
exhibits.limits: Read-only mapping; modeled detectors are not retrospective proof of detection.

exhibits.title: Find High-to-Low covert channels in a matrix
exhibits.action: Toggle Reference and Modify permissions for secret and public tasks on shared resources.
exhibits.outcome: A channel is flagged when High can modify an attribute Low can read, with storage/timing classification.
exhibits.limits: Abstract five-attribute permissions exercise.

exhibits.title: Compare live capacity, reliability and observability
exhibits.action: Select one of eight seeded carrier models in the trade-off instrument.
exhibits.outcome: Meters show different capacity, delivery and detectability for the same demo message.
exhibits.limits: Fixed illustrative model settings; metrics are not field measurements.

exhibits.title: Review cross-channel defensive practices
exhibits.action: Read defensive principles and grouped primary references.
exhibits.outcome: The synthesis distinguishes monitoring suspicious statistics, disrupting carriers and accepting residual uncertainty.
exhibits.limits: Explanatory reference page, not a deployed control.

exhibits.title: Test cross-channel distinctions
exhibits.action: Answer questions and reset the score.
exhibits.outcome: Each answer reveals an explanation and the total score updates.
exhibits.limits: Instructional quiz; no empirical detector run.

exhibits.title: Search covert-channel and detection terminology
exhibits.action: Filter definitions by term or explanation.
exhibits.outcome: Matching entries and count update as the query changes, clarifying capacity, anomaly baselines, carriers and related terms.
exhibits.limits: Searchable reference; no channel or detector execution.

exhibits.title: All-or-Nothing Credential Baseline
exhibits.action: Prove an age claim with the conventional signed credential baseline.
exhibits.outcome: The verifier receives and checks the full credential payload, exposing fields beyond the requested predicate.

exhibits.title: BBS Selective Disclosure
exhibits.action: Choose revealed claims, generate a presentation, and step through the BBS proof.
exhibits.outcome: A fresh proof verifies the issuer’s signature on revealed claims while hidden fields remain undisclosed.

exhibits.title: Tamper a Revealed Claim
exhibits.action: Change a disclosed class claim after proof generation and reverify the honest presentation.
exhibits.outcome: The actual verifier rejects changed revealed bytes and accepts the original proof.

exhibits.title: BBS and Ed25519 Three-Presentation Comparison
exhibits.action: Make three BBS presentations and three Ed25519 showings, then inspect verification and shared byte runs.
exhibits.outcome: Randomized BBS proofs differ while a conventional signature repeats, subject to disclosed-data and metadata linkability.
exhibits.limits: Unique revealed claims, headers, issuer keys, and status identifiers can still correlate presentations.

exhibits.title: Age Predicate without Birth Date
exhibits.action: Prove a qualifying 1999 birth date, try an honest underage 2010 date, or force a forged proof.
exhibits.outcome: The real pairing and range-proof checks accept the qualifying claim and reject the underage or forged claim without disclosing DOB.
exhibits.section: 4 · Predicate proof: "over 18" without a birth date
exhibits.limits: The custom range construction is a teaching implementation, not a production credential system.

exhibits.title: Status-List Revocation Tradeoff
exhibits.action: Toggle credential #17’s status and ask the verifier to check its proof and published status bit.
exhibits.outcome: The proof binds the claimed index, so revocation works but the stable index reconnects otherwise randomized showings.
exhibits.limits: The status list does not provide zero-knowledge non-revocation; accumulator designs are compared in prose only.

exhibits.title: Credential Privacy Comparison
exhibits.action: Read the table of issuer visibility, verifier visibility, linkability, and selective disclosure.
exhibits.outcome: Compare plain signed credentials, BBS, blind signatures, and other credential patterns by whose information is hidden.

exhibits.title: Curve Explorer
exhibits.action: Switch between smooth real-number geometry and a finite field of 17; select points P and Q on the plotted curve.
exhibits.outcome: See the third intersection, reflection and resulting P+Q, with finite-field line segments wrapping modulo 17.
exhibits.limits: Tiny teaching field and real-number picture are analogies; production curves have large finite fields.

exhibits.title: Break the Discrete Log
exhibits.action: Generate a new toy secret and solve its public point by brute force.
exhibits.outcome: Watch candidate scalar multiples until the small-curve private scalar is found.
exhibits.limits: Toy small-field brute force does not estimate practical attacks on production curves.

exhibits.title: ECDH Live Demo
exhibits.action: Choose a supported real curve, generate fresh Alice and Bob keypairs, and inspect their public values and shared outputs.
exhibits.outcome: Compare the matching raw shared value Z and the transcript from both parties; an X25519-only expandable note explains low-order all-zero rejection.
exhibits.limits: Private scalars are intentionally displayed for teaching; Z is not yet an application key and must go through a KDF. The panel generates valid peer keys and does not test attacker-supplied low-order inputs.

exhibits.title: Scalar Multiplication
exhibits.action: Switch between a small field and supported real curve, change scalar, and inspect the resulting public point.
exhibits.outcome: See an exact small-field double-and-add trace and a real curve result with its actual output encoding.
exhibits.limits: The trace is for the toy field only; X25519 uses a Montgomery ladder and real short-Weierstrass implementations use different optimized algorithms. JavaScript timing is not a side-channel guarantee.

exhibits.title: Curve Comparison
exhibits.action: Read parameter and subgroup information across the supported curves.
exhibits.outcome: Compare named curve families and their metadata alongside small-field analogy plots.
exhibits.limits: Mini-plots are small-field analogies, not production-field points; no quantum attack is executed.

exhibits.title: Security margin and field prime
exhibits.action: Read the logarithmic work-factor scale and Goldilocks prime representation.
exhibits.outcome: Compares nominal classical 128-bit and 224-bit security tiers and the field p=2^448−2^224−1.
exhibits.limits: Security levels are estimates of generic classical attacks, not measured break times.

exhibits.title: Toy curve scalar multiplication
exhibits.action: Move k from 1 to 28 and inspect k·G on a small plotted curve.
exhibits.outcome: Shows point addition and scalar multiplication before the real X448 exchange.
exhibits.limits: The 29-point plot is illustrative and unrelated in security scale to X448.

exhibits.title: X448 Diffie-Hellman exchange
exhibits.action: Run Alice and Bob key agreement, compare their shared values, reveal private scalars and inspect clamped bits.
exhibits.outcome: Displays matching 56-byte shared outputs, public-key wire view and RFC 7748 scalar clamping.
exhibits.limits: Bare unauthenticated DH is vulnerable to an active man in the middle; it is not a complete secure channel.

exhibits.title: Sign and verify Ed448
exhibits.action: Generate a key pair, sign a message under an optional context, verify, then tamper with message or signature.
exhibits.outcome: Shows signature acceptance or rejection and public and private material in the teaching UI.
exhibits.limits: In-tab private seed must not be used as a persistent production key.

exhibits.title: Seed expansion and domain separation
exhibits.action: Expand one seed with SHAKE256 and SHA-512, then sign the same message under two contexts and cross-check.
exhibits.outcome: Displays differing expansion bytes and context-bound signatures that do not interchange.
exhibits.limits: Hash comparison is explanatory; SHA-512 output is not an alternate interoperable Ed448 key derivation.

exhibits.title: Curve25519 versus Curve448
exhibits.action: Generate live keys, signatures and timing/size comparison.
exhibits.outcome: Shows key/signature byte and operation tradeoffs for the two curve families.
exhibits.limits: Local timings are browser and device dependent, not universal benchmarks.

exhibits.title: Recomputed RFC vectors
exhibits.action: Open the reference-vector disclosure after automatic on-load recomputation.
exhibits.outcome: Shows computed X448 and Ed448 values beside published expected outputs.
exhibits.limits: Known-answer vectors check selected examples; they are not a complete implementation audit.

exhibits.title: Curve selection guide
exhibits.action: Expand decision tree and deployment examples.
exhibits.outcome: Summarizes classical security and performance tradeoffs and points to post-quantum alternatives.
exhibits.limits: Guidance is explanatory and can age as deployment profiles change.

exhibits.title: Atbash substitution
exhibits.action: Explore Hebrew and Latin letter mappings, load a Jeremiah example and enter text.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect fixed substitution output and unchanged frequency-shape and index of coincidence.

exhibits.title: Caesar cipher and frequency attack
exhibits.action: Choose a shift, encode text and run frequency alignment against ciphertext.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect ranked English shift candidates from chi-squared frequency scoring.

exhibits.title: Vigenère and Kasiski examination
exhibits.action: Enter plaintext and key, encrypt, then run Kasiski examination on ciphertext.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect repeated sequences, spacings, likely period and columnwise shift recovery.
exhibits.limits: Short or unsuitable ciphertext may not yield a reliable key-length estimate.

exhibits.title: One-time pad and reused-key attack
exhibits.action: Generate a key, encrypt text and reuse the same pad for two messages; try crib dragging.
exhibits.outcome: The XOR of two ciphertexts equals the XOR of the two plaintexts when a pad is reused.

exhibits.title: AES-256-GCM and tamper detection
exhibits.action: Encrypt text, decrypt, inspect GHASH and flip a ciphertext bit before verifying.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect real ciphertext and integrity-check rejection after the bit flip.

exhibits.title: The historical cipher arc
exhibits.action: Inspect the timeline of five eras, each cipher’s fatal flaw and what its successor fixed.
exhibits.outcome: Compare substitution, frequency, repeating-key, pad-reuse and authenticated-encryption lessons in one historical synthesis.

exhibits.title: Passive Diffie-Hellman and Discrete Log
exhibits.action: Run finite-field DH with toy primes and invoke baby-step giant-step to recover an exponent.
exhibits.outcome: Displays public shares, matching private secrets, measured attack work, and a cost chart.
exhibits.section: Eve is watching — and it doesn't help her
exhibits.limits: Toy primes make the attack feasible; the generic cost chart is not a real finite-field security estimate.

exhibits.title: Active Man-in-the-Middle Relay
exhibits.action: Choose Alice, Bob, and Mallory exponents, run the replacement exchange, and send a message through Mallory.
exhibits.outcome: Shows two distinct shared keys; Mallory decrypts, optionally edits, and re-encrypts a message.

exhibits.title: ECDSA Authenticated DH
exhibits.action: Run a clean signed handshake and one where Mallory substitutes an ephemeral share.
exhibits.outcome: WebCrypto P-256 ECDSA validates the honest transcript and rejects the swapped one.
exhibits.limits: A full SIGMA-like AKE also MACs the transcript and binds negotiated parameters.

exhibits.title: Generic BSGS versus Finite-Field NFS
exhibits.action: Read the references and glossary comparing the demo’s BSGS discrete log with finite-field NFS and reused-prime precomputation.
exhibits.outcome: Clarifies why the toy attack and square-root cost chart do not set real finite-field DH security.
exhibits.limits: NFS and Logjam are cited, not executed or measured.

exhibits.title: Identity Binding in Deployed DH Protocols
exhibits.action: Read the TLS, Signal X3DH, and SSH examples beneath the signed exchange.
exhibits.outcome: Compares transcript signatures, signed prekeys with identity-key DH inputs, and host-key exchange hashes as distinct ways to authenticate ephemeral DH.
exhibits.limits: The panel describes these protocol patterns; the live exercise only signs a simplified P-256 ECDSA delivery.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 1: Watch the Loop
exhibits.action: Choose ML-DSA parameters, sign once or step through attempts, regenerate a key, flip a signature byte and reverify.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect each acceptance check, retry reason and final signature verification or tamper rejection.
exhibits.limits: Instrumented signing exposes internal attempts in a teaching implementation; the display is not a production constant-time guarantee.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 2: Histogram of Iterations
exhibits.action: Run batches of 100 or 1000 signatures and inspect or export the iteration histogram and rejection reasons.
exhibits.outcome: The empirical retry distribution and category counts illustrate variable loop length.
exhibits.limits: Finite batches fluctuate and should not be read as timing leakage or key recovery.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 3: Real Signing Times (Measured)
exhibits.action: Measure 2000 actual signature operations and inspect or export timing samples.
exhibits.outcome: The chart reports browser-observed latency distribution separately from instrumented iteration counts.
exhibits.limits: Browser timing includes scheduling and environment noise; a distribution alone does not establish exploitable key-dependent leakage.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 4: Why Each Check Exists
exhibits.action: Expand the four checks and show examples for z, r0, c·t0 and hint-weight rejection.
exhibits.outcome: The panel explains each bound and displays an illustrative accepted or rejected candidate.
exhibits.limits: Examples explain checks; they do not prove the full security reduction.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 5: Comparing Signature Schemes
exhibits.action: Compare the scheme summary for ML-DSA and other signatures.
exhibits.outcome: The displayed table relates signature and key sizes, operation style and rejection behavior.
exhibits.limits: Comparison values are informational and can depend on selected parameterization and implementation.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 6: Is Iteration Count Distinguishable?
exhibits.action: Run the KS comparison and guess which of two populations has a deliberately leaky setting.
exhibits.outcome: The lesson reports the sample test and feedback while explaining why variable time is not automatically key leakage.
exhibits.limits: The leaky population is constructed for teaching; the test does not prove real ML-DSA secret recovery.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 7: Symbols & Further Reading
exhibits.action: Read the notation and linked source material for the signing checks.
exhibits.outcome: The glossary connects the parameters and variables used in the interactive panels.
exhibits.limits: A reference glossary rather than a separate cryptographic experiment.

exhibits.title: Seal a Document
exhibits.action: Choose an ML-DSA parameter set, generate keys, enter document text, seal and verify the exported JSON; tamper with the text and verify again.
exhibits.outcome: The browser signs the document content with FIPS 204 ML-DSA and verifies it under the included public key. Recomputing an ordinary SHA-256 content hash after an edit cannot make the old ML-DSA signature verify.
exhibits.limits: The JSON package signs only content. The signer label and timestamp are unsigned, and its included public key is not bound to a trusted human identity; successful verification alone does not establish signer identity.

exhibits.title: Choosing a parameter set
exhibits.action: Read the protocol and policy questions and compare ML-DSA-44, -65 and -87 by NIST strength category, key size and signature size.
exhibits.outcome: The panel explains how interoperability requirements and security category guide a parameter choice; it does not run ML-DSA internals in this section.
exhibits.limits: This is conceptual guidance and a static FIPS parameter table. It does not establish a one-size-fits-all best parameter set or run signing inside the guidance panel.

exhibits.title: Signature Size Comparison
exhibits.action: Compare the signature-size bars for RSA-PSS, ECDSA, Ed25519, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA.
exhibits.outcome: The page draws bars from specified byte counts; its ML-DSA-44, -65 and -87 counts are FIPS 204 Table 2 values, not fresh signatures computed by this chart.
exhibits.limits: This chart visualizes transcribed specification sizes. Separate signing and benchmark controls perform real ML-DSA operations.

exhibits.title: ML-DSA Mechanism and Rejection Loop
exhibits.action: Walk through key generation, signing, verification, hard problems, and quantum resistance; inspect the Fiat–Shamir visualization.
exhibits.outcome: The explanation separates lattice arithmetic from an illustrative view of challenges and rejection sampling.

exhibits.title: Signing Timing Variability
exhibits.action: Run repeated signatures and compare variability against verification as a control.
exhibits.outcome: The measurements expose the signing rejection loop and local timing spread without inferring a secret-key leak.
exhibits.section: The loop you cannot see, measured
exhibits.limits: Browser timing observations are not a side-channel exploit or constant-time audit.

exhibits.title: Browser Benchmark and Classical Baseline
exhibits.action: Run local ML-DSA operations and compare timings and byte sizes with a measured classical signature.
exhibits.outcome: The panel reports environment and distribution summaries for key generation, signing and verification.
exhibits.limits: Local timing is environment-dependent and is not a universal algorithm ranking.

exhibits.title: NIST PQC Trio and Deployment
exhibits.action: Compare ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA roles, a complete post-quantum system, deployment contexts and standardization timeline.
exhibits.outcome: The panel distinguishes key establishment from two signature families.

exhibits.title: Implementation Fidelity and Limitations
exhibits.action: Inspect what runs locally, the standard-versus-legacy name distinction, parameter references, integrity pin, and security limits.
exhibits.outcome: The disclosures distinguish real ML-DSA signing from explanatory diagrams and make library and policy constraints visible.

exhibits.title: Run distributed key generation rounds
exhibits.action: Choose parties and threshold; step or run the ceremony, optionally arming a cheating dealer.
exhibits.outcome: Shows commitments, private shares, public complaints and reveals, QUAL, and assembled public key; bad shares are detected.
exhibits.limits: One browser tab plays every party, so private channels are only modeled and visible for teaching.

exhibits.title: Reconstruct from t shares and compare t−1
exhibits.action: Select the threshold-size and undersized sets, then reconstruct and compare with the public commitment.
exhibits.outcome: Shows t shares recovering the group public key and too few shares failing the comparison.
exhibits.limits: The UI is a local demonstration, not a distributed signing system; exposure of shares in the page is intentional.

exhibits.title: Compare rushing key bias with a hiding-commitment fix
exhibits.action: Choose naive or GJKR mode, malicious dealer count and target nibble; run one or twenty rounds.
exhibits.outcome: Displays subset-sum candidate public keys and how commit-then-reveal removes the attacker’s advance view.
exhibits.limits: Faithful bias model with real commitment and subset-sum arithmetic; it is not a second full extraction-phase ceremony.
exhibits.section: Exhibit 3 · Bias the key — the GJKR attack & fix

exhibits.title: Pinned DNSSEC Chain of Trust
exhibits.action: Choose a validation clock and inspect each signed link from the IANA root anchor through .com to cloudflare.com.
exhibits.outcome: Cryptographic checks validate the pinned capture at a chosen time, exposing DS-to-DNSKEY and RRSIG links and any timing failure.
exhibits.section: A real chain of trust, one link at a time
exhibits.limits: A committed DNS capture is checked at a selected instant; the page does not perform a live DNS lookup.

exhibits.title: Diagnose Broken Chain Links
exhibits.action: Select stale DS, missing key tag, bad time, rogue signer, tampered answer, and other failure cases.
exhibits.outcome: A signed teaching hierarchy is validated and the named failure is reported at the offending link.
exhibits.section: Break each link, and read the diagnosis

exhibits.title: Unsigned Delegation Versus Bogus Chain
exhibits.action: Switch between a signed no-DS delegation, a broken chain, and captured opt-out evidence.
exhibits.outcome: The resolver distinguishes authenticated INSECURE status from BOGUS validation failure.
exhibits.section: A chain that ends is not a chain that broke

exhibits.title: Enumerate a Zone through NSEC
exhibits.action: Follow successive signed denial-of-existence records and try a forged denial.
exhibits.outcome: Each proof discloses the next existing owner name, enabling a complete zone walk while bad denial signatures fail validation.
exhibits.section: The proof that a name is absent tells you which names are present

exhibits.title: NSEC3 Offline Guessing
exhibits.action: Run the same dictionary against two signed zones and inspect the hash trace and recovered-name meter.
exhibits.outcome: Hashed denial removes plain next-name pointers but guessable names can still be recovered offline.
exhibits.section: NSEC3 turns the walk into an offline guessing problem
exhibits.limits: The dictionary is a finite teaching wordlist; unrecovered labels are not proved unguessable.

exhibits.title: Precomputed Versus On-Demand Denial
exhibits.action: Switch between a precomputed NSEC chain and a captured on-demand black-lie response.
exhibits.outcome: The on-demand proof reveals no neighbouring owner name and illustrates the need for an online signing key.
exhibits.section: Making the denial up, one query at a time
exhibits.limits: The response is captured or synthesized locally; no online nameserver is queried.

exhibits.title: DNSSEC Key Rollover and Cached DS
exhibits.action: Advance through overlapping key publication/signing stages and inspect a cached-parent-DS failure.
exhibits.outcome: The validator demonstrates how overlap keeps the chain available and how stale delegation data can break it.
exhibits.section: Replacing a key without going dark

exhibits.title: Strip the hybrid group
exhibits.section: Break it yourself: strip the offer
exhibits.action: Delete X25519MLKEM768 from supported_groups, choose transcript binding and policy, then run or compare handshakes.
exhibits.outcome: An unbound model can complete on x25519; TLS 1.3-style transcript binding detects the altered offer at Finished verification.
exhibits.limits: The wire and unbound pre-TLS-1.3 counterfactual are scripted; no full TLS record or certificate exchange.

exhibits.title: Preferred versus required hybrid policy
exhibits.section: One config line: PQC preferred vs required
exhibits.action: Run the same unbound strip with PQC preferred and PQC required.
exhibits.outcome: Preferred can accept classical-only; required aborts and exposes an availability tradeoff.
exhibits.limits: The comparison isolates one policy under the same scripted strip and deliberately unbound transcript.

exhibits.title: Version rollback sentinel
exhibits.section: The weaker cousin: the downgrade sentinel
exhibits.action: Toggle server sentinel writing and client checking for a TLS 1.3-capable server negotiating TLS 1.2.
exhibits.outcome: Displays ServerHello.random tail bytes and whether the client detects a version rollback.
exhibits.limits: A marker only covers version rollback, not a group strip inside TLS 1.3; the panel models the TLS 1.2 case.

exhibits.title: Retry downgrade after failure
exhibits.action: Choose a fail-open or fail-closed retry policy and run two broken handshakes.
exhibits.outcome: A retry that drops PQ can yield a classical-only connection despite prior transcript protection.
exhibits.limits: Scripted retry policy rather than an actual network client; failure does not imply TLS 1.3 itself accepted a stripped transcript.

exhibits.title: FREAK, Logjam and POODLE context
exhibits.section: The same shape, for thirty years
exhibits.action: Read historical downgrade patterns.
exhibits.outcome: Relates export-grade key exchange and version rollback to negotiation before authentication.
exhibits.limits: Historical cards do not reproduce these attacks.

exhibits.title: Two totals leak one salary
exhibits.action: Run a differencing attack against exact and noisy aggregate releases.
exhibits.outcome: Subtracting exact neighboring totals reveals one salary; noisy releases vary while each query spends privacy budget.
exhibits.section: Two harmless totals, one person's salary

exhibits.title: Generalization and homogeneity attack
exhibits.action: Choose quasi-identifier generalization and inspect the measured k and salary-band classes.
exhibits.outcome: A class can satisfy k-anonymity while its unanimous sensitive value reveals Alice’s salary band.
exhibits.limits: The table is a small local example; measured k does not guarantee attribute privacy.
exhibits.section: What about anonymising the table instead?

exhibits.title: The differential privacy guarantee
exhibits.action: Adjust epsilon and mechanism to inspect neighboring database output distributions and their likelihood ratio rails.
exhibits.outcome: The charts compute exact probabilities and check the epsilon bound or a measured delta needed for the selected mechanism.
exhibits.limits: Gaussian calibration derives from a continuous bound but the panel samples a discrete approximation.

exhibits.title: Guess the neighboring world
exhibits.action: Draw 2,000 outputs from both worlds, deal a release and guess Alice’s presence.
exhibits.outcome: Compare sampled histograms to exact probabilities and see guessing results against the privacy bound.
exhibits.section: Can you tell which world you are in?

exhibits.title: Epsilon utility dial
exhibits.action: Move epsilon and release multiple noisy answers or a post-processed mean.
exhibits.outcome: See how noise and usefulness change and that deterministic post-processing spends no additional privacy budget.
exhibits.section: The dial: what ε costs in usefulness

exhibits.title: Declare sensitivity before release
exhibits.action: Choose a public clipping bound and a policy for an out-of-range thirteenth record.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect clipping or exclusion bias and why data-dependent sensitivity would misstate the privacy guarantee.
exhibits.section: Where does Δ come from? You have to answer

exhibits.title: Composition ledger and averaging
exhibits.action: Issue queries against a finite epsilon ledger and run repeated queries without a budget.
exhibits.outcome: See summed privacy cost and how averaging many noisy releases can expose the signal.
exhibits.section: Composition: ε is a budget, not a setting

exhibits.title: Privacy parameters in deployed systems
exhibits.action: Inspect deployment ε values, provenance labels, belief bounds and four accounting conversions for one Census release.
exhibits.outcome: Compare e^ε and posterior bounds and see how differing accountants can label the same underlying ρ budget.
exhibits.limits: The figures have different published, measured or derived provenance and accounting choices; a raw ε comparison alone is incomplete.

exhibits.title: Differential privacy transfer challenge
exhibits.action: Answer four new scenario questions and inspect tailored feedback or linked interactions to revisit.
exhibits.outcome: Test whether lessons about releases, mechanisms, inference and accounting transfer beyond the page’s worked examples.
exhibits.section: Four situations this page has not shown you

exhibits.title: Fresh masks cancel
exhibits.action: Choose one sender and one message byte, draw a new mask for every edge, or load the fixed independently checked fixture.
exhibits.outcome: Displays every participant input, pairwise mask and public broadcast, then recomputes the XOR aggregate and its equality with the input XOR.
exhibits.limits: Information-theoretic anonymity is conditional on independent uniform secret one-use masks and the declared observer model; WebCrypto random generation is a concrete CSPRNG-backed execution, not a proof of that theorem.

exhibits.title: Observer and coalition views
exhibits.action: Select an external observer, one participant or a coalition and compare uniform with deliberately skewed sender priors.
exhibits.outcome: Removes exactly the masks known to the selected view, derives remaining connected components and component XORs, then enumerates compatible exactly-one-sender distributions and renormalizes the supplied priors.
exhibits.limits: The compatible-sender set requires the displayed exactly-one-sender assumption; with multiple senders, component parity is not a sender list, and equal likelihoods do not create uniform priors.

exhibits.title: Collision parity and byte XOR
exhibits.section: The output is parity, not a headcount
exhibits.action: Run zero, one, two or three simultaneous one-bit senders, then compare identical and distinct one-byte concurrent payloads.
exhibits.outcome: Shows the public broadcasts and XOR result beside the private simulator trace, demonstrating even/odd parity and byte values that cancel or remain structurally plausible.
exhibits.limits: Basic DC-net reveals an XOR, not a sender count or a reliable collision marker; the private sender trace is omniscient teaching state and is not available to protocol observers.

exhibits.title: Malformed, jammer and dropout cases
exhibits.section: Shape checks are not honesty checks
exhibits.action: Compare an honest round with a wrong-width contribution, a correctly shaped arbitrary contribution, a missing participant and a reformed graph using replacement masks.
exhibits.outcome: Rejects malformed input, accepts but exposes the changed aggregate from the shaped jammer, aborts the incomplete round with its uncancelled boundary-mask equation, and runs a new four-member round.
exhibits.limits: Structural validation does not prove equation compliance or identify a jammer. A missing contribution aborts the current round; continuing requires new membership, a new graph and genuinely fresh masks.

exhibits.title: Bounded commit before reveal
exhibits.action: Compute SHA-256 commitments for every encoded contribution and context before reveal, then change each bound field, precommit a dishonest byte and withhold one reveal.
exhibits.outcome: Accepts the honest openings, rejects changed openings under the stated hash assumptions, still accepts a precommitted jammer and aborts when a participant withholds its reveal.
exhibits.limits: This narrow adaptation assumes SHA-256 collision and second-preimage resistance and claims no formal hiding theorem; it does not authenticate identity, prove the DC-net equation, force reveal or provide Dissent/Verdict accountability.

exhibits.title: Mask reuse and later disclosure
exhibits.action: Reuse every edge mask across a known-empty and a message round, compare a distinct deterministic-mask control, then disclose both masks incident to one recorded participant.
exhibits.outcome: Cancels each participant’s reused masks to recover every second input, shows the distinct control does not retain that identity, and reconstructs the recorded participant’s past input after full incident-mask disclosure.
exhibits.limits: The identity requires every mask incident to a participant to repeat; the distinct deterministic control is not a randomness proof. JavaScript cannot establish secure erasure or prevent later key retention.

exhibits.title: Choose one declared distance-bounding session
exhibits.action: Choose one of six actor views, set exact timing and error parameters, select broken assumptions, and run a freshly derived verifier-nonce session.
exhibits.outcome: The page derives response registers, challenges, round trips, verdicts and applicable exact probabilities from the displayed inputs, while changed inputs retire the prior result.
exhibits.limits: The declared synchronous HMAC-SHA-256 profile is one teaching instantiation of the paper's hash function, not an interoperable radio protocol or a proof that the hand-rolled PRF is secure.

exhibits.title: Authentication is not proximity
exhibits.action: Relay an ordinary domain-separated HMAC-SHA-256 challenge and response, then alter the returned tag as a negative control.
exhibits.outcome: The genuine relayed tag authenticates without proving proximity, while the altered tag is rejected; no rapid phase or distance verdict is fabricated.
exhibits.limits: This is a bounded authentication contrast, not a complete deployed authentication protocol; it intentionally makes no timing or distance claim.

exhibits.title: Exact rapid rounds and a late online relay
exhibits.action: Compare an honest in-range session with an online relay whose answers are all correct but whose complete modeled path is charged to every round trip.
exhibits.outcome: Exact threshold arithmetic accepts the honest transcript and rejects the relay on timing; late answers cannot consume the separate content-error allowance.
exhibits.limits: All distances, speeds and delays are declared exact model quantities; no browser or network clock measures physical propagation.

exhibits.title: Mafia fraud by pre-asking
exhibits.action: Choose how many rounds the nearby attacker pre-asks, how many content errors are tolerated, and whether challenges are predictable or the verifier nonce is reused.
exhibits.outcome: The attacker answers from stored oracle results without receiving the key or registers; the page computes the applicable exact full or partial pre-ask probability and withdraws formulas when their assumptions are broken.
exhibits.limits: The exact formulas assume ideal independent response bits, unpredictable challenges and a fresh verifier nonce; physical-layer early-detect/late-commit behavior is outside the model.

exhibits.title: Dishonest-prover distance fraud
exhibits.action: Run a distant legitimate key holder that commits before seeing each challenge, vary its actual delay, and compare the realized register-distance probability with the ideal ensemble average.
exhibits.outcome: The page keeps this actor distinct from a relay, computes success from the current response table's Hamming distance, and exposes when an unsafe processing-delay floor makes the prover appear nearer.
exhibits.limits: The return trip begins only after challenge arrival and removes processing delay rather than modeling scheduled radio pre-transmission or physical synchronization.

exhibits.title: Exact independent-noise acceptance
exhibits.action: Set a rational per-bit error probability and content-error allowance for an honest prover, then inspect the sampled transcript and exact acceptance and false-rejection probabilities.
exhibits.outcome: Rejection sampling realizes the requested rational probability without binary-floor approximation, while timing failures remain outside the content allowance.
exhibits.limits: Independent bit flips are not a model of correlated, bursty, multipath or capture-shaped radio errors; the reduced rational denominator is bounded at 2^32.

exhibits.title: Model and source boundary
exhibits.section: What this lesson does not do
exhibits.action: Read the implementation limits and the exact primary-source sections used for timing, protocol, attack vocabulary and noisy-channel reasoning.
exhibits.outcome: The page distinguishes this exact arithmetic and event simulator from ranging hardware, localisation, Brands–Chaum, physical-layer attacks, terrorist fraud and production parameter guidance.
exhibits.limits: The source list and exclusions explain the model; they are not additional executed protocols, attacks or empirical measurements.

exhibits.title: Equal file, three encryption choices
exhibits.action: Edit one synthetic file and run fresh-key, local message-locked and server-aided uploads for Alice and Bob.
exhibits.outcome: Displays both data keys and ciphertexts, exact equality, unique blobs, distinct capsules, counted bytes and the data-deduplication ratio for each mode.
exhibits.limits: Counted storage includes unique data ciphertext and capsules but excludes identifiers, indexes, allocator overhead and protocol traffic.

exhibits.title: Dictionary pressure and the online boundary
exhibits.section: Dictionary pressure and the online boundary
exhibits.action: Run equal-length local guesses and RFC 9497 VOPRF guesses across request budgets, identities, epochs, proof tampering and key-server compromise.
exhibits.outcome: Shows exact ciphertext confirmation offline, recovery or delay within a modeled online budget, principal refusal, renewed budgets and proof rejection.
exhibits.limits: The allowlist and quota are teaching state, not an authentication protocol, Sybil defense or enforceable production rate limit.

exhibits.title: Who learns what?
