exhibits.action: Compare the values and capabilities exposed to the client, key server, storage server and three attacker views for the computed run.
exhibits.outcome: Separates blinded VOPRF traffic, stored equality and metadata, quota-bound guessing, local-MLE guessing and combined-compromise confirmation.
exhibits.limits: All roles execute in one browser origin, so the distinct views are a pedagogical model rather than process, network or hardware isolation.

exhibits.title: Boundaries: possession, authorization, deletion, revocation, rotation
exhibits.section: Boundaries: possession, authorization, deletion, revocation, rotation
exhibits.action: Execute fresh-nonce possession, owner reads, cross-owner refusal, reference-count deletion, revocation, cached opening, VOPRF rotation and proof tampering.
exhibits.outcome: Reports each boundary independently, including replay rejection, last-reference deletion, prospective revocation and old-capsule survival after rotation.
exhibits.limits: The short response still makes both modeled parties read the complete ciphertext and is not a scalable leakage-resilient proof-of-ownership construction.

exhibits.title: Construction, adaptation, and limits
exhibits.action: Inspect the exact local and server-aided formulas, primitive choices, primary sources, adaptations and nonclaims beside the executable results.
exhibits.outcome: Distinguishes the modern P-256 VOPRF and RFC 5297 capsule substitutions from exact DupLESS and keeps the fixed-counter, proof, isolation and revocation assumptions visible.
exhibits.limits: The original DupLESS proof does not automatically transfer to the substituted VOPRF and capsule construction, and no production hardening is claimed.

exhibits.title: HMAC_DRBG State and Reseeding
exhibits.action: Supply or generate entropy, generate bytes, repeat the seed, flip a seed digit, and reseed.
exhibits.outcome: Shows output and K/V state updates, determinism, avalanche, and fresh-entropy change.

exhibits.title: CTR_DRBG and HMAC Comparison
exhibits.action: Generate with AES-based CTR_DRBG, repeat the seed, and compare against HMAC_DRBG.
exhibits.outcome: Shows key/counter state, generated bytes, and browser timing of both mechanisms.
exhibits.limits: Timing reflects this browser and implementation.

exhibits.title: Hash_DRBG Output and State
exhibits.action: Choose a hash and output length, generate bytes, and inspect V and C.
exhibits.outcome: Displays generated bytes and a three-construction comparison.

exhibits.title: Statistical Output Quality
exhibits.action: Run simplified tests on the DRBGs and compare their byte grids to a weak LCG.
exhibits.outcome: Reports statistics and visual differences while showing that passing tests cannot establish unpredictability.
exhibits.limits: Simplified SP 800-22-style checks are not certification or proof of cryptographic security; Dual_EC is simulated.

exhibits.title: Stolen State and Reseed
exhibits.action: Seed two generators, steal their states, attempt past/future recovery, and reseed from fresh entropy.
exhibits.outcome: Counts recovered bytes and contrasts backtracking and prediction resistance with a deliberately defective control.
exhibits.limits: The CTR-no-update construction is deliberately defective; future prediction after compromise needs fresh entropy to recover.

exhibits.title: RBG Construction Classes
exhibits.action: Select RBG1, RBG2, RBG3, or RBGC and toggle modeled source availability and health.
exhibits.outcome: Describes which source request is allowed and what claim about prediction resistance can be made.
exhibits.section: From a DRBG mechanism to an RBG system
exhibits.limits: The class panel generates no bytes and is not NIST validation.

exhibits.title: Entropy Credit Routing
exhibits.action: Choose how source B reaches a Hash_DRBG reseed and toggle modeled validation, health, and freshness.
exhibits.outcome: Shows an entropy-credit ledger and compares actual generated bytes without treating changed output as credited entropy.
exhibits.limits: Source status and credited bits are modelled assumptions, not measurements of entropy.

exhibits.title: Live DRBG Conformance Check
exhibits.action: Run the lab’s known-answer checks.
exhibits.outcome: Displays pass or failure against reference output vectors.
exhibits.limits: Known-answer agreement does not certify a complete RBG system.

exhibits.title: DRBG Seed, Reseed, and Compromise Directions
exhibits.action: Read the seed-to-output flow and contrast backtracking with prediction resistance.
exhibits.outcome: Explains why a state theft threatens future outputs until a fresh-entropy reseed, while one-way state updates protect prior outputs.
exhibits.limits: The panel teaches security definitions; the later state-theft exhibit tests behavior.

exhibits.title: CTR_DRBG Seed-Length Illusion
exhibits.action: Supply a short hex entropy input and generate CTR_DRBG output, then read the supplied-bit count and zero-fill warning.
exhibits.outcome: Separates a full-looking 48-byte AES-256 seed from the much lower entropy actually supplied by a short input.
exhibits.limits: The lab pads for demonstration and labels it under-seeded; SP 800-90A instantiation would reject this input.

exhibits.title: Validated Source Versus Extra Input
exhibits.action: Open the disclosure on source-credit requirements and the cited external-conditioner analysis.
exhibits.outcome: Distinguishes the lab’s model of validated-source access from optional additional input and identifies the broader RBGC proposal as unadopted by this experiment.
exhibits.section: What is required, and what is Hill’s analysis?
exhibits.limits: Credited bits are hypothetical source assumptions; the fixed public inputs prove influence only, and the cited proposal is not treated as a standard.

exhibits.title: Noisy Source
exhibits.action: Sample a modelled device twice and compare bit grids and SHA-256 digests.
exhibits.outcome: Shows read differences, the model-derived min-entropy estimate and how even one changed bit yields a different hash-derived result.
exhibits.limits: No physical device is sampled; cell skew and bit error rate are independently set teaching parameters.

exhibits.title: Enrol & Reproduce
exhibits.action: Enrol a source reading with a random codeword and published XOR helper, then take another reading and step through correction and key derivation.
exhibits.outcome: A BCH decoder attempts to reconstruct the codeword and reading; HKDF-SHA-256 derives the same key when errors fit the correction radius.
exhibits.limits: Reproduction can fail beyond the selected BCH radius; publishing helper bits leaks information about the source.

exhibits.title: Measured Reliability
exhibits.action: Run a sweep of repeated enrol-and-reproduce trials at different bit-error rates.
exhibits.outcome: Compare measured key mismatch frequency with the binomial prediction for the code correction radius.
exhibits.limits: The plotted prediction assumes independent flips under the source model, not measured physical device reliability.

exhibits.title: What the Helper Costs
exhibits.action: Select a cell-bias scenario and run the attacker against the published helper for one enrolment or repeated trials.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect posterior bit estimates and security-budget calculations as source bias raises an attacker’s confidence.
exhibits.limits: The attacker and entropy accounting rely on the stated independent-cell model; results do not certify real PUF secrecy.

exhibits.title: Enrolling Twice
exhibits.action: Create two enrolments of the same source word and inspect the public helper XOR.
exhibits.outcome: The comparison exposes relationships between reused readings and codewords that would be hidden with one enrolment.
exhibits.limits: Reuse conclusions apply to this code-offset construction and source model; repeated enrolment must be evaluated for a concrete scheme.

exhibits.title: Why It Matters
exhibits.action: Follow the guided five-step path or read the deployment context and model disclosure.
exhibits.outcome: The tour connects noisy readings, correction, reliability and helper leakage to device-key use.
exhibits.limits: The guided path repeats the full-lab mechanisms with a modelled source; it is not evidence of a physical device’s entropy.

exhibits.title: Watch two CSS variant registers produce bytes
exhibits.action: Clock eight times or generate a new sample key.
exhibits.outcome: Shows the 17- and 25-cell registers, tapped bits, byte addition and carry.
exhibits.limits: Implements Boneh–Shoup’s teaching variant, not deployed DVD sector scrambling.

exhibits.title: Search small-register states to recover a CSS variant key
exhibits.action: Choose known keystream byte count or supply bytes; enumerate 65,536 small-register guesses.
exhibits.outcome: Shows survivor count and, only for a unique candidate with private continuation, the recovered key and predicted bytes.
exhibits.limits: Three public bytes leave many survivors; manual samples without a private continuation are never labelled recovered.

exhibits.title: Measure survivor counts and search cost
exhibits.action: Count survivors for eight independent keys and inspect subtraction of the first three bytes.
exhibits.outcome: Displays the 24-bit seed deduction and survivor histogram, with measured candidate rate and extrapolated 2^40 work.
exhibits.limits: 2^40 time is extrapolated; the page runs only the 2^16 guess search.

exhibits.title: Run an E91 Bell test
exhibits.action: Choose an ideal, intercept-resend Eve, noisy, misaligned, or lossy channel; choose pair count and seed; run the simulation.
exhibits.outcome: The page samples singlet-pair measurements and displays measured CHSH |S|, a conservative joint 95% interval, expected correlations and candidate sifted-key agreement.
exhibits.limits: A Bell violation under this idealized model is not a QKD key-security proof; the lab omits authenticated discussion, reconciliation, privacy amplification, finite-key security, and realistic device behavior.

exhibits.title: Vary Eve, depolarization, alignment, and loss
exhibits.action: Switch between channel scenarios and adjust their parameter slider, then compare measured Bell correlations, coincidence rates, and candidate-key agreement.
exhibits.outcome: Intercept-resend uses a fixed Eve basis, depolarization randomly replaces a pair, fixed analyzer offset shifts Bob's angle, and independent photon loss reduces coincident rounds.
exhibits.limits: These are specified textbook channel models, not evidence that every eavesdropper is detected. Loss is independent and fair-sampling behavior is assumed.

exhibits.title: Bell Inequality and Protocol Flow
exhibits.action: Read the CHSH inequality, measurement settings, singlet correlation curve, and protocol steps.
exhibits.outcome: The diagrams relate ideal quantum correlations to the classical bound and explain how channel noise changes interpretation.

exhibits.title: E91 versus BB84
exhibits.action: Compare entanglement-based E91 with BB84 prepare-and-measure key distribution.
exhibits.outcome: The section maps preparation, tests, and trust assumptions without claiming the simulated Bell statistics form a security proof.

exhibits.title: Experiments and Deployment Context
exhibits.action: Read Bell-test, satellite, and device-independent QKD examples.
exhibits.outcome: The examples place the idealized simulation beside real experiments and its missing finite-key and detector analysis.

exhibits.title: Physics Sources and Scope
exhibits.action: Inspect primary references, further reading, and the explicit simulation scope.
exhibits.outcome: The source list supports the physics narrative and states that post-processing and a deployable key are not implemented.

exhibits.title: Selective detection and fair sampling
exhibits.section: The Bell test, explained — biased coincidences
exhibits.action: Switch between all emitted rounds and only two-click rounds in an eight-instruction local classical model.
exhibits.outcome: Compare the same preassigned instructions at |S|=2 with a selectively retained 25% of each setting pair that yields apparent |S|=4.
exhibits.limits: Exact constructed classical toy, not a physical detector exploit or a QKD key-security proof; the main E91 loss slider remains setting- and outcome-independent.

exhibits.title: What an elliptic curve is
exhibits.action: Read the Weierstrass equation and inspect the rendered real-curve construction.
exhibits.outcome: The smooth curve, mirrored points, point at infinity, and finite-field bridge are shown.
exhibits.limits: Introductory geometric explanation; the displayed real curve is not a cryptographic group.

exhibits.title: Point addition over the reals
exhibits.action: Drag P and Q, toggle doubling or reflection, or choose the inverse and y=0 example chips.
exhibits.outcome: The chord or tangent and algebraic sum update, including P + (-P) = O and 2P = O edge cases.
exhibits.limits: Floating-point geometry over the reals illustrates the group law; cryptographic arithmetic is over finite fields.

exhibits.title: Point addition over a finite field
exhibits.action: Switch to the finite-field tab and select P and Q on a small lattice or choose secp256k1 preset points.
exhibits.outcome: Exact modular point sums and special cases appear; secp256k1 gives a numeric readout instead of an impossible lattice plot.
exhibits.limits: Small lattices are teaching curves; secp256k1 coordinates are computed numerically, not plotted.

exhibits.title: Scalar multiplication: k · P
exhibits.action: Choose a curve, k, and repeated-addition or double-and-add method; step or play the trace.
exhibits.outcome: The point accumulator, binary-bit trace, and operation counts expose the O(k) versus O(log k) gap and order edge cases.
exhibits.limits: Naive addition is capped at k=2000 to keep the browser responsive.

exhibits.title: Why you cannot go backwards (ECDLP)
exhibits.action: Choose a new hidden scalar and step or play successive multiples of G on the F97 teaching curve.
exhibits.outcome: The walk locates Q=kG after k steps and compares the toy group with the approximate generic attack cost for secp256k1.
exhibits.limits: The interactive walk is a 99-element toy subgroup, not an actual solver for a cryptographic curve; generic square-root cost is explanatory.

exhibits.title: ECDSA Key Generation, Signing, Verification
exhibits.action: Generate a P-256 or secp256k1 keypair, sign a message with random or RFC 6979 nonce, and verify.
exhibits.outcome: The signature’s r and s values and verification result connect the private scalar to the public point.

exhibits.title: Curve Geometry and Finite-Field Arithmetic
exhibits.action: Inspect visual real-coordinate point addition and try finite-field curve arithmetic.
exhibits.outcome: The visual and toy finite-field views clarify scalar multiplication without claiming the real-coordinate picture is the production curve.
exhibits.limits: The real-coordinate drawing is explanatory and distinct from finite-field ECDSA.

exhibits.title: ECDSA Nonce-Reuse Key Recovery
exhibits.action: Try the two-signature equations on a toy curve and run full compromise on 256-bit keys.
exhibits.outcome: Repeated r permits recovery of nonce k and private key d, followed by a forged signature that verifies.
exhibits.limits: The full-compromise run deliberately injects reuse; it is not an attack on correctly generated nonces.

exhibits.title: Deterministic Nonce Defense
exhibits.action: Sign repeated inputs with random and RFC 6979 nonces, then try the reuse attack against deterministic signing.
exhibits.outcome: Nonce samples and attack control show why RFC 6979 derives k from private key and message rather than relying on fresh randomness.

exhibits.title: ECDSA Use Cases and Ed25519 Comparison
exhibits.action: Read examples across TLS, cryptocurrencies, SSH, JWT, WebAuthn, and the ECDSA versus Ed25519 table.
exhibits.outcome: The explanatory material places signatures in deployed protocols and distinguishes the two designs.

exhibits.title: Sign and tamper with a note
exhibits.section: Start here: sign a note, then change it
exhibits.action: Generate a keypair, sign a note, verify it and change one character before checking again.
exhibits.outcome: The original note verifies and a modified note fails against the same signature.
exhibits.limits: Keys are generated in the browser for teaching and are not stored as production credentials.

exhibits.title: Key derivation and scalar walk
exhibits.action: Generate a 32-byte seed and walk the initial scalar double/add operations toward its public point.
exhibits.outcome: Shows a compressed public key, exact prefix group steps and a separate summary jump to the exact endpoint.
exhibits.limits: The animation skips remaining operations and plots approximate coordinates; it does not show a full literal path.

exhibits.title: Deterministic Ed25519 signatures
exhibits.action: Sign a message and sign the same message again.
exhibits.outcome: Compares signature bytes; identical key and message produce identical Ed25519 signatures.
exhibits.limits: A changed message or key changes the deterministic input; this does not make repeated signing unsafe by itself.

exhibits.title: Verification and tamper presets
exhibits.action: Enter public key, message and signature; verify, tamper or load a wrong-key or modified-message preset.
exhibits.outcome: Displays accepted or rejected verification against the entered bytes.
exhibits.limits: Acceptance depends on verification rule and correctly trusted public-key identity.

exhibits.title: ECDSA nonce reuse recovery
exhibits.action: Reuse an ECDSA nonce to recover a private key, run fresh-nonce control and compare repeat Ed25519 signatures.
exhibits.outcome: Shows a private-key recovery from two ECDSA signatures with a repeated nonce and why deterministic Ed25519 differs.
exhibits.limits: A controlled ECDSA example; the fresh-nonce control does not prove all real implementations safe.

exhibits.title: Small-order public-key edge case
exhibits.action: Forge against a small-order key and compare cofactored ZIP215 and strict RFC verification of identical bytes.
exhibits.outcome: One rule accepts while strict verification rejects, demonstrating rule-dependent signature meaning.
exhibits.limits: The constructed small-order key is an edge-case counterexample; the result depends on the exact verifier rule.

exhibits.title: ElGamal encryption
exhibits.action: Generate a keypair in a toy or RFC 3526 group, encrypt an integer or text repeatedly and decrypt.
exhibits.outcome: Compare randomized ciphertexts of the same message and recovered plaintext.
exhibits.limits: The p=2039 teaching group is insecure; the larger group option is distinct.

exhibits.title: Guided ElGamal arithmetic walkthrough
exhibits.action: Step forward or backward through ten stages of a fresh toy encryption and decryption run.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect computed private and public keys, ephemeral mask, both ciphertext components and recovered message.
exhibits.limits: Uses the intentionally small toy group.

exhibits.title: Multiplicative homomorphism
exhibits.action: Encrypt two toy-group integers, multiply their ciphertext components and decrypt.
exhibits.outcome: Observe that the decrypted product corresponds to the product of plaintexts.
exhibits.limits: This algebraic property does not provide integrity.

exhibits.title: Ciphertext re-randomization and mix net
exhibits.action: Re-randomize a ciphertext or simulate shuffling three encrypted toy messages.
exhibits.outcome: See changed ciphertext with preserved plaintext, plus shuffled output order.
exhibits.limits: The three-message mix net is a local simulation, not an end-to-end anonymity system.

exhibits.title: Toy discrete-log key cracking
exhibits.action: Crack a fresh toy private key.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect recovered private exponent by solving the small group’s discrete logarithm.
exhibits.limits: The attack only demonstrates the deliberately tiny group.

exhibits.title: Ephemeral reuse and malleability
exhibits.action: Reuse an ephemeral k across messages, then multiply a ciphertext to tamper without the key.
exhibits.outcome: Recover the second plaintext from a known first message and see unauthenticated decryption silently change.

exhibits.title: Cramer–Shoup authenticated encryption
exhibits.action: Run round trip, probe a decryptor with invalid queries, try tampering and search a toy hash collision.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect the ciphertext validity check and rejection behavior alongside toy limits of the hash challenge.
exhibits.limits: The toy group and toy collision search demonstrate failure modes; they are not production security parameters.
exhibits.section: Defense: Cramer–Shoup — A Check the Attacker Cannot Learn From

exhibits.title: ElGamal signatures and nonce reuse
exhibits.action: Sign and verify, then reuse a signature nonce across two messages.
exhibits.outcome: Recover the nonce and signing key in the reuse experiment.

exhibits.title: Toy discrete-log scatter plot
exhibits.action: Drag or randomize the exponent slider in the small group.
exhibits.outcome: Watch computed y = g^x mod p points and the selected point on the plot.
exhibits.limits: The tiny group is exhaustively plotted and insecure; visual irregularity is not a proof of hardness.

exhibits.title: Quadratic-character leakage experiment
exhibits.action: Choose a group and one of three message-encoding settings, then run repeated public-value IND-CPA guesses.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect Legendre symbols, decryption checks, transcripts and win tallies as raw message character leaks in two modes.
exhibits.limits: Equal symbols only defeat this particular distinguisher; small toy parameters remain insecure, and this is not an attack on prime-order elliptic-curve ElGamal.

exhibits.title: Authenticated ElGamal tamper rejection
exhibits.action: Enter a message and attacker factor, encrypt with a shared-secret-derived MAC, then multiply ciphertext c2.
exhibits.outcome: Honest ciphertext decrypts and changed ciphertext fails the MAC check.
exhibits.limits: Uses small teaching parameters; authentication sacrifices unmodified homomorphism and re-randomization.

exhibits.title: ElGamal versus RSA table
exhibits.action: Inspect the six-property comparison of assumptions, ciphertext shapes, randomness and use.
exhibits.outcome: Contrast the primitives’ structural differences and shared lack of post-quantum security.

exhibits.title: ElGamal-derived applications
exhibits.action: Inspect the named signature, threshold, voting and elliptic-curve variants.
exhibits.outcome: Connect ElGamal algebra to the listed modern applications without running those separate protocols.
exhibits.limits: These variants are listed as context and are not implemented by this panel.

exhibits.title: Double Ratchet Wire View
exhibits.action: Step a scripted conversation or send a custom message and inspect the captured packet and key progression.
exhibits.outcome: Shows plaintext at endpoints, ciphertext/header/tag on the wire, and fresh chain-key fingerprints.
exhibits.section: A real Double Ratchet, and what the network sees

exhibits.title: Eavesdropping and Packet Tamper
exhibits.action: Try to read a captured packet without keys or flip its ciphertext and deliver it.
exhibits.outcome: Shows opaque content and authentication rejection of modified packets without advancing the ratchet.
exhibits.section: Break it yourself — try to read or forge the wire

exhibits.title: Endpoint Implant Pivot
exhibits.action: Deploy or remove a modelled implant and send messages.
exhibits.outcome: Shows plaintext captured before encryption or after decryption while ciphertext remains sound.
exhibits.section: The pivot: compromise the endpoint, not the cipher
exhibits.limits: The implant is a local model; it does not compromise a real device.

exhibits.title: Encryption and Endpoint Verdicts
exhibits.action: Compare the encryption, endpoint-integrity, and system signals as packet and implant experiments run.
exhibits.outcome: Keeps a mathematically sound cipher distinct from an unsafe endpoint outcome.

exhibits.title: Independent Update Authorities and Endpoint Reach
exhibits.action: Select independent or shared administration, compromise signing and routing roles, and run encrypted probes.
exhibits.outcome: Shows whether attacker updates install, identity binding changes, and plaintext becomes available across users under each modeled policy.
exhibits.section: When does one compromise reach every device?
exhibits.limits: The authorization policy is illustrative, not a reconstruction of Encrochat updates; signatures and ciphertext probes execute, but installation permissions are modeled.

exhibits.title: 1 · The Machine
exhibits.action: Set rotor order, ring settings, start positions, reflector and plugboard, then encrypt or decrypt text.
exhibits.outcome: Watch rotors step and output letters; identical settings reverse the transformation.
exhibits.limits: Models Wehrmacht three-rotor Enigma I with rotors I–V and UKW-B/C, not naval M4 or Lorenz.

exhibits.title: Signal Path
exhibits.action: Step a letter through plugboard, forward rotors, reflector and reverse path, and trigger a double-step demo.
exhibits.outcome: The visualizer traces contacts and rotor windows before and after stepping.
exhibits.limits: Visualization follows the implemented Enigma I model rather than a physical electromechanical machine.

exhibits.title: 2 · The Flaw
exhibits.action: Examine the no-self-encryption invariant and try crib placements against ciphertext.
exhibits.outcome: Positions where a crib letter would match its own ciphertext letter are rejected before search.
exhibits.limits: This filter eliminates impossible placements but does not alone reveal the key.

exhibits.title: 3 · The Break
exhibits.action: Choose a surviving crib offset, inspect its constraint menu and run or cancel the simulated Bombe over rotor positions and optional orders or rings.
exhibits.outcome: The logical search prunes contradictions, reports candidate stops and allows loading a stop into the machine.
exhibits.limits: A teaching-scale logical search, not cycle-accurate Bombe hardware; stops verify the crib but undetermined plugboard pairs can leave other plaintext wrong.

exhibits.title: Why it looked unbreakable — and why it broke
exhibits.section: Why it looked unbreakable — and why it broke
exhibits.action: Compare keyspace and exploitable structure, then inspect live engine vectors, invariants and model limits.
exhibits.outcome: The appendix computes examples from the same machine and contrasts apparent combinatorial strength with predictable cribs and structural constraints.
exhibits.limits: Historical comparison is explanatory; the live vectors test the implemented machine, not every Enigma variant.

exhibits.title: Clone a DRBG state and predict the next outputs
exhibits.action: Snapshot and restore two simulated machines, step outputs, then give one server fresh entropy.
exhibits.outcome: Cloned HMAC_DRBG state produces matching future outputs until a true entropy divergence.
exhibits.limits: Machines and snapshots are modeled, while DRBG outputs are computed in browser.
exhibits.section: Clone the machine, clone every secret

exhibits.title: Simulate a child inheriting its parent’s DRBG state
exhibits.action: Fork the modeled process and step the parent and child streams.
exhibits.outcome: Shows matching next nonce and secret key from copied state.
exhibits.limits: Process forking itself is simulated, not an operating-system fork.
exhibits.section: A child inherits the parent’s next secret

exhibits.title: Enumerate low-entropy DRBG seeds
exhibits.action: Adjust effective seed entropy and run recovery within the enumerable range.
exhibits.outcome: Tests candidate seeds against observed output and recovers future generator output when the tiny search completes.
exhibits.limits: High entropy settings are not exhaustively searched; source entropy is modeled.
exhibits.section: Starve the seed, enumerate the key

exhibits.title: Compare a true reseed with a silent no-op
exhibits.action: Run proper and silent no-op reseed scenarios.
exhibits.outcome: Displays cryptographic output and security verdicts that distinguish changed counter from changed unpredictable state.
exhibits.limits: Reseed source health is modeled; a counter increment alone is not new entropy.
exhibits.section: A healthy counter over a stale seed

exhibits.title: Inspect two entropy failures
exhibits.action: Read the historical cases and relate them to the simulated collapse paths.
exhibits.outcome: Shows the operational source-failure context of repeated or predictable random output.
exhibits.limits: Historical explanation is contextual; the browser simulations do not reproduce those systems.
exhibits.section: Two real collapses, no attacker in either

exhibits.title: Envelope Operations
exhibits.action: Create a KEK, enter plaintext and context, seal and open an envelope, change tenant context, rotate the KEK and re-wrap.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect the envelope and operation timeline; changing the authenticated context makes AES-GCM opening fail, while key version rotation and re-wrap are visible.
exhibits.limits: The payload context is GCM AAD; RFC 3394 wrapping does not accept separate AAD. In-browser key storage is not a hosted KMS or HSM.

exhibits.title: Who may use this key?
exhibits.action: Run the same wrapped DEK through a log-only decrypt API and an opt-in caller/key/operation grant.
exhibits.outcome: Compare unauthorized Mallory receiving a DEK from an unguarded API, denial by a grant check, and allowed Alice unwrapping the same DEK.
exhibits.limits: Alice and Mallory are caller-supplied labels; no login, verified IAM principal, HSM, or real non-extractable key boundary.

exhibits.title: Key-Handle Roles and Wrap-Then-Decrypt Disclosure
exhibits.action: Choose fixed roles or intentionally unsafe mutable usages and a sensitive wrappable or nonextractable target, then run the wrap-then-decrypt trace or wrap and unwrap to a handle.
exhibits.outcome: For a wrappable target, the unsafe policy returns 32 key bytes that independently open an AES-GCM challenge. Fixed roles refuse byte-returning decrypt while protected unwrap still opens the challenge; a nonextractable target refuses wrapping under either policy.
exhibits.limits: The token policy is a browser model using real RFC 3394 AES-KW and WebCrypto AES-GCM, not a hardware token or full PKCS #11 emulator. This section executes one API trace; the separate bounded explorer covers declared additional presets but not unmodeled calls. The wrapping key is generated internally and is nonextractable. Copy, derive, authenticated callers and cross-session security are outside scope. Protected unwrap cannot revoke existing key copies.

exhibits.title: Bounded Key-Handle State Search
exhibits.action: Choose the mutable-role, known-key-import or same-value-handle preset, fixed or intentionally unsafe policy, and state cap, then explore the bounded state space.
exhibits.outcome: Compare bounded no-witness, explicit incomplete-cutoff and shortest-disclosure results. Found witnesses are revalidated from terminal symbolic state, replayed with real RFC 3394 and independently checked with a fresh AES-GCM challenge; the same-value case retains two distinct equal-byte handles with complementary roles.
concepts: distinct handles with equal key values
exhibits.limits: The result covers exactly the displayed three presets, four successful calls, at most four handles and blobs, three templates and the selected operational cap. A cap hit is incomplete, while fixed-policy exhaustion means only no witness within these bounds. This is not a PKCS #11 implementation, HSM assessment, vendor vulnerability claim, exhaustive search or security proof.
exhibits.section: Can another call sequence expose it?

exhibits.title: Steal one KEK: what still opens?
exhibits.action: Choose isolated tenant KEKs or one shared KEK, then run the compromise experiment.
exhibits.outcome: Read actual successful decrypt counts for archived copies, current wraps, retained DEKs, future data and owner access across maintenance stages.
exhibits.limits: Attacker holds stolen raw KEK material and archived envelopes, with no further KMS API access; results do not imply re-wrapping erases archived plaintext.
exhibits.section: Steal one KEK: what still opens?

exhibits.title: Root, KEK, and Wrapped DEK Hierarchy
exhibits.action: Create keys and envelopes, then inspect the evolving hierarchy diagram.
exhibits.outcome: The diagram links root boundary, versioned KEKs, and wrapped DEKs to show which key protects which envelope.
exhibits.limits: The root/HSM boundary is modeled in browser, not an actual hardware security module.

exhibits.title: KMS Request Flow
exhibits.action: Switch GenerateDataKey, Encrypt, Decrypt, and ReEncrypt request paths.
exhibits.outcome: A step list identifies client, KMS, and storage exchanges and approximate wire bytes for each operation.
exhibits.limits: The request/response paths and byte estimates are modeled rather than live network KMS calls.

exhibits.title: KEK Rotation and Rewrap Drill
exhibits.action: Rotate a KEK and rewrap envelopes, then inspect the ordered timeline.
exhibits.outcome: Version changes and rewrapping distinguish replacing a KEK wrapper from re-encrypting payload data.
exhibits.limits: The KMS is an in-browser model; persistent cloud key custody is absent.

exhibits.title: Hash-Linked KMS Audit Log
exhibits.action: Inspect operation entries, tamper entry #1, and inspect the resulting hash-chain verification.
exhibits.outcome: The viewer identifies a changed content hash or broken predecessor link in the modeled log.
exhibits.limits: A local hash chain is not an independently protected external audit service.

exhibits.title: Security Properties Under Weakened Conditions
exhibits.action: Run all security experiments in defended or weakened mode and inspect each result.
exhibits.outcome: Compare defended and weakened results for context binding, ciphertext authentication, tenant key isolation, wrapped-key integrity and rotation preserving access.
exhibits.section: Security Properties — Try to Break It
exhibits.limits: The browser model does not reproduce IAM, HSM, operational logging, or cloud service failure modes.

exhibits.title: Key-Evolving Audit Log After Compromise
exhibits.action: Build paired static-key and key-evolving HMAC-SHA-256 logs at a selected compromise boundary, then attempt a pre-compromise rewrite, forge from the exposed period, delete the suffix, and vary trusted CLOSE and heartbeat inputs.
exhibits.outcome: The static key authenticates an earlier rewrite while the evolving track rejects it under the stated one-way-evolution and erasure assumptions; both tracks authenticate a replacement suffix from the compromised period. The retained checkpoint anchors only its prefix, while completeness and freshness change only with their separate external evidence.
exhibits.limits: This is a bounded, single-logger/private-verifier teaching adaptation, not the full Schneier–Kelsey protocol, Bellare–Yee's exact proven construction, a standardized wire format, or a security proof. Symmetric verifier state can forge; JavaScript cannot guarantee erasure; messages remain plaintext; the checkpoint does not establish completeness, freshness, availability, global consistency, or split-view resistance, and external CLOSE or heartbeat inputs establish only their stated bounds.

exhibits.title: TEA1 Keystream Generator
exhibits.action: Supply an 80-bit key, frame number, and 4–32 output bytes, then generate TEA1 output.
exhibits.outcome: The byte stream and known-answer verdict compare the TypeScript core to a published reference fixture.
exhibits.limits: It isolates a cipher and frame value, not a complete radio protocol.

exhibits.title: 80-Bit Input to 32-Bit Working Register
exhibits.action: Step through or run all ten key-byte loading rounds.
exhibits.outcome: A bit grid, register readout, and round trace expose the reduction that bounds effective state at 32 bits.

exhibits.title: Known-Plaintext Register Search
exhibits.action: Provide known plaintext and start or cancel a real register-candidate search.
exhibits.outcome: A worker tests a 2^16 candidate window and verifies a recovered register against the TEA1 stream.
exhibits.limits: The browser searches only the 2^16 window containing the local fixture, not the entire 2^32 space; this is not a live interception tool.

exhibits.title: Local Search-Rate Wall
exhibits.action: Measure local candidate throughput and inspect projected search time.
exhibits.outcome: Observed rate is used to scale from the sampled window to a larger key-space wall.
exhibits.limits: One browser/device rate is not a real adversary forecast.

exhibits.title: Paper Attacks Versus Practical Break
exhibits.action: Inspect published attack data and contrast a weakness that reduces the key-space search with small reductions in AES work.
exhibits.outcome: The chart and explanation distinguish attack complexity claims from a demonstrated browser run.
exhibits.limits: The complexity figures are cited research context, not live attacks on full AES.

exhibits.title: Compliance, Intentional Weakness, and Deployment
exhibits.action: Read the historical framing and radio-to-end-to-end boundary.
exhibits.outcome: The context separates export rules, engineering choices, radio-link confidentiality, and application-layer protection.

exhibits.title: Seven factoring methods
exhibits.action: Choose a bounded N and run trial division, Fermat, Pollard rho, p−1, p+1, ECM and quadratic sieve sequentially or individually.
exhibits.outcome: A board reports factors, verified or bounded failures, method traces and measured work for one N.
exhibits.limits: Real browser BigInt at teaching sizes and runtime caps; giving up under a cap is not evidence N is unfactorable.

exhibits.title: Recursive splitting
exhibits.action: Factor an N with more than two factors recursively.
exhibits.outcome: Displays a factor tree with methods used at successive splits.
exhibits.limits: Bounded methods may stop before full factorization.

exhibits.title: Forge a weak RSA modulus
exhibits.action: Select weakness and a 48–72-bit size, generate N, run exploiting and negative-control methods, then send it to the factoring board.
exhibits.outcome: Shows which method succeeds for a deliberately weak modulus and corresponding key-generation rule.
exhibits.limits: Tiny generated moduli are intentionally insecure; a bounded negative run is only a result under its selected cap.

exhibits.title: Algorithm step trace
exhibits.action: Choose a completed factoring run and step or reveal its trace.
exhibits.outcome: Shows rho gcds, Fermat walks, ECM denominators or sieve relation/dependency details as applicable.
exhibits.limits: Only completed runs produce a trace; the display is tied to the bounded local run.

exhibits.title: Method-specific work curves
exhibits.action: Inspect each method plotted against the property it depends on, with measured points from local runs.
exhibits.outcome: Separates cost models from measurements and compares only suitable N-based curves on a common axis.
exhibits.limits: Dashed complexity models are projections, not browser execution at cryptographic sizes.

exhibits.title: RSA generation rules and Shor
exhibits.action: Compare classical weakness-specific rules with Shor period finding.
exhibits.outcome: Shows why key-generation constraints resist certain classical methods but do not remove quantum order finding.
exhibits.limits: The lab does not run Shor or model quantum hardware.

exhibits.title: Batch GCD across a key corpus
exhibits.action: Generate seeded keys under an entropy slider, run batch and naive GCD, audit a key and inspect product/remainder trees.
exhibits.outcome: Reports shared factors and independently verifies recovered p×q=N, with collision predictions and measured timings.
exhibits.limits: The corpus is generated locally and seeded for experiments; predictions assume independent draws and do not prove a particular key secure.

exhibits.title: Illustrative signing and public-key-only forgery
exhibits.action: Generate an illustrative keypair, sign and verify a message, run the tamper test, then try the short-vector forgery with only the public key.
exhibits.outcome: Displays a generated signature and norm check; message tampering is rejected, while the short-vector forgery may pass this panel's illustrative verifier because the signer never uses the private trapdoor.
exhibits.limits: This panel's signing flow is intentionally forgeable and is not Falcon or an unforgeability demonstration; it never reads the private trapdoor. The real Falcon WASM run is a separate panel.

exhibits.title: Simulated sampler timing and correlation attack
exhibits.section: Panel 5 — Side-Channels, Use Cases, and Warnings
exhibits.action: Toggle leaky versus constant-time simulated sampler, run 512 samples, then run the attack over 200 simulated signatures.
exhibits.outcome: Plots modeled timing strata and a round-by-round correlation and distribution estimate; the chosen timing formula creates a leak in leaky mode and flattens it in constant-time mode.
exhibits.limits: No browser clock or physical leakage is measured. The leaky/flat timing formulas predetermine this model's outcome; it does not reproduce the cited hardware power attacks or certify an implementation's side-channel resistance.

exhibits.title: Run Falcon-1024 reference WebAssembly
exhibits.action: Enter a message and click Run real Falcon-1024 on your message.
exhibits.outcome: Loads the falcon-crypto WASM module, generates a keypair, signs and verifies the message, rejects a tampered message, and reports the measured key/signature byte lengths and operation times.
exhibits.limits: Uses the packaged Falcon-1024 reference WASM path only, with its padded signature wrapper; timings vary by device and loading may fail offline or without WebAssembly. It is separate from the page's illustrative signer and toy trapdoor.

exhibits.title: NTRU trapdoor signing versus incomplete-key attempts
exhibits.section: Panel 7 — Real NTRU trapdoor at toy scale (n = 8, Babai round-off)
exhibits.action: Generate an n=8 trapdoor key, sign with its full basis, then try an incomplete basis, a public-key-only forgery and a damaged coefficient of F.
exhibits.outcome: Checks the exact NTRU equation, verifies the full-basis signature against the public key and norm bound, and displays how missing or damaged trapdoor information affects signing attempts.
exhibits.limits: The n=8 lattice offers no security; Babai round-off is an NTRUSign-style teaching mechanism with known leakage, not Falcon's Gaussian sampler or production signer.

exhibits.title: NTRU Lattice and Basis Trapdoor
exhibits.action: Place a lattice target and compare closest-vector decoding with short private and long public bases.
exhibits.outcome: The small geometric model shows the basis asymmetry used to motivate trapdoor signing.
exhibits.limits: This small visual analogy is not the n=512/1024 Fast Fourier Sampler.

exhibits.title: Illustrative NTRU Public-Key Generation
exhibits.action: Choose a parameter set and generate short f,g and a public h through negacyclic ring inversion.
exhibits.outcome: The code computes a genuine NTRU-form public key while exposing the missing full trapdoor completion required for signing.
exhibits.limits: The (F,G) completion and real Falcon sampling are absent here; the illustrative Panel 3 signer never reads the private key.

exhibits.title: Falcon, ML-DSA, and SLH-DSA Comparison
exhibits.action: Compare size bars and published category 1/2 and category 5 rows while editing the message length.
exhibits.outcome: The table separates signature size, algorithmic assumptions, and implementation complexity across the three schemes.
exhibits.section: Panel 4 — Falcon vs ML-DSA vs SLH-DSA
exhibits.limits: Published values and indicative timing are not same-hardware measurements; the smallest ML-DSA set targets category 2.

exhibits.title: Falcon References and Fidelity Warnings
exhibits.action: Inspect references and the explicit boundary between illustrative signing, toy n=8 trapdoor signing, and real WebAssembly Falcon.
exhibits.outcome: The source notes prevent a norm-only illustrative verifier from being mistaken for unforgeable Falcon.

exhibits.title: One Feistel round
exhibits.action: Choose a block, key and round function, step through DES round values and undo a round.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect halves, subkey, F output and XOR; decryption reverses a round without inverting F.

exhibits.title: DES round trip and weak keys
exhibits.action: Encrypt and decrypt a block under a key, then choose a weak or semi-weak DES key.
exhibits.outcome: Compare recovered plaintext and unusual weak-key behavior.

exhibits.title: DES complementation
exhibits.action: Compute encryption of a key/plaintext and their bitwise complements, then race toy searches.
exhibits.outcome: Check the complementation identity and its work-factor implication.

exhibits.title: Double DES meet in the middle
exhibits.action: Run a bounded key search on two known pairs with fresh hidden victim keys.
exhibits.outcome: Recover candidate key pairs by joining forward encryption and backward decryption results.
exhibits.limits: The runnable keyspace is scaled down; full DES cost is projected.

exhibits.title: Birthday collision and CBC cookie recovery
exhibits.action: Measure truncated DES collisions and run a simulated CBC stream cookie-recovery experiment.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect collision counts and how a colliding attacker-controlled block can expose a secret block.
exhibits.limits: The collision measurement uses truncated outputs and the cookie scenario is a local model.

exhibits.title: Feistel round-count experiment
exhibits.action: Select random or DES round functions, number of rounds and trials, then run a distinguishing matrix.
exhibits.outcome: Compare empirical distinguisher rates and a four-round shared-function fixture.
exhibits.limits: Finite toy experiments illustrate distinguishers rather than proving PRP security.

exhibits.title: Archived NIST DES vector runner
exhibits.action: Run all known-answer vector families again and inspect per-row encrypt and decrypt checks.
exhibits.outcome: Compare local DES ECB/CBC results with archived published ciphertext and plaintext answers in both directions.
exhibits.limits: The source standards are withdrawn; matching historical vectors checks implementation agreement, not present-day DES security.

exhibits.title: BFV Encrypt, Add, Decrypt
exhibits.action: Choose two small integers, encrypt each, add ciphertexts, and decrypt the result; repeat encryption of one value.
exhibits.outcome: Shows homomorphic addition, ciphertext randomization, and the measured noise budget.
exhibits.section: Exhibit 2 · Encrypt, Add, Decrypt — and See the Noise
exhibits.limits: Insecure toy BFV uses small parameters and Math.random; it illustrates algebra, not secure deployment.

exhibits.title: Noise Budget Exhaustion
exhibits.action: Add, multiply, auto-multiply until failure, refresh, and attempt decryption.
exhibits.outcome: Plots noise magnitude and remaining bits, showing how correctness ceases to be guaranteed at overflow.
exhibits.section: Exhibit 3 · The Noise Budget: Add Is Cheap, Multiply Is Not
exhibits.limits: The refresh uses the secret key; real bootstrapping is different and cannot repair destroyed data.

exhibits.title: Ciphertext Multiply and Relinearize
exhibits.action: Encrypt two values, multiply without relinearization, relinearize, and decrypt.
exhibits.outcome: Shows ciphertext component growth and return to a shorter form with the result.
exhibits.section: Exhibit 4 · Multiply, Relinearize, and Pack (Batched Add)
exhibits.limits: Toy parameters provide no practical security.

exhibits.title: Packed Homomorphic Addition
exhibits.action: Enter two short vectors, encrypt, add, and decrypt them.
exhibits.outcome: Shows multiple coefficient values combined by one ciphertext addition.
exhibits.section: Coefficient packing: one add, many values
exhibits.limits: This coefficient encoding is not production SIMD batching; packed multiplication mixes slots.

exhibits.title: Scheme and Parameter Explorer
exhibits.action: Compare BGV, BFV, and TFHE; change the nominal ring-size slider and time toy BFV addition.
exhibits.outcome: Displays conceptual tradeoffs and rough depth estimates alongside local toy timing.
exhibits.section: Exhibit 5 · BGV vs BFV vs TFHE — Choosing a Scheme
exhibits.limits: The parameter slider uses rough estimates and the benchmark is toy BFV, not production performance.

exhibits.title: Encrypted Vote Tally
exhibits.action: Choose ballots, encrypt each vote, add ciphertexts, then decrypt only the total.
exhibits.outcome: Displays a homomorphic sum without exposing individual votes to the modeled server.
exhibits.section: Try it live: an encrypted vote tally
exhibits.limits: Toy BFV is not a deployable private voting protocol.

exhibits.title: Locked-Box Computing and Scheme Families
exhibits.action: Follow the client/server ciphertext flow and compare BGV, BFV, TFHE, and CKKS.
exhibits.outcome: Explains encrypted addition and multiplication, BFV scaling versus BGV modulus switching, and integer, bit, and approximate workloads.
exhibits.section: Exhibit 1 · The Idea: Compute on Locked Boxes
exhibits.limits: The live arithmetic is toy BFV; other families are compared in prose and tables.

exhibits.title: FHE Application Boundaries
exhibits.action: Read examples of private queries, genomics, inference, and aggregate tallying.
exhibits.outcome: Connects homomorphic evaluation to use cases and flags that decrypted-result exposure and failure feedback need separate analysis.
exhibits.limits: Application examples are explanatory; the separate ballot demo is the live computation.

exhibits.title: Watch the missing term appear
exhibits.action: Advance from two satisfying instances through a naive fold, cross-term commitment and corrected relaxed fold.
exhibits.outcome: The residual shows r·T for the naive combination and zero after E′ absorbs the cross term.
exhibits.limits: Uses a small demonstration circuit over the ristretto255 scalar field; no recursive circuit or complete proof system is built.

exhibits.title: The large values stay out of this lane
exhibits.section: The large values stay out of this lane
exhibits.action: Inspect the public inputs and opaque commitments accepted by the per-fold verifier.
exhibits.outcome: The panel counts group operations while private W and E stay out of that verifier lane.
exhibits.limits: This public verifier is not embedded in a recursive augmented step circuit.

exhibits.title: Change the history, not the verifier’s per-fold work
exhibits.section: Change the history, not the verifier’s per-fold work
exhibits.action: Choose 2 to 64 steps of y = x³ + 3, run the fold and open final W′ and E′.
exhibits.outcome: The transcript and per-fold work display update, while the final opening checks one step-wide instance.
exhibits.limits: UI caps history at 64 steps; one final opening is not a succinct SNARK or zero-knowledge proof.

exhibits.title: Three attacks, one ordering mistake that wins
exhibits.section: Three attacks, one ordering mistake that wins
exhibits.action: Tamper a folded witness or Com(T), then reveal r before committing T in the broken mode.
exhibits.outcome: The first two are caught; early challenge exposure permits a backward-selected correction accepted by the altered protocol.
exhibits.limits: The successful attack changes the protocol ordering; it is not a forgery against the correctly ordered transcript.

exhibits.title: Nothing hidden behind the diagram
exhibits.action: Open R1CS matrices, transcript and commitment details, edge-case notes and the scope disclosure.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect concrete witness layout, hash-to-group and challenge inputs, and boundaries of recursion and zero knowledge.
exhibits.limits: Commitments here are unblinded; no curve cycle, recursive verifier, compressing SNARK or zero-knowledge proof is implemented.

exhibits.title: Encrypt and decrypt a numeric string with FF1
exhibits.action: Enter digits and run the FF1 starter encryption.
exhibits.outcome: Ciphertext preserves the selected numeric format and decrypts back.
exhibits.limits: FF1 preserves shape, not confidentiality of format or equality patterns.
exhibits.section: Start here — the whole idea in one encrypt

exhibits.title: Tokenize a card number with FF1
exhibits.action: Enter card digits, generate or set AES key and tweak, encrypt and decrypt.
exhibits.outcome: Displays format-preserving ciphertext with the expected digit structure.
exhibits.limits: A format-preserving ciphertext is not a payment tokenization service or a complete card-data compliance control.

exhibits.title: Compare FF1 and FF3-1 over a chosen format
exhibits.action: Generate a key and run both algorithms over the sample.
exhibits.outcome: Side-by-side outputs and domain information expose their differences.
exhibits.limits: The UI warns FF3-1 is being withdrawn; comparison does not recommend new FF3-1 deployment.

exhibits.title: Trace FF1 Feistel rounds
exhibits.action: Trace rounds and step or play through the swap and round-function calculation.
exhibits.outcome: Shows per-round halves, AES round function inputs and outputs, and modular-radix addition.
exhibits.limits: Detailed trace is for teaching and should not be used as a secure handling environment for real secrets.

exhibits.title: Compare equality leak, tweak change and domain size
exhibits.action: Run repeated-value encryptions and a flipped-tweak comparison, then use the domain calculator.
exhibits.outcome: Displays deterministic equality for a fixed key/tweak, changed outputs with a tweak bit, and small-domain warnings.
exhibits.limits: Tweak changes do not erase small-domain or other structural leakage.
exhibits.section: Failure Lab — Why FPE Still Leaks

exhibits.title: Recover a small-domain FF3-1 plaintext by enumeration
exhibits.action: Choose a short decimal length and run the codebook attack.
exhibits.outcome: Enumerates domain values and reports recovered plaintext and query count without knowing the key.
exhibits.limits: The executable attack enumerates tiny domains; larger attack estimates in the page are not run.
exhibits.section: Live: break FF3-1 by codebook recovery

exhibits.title: Preserve SSN and phone punctuation while encrypting digits
exhibits.action: Choose SSN, phone or ZIP, enter a value and run FF1 encryption and decryption.
exhibits.outcome: SSN and phone digits change while separators and mask remain; five-digit ZIP is refused under the enforced domain floor.
exhibits.limits: ZIP refusal is the teaching outcome; format retention gives no integrity or full semantic validity.

exhibits.title: Encrypt over a user-defined alphabet with FF1
exhibits.action: Set an alphabet, plaintext, AES-256 key and tweak, then encrypt and decrypt.
exhibits.outcome: Ciphertext stays within the supplied alphabet and length, while round-trip recovers the original string.
exhibits.limits: Requires distinct alphabet symbols and supported domain parameters; no authentication.

exhibits.title: Trace FF3 to FF3-1 withdrawal and alternatives
exhibits.section: Scope — FF3-1 is being withdrawn, and that is the lesson
exhibits.action: Read the attack chronology, finite-domain and tweak-schedule discussion, then compare alternatives.
exhibits.outcome: Explains why shorter tweak did not fix the alternating schedule and why FF1 or other designs are preferred by use case.
exhibits.limits: Historical and design explanation; live codebook demo is a separate simplified small-domain attack.

exhibits.title: Match encrypted records by retained format
exhibits.section: Format can identify a record without decrypting it
exhibits.action: Encrypt eight synthetic records with fresh FF1 tweaks and match name/city shapes against an auxiliary roster; compare padded AES-GCM records.
exhibits.outcome: Public format-only matching narrows candidate sets and computes uniform-prior Shannon leakage; the equal-length padded control leaves all eight candidates.
exhibits.limits: Invented complete roster and uniform prior; unique candidate is not real-world identity proof. No FF1 key recovery and no general anonymity guarantee from padding.

exhibits.title: Toy LWE from First Principles
exhibits.action: Choose a three-component secret and noise magnitude, generate samples, solve clean and noisy equations, and animate A·s+e.
exhibits.outcome: Exact modular solving succeeds without error and becomes inconsistent with sampled error, illustrating the LWE problem.
exhibits.section: Learning With Errors (LWE) from first principles
exhibits.limits: The n=3, q=97 system is deliberately tiny and not cryptographically secure.

exhibits.title: FrodoKEM Key Generation and Sizes
exhibits.action: Choose FrodoKEM-640, -976, or -1344 and generate a keypair.
exhibits.outcome: liboqs WASM returns actual public and secret keys; a size chart relates the unstructured matrix to large public keys.
exhibits.limits: The first invocation loads WASM; in-browser timings are device dependent.

exhibits.title: FrodoKEM Encapsulation and Tamper
exhibits.action: Generate Alice’s keypair, let Bob encapsulate, let Alice decapsulate, and tamper with ciphertext.
exhibits.outcome: The two parties derive matching shared secrets when unaltered; a tampered ciphertext yields an unrelated implicit-rejection secret.
exhibits.limits: This few-ciphertext eFrodoKEM variant limits use of one public key to 255 ciphertexts; it is not a reusable deployment.

exhibits.title: FrodoKEM Versus ML-KEM
exhibits.action: Run a browser benchmark of FrodoKEM-976 and ML-KEM-768 and inspect published sizes and security data.
exhibits.outcome: Measured median, range, and load times show the cost of avoiding ring structure alongside specification values.
exhibits.limits: Measured milliseconds are browser/device specific and are not production benchmarks.

exhibits.title: Hybrid KEM Derivation
exhibits.action: Run both liboqs KEMs and combine their derived secrets.
exhibits.outcome: The walkthrough computes a hybrid shared value and relates it to the hedge against a broken family.

exhibits.title: Error Distribution and Toy Failure
exhibits.action: Sample 1,000 errors and run a toy decryption failure or probability chart.
exhibits.outcome: Histograms and q=17 calculations expose the correctness versus noise-width tradeoff.
exhibits.limits: The q=17 failure model is a toy; its failure rates are not FrodoKEM deployment failure rates.

exhibits.title: Post-Quantum KEM Landscape
exhibits.action: Read the table and cross-demo links comparing FrodoKEM, ML-KEM, and code-based options.
exhibits.outcome: Published status and size context explains why the conservative plain-LWE option is not the default.
exhibits.section: FrodoKEM in the PQ KEM landscape

exhibits.title: Structureless Versus Structured Lattice Bets
exhibits.action: Read the sourced comparison of NIST, China’s S-Cloud+, and FrodoKEM positions.
exhibits.outcome: The analysis locates the extra algebraic structure tradeoff and hedging decisions.

exhibits.title: Threshold key generation
exhibits.action: Choose n and t, generate shares, and reveal points on the toy polynomial plot.
exhibits.outcome: Shows group public key, individual shares and the threshold reconstruction intuition.
exhibits.limits: The p=97 plot is illustrative; the live FROST path uses real scalar shares and a trusted initial dealer.

exhibits.title: Choose a threshold subset
exhibits.action: Toggle signers until exactly t are selected and continue.
exhibits.outcome: Shows a quorum needed to proceed and later permits another valid subset under the same group key.
exhibits.limits: A scripted browser roster, not a distributed network or dealerless setup.

exhibits.title: Round 1 nonce commitments
exhibits.action: Enter a message and run Round 1 for the selected signers.
exhibits.outcome: Displays nonce commitments before shares are computed.
exhibits.limits: The UI orchestrates the round in one browser; no transport or independent devices.

exhibits.title: Round 2 signature shares
exhibits.action: Run Round 2 after commitments.
exhibits.outcome: Displays each participant’s signature share and binding inputs.
exhibits.limits: Shares are generated by in-page parties; this does not model malicious transport.

exhibits.title: Aggregate and verify FROST
exhibits.action: Aggregate shares and test verification or a failure case.
exhibits.outcome: Produces a single group signature and reports verifier acceptance or rejection.
exhibits.limits: Correctness of the selected run is checked; this is not a general active-adversary security proof.

exhibits.title: Try another valid quorum
exhibits.action: Pick and sign with a different threshold subset.
exhibits.outcome: Compares verified signatures under the same group public key without revealing signers from a signature alone.
exhibits.limits: The UI retains local history for comparison; it is not a metadata privacy guarantee.

exhibits.title: Private FROST versus accountable BLS
exhibits.action: Sign the same quorum with BLS ATS, edit signer bitmap, test threshold guard, absent signer framing, corrupt share, rogue key and dealer framing.
exhibits.outcome: Shows which verifications and registration checks reject attacks, while a trusted dealer who knows all shares can frame signers.
exhibits.limits: ATS is a separate BLS construction; drand quicknet vector is a private-BLS check, not an accountable-signature example.

exhibits.title: Nonce reuse and binding checks
exhibits.action: Reuse signing nonces to recover and forge, run a fresh-nonce control and binding-term consistency controls.
exhibits.outcome: Displays key-recovery/forgery in the misuse example and contrast with checks under safe inputs.
exhibits.limits: Attack harness is a separate TypeScript/noble construction; main signing walkthrough uses Rust/WASM FROST.

exhibits.title: Adaptive corruption research boundary
exhibits.section: Adaptive corruption: what this lesson does and does not show
exhibits.action: Read parameter-dependent research context and roster/corruption notation.
exhibits.outcome: Distinguish public verifying shares from secret shares, the 2025 proof baseline, and the October 2026 canonical-point 488/173 attack versus adversarial-point 228/114 subset-search measurement.
exhibits.limits: The cited preprint has distinct attack models; the 228/114 measurement is a successful subset search, not an end-to-end attack on this small browser signing lesson. This panel does not execute adaptive corruption.

exhibits.title: Interactive versus Fiat–Shamir
exhibits.action: Advance the transformation from an interactive Schnorr proof to a hash-derived challenge.
exhibits.outcome: See how who chooses the challenge and which transcript fields enter the hash changes the proof.
exhibits.section: Interactive → non-interactive: who chooses the challenge?

exhibits.title: Frozen Heart transcript omission
exhibits.action: Choose which fields the challenge hash covers, then try to forge a proof for Alice’s public key or create an honest control proof.
exhibits.outcome: When R is omitted, algebra chooses a response and solves for the commitment so the verifier equation holds without Alice’s witness.
exhibits.limits: The lab exercises a Schnorr-style demonstration, not a reproduction of every affected production protocol.

exhibits.title: Omission ladder
exhibits.action: Inspect which omitted transcript fields enable which attack outcomes.
exhibits.outcome: Compare verification and forgery conditions across field-binding choices.
exhibits.section: The omission ladder — which omissions actually matter

exhibits.title: Fiat–Shamir audit checklist
exhibits.action: Inspect the audit section and its challenge-binding checklist.
exhibits.outcome: Identify fields that an implementation must tie into a non-interactive proof challenge.
exhibits.section: How to audit this in real code

exhibits.title: Frozen Heart historical disclosure context
exhibits.action: Inspect the named 2022 disclosure cases and random-oracle-model explanation.
exhibits.outcome: Relate incomplete challenge transcripts to several independent systems while distinguishing the lab’s minimal Schnorr illustration from product-specific exploits.
exhibits.limits: The lab does not reproduce a specific deployment exploit or prove a formal random-oracle theorem.
exhibits.section: Frozen Heart: one bug, many independent systems

exhibits.title: Regex to Minimized DFA
exhibits.action: Choose a format regex and output length, then inspect the minimized automaton and count table.
exhibits.outcome: Shows state transitions, accepted-string count, and payload capacity for each length.

exhibits.title: Format-Transforming Encryption
exhibits.action: Enter a message, passphrase, and regex; encode to a string accepted by the format.
exhibits.outcome: Shows ciphertext to integer, FF1 cycle walk, DFA unranking, output string, and transmission metadata.
exhibits.section: Encode a message into the format
exhibits.limits: Format conformance alone does not make traffic distribution realistic or authenticate the string.

exhibits.title: Regex Classifier Challenge
exhibits.action: Run an anchored classifier rule against alternate ciphertext encodings and the stego string.
exhibits.outcome: Compares which wire strings match the chosen rule.
exhibits.limits: Defeats the selected regular-expression rule, not arbitrary traffic analysis.

exhibits.title: Recover Message
exhibits.action: Supply stego string, passphrase, and salt to invert the cycle walk and rank mapping.
exhibits.outcome: Displays the decoded message or a specific refusal.
exhibits.limits: Unauthenticated decoding can leak failure detail.

exhibits.title: Statistical and Length Leakage
exhibits.action: Play spot-the-fake and inspect output length versus message size.
exhibits.outcome: Exposes distribution mismatch and a length side channel despite regex acceptance.

exhibits.title: Unauthenticated String Substitution
exhibits.action: Run 60 replacements drawn from the same format and pass each through the receiver decoder.
exhibits.outcome: Counts accepted and rejected substitutions and shows distinct decoder outcomes.

exhibits.title: Authenticated Sealing and Replay Controls
exhibits.action: Seal and open a formatted message, then run the substitution attack against the authenticated variant.
exhibits.outcome: Shows a verification gate and uniform refusal before revealing plaintext.
exhibits.limits: The lab illustrates safeguards and discusses branchless ranking; it is not a production FTE transport.

exhibits.title: Unauthenticated Key Agreement for FTE
exhibits.action: Run an ephemeral X25519 or P-256 exchange and compare derived roots.
exhibits.outcome: Shows matching shared roots that never cross the channel while warning that an unbound peer key permits a relay attacker.
exhibits.limits: The exchange is unauthenticated; transcript signatures or pinned identities are outside this control.

exhibits.title: Authenticated FTE Fragments
exhibits.action: Seal a message into several phone-number strings, reassemble it, then alter one fragment.
exhibits.outcome: Shows how one tag covers all pieces while the counter supplies order, and tampering is refused.
exhibits.section: Fragments, so a phone number can carry a tag after all
exhibits.limits: A sequence of phone numbers can still reveal traffic patterns even when each string matches the regex.

exhibits.title: Freshness for Formatted Messages
exhibits.action: Open authenticated fragments twice and reset the used-counter window.
exhibits.outcome: Shows a valid tag alone accepts old bytes but the local replay window rejects a repeated counter.
exhibits.limits: The replay window is a local protocol demonstration, not a deployed transport.

exhibits.title: Regex to Minimized DFA
exhibits.action: Edit the format, inspect the graph or transition table, then scrub an encoded string’s state path.
exhibits.outcome: Shows Thompson NFA construction, determinization, Hopcroft minimization, alphabet classes, and the accepting path used by the FTE rank mapping.
exhibits.limits: Only supported regex syntax and the lab’s bounded state space are accepted.

exhibits.title: Exact-Language Counting and Capacity
exhibits.action: Change the regex and length, then inspect C[q0][k], the capacity curve, and the shortest length that fits a payload.
exhibits.outcome: Relates exact accepted-string counts to floor(log2 C) payload bits and the encoder’s selected length.
exhibits.limits: Finite length and memory limits bound the count; capacity does not imply a realistic cover-traffic distribution.

exhibits.title: Authentication Tag Capacity Cost
exhibits.action: Compare maximum formatted message sizes after paying for a framing byte and 32-, 64-, or 128-bit tags.
exhibits.outcome: Shows how an integrity tag competes with plaintext for a finite regex language and makes narrow formats unusable.
exhibits.limits: The capacity table is computed for this language model and tag sizes, not a complete transport design.

exhibits.title: Branchless Ranking Versus Constant Time
exhibits.action: Read the production panel’s caveat about the revised unranking loop.
exhibits.outcome: Separates removed secret-dependent loop exits from remaining variable-time BigInt arithmetic and JIT behavior.
exhibits.limits: The browser implementation is not constant-time against local or co-resident attackers.

exhibits.title: FF1 Known-Answer Vectors in Browser
exhibits.action: Open the vector disclosure and run the published FF1 radix-10 and radix-36 samples through encryption and decryption.
exhibits.outcome: Reports exact matches for browser-supported cases and labels the AES-192 cases unsupported rather than failures.
exhibits.section: Known-answer tests — run the nine NIST vectors in this browser
exhibits.limits: Only six vector cases execute in browser WebCrypto; three AES-192 cases are unsupported there and are covered separately by Node tests.

exhibits.title: One key, one authorized answer
exhibits.action: Encrypt a chosen vector and compare an authority with basis-vector keys against an analyst holding one functional key.
exhibits.outcome: The authority recovers each coordinate from ciphertext; the analyst receives only the authorized bounded inner product.
exhibits.limits: The scheme uses a deliberately bounded plaintext range and toy-sized interactive examples; an authorized answer can itself reveal private information.

exhibits.title: Decryption finishes before the answer arrives
exhibits.section: Decryption finishes before the answer arrives
exhibits.action: Apply the functional key, then run the bounded discrete-log search with a chosen bound.
exhibits.outcome: The group element is derived first; baby-step giant-step recovers a signed integer only when within range, with search-work diagnostics.
exhibits.limits: A missed result can be a bound failure, not failure of the functional-key algebra; practical large-range decoding is expensive.

exhibits.title: Each independent key removes one degree of freedom
exhibits.section: Each independent key removes one degree of freedom
exhibits.action: Request several functional keys and inspect ranks, equations and candidate vectors.
exhibits.outcome: Independent outputs shrink the affine family until sufficient rank determines the encrypted vector.
exhibits.limits: The leakage comes from authorized outputs together; issuing several individually valid keys can reveal more than intended.

exhibits.title: Enough keys are the master secret — with no ciphertext at all
exhibits.section: Enough keys are the master secret — with no ciphertext at all
exhibits.action: Issue or block key requests, optionally override the rank gate and try a newly derived key for an unapproved function.
exhibits.outcome: Full-rank pairs (y, sk_y) solve for the master secret and generate a genuine key that decrypts a fresh ciphertext.
exhibits.limits: This is a key-issuance failure when the authority releases a spanning set, not a cryptographic break under an appropriate authorization policy.

exhibits.title: What backs the four stages up
exhibits.section: What backs the four stages up
exhibits.action: Inspect test fixtures, the deliberately wrong fixture, FE-versus-ABE-versus-FHE comparison and scope.
exhibits.outcome: The evidence panel distinguishes computed behavior, model choices and unimplemented capabilities.
exhibits.limits: Comparison is conceptual; the lab executes its particular inner-product FE construction, not ABE or FHE.

exhibits.title: Solve a private 3-bit wealth comparison
exhibits.action: Set Alice and Bob values and run the comparator.
exhibits.outcome: Returns only the greater-than/equal verdict while displaying the garbled-circuit framing.
exhibits.limits: Tiny 3-bit example and semi-honest participants; private values are available within one local browser for teaching.

exhibits.title: Garble and evaluate one AND gate
exhibits.action: Garble a gate, choose two inputs, evaluate and reveal the output mapping.
exhibits.outcome: Shows opaque wire labels, point-and-permute row choice and one decrypted row.
exhibits.limits: Labels and secrets are shown for pedagogy; real evaluator visibility is restricted.

exhibits.title: Deliver one selected input label by oblivious transfer
exhibits.action: Select Bob’s bit and run one Chou–Orlandi OT.
exhibits.outcome: Shows only the chosen label box opening while Alice’s view does not identify Bob’s choice.
exhibits.limits: One browser simulates both parties and exposes internal steps for learning.

exhibits.title: Step through the garbled comparator
exhibits.action: Set 3-bit values, garble, then step or autoplay evaluation and toggle God view.
exhibits.outcome: Tracks label propagation across XOR, AND and OR gates until the output verdict.
exhibits.limits: The revealed God view is outside Bob’s protocol view; this is a small fixed comparator.

exhibits.title: Show a single-use rule violation
exhibits.action: Garble a gate and run the label-reuse attack.
exhibits.outcome: Bob obtains both labels for his wire, decrypts two rows, and infers Alice’s hidden bit.
exhibits.limits: The lab does not implement malicious-party protections such as cut-and-choose.

exhibits.title: Explore garbled-circuit application families
exhibits.action: Inspect application cards and the MPC family tree.
exhibits.outcome: Maps private set intersection, private inference, sealed-bid auctions and threshold signature techniques to related protocols.
exhibits.limits: Application cards are explanatory; they do not implement those systems or prove deployment properties.

exhibits.title: Why Threshold ECDSA Is Hard
exhibits.action: Read the ECDSA reciprocal-product dependency and compare with FROST Schnorr signing.

exhibits.title: Paillier Homomorphic Primitive
exhibits.action: Run the Paillier encryption example and inspect additive and scalar homomorphisms.

exhibits.section: Exhibit 2 — Paillier Encryption: The MPC Primitive
exhibits.limits: The lab uses 1024-bit Paillier for tractability, below production recommendations.

exhibits.title: Two-Party Distributed Key Generation
exhibits.action: Generate each party’s share and Paillier key, then open commitments to obtain a joint public key.
exhibits.outcome: No full private key is reconstructed in the browser’s protocol state.

exhibits.title: MtA Share Conversion
exhibits.action: Load a real-number MtA example and step through the Paillier computation.
exhibits.outcome: The encrypted product becomes two additive shares without disclosing the inputs.

exhibits.action: Enter a message, run all signing rounds, inject a cheating condition, verify with noble curves, or run 25 random self-tests.

exhibits.title: GG20 Security versus FROST
exhibits.action: Read the security and deployment table.

exhibits.title: Identifiable-Abort Obligations

exhibits.outcome: The table distinguishes implemented detection from the proofs a production GG20 signer needs for party attribution.
exhibits.limits: The full proof stack is documented, not executed in this demo.

exhibits.title: Threshold ECDSA in Production
exhibits.action: Read wallet deployment snapshots, MPC versus multisig, and further reading.
