exhibits.title: Private and public lattice bases
exhibits.action: Choose dimension and seed, generate a key pair, compare shapes and compute HNF for both bases.
exhibits.outcome: Proves the unimodular basis change and canonical HNF equality by integer arithmetic and plots a two-dimensional projection.
exhibits.limits: The plot is a projection; HNF equality is a mathematical property and does not conceal all side channels by itself.

exhibits.title: Babai decryption with two bases
exhibits.action: Select error distribution, encrypt and decrypt using private and public bases.
exhibits.outcome: Shows the decryption bound and contrasting nearest-plane outcomes for the same ciphertext.
exhibits.limits: Small integer lattices and chosen error distributions are educational, not secure public-key parameters.

exhibits.title: Reduce the public basis
exhibits.action: Run LLL on the public basis before either named break.
exhibits.outcome: Shows how much ordinary reduction already helps at these small dimensions.
exhibits.limits: The result is parameter dependent and does not generalize to real lattice security levels.

exhibits.title: GGH encryption error congruence
exhibits.action: Step through the public-basis attack under ±3 errors, then alter the distribution.
exhibits.outcome: Uses e congruent to 3 modulo 6 to expose a residue and tests whether the original structure survives.
exhibits.limits: This attack relies on the special ±3 distribution; other choices can remove this particular congruence.

exhibits.title: Signature cloud basis recovery
exhibits.action: Collect round-off signatures and run shape recovery, then compare a Gaussian-signature control.
exhibits.outcome: Visualizes offset cloud and separate checks for useful forged basis versus actual private basis recovery.
exhibits.limits: A different signature scheme from Act 2; a forgery check and secret-basis recovery check are distinct.

exhibits.title: Modern lattice construction changes
exhibits.action: Read post-attack design comparison.
exhibits.outcome: Explains why public canonical bases and altered sampling address exposed structural weaknesses.
exhibits.limits: The panel is context, not an implementation or proof of modern schemes.

exhibits.title: Commit-by-commit secret leak
exhibits.action: Advance a synthetic repository through credential insertion, redaction and file deletion; inspect commit graph and file contents.
exhibits.outcome: See computed Git object identifiers and the sensitive blob remain reachable after a clean working tree.
exhibits.limits: The repository is generated in memory, not a live remote Git host.

exhibits.title: HEAD versus history secret scan
exhibits.action: Scan HEAD and the entire reachable history using the same scanner.
exhibits.outcome: Compare a clean HEAD result against a historical finding with path, line, blob and reachable commits.

exhibits.title: Entropy and format-rule detector
exhibits.action: Switch between sample strings and enter a candidate to inspect scanner scoring.
exhibits.outcome: See why Shannon entropy thresholds and format rules flag or miss candidate secrets.

exhibits.title: Credential rotation control
exhibits.action: Rotate the synthetic credential at its provider and rescan the history.
exhibits.outcome: The same blob and scanner finding remain, while the modeled credential becomes revoked.
exhibits.limits: Provider rotation is a simulated status change; no real credential or provider is contacted.

exhibits.title: Secret scan and history cleanup limits
exhibits.action: Read the threat-boundary list below the four panels.
exhibits.outcome: See why one branch’s parent chain, entropy thresholds and history rewriting cannot establish repository-wide absence or erase distributed copies.

exhibits.title: Build a Chow White-Box AES Program
exhibits.action: Choose or generate an AES-128 key and build the table network.
exhibits.outcome: Shows compiled tables and independent AES checks for the resulting program.
exhibits.limits: The program intentionally contains a recoverable key in the browser.

exhibits.title: Instrumented Table-Lookup Trace
exhibits.action: Choose a trace count and record table outputs while encrypting random inputs.
exhibits.outcome: Displays bit-level recordings used as the attack surface.
exhibits.section: Make the program tell on itself
exhibits.limits: The page instruments itself; it does not attach a debugger to an external binary.

exhibits.title: Differential Computation Analysis
exhibits.action: Choose the attack surface, bit prediction, and trace count, then run the key-recovery analysis.
exhibits.outcome: Scores candidates using difference of means and reports recovered bytes with confidence and trace data.
exhibits.section: Take the key out of the trace
exhibits.limits: A failed run at one trace count is not evidence that a scheme is secure.

exhibits.title: External Encoding Placement Sweep
exhibits.action: Move encodings inside or outside the program and measure combinations across attack surfaces.
exhibits.outcome: Shows when the trace-based hypotheses remain available and when external data hides them.
exhibits.section: What actually stops it: where the encoding lives
exhibits.limits: The result is scoped to this construction and DCA; outside encodings do not defeat the algebraic attack.

exhibits.title: BGE Algebraic Step A1
exhibits.action: Run the first algebraic recovery step against built tables.
exhibits.outcome: Shows an encoding relation recovered without recorded execution traces.
exhibits.section: The algebraic route, which needs no traces at all
exhibits.limits: Only step A1 is executed; the rest of BGE is explained, not run.

exhibits.title: White-Box Attacker and Encoded Table Network
exhibits.action: Read the first act’s machine-owner threat model and lookup-table explanation.
exhibits.outcome: Explains why Chow-style AES embeds the key into tables and scrambles intermediate wires when an attacker can read and trace the running program.
exhibits.limits: The lab builds a specific Chow-style construction; the threat model does not imply security of arbitrary white-box designs.

exhibits.title: Later Algebraic and Statistical Attacks
exhibits.action: Read the final act’s research map for improved BGE work and DCA against wider encodings.
exhibits.outcome: Places the live trace and table attacks alongside follow-on results, while explaining why nibble width is not a general security boundary.
exhibits.limits: Later attacks are summarized with primary sources, not reproduced by the live program.

exhibits.title: Browser randomness as dice
exhibits.action: Roll five dice several times using the browser random source.
exhibits.outcome: Five faces and the consumed/discarded byte count appear; repeated rolls are compared without treating an accidental repeat as an error.
exhibits.limits: A few rolls do not test or prove entropy quality; the demo relies on crypto.getRandomValues and the host environment.

exhibits.title: Deterministic bytes from a recipe
exhibits.section: Now a computer, following a recipe
exhibits.action: Enter a seed phrase and roll twice without changing it, then alter the phrase and compare.
exhibits.outcome: A SHA-256-derived ChaCha20 generator produces dice and bytes that repeat exactly for the same input.
concepts: cryptographic deterministic random bit generator intuition
exhibits.limits: The seeded generator uses a fixed internal nonce for reproducibility and a guessable input; it is intentionally not a safe key-generation recipe.

exhibits.title: Two keys that look alike
exhibits.section: Step 2 Two keys. Tell them apart.
exhibits.action: Generate a browser-random 32-byte key and a 32-byte ChaCha20-derived key from a four-digit PIN, and inspect both sets of four visual checks.
exhibits.outcome: The two byte strings and simple check results appear side by side; they can both pass despite radically different seed search spaces.
concepts: visual randomness tests cannot prove security
exhibits.limits: Passing these four checks does not establish CSPRNG security. The seeded key is intentionally guessable despite its 256-bit length.

exhibits.title: Checks catch an obvious pattern
exhibits.section: Do those checks do anything at all?
exhibits.action: Run the same four checks on a byte counter.
exhibits.outcome: Failed checks and pattern explanations show what the superficial tests can detect and why passing them proves much less.
exhibits.limits: This is a deliberately obvious nonrandom source and does not validate the sufficiency of the tests for cryptographic use.

exhibits.title: Guess the PIN and recover the seeded key
exhibits.section: Step 3 Guess the seed, take the key
exhibits.action: Try one PIN, then enumerate all 10,000 four-digit PINs against an AES-256-GCM encrypted message made under the seeded key.
exhibits.outcome: AEAD authentication rejects wrong candidate keys; a successful candidate opens the message and reveals the PIN, recovered key and search cost.
exhibits.limits: The full sweep covers exactly four-digit PINs, not every possible seed; the lab does not break ChaCha20, AES-GCM or a well-seeded generator.

exhibits.title: Run the same search against browser randomness
exhibits.action: After making keys, search the same 10,000 candidate PINs against the browser-random key ciphertext and compare with the seeded case.
exhibits.outcome: No candidate opens the browser-random-key message in the expected run; a table contrasts identical cipher, key length and tests with different key origin and observed search result.
concepts: same AES-GCM algorithm different key origins
exhibits.limits: A failed 10,000-PIN search shows only that this key was not found in that candidate set; it does not prove all attacks infeasible or assess host entropy.

exhibits.title: Published and derived cipher checks
exhibits.section: How this demo checks its own results
exhibits.action: Read the on-load vector verdict and optionally expand the individual published and locally derived cases.
exhibits.outcome: ChaCha20 implementation outputs are checked against RFC 8439 vectors and separate changed-input cases, with source provenance and disagreements visible.
exhibits.limits: Passing a finite vector set checks specified cases; it is not a formal proof or security audit of the entire implementation.

exhibits.title: What Randomness Checks Cannot Establish
exhibits.action: Read the recap, real incidents, and four closing questions.
exhibits.outcome: The narrative separates surface statistical checks from unpredictability and explains why seed recovery changes the earlier verdict.

exhibits.title: Birthday Table and Floyd Collision Search
exhibits.action: Choose truncation width and a memory strategy, then hunt a real shortened-hash collision and verify a 9-bit near miss.
exhibits.outcome: The two inputs share a truncated digest while their full SHA-256 digests differ; Floyd output includes measured walk lengths.
exhibits.limits: The output truncation is deliberate; full SHA-256 is not attacked.

exhibits.title: Opposite-Meaning Letter Forgery
exhibits.action: Find colliding dismissal and recommendation letters, reject same-type matches, and submit a tag against the other letter.
exhibits.outcome: A real WebCrypto HMAC verifies the swapped letter because the application MACs only a short digest; modifying the tag fails.
exhibits.limits: HMAC is not broken; the intentionally truncated unhashed input to HMAC is collision-prone.

exhibits.title: Full Lookup versus Chained Tables
exhibits.action: Set hash width, domain, Hellman starts, columns, and table count; build tables and invert 32 targets.
exhibits.outcome: Measured coverage, chain merges, verified preimages, and misses distinguish full lookup from regenerated chains.
exhibits.section: A lookup table is not a rainbow table
exhibits.limits: The K–L relation is a heuristic model and does not promise its estimated coverage for arbitrary parameters.

exhibits.title: Salted Target Experiment
exhibits.action: Precompute an unsalted table, draw fresh per-user salts, then test old candidates and guess each salted target.
exhibits.outcome: Old table hits mostly fail salted verification while per-user guessing still recovers valid preimages.
exhibits.section: Precompute first. Learn the salt afterward.
exhibits.limits: With a 12-bit digest, accidental matches and multiple preimages are common; recovery of a preimage does not identify the original password.

exhibits.title: Joux Multicollision and Concatenation
exhibits.action: Build b forks in a toy iterated hash, enumerate or flip combinations, and search H1‖H2.
exhibits.outcome: A linear number of small collision searches yields exponentially many H1-equivalent messages and can weaken naive concatenation.
exhibits.section: Build exponentially many messages from a linear chain of forks
exhibits.limits: The compression output is deliberately tiny; this does not attack full SHA-256 or contradict Merkle–Damgård collision-preservation results.

exhibits.title: Unkeyed versus secret-key hash-table buckets
exhibits.section: When the hash table becomes the target
exhibits.action: Search attacker-chosen names for one exposed bucket, insert them with linear probing, then reuse the same names under a fresh secret HMAC-SHA-256 bucket map.
exhibits.outcome: Compare measured slot visits and per-insertion probes for public versus keyed starting buckets in the same small table.
exhibits.limits: The public mapping is a deliberately weak FNV-1a bucket index and the keyed comparator uses WebCrypto HMAC, not SipHash. Slot visits in this toy are not a SHA-256 collision, a server benchmark, or a proven denial-of-service exploit.

exhibits.title: Live SHA-256 fingerprint
exhibits.section: Start here - What is a hash?
exhibits.action: Type input and watch a SHA-256 digest update.
exhibits.outcome: Shows fixed-size output and changes from small input edits.
exhibits.limits: A small changed-input example does not establish one-wayness or collision resistance.

exhibits.title: Compare three 256-bit digests
exhibits.action: Enter a message and hash with SHA-256, SHA3-256 and BLAKE3; reveal timing details.
exhibits.outcome: Displays three actual digests and indicative local timing.
exhibits.limits: Timing uses portable single-threaded JavaScript BLAKE3 and is not a cross-implementation benchmark.

exhibits.title: Single-bit flip and sweep
exhibits.action: Pick an input bit, inspect changed digest bits, and sweep every bit or a sample for long messages.
exhibits.outcome: Displays Hamming-distance percentage and distribution around half the output bits.
exhibits.limits: Long inputs are sampled rather than exhaustively swept; avalanche statistics alone are not a full security proof.

exhibits.title: Merkle–Damgård, sponge and tree
exhibits.action: Inspect diagrams and information tabs for SHA-256, SHA-3 and BLAKE3.
exhibits.outcome: Compares exposed chaining state, hidden sponge capacity and parallelizable tree structure.
exhibits.limits: The diagrams describe constructions; native BLAKE3 SIMD and multicore speed is not demonstrated by this page.

exhibits.title: Forge a bare SHA-256 prefix MAC
exhibits.action: Supply a demonstration secret and attacker suffix, then continue hashing from a published tag.
exhibits.outcome: Recomputed SHA-256 verifies an extended secret-prefix message without knowing secret bytes when their length is known.
exhibits.limits: This attacks bare SHA-256(secret||message), not HMAC-SHA256 or a proper authenticated protocol.

exhibits.title: Block cipher compression and fixed points
exhibits.section: Section D — A hash from a block cipher
exhibits.action: Compute AES-128-based compression, remove feed-forward, find a preimage or fixed point, and compare padding choices for message chaining.
exhibits.outcome: Shows one-block Davies–Meyer behavior, an invertible broken variant, and length-preserving padding controls.
exhibits.limits: Teaching AES-based construction and chosen-IV demonstrations are not SHA-256 or published AES hash vectors.

exhibits.title: Reduced-round SHA-2 research context
exhibits.action: Read citations and full-round boundary.
exhibits.outcome: Distinguishes reported reduced-step collision work from a full SHA-256 break.
exhibits.limits: No reduced-round collision search or pair verification executes here.

exhibits.title: Run a toy module-LIP public-key recovery
exhibits.action: Choose toy ring degree n=4 or n=8 and click Recover the key from the public key.
exhibits.outcome: Generates a separate toy unimodular basis, publishes Gram matrix Q, builds the tau-cocycle lattice from Q, applies LLL/enumeration and parity filtering, then displays a recovered equivalent basis B′ whose Gram matrix equals Q when successful.
exhibits.limits: Toy n=4/8 reduction on a separate genuinely unimodular toy key, not key recovery on this demo's HAWK-512/1024 keys or a production-scale HAWK key. Plain LLL substitutes for the large-scale shortest-vector procedure.

exhibits.title: Draw from the standalone Gaussian CDT and compare samplers
exhibits.action: Sample both distributions with 4,096 draws each and step through one CDT threshold walk.
exhibits.outcome: Displays measured histogram, theoretical PMF, distribution statistics and elapsed times for table-T1 discrete draws versus a Falcon-style accept/reject comparison; the walk exposes threshold comparisons and sign selection.
exhibits.limits: The T1 table runs here and in the sampler-gap bench, but this build's default signing path substitutes a mod-2 linear solve and does not call T1; the Falcon-style comparison is educational, not a full Falcon implementation or a side-channel certification.

exhibits.title: Sign, verify and forge using the demo's public parity basis
exhibits.action: Choose HAWK-512 or HAWK-1024, enter a message, generate a keypair and sign, then click Forge with only the public key and inspect the unmodified verifier's result.
exhibits.outcome: Computes a lattice signature and public-key verification checks, then derives a second signature from public data alone and reports whether the same verifier accepts it.
exhibits.limits: This educational signing implementation is forgeable by design because it publishes B mod 2 and does not use the production HAWK trapdoor or default Gaussian coset sampler; success of this demo's verifier is not HAWK unforgeability or deployment approval. HAWK was withdrawn in July 2026.

exhibits.title: Measure whether Gaussian sampling fixes the demo forgery
exhibits.action: After generating a keypair, click Measure the sampler gap to compare the mod-2 linear solve with a T1 discrete-Gaussian coset offset on that same key and message.
exhibits.outcome: Reports measured coefficient changes, additivity over integers and mod 2, value diversity, norm inflation and whether public-key-only forgeries under both columns pass the unmodified verifier.
exhibits.limits: The added Gaussian samples the public parity coset using T1, not production HAWK's basis-dependent lattice-coset sampler; it compares this build's exposed-public-basis failure and cannot establish a vulnerability of a correctly implemented HAWK signer.

exhibits.title: Three Lattice Signature Designs
exhibits.action: Compare Falcon, ML-DSA, and HAWK design sketches and at-a-glance figures.
exhibits.outcome: The panel identifies distinct lattice assumptions, sampling strategies, and deployment statuses.

exhibits.title: Standardization Roadmap
exhibits.action: Read the chronology and the lab’s 2026 security update for HAWK.
exhibits.outcome: The panel ties scheme status to its reported key-recovery margin change without treating this demo as a deployable signer.

exhibits.action: Read use cases for deployed PQ signatures, constrained devices, and adjacent research.
exhibits.outcome: The section presents algorithm choice context alongside links to related experiments.

exhibits.action: Choose RSA-PSS, Ed25519, ECDSA high-S or textbook RSA tactics, then ask and forge.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect real verifier outcomes and whether a candidate is a new-message forgery or merely new signature bytes on an old message.

exhibits.title: PRP and PRF collision curve
exhibits.action: Set domain size, query count and trials, then measure a switching-lemma collision curve.
exhibits.outcome: Compare empirical distinguishability as queries approach the birthday scale.

exhibits.title: DDH reduction wrapper
exhibits.action: Select a random or re-encrypting adversary and run the reduction over trials.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect how an adversary’s advantage transfers through the wrapper.

exhibits.title: Security game boundaries
exhibits.action: Expand the scope comparison and nearby-definition table.
exhibits.outcome: Distinguish ideal PRP/PRF oracles from real crypto operations and identify CCA1, NM-CPA and KEM security as separate notions.
exhibits.section: What this lab is, and is not

exhibits.title: Multi-key rare-signal advantage toy
exhibits.section: One hidden bit, several independent keys
exhibits.action: Set independent user instances, queries per user, and a per-query reveal chance, then run a sample game.
exhibits.outcome: Compare the toy’s exact distinguishing advantage 1−(1−ε)^Q with the union ceiling min(1,Qε); see whether any tagged leak disclosed the shared challenge bit.
exhibits.limits: Abstract tagged-leak game, not encryption, AES, a proof for a real scheme, or a reason to multiply a bound that already counted queries. One sample outcome does not estimate advantage.

exhibits.title: Adjacent hybrids and verified hard-core reconstruction
exhibits.section: Move one game at a time
exhibits.action: Advance through H0–H5 one adjacent hop at a time, run the AES and ideal-oracle boundary checks, inspect the exposed predicate, then run the bounded reconstruction.
exhibits.outcome: Classify exact rewrites, the symbolic AES-PRP replacement and the exact q(q−1)/2^129 collision ceiling; then independently verify a candidate recovered from the stipulated inner-product predictor without giving the decoder x.
exhibits.limits: The route combines real AES-128 with exact finite bookkeeping and lazily sampled ideal oracles, but leaves the AES-PRP term symbolic. Its n=8 hash fixture and stipulated fixed-x predictor are exhaustible teaching devices, not a one-way-function premise, a SHA-256 attack or an asymptotic theorem experiment. Reconstruction is probabilistic and accepts candidates only after an independent f(candidate)=y check.

exhibits.title: Target collision resistance as an order-of-play game
exhibits.section: The same family, two orders of play
exhibits.action: Choose the planted-pair or nibble-fold family and an adversary strategy, then play target-before-key and key-first state machines or exhaust the complete 8-bit key space.
exhibits.outcome: Compare accepted and refused moves, the planted strategy’s exact 2-of-256 target-first and 256-of-256 key-first counts, family-winnability controls, bounded samples, and the signed (key, digest) application boundary.
exhibits.limits: The fixed length-preserving 8-to-8-bit family is an exhaustible order-of-play model, not a UOWHF construction, an asymptotic separation or evidence about a real hash. The signed-pair panel does not establish malicious-signer non-repudiation.

exhibits.title: HPKE KEM, KDF, and AEAD Pipeline
exhibits.action: Change message, info, AAD, and keys, select a mode, and seal messages.
exhibits.outcome: Shows X25519 encapsulation, labeled HKDF schedule, AEAD ciphertext, and changing downstream bytes.
exhibits.section: The pipeline — three primitives, one envelope
exhibits.limits: Runs in browser with generated keys; its Base mode does not authenticate the sender.

exhibits.title: HPKE Base, PSK, Auth, AuthPSK
exhibits.action: Switch modes and inspect changed key-schedule context bytes and extra inputs.
exhibits.outcome: Highlights mode byte, PSK identifier hash, and authenticated second DH differences.

exhibits.title: HPKE Nonce Derivation
exhibits.action: Seal successive messages in one context and inspect the per-sequence nonce table.
exhibits.outcome: Shows base_nonce XOR sequence number and the changing nonce bytes.
exhibits.section: The nonce is a counter in disguise

exhibits.title: Sender and Receiver Binding Breaker
exhibits.action: Change info, AAD, or mode on one side, seal and open, then replay into a fresh context.
exhibits.outcome: Shows matching contexts decrypt, mismatched bindings reject, and a fresh context can open the same packet again.
exhibits.limits: HPKE provides no built-in replay protection across fresh receiver contexts.

exhibits.title: HPKE Application Responsibilities
exhibits.action: Read RFC 9180 non-goals covering ordering, negotiation, replay, compromise, randomness, and plaintext length.
exhibits.outcome: Shows which security properties the envelope leaves to the carrying application.
exhibits.section: What HPKE deliberately does not do (RFC 9180 §9.7)

exhibits.title: Post-Quantum HPKE KEM Seam
exhibits.action: Read the named hybrid KEM substitution at the shared-secret input to the key schedule.
exhibits.outcome: Explains how a KEM can change while HPKE KDF and AEAD mechanics remain structurally the same.
exhibits.section: Post-quantum HPKE: swap one stage (named, not built)
exhibits.limits: The post-quantum KEM is described here, not built or exercised in this lab.

exhibits.title: HPKE Auth KCI and Identity-Bound Sign-then-Encrypt
exhibits.action: Generate a fresh three-party key set, then run nine cases spanning honest delivery, outsider tampering, recipient-key KCI, recipient and sender compromise, forwarding, public evidence and replay.
exhibits.outcome: Executes an Auth ciphertext forgery with recipient skR and public sender pkS, then contrasts it with strict Ed25519 evidence over sender, recipient, independently expected context and message.
exhibits.section: Sender evidence under key compromise: Auth versus Sign-then-Encrypt
exhibits.limits: Bounded teaching profile, not a standardized signcryption wire format or proof transfer. Evidence proves only that a separately pinned key signed the exact disclosed fields; it does not prove transmission, receipt, time, human intent or legal non-repudiation, and replay remains application state.

exhibits.title: Timing Oracle Lab
exhibits.action: Choose secret weight, timing noise, queries per position and a preset, then run a chosen-bit-flip timing attack.
exhibits.outcome: Per-position average times are thresholded into a recovered support, with bit accuracy, query count and observed gap.
exhibits.limits: Decode time is modelled as base plus error-weight work plus Gaussian noise; no full HQC or real BCH decoder runs.

exhibits.title: Why averaging works: the distinguisher
exhibits.action: Toggle constant-time and side-by-side modes, and vary query count or noise to compare vulnerable and defended distributions.
exhibits.outcome: Shows single-query and averaged bells, theoretical overlap and measured recovery; constant-time mode flattens the timing signal.
exhibits.limits: The defense is applied to this abstract model; a real implementation needs independent timing and compiler review.

exhibits.title: Four Leaks, One Scheme
exhibits.action: Read the attack timeline and the Closing the Channel recommendations.
exhibits.outcome: The narrative distinguishes reported historical attacks from modelled results and lists implementation mitigations.
exhibits.limits: The timeline is reported context; timing numbers inside the live simulator are illustrative, not measurements from HQC.

exhibits.title: Compare source-level select and optimized binary behavior
exhibits.action: Inspect side-by-side source and compiler-output narrative.
exhibits.outcome: Identifies a secret-dependent branch and cache access introduced in the vulnerable optimized binary.
exhibits.limits: The page presents a faithful model; it does not compile or inspect a live HQC binary.

exhibits.title: Recover simulated HQC plaintext bits from cache probes
exhibits.action: Adjust secret size, repetitions, probe count, noise, defense state and seed, then run.
exhibits.outcome: Shows per-position cache hit rates and hard-majority versus reliability-weighted recovery accuracy.
exhibits.limits: A repetition-code stand-in replaces HQC Reed–Muller; no actual cache trace, HQC decapsulation, or key recovery occurs.

exhibits.title: Compare vulnerable and verified constant-time modes
exhibits.action: Hold seed constant and compare optimized vulnerable and constant-time settings.
exhibits.outcome: Shows a modeled signal in the leaking binary and no secret-dependent cache signal in the fixed binary.
exhibits.limits: A silent model channel does not prove a real compiled artifact is side-channel free.

exhibits.title: Trace four HQC timing and cache side channels
exhibits.action: Read the four dated incident cards and their fixes.
exhibits.outcome: Places decoder weight, cache access, variable division and compiler-induced branch leakage in a progression.
exhibits.limits: Read-only historical synthesis, not four reproduced attacks.

exhibits.title: Inspect mitigation and anti-pattern lists
exhibits.action: Read recommended binary inspection, optimization barriers and tooling against common unsafe assumptions.
exhibits.outcome: Explains that constant-time claims apply to a compiled artifact and build configuration.
exhibits.limits: Mitigation guidance; simulation does not establish any production binary is constant-time.

exhibits.title: Generate an illustrative HQC keypair
exhibits.action: Select HQC-128, -192 or -256 and generate a fresh illustrative sparse-vector keypair.
exhibits.outcome: Computes toy public relation s = x + h·y over a quasi-cyclic bit representation and displays actual sparse supports and public values alongside separately sourced specification sizes.
exhibits.limits: The generated n and private-key representation are illustrative. The published 2026 HQC decapsulation key defaults to a 32-byte seed; this page does not generate production HQC keys.

exhibits.title: Run illustrative HQC encapsulation and decapsulation
exhibits.action: After keygen, run encap and decap and optionally show the intermediate code and Fujisaki–Okamoto steps.
exhibits.outcome: Calculates u, v, d and a shared secret, decodes Reed-Muller/Reed-Solomon layers, reports corrected errors, FO verification and whether Alice/Bob secrets match.
exhibits.limits: Runs an educational reduced-parameter KEM inspired by HQC, not a standard-conformant production HQC encapsulation. Its implicit-rejection fallback differs from the published specification.

exhibits.title: Change ciphertext error placement and measure decoding
exhibits.section: 6. Bit-flip lab — watch the error budget at work

exhibits.outcome: Counts which flipped bits actually reach the toy decoder, reports Reed-Muller/Reed-Solomon corrections and exact seed recovery, and separately reports FO acceptance.
exhibits.limits: The illustrative decoder has small parameters and its observed correction rate is not a production HQC decapsulation-failure estimate.

exhibits.action: Choose u, v or d, enter a bit index, flip it and decapsulate the modified illustrative ciphertext.

exhibits.limits: This is a toy behavior demonstration, not an IND-CCA proof. Physical fault attacks on other decapsulation steps are discussed as research context and not executed.

exhibits.title: Measure a secret-indexed lookup timing toy
exhibits.action: Run the browser timing experiment for naive early-return and full-scan lookups at six planted marker positions.
exhibits.outcome: Measures and plots time per lookup on the current device, after verifying each lookup returned the planted index.
exhibits.limits: The code times a JavaScript array toy, not HQC FPGA or real hardware leakage. A full scan in JavaScript does not prove constant-time machine behavior; the 2026 masked-HQC profiling paper is cited context only.

exhibits.title: Compare HQC, BIKE and ML-KEM published sizes
exhibits.action: Choose security level 1, 3 or 5 and inspect the side-by-side KEM table and size bars.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 2 — Encrypt Before Recipient Exists
exhibits.action: Encrypt a message to Bob’s identity, then enroll Bob with the PKG and decrypt.
exhibits.outcome: The pairing-derived shared value lets the extracted identity key recover the message even though Bob had no key at encryption time.
exhibits.limits: BasicIdent is a teaching construction and does not supply modern authenticated-encryption or chosen-ciphertext security by itself.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 3 — Wrong Identity = Garbage
exhibits.action: Try decrypting with a key extracted for an identity different from the recipient.
exhibits.outcome: The wrong pairing value yields incorrect plaintext bytes alongside the correct identity result.
exhibits.limits: Unauthenticated BasicIdent can produce garbage without an integrity verdict; this comparison is not AEAD tamper detection.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 4 — Time-Limited Capabilities
exhibits.action: Encrypt to an email-plus-date identity, then have the PKG issue, refuse or improperly issue the matching private key.
exhibits.outcome: An issued matching key decrypts; when the PKG refuses, Bob’s available undated key produces garbage, while a colluding PKG can issue early and defeat the policy.
exhibits.limits: Time scoping depends on PKG key issuance and ciphertext identity conventions; it does not revoke an already issued matching key.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 5 — The PKG Escrow Tradeoff
exhibits.action: Run the PKG escrow example and inspect feature, privacy tradeoff and named mitigations.
exhibits.outcome: The authority extracts the recipient’s private key and decrypts the ciphertext.
exhibits.limits: BasicIdent implements none of the listed escrow mitigations; the PKG must be trusted with all identities.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 6 — A Parent Key Really Derives Its Descendant
exhibits.section: Exhibit 6 — A Parent Key Really Derives Its Descendant
exhibits.action: Build a three-level identity, delegate parent-to-child keys without the master secret, then compare descendant, sibling and root-PKG results.
exhibits.outcome: The delegated descendant and fresh PKG key recover the target message; the same-depth sibling runs the pairing algebra but recovers a different secret, while root escrow remains.
exhibits.limits: Bounded depth-three Type-3 KEM/DEM teaching adaptation; it does not claim the paper's full proof and delegation does not remove root escrow.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 7 — Who Must Be Compromised?
exhibits.action: Run PKI, IBE and bounded certificateless routes for one identity, then compare Type-I, Type-II, combined-compromise, key-replacement and tag-tamper outcomes.
exhibits.outcome: The certified PKI and escrowed IBE routes succeed; neither certificateless adversary class decrypts alone, the combined compromise accepts, and displacement or tag mutation rejects.
concepts: PKI versus IBE versus certificateless ownership
exhibits.limits: Bounded Huang–Wong mechanics adaptation using BasicIdent, so the cited IND-CCA theorem does not apply; one-shot actors are not full adaptive games, JavaScript is not constant-time, and key replacement can still deny service without an authenticated directory.

exhibits.title: JWS Token Inspection and Editing
exhibits.action: Decode or paste a compact JWS, edit header and claims, re-sign with a held key or preserve the old signature, and inspect a diff.
exhibits.outcome: Readable header and claims show that JWS is signed rather than encrypted; changing signed bytes without re-signing is rejected.
exhibits.limits: The page uses invented session keys and tokens; pasted data should be non-sensitive.

exhibits.title: Verifier Policy and Decision Trace
exhibits.action: Choose accepted algorithms, held key, and correct or vulnerable verifier; verify the current token.
exhibits.outcome: The decision trace shows token algorithm, application policy, key type, signature check, and claim checks.
exhibits.limits: The vulnerable path is deliberately broken for demonstration and must not be used for application authentication.

exhibits.title: alg:none Forgery
exhibits.action: Launch an unsigned admin token and compare vulnerable and correct verification.
exhibits.outcome: The vulnerable verifier accepts the attacker-controlled no-signature token while the policy-driven verifier rejects it.

exhibits.title: RS256 to HS256 Key Confusion
exhibits.action: Re-sign with HS256 using the RSA public key bytes as an HMAC secret, then compare verifiers.
exhibits.outcome: A verifier that follows the untrusted header accepts the forgery; typed key binding rejects it.

exhibits.title: Silent Claim Tamper Control
exhibits.action: Change a claim but keep the original signature and run both verifiers.
exhibits.outcome: Both reject the modified signed content, isolating the structural implementation bugs in the other attack cases.

exhibits.title: Four KDFs on one password
exhibits.action: Enter a password, set cost parameters and run PBKDF2-SHA256, scrypt, Argon2id and HKDF sequentially.
exhibits.outcome: Shows derived output, measured time and defined nominal memory for compute-hard, memory-hard and fast extract-expand functions.
exhibits.limits: Nominal memory is algorithm-defined, not measured RAM; local timings are device dependent and HKDF is unsuitable for password slowing.

exhibits.title: Salt reuse control
exhibits.action: Toggle fresh versus reused salt for repeated password runs.
exhibits.outcome: Identical password and salt reproduce derived keys; new salts change output.
exhibits.limits: Salt reuse is a teaching misuse; a salt is public and does not add password entropy.

exhibits.title: Weaken KDF work factors
exhibits.action: Apply a 1,000-iteration PBKDF2 or 8 MiB Argon2id preset and rerun.
exhibits.outcome: Shows reduced time and nominal resource cost under weaker parameters.
exhibits.limits: One local derivation measures defender cost; it does not benchmark GPU attackers or quantify breach resistance.

exhibits.title: HKDF: Extract and Expand
exhibits.action: Change input key material, salt, context info and output length, then derive.
exhibits.outcome: Show computed PRK, OKM, expansion blocks and a two-phase diagram populated with the actual derived bytes.
exhibits.limits: HKDF expects high-entropy input key material; it is not a password-stretching function.

exhibits.title: Argon2id: Modern Password Hashing
exhibits.action: Set password, salt, time, memory, parallelism and tag length, then derive an Argon2id output.
exhibits.outcome: Read the output, browser runtime, selected memory cost and estimated password-guessing attack cost.
exhibits.limits: Browser timing and attacker-cost estimates are illustrative; memory-hardness does not guarantee a side-channel-free implementation or make GPU and ASIC attacks impossible.

exhibits.title: Stretch then Fan Out
exhibits.action: Supply one password and salt, edit three context strings, then run Argon2id followed by HKDF expansion.
exhibits.outcome: See one derived root and separately labelled context-specific output keys in a fan-out diagram, including the total runtime.
exhibits.limits: A teaching composition with fixed Argon2id parameters; this does not model a whole TLS, Signal or vault key schedule.
exhibits.section: The KDF Chain: Stretch then Fan Out

exhibits.title: PBKDF2 Password Stretching
exhibits.action: Set password, salt, iterations and length; derive or benchmark 100k, 600k and 1M iterations.
exhibits.outcome: Compare HMAC-SHA-256 and HMAC-SHA-512 output and measured browser time plus an attack-cost estimate.
exhibits.limits: Browser benchmark measures this device; offline-attack cost is an estimate. PBKDF2 is CPU-hard, not memory-hard.

exhibits.title: scrypt Memory-Hard Stretching
exhibits.action: Adjust N, r, p, salt and password; derive a key or compare three N values.
exhibits.outcome: See output bytes, measured runtime and estimated memory consumption; very large settings may exceed browser memory.
exhibits.limits: Benchmarks depend on the device and may fail under browser memory limits; they do not directly measure GPU attack throughput.

exhibits.title: Why Memory Hardness Beats GPUs
exhibits.action: Move among labelled memory-cost settings and animate the access grid.
exhibits.outcome: See a teaching visualization where a one-MiB cell scale and waiting cores illustrate greater per-guess memory demand.
exhibits.limits: A single-bus visualization, not an instrumented GPU trace or measured attack cost.

exhibits.title: KDF Decision Tree and Comparison
exhibits.action: Choose entropy source, key fan-out need and legacy constraints, then request a recommendation.
exhibits.outcome: A table compares password and high-entropy KDF roles, memory hardness, GPU resistance and parameters.

exhibits.title: Salt and Domain Separation
exhibits.action: Run the no-salt, random-salt, context-binding and domain-separation buttons.
exhibits.outcome: Outputs show repeated unsalted passwords match while different salts or HKDF info strings separate derivations.

exhibits.title: One Password Across Four KDF Settings
exhibits.action: Run PBKDF2 at two costs, scrypt and Argon2id on one password, then select an attack target.
exhibits.outcome: The panel plots local derivation time alongside modeled attacker cost.
exhibits.section: Cost Comparison: One Password, Every KDF
exhibits.limits: Attack-cost estimates are modeled and timing is browser-specific.

exhibits.title: Published RFC Known-Answer Checks
exhibits.action: Run bundled RFC test vectors and inspect expected and actual bytes.
exhibits.outcome: The panel reports per-vector pass or failure for the implemented KDF paths.

exhibits.title: ML-KEM implicit rejection
exhibits.action: Flip one ciphertext bit or restore validity and step through Fujisaki–Okamoto decapsulation.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect re-encryption comparison and selection of the normal or pseudorandom fallback secret.
exhibits.limits: A malformed ciphertext length fails the input check before the implicit-rejection branch.

exhibits.title: Same ciphertext, safe and fail-open callers
exhibits.action: Compare two calling programs after changing the ciphertext.
exhibits.outcome: The same decapsulation returns 32 bytes, but caller policy determines whether the session is trusted.
exhibits.limits: Callers are deliberately small teaching models built around real ML-KEM operations.

exhibits.title: Malformed length and output buffer
exhibits.action: Corrupt the ciphertext length and choose what a caller-owned output buffer held beforehand.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect a return-code error that leaves the buffer unchanged and a broken caller deriving from stale bytes.

exhibits.title: Verbose caller response channels
exhibits.action: Compare valid and invalid ciphertext responses from safe and chatty callers.
exhibits.outcome: Message, response length and code-path differences expose a validity signal.
exhibits.limits: Timing is modeled as branch behavior and is not measured in the browser.
exhibits.section: 4 · The oracle a chatty caller hands out

exhibits.title: Wrong recipient and key confirmation
exhibits.action: Compare Bob and Carol decapsulating a ciphertext sent to Bob.
exhibits.outcome: Both receive bytes, but only the intended recipient agrees with the sender; confirmation MAC distinguishes the mismatch.
exhibits.section: 5 · “32 bytes arrived” is not “a secret with the intended party”

exhibits.title: Truncated ciphertext comparison case study
exhibits.action: Expand the research-update panel and compare a full eight-byte equality check with a faulty seven-byte prefix check.
exhibits.outcome: One changed final bit is rejected by full comparison but accepted by the deliberately truncated check.
exhibits.limits: Eight schematic bytes, not ML-KEM wire data; does not reproduce paper key recovery or compromise correct ML-KEM.
exhibits.section: Research update: what if the comparison skips a byte?

exhibits.title: Needham–Schroeder Public-Key Flow
exhibits.action: Select the original public-key protocol and step its messages.
exhibits.outcome: Shows nonce exchange under RSA-OAEP and the ambiguous responder identity in message two.
exhibits.limits: RSA-OAEP is a browser substitution for the older protocol’s encryption; the relay property remains.

exhibits.title: Lowe Man-in-the-Middle Attack
exhibits.action: Run the same protocol with Mallory relaying between Alice and Bob.
exhibits.outcome: Shows Bob accepts Mallory as Alice because the second message lacks responder identity binding.

exhibits.title: Lowe Identity-Binding Fix
exhibits.action: Replay Mallory’s relay against the patched message-two format.
exhibits.outcome: Shows Alice reject the mismatch before forwarding the final nonce.

exhibits.title: Kerberos AS, TGS, AP Exchanges
exhibits.action: Run the Kerberos v5 flow and inspect tickets, key types, preauthentication, and swimlane messages.
exhibits.outcome: Shows KDC-issued TGT and service ticket plus accepted or rejected application authentication.
exhibits.limits: Teaching profile omits PAC, several KDC options, and wire KRB-ERROR messages.

exhibits.title: Kerberos Replay and Clock Checks
exhibits.action: Shift the client clock and replay the last AP-REQ.
exhibits.outcome: Shows skew, validity-window, and replay-cache decisions against authenticators and tickets.

exhibits.title: AS-REP Roasting and Preauthentication
exhibits.action: Inspect the threat cards: request an AS-REP without preauthentication, try a four-word offline dictionary, then send the same request to an account requiring preauth.
exhibits.outcome: Shows password-derived ciphertext yielded by the first account and refusal to issue it for the protected account.
exhibits.limits: A throwaway KDC and four-word list demonstrate mechanism, not realistic cracking scale.

exhibits.title: Ticket Expiry and Pass-the-Ticket
exhibits.action: Inspect the threat cards for an expired service ticket and a stolen still-valid ticket.
exhibits.outcome: Shows expiry rejection but accepted possession-based use within lifetime; Kerberos does not bind a ticket to a machine in this model.
exhibits.limits: The pass-the-ticket probe models possession of valid material; endpoint protection remains outside the protocol.

exhibits.title: Kerberos AES-256 Encryption Type
exhibits.action: Inspect the generated encryption and integrity subkeys, ciphertext and decrypt round trip for etype 18.
exhibits.outcome: Shows key-usage separation and AES256-CTS-HMAC-SHA1-96 processing of the demo plaintext.
exhibits.limits: Ticket bodies are encrypted JSON in this teaching profile, not RFC 4120 ASN.1/DER wire encodings.

exhibits.title: Before public keys: Merkle puzzles
exhibits.action: Build weak-key AES puzzles, let Bob solve one, run Eve’s search and flip Bob’s copy.
exhibits.outcome: The work meter compares Bob’s one-puzzle work to Eve’s many-puzzle search and shows the shared secret or tamper failure.
exhibits.limits: Weak suffix sizes make the demonstration feasible; practical public-key exchange relies on stronger modern primitives.

exhibits.title: Live Diffie–Hellman
exhibits.action: Change a, b and small group parameters, compute public shares and shared value, then brute-force a discrete logarithm.
exhibits.outcome: Both parties agree, while the attacker can enumerate the toy group to recover an exponent.
exhibits.limits: Tiny parameters are deliberately breakable and are not suitable for real key exchange.

exhibits.title: What DH does NOT give you
exhibits.section: What DH does NOT give you
exhibits.action: Substitute Eve’s shares, relay an AES-GCM-protected message, then repeat with signed key shares.
exhibits.outcome: Unauthenticated DH permits Eve to derive two leg keys and alter a relayed message; a verified identity signature rejects substituted shares.
exhibits.limits: Small DH values are teaching-only; signature verification presupposes an independently trusted identity key.

exhibits.title: Live ECDH
exhibits.action: Choose scalars on the small demonstration curve and walk a·G one addition at a time.
exhibits.outcome: The elliptic-curve public points and matching shared point show the analogous DH operation.
exhibits.limits: The plotted curve is small and breakable; the Curve25519 comparison is explanatory, not an X25519 run.

exhibits.title: The mechanic shift: KEM vs DH
exhibits.section: The mechanic shift: KEM vs DH
exhibits.action: Run ML-KEM-768 keygen, encapsulation and decapsulation, then flip a ciphertext bit.
exhibits.outcome: Compare Bob’s and Alice’s shared secrets; tampered ciphertext decapsulates to a different secret through implicit rejection.
exhibits.limits: The page executes library ML-KEM; a differing secret after tampering is not a visible explicit reject bit.

exhibits.title: Hybrid combine
exhibits.action: Combine the toy DH value from the earlier panel with the ML-KEM secret through HKDF.
exhibits.outcome: Displays each input and derived session key, alongside the conditional hybrid-security explanation.
exhibits.limits: The DH half is a toy integer, not X25519; this panel is not a production authenticated TLS handshake.

exhibits.title: Shor’s algorithm — the threat
exhibits.action: Select a tiny composite and coprime base, observe classical period finding and gcd post-processing.
exhibits.outcome: The model shows factors for suitable periods and retry cases for odd or trivial periods.
exhibits.limits: The period is found by classical brute force; no quantum Fourier transform or quantum hardware is run.

exhibits.title: Module-LWE — the new hard problem
exhibits.action: Resample the tiny matrix instance and solve A·s = b with and without the error vector.
exhibits.outcome: Noiseless Gaussian elimination recovers s, while treating a noisy instance as exact yields a wrong vector.
exhibits.limits: q=11 and 3×3 matrices are illustrations; wrong naive elimination does not establish hardness of ML-KEM parameters.

exhibits.title: All five at once
exhibits.action: Read the five-generation table, size comparison, dated history and production context.
exhibits.outcome: The summary places Merkle puzzles, DH, ECDH, KEM and hybrid approaches in a historical and deployment view.
exhibits.limits: Static context and estimates are not live protocol interoperability tests.

exhibits.title: Short-code pairing and commitment
exhibits.section: What DH does NOT give you — Pairing check
exhibits.action: Run honest, active-relay-without-commitment, and active-relay-with-commitment scenarios; compare the displayed codes and commitment check.
exhibits.outcome: The toy short code can collide across two substituted key-share transcripts; binding a nonce before reveal causes the attempted late choice to fail verification and abort.
exhibits.limits: A three-digit toy code and SHA-256 demonstration, not Bluetooth f4/f5/f6/g2 or its six-digit security probability. The original DH/Ed25519 panel remains separate.

exhibits.title: Key lifecycle decisions
exhibits.section: Follow the key, from creation to retirement
exhibits.action: Choose between two decisions at each of ten stages and move through the path.
exhibits.outcome: Feedback explains generation, binding, purpose separation, rotation, custody, recovery, compromise, lifetimes, destruction and public-key trust.
exhibits.limits: Policy scenarios only; choices do not perform transfer, backup, revocation, sanitization or public-key verification.

exhibits.title: Historical key compromise
exhibits.action: Encrypt records, rotate to B, copy old Key A, and run attacker decryption.
exhibits.outcome: WebCrypto AES-256-GCM ciphertext remains under A after rotation; independent captured A decrypts an archived record and validates its tag.
exhibits.limits: Fictional records and simulated custody incident; real browser cryptography does not model production key service or persistent storage.

exhibits.title: Re-encryption and key retirement
exhibits.action: Re-encrypt remaining library records under B, discard the library’s A reference, and compare readability with the attacker’s archived copy.
exhibits.outcome: Current record epochs change while a captured A ciphertext remains exposed; discarding A may make remaining old records unreadable.
exhibits.limits: Deleting a JavaScript CryptoKey reference is not secure erasure of all copies or backups.

exhibits.title: Authenticated encryption tampering
exhibits.action: After encrypting, press Try tampering.
exhibits.outcome: A modified ciphertext byte is rejected by WebCrypto AES-GCM; this check does not reveal key theft.
exhibits.limits: Only one deliberate byte flip; successful authentication of an unmodified record says nothing about key custody.

exhibits.title: Ciphertext Custody and Rotation Limits
exhibits.action: Inspect the ciphertext table, historical attacker copy and the actual cryptography and limits disclosure.
exhibits.outcome: Successful AES-GCM authentication says nothing about whether an old key escaped; dropping a JavaScript key reference is not secure erasure.
exhibits.section: Ciphertext and key custody / Why the result matters

exhibits.title: Run a key-directory split view and message detour
exhibits.action: Advance or run the malicious directory steps.
exhibits.outcome: Alice receives Mallory’s substituted key, encrypts with X25519/HKDF/AES-GCM, and Mallory decrypts and reseals to Bob while Carol sees Bob’s legitimate key.
exhibits.limits: Roles and directory coexist in one browser; this is a teaching attack, not an external service compromise.
exhibits.section: 1 · The lie — one directory, two truths

exhibits.title: Test progressively stronger key-transparency checks
exhibits.action: Select signature, inclusion, consistency or gossip layer and run both lookups, optionally retaining earlier anchors.
exhibits.outcome: Signature and per-view Merkle proofs can pass under a split view; gossip detects conflicting signed roots.
exhibits.limits: Detection needs cross-view comparison or monitoring; one isolated client can be consistently lied to.
exhibits.section: 2 · The defense — each layer earned by the attack it fails to stop

exhibits.title: Step through byte-level consistency proofs
exhibits.action: Advance one hash step or run all proof steps.
exhibits.outcome: Shows node hashes and the old and new root reconstruction for append-only history.
exhibits.limits: A consistency proof covers one view; separate consistent forks can evade an isolated client.

exhibits.title: Derive and tamper a private directory label
exhibits.action: Derive a label with the VRF and flip a byte in its proof.
exhibits.outcome: Shows deterministic private label and rejection of tampered proof.
exhibits.limits: This isolates lookup label privacy; it does not conceal every form of metadata.
exhibits.section: 4 · Label privacy — the directory that doesn’t leak its users

exhibits.title: Audit a user’s own key history
exhibits.action: Run Bob’s audit of his directory key history.
exhibits.outcome: Displays whether an unauthorized key change is visible in the monitored log.
exhibits.limits: A monitor must receive and check relevant tree history; detection can occur after a message was intercepted.
exhibits.section: 5 · Monitoring — the attacker must leave a receipt

exhibits.title: Sponge Construction and Shared Core
exhibits.action: Read the sponge primer and six-step side-by-side pipeline table.
exhibits.outcome: Four fresh SHA3, SHAKE, cSHAKE, and KMAC runs share one Keccak-f[1600] primitive while domain and absorption steps differ.

exhibits.title: SHA3-256 Absorption Trace
exhibits.action: Change the message and step across absorbed blocks.
exhibits.outcome: The digest, padding markers, lane view, and permutation trace derive from the real sponge implementation.

exhibits.title: SHAKE Extendable Output
exhibits.action: Set SHAKE strength and requested output length and inspect output.
exhibits.outcome: The same sponge is squeezed beyond a fixed digest while the mode suffix separates SHAKE from SHA3.

exhibits.title: cSHAKE Customization and Empty-Parameter Equivalence
exhibits.action: Edit function name and customization string and compare cSHAKE output with SHAKE under empty parameters.
exhibits.outcome: The absorbed prefix changes domains; empty parameters reproduce SHAKE exactly as SP 800-185 requires.

exhibits.title: KMAC Tag and Verification
exhibits.action: Set key, message, output length or XOF mode; compute, verify, tamper, and clear a tag.
exhibits.outcome: The tag check responds to changed inputs and the live view shows encoded key and output-length binding.

exhibits.title: KMAC Versus Naive Prefix MAC
exhibits.action: Compare KMAC with SHA-256(key ‖ message) for the same inputs.
exhibits.outcome: Computed tags and explanatory facts show construction differences and why a naive Merkle–Damgård prefix MAC is not a substitute.

exhibits.title: NTRU+ key encapsulation
exhibits.action: Run NTRU+768 WASM keygen, encapsulate and decapsulate, then flip one ciphertext bit.
exhibits.outcome: Compares sender and recipient 32-byte secrets and re-encryption rejection of modified ciphertext.
exhibits.limits: Reference WASM is not guaranteed constant-time or production ready; an honest round trip does not prove NTRU hardness.

exhibits.title: Ring-term wrap
exhibits.section: Watch a term wrap through the real ring
exhibits.action: Choose monomial degrees and multiply across the 768-coefficient quotient ring.
exhibits.outcome: Shows reduction by X^768=X^384−1 and the resulting polynomial terms.
exhibits.limits: One term multiplication illustrates ring arithmetic; it is not a KEM security test.

exhibits.title: AIMer historical signature
exhibits.section: A signature from a symmetric one-way function
exhibits.action: Run AIMer-128f reference keygen, sign and verify, then flip a transcript bit.
exhibits.outcome: Shows computed AIM2 image versus public key, 33 proof blocks and local verifier behavior.
exhibits.limits: A reported public-key-only AIM2 forgery means honest KATs and bit-tamper rejection do not establish unforgeability; this page does not reproduce the attack.

exhibits.title: KpqC algorithm families
exhibits.action: Compare NTRU+, SMAUG-T, AIMer and HAETAE by KEM or signature role and mathematical family.
exhibits.outcome: Shows how Korean competition selections span different foundations and links sibling lab implementations.
exhibits.limits: Only NTRU+ and historical AIMer run here; selection is not a proof of security.

exhibits.title: ML-KEM stepper
exhibits.action: Select ML-KEM-512, 768, or 1024 and advance KeyGen, Encaps, and Decaps.
exhibits.outcome: Displays generated artifacts, operation timings, and a byte-for-byte match of both parties' 32-byte shared secrets.
exhibits.limits: Local browser library is not a FIPS-validated module and the flow has no peer authentication; final FIPS 203 ML-KEM is not byte compatible with every pre-standard Kyber protocol.

exhibits.title: Full hybrid encryption (ML-KEM + AES-256-GCM)
exhibits.action: Enter plaintext, encrypt and decrypt it, then flip a byte of the ML-KEM ciphertext and try decryption again.
exhibits.outcome: Runs ML-KEM encapsulation, HKDF-SHA256, and AES-256-GCM; shows authentication/decryption result or failure after tampering.
exhibits.limits: Teaching-only encryption path lacks peer authentication and independent audit. ML-KEM ciphertext modification by itself may yield a different decapsulated secret; GCM then rejects the derived-key mismatch.

exhibits.title: Learning With Errors: the noise is the whole point
exhibits.section: Learning With Errors: the noise is the whole point
exhibits.action: Generate a tiny q=17 scalar LWE instance; solve its clean and noisy equations by Gaussian elimination and count toy candidates.
exhibits.outcome: Shows when exact linear algebra recovers the secret from clean equations and how noise usually changes that result.
exhibits.limits: 4x4 scalar toy with Math.random; it is intentionally searchable, sometimes singular, and does not implement ML-KEM's module lattice or estimate its security.

exhibits.title: Cyclic NTT polynomial multiplication
exhibits.action: Run an eight-point cyclic NTT on two small polynomials, step butterflies, and compare the inverse result with schoolbook multiplication.
exhibits.outcome: Displays NTT, pointwise product, inverse transform, butterfly trace, and a match or mismatch verdict for the toy cyclic ring.
exhibits.limits: Computes Z_3329[X]/(X^8-1), not FIPS 203's incomplete negacyclic ML-KEM NTT or its base-case multiplication.

exhibits.title: ML-KEM parameter sets and fresh key-establishment wire cost
exhibits.action: Compare FIPS 203 key and ciphertext sizes and select a profile to use in the real ML-KEM stepper.
exhibits.outcome: Shows parameter categories and construction-level bytes for X25519, ML-KEM-512/768/1024, and X25519 plus ML-KEM-768.
exhibits.limits: Static construction-level payload accounting excludes certificates, signatures, framing, retransmissions and protocol-specific key caching; categories are not exact bit-strength values.

exhibits.title: Browser benchmark
exhibits.action: Run warm-up and repeated ML-KEM KeyGen/Encaps/Decaps timings and optional native X25519 timings; export JSON or CSV samples.
exhibits.outcome: Shows local median and p95 timing, environment metadata and raw sample exports.
exhibits.limits: Pure-JavaScript ML-KEM and native Web Crypto X25519 backends differ; these local wall-clock timings are not portable rankings or side-channel measurements. X25519 result may be unavailable in a browser.

exhibits.title: KEM and Implementation Boundary
exhibits.action: Read the KEM roles and the boundary between the two toy primers and the actual ML-KEM operation.
exhibits.outcome: The panel distinguishes shared-secret establishment from message encryption and toy arithmetic.
exhibits.section: What is a KEM? / Two primers, one real implementation

exhibits.title: Final ML-KEM and Earlier Kyber
exhibits.action: Inspect deployment examples, standards status and the exact library implementation.
exhibits.outcome: The disclosures separate FIPS 203 ML-KEM from pre-standard CRYSTALS-Kyber variants and identify the browser code path.
exhibits.section: Deployment examples / Standards status / What exactly runs here

exhibits.title: LWE Primer and Vocabulary
exhibits.action: Read the LWE mechanism narrative and expand the jargon definitions.
exhibits.outcome: The section ties noise, lattices and polynomial arithmetic vocabulary back to the KEM stepper.

exhibits.title: Vulnerable division versus Barrett reduction
exhibits.action: Toggle vulnerable reference C and patched Barrett-reduction code.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect the secret-dependent division path and why the multiply-and-shift replacement avoids that branch.

exhibits.title: Timing distribution experiment
exhibits.action: Choose a simulated Cortex platform and run single or hundred-measurement batches; compare distributions before and after patching.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect noisy model cycle counts and statistical separation across secret-dependent inputs.
exhibits.limits: The browser uses deterministic modeled timings rather than CPU division measurements.

exhibits.title: KyberSlash key-recovery simulation
exhibits.action: Launch the vulnerable or patched attack, control speed and inspect per-coefficient progress and exported timing samples.
exhibits.outcome: The model infers a narrowed ML-KEM-768 secret vector from crafted-ciphertext timing; the patched path is the control.
exhibits.limits: Uses a narrowed coefficient range and deterministic leakage model; not a browser timing attack on maintained libraries.

exhibits.title: KyberSlash disclosure timeline
exhibits.action: Inspect implementation and patch history in the timeline.
exhibits.outcome: Compare reported vulnerable and patched paths as a historical case study.

exhibits.title: Two-probe coefficient inference
exhibits.action: Choose a hidden coefficient and compare two crafted probe timings in slow motion.
exhibits.outcome: The truth table maps fast/slow pairs to the selected toy secret coefficient.
exhibits.limits: The walkthrough reduces coefficient values to −1, 0, +1 and uses adjacent probes rather than the paper’s full attack procedure.
exhibits.section: How two probes read one secret coefficient

exhibits.title: KyberSlash deployment lesson
exhibits.action: Read the deployment lessons and KyberSlash2 callout.
exhibits.outcome: See why encryption of public data can become a secret-dependent timing oracle when reencryption runs inside decapsulation.
exhibits.section: What this means for PQ deployment

exhibits.title: Lattice Signal Puzzle
exhibits.action: Adjust a two-vector basis, inspect distorted dots, and select a short or nearby lattice point across missions.
exhibits.outcome: Measures choices and shows how integer combinations generate the same underlying dot set.
exhibits.limits: The small visual puzzle is not a cryptographic lattice attack.

exhibits.title: Vector Flight
exhibits.action: Use positive or negative basis-vector thrusts to visit numbered beacons, with optional hint.
exhibits.outcome: Counts moves against a computed best route through each mission.
exhibits.limits: This is a navigation game, not ML-KEM cryptanalysis.

exhibits.title: Basis Match
exhibits.action: Choose which alternate pair of arrows generates exactly the original lattice.
exhibits.outcome: Reveals lattice dots and distinguishes equivalent unimodular basis changes from missing or extra points.

exhibits.title: Toy LWE Secret Search
exhibits.action: Guess the small secret in t=A·s+e and run an exhaustive search, then change problem scale.
exhibits.outcome: Displays residual error and brute-force work estimates.
exhibits.section: A private key small enough to steal
exhibits.limits: The toy search is not a state-of-the-art lattice reduction attack.

exhibits.title: ML-KEM Exchange and Tamper
exhibits.action: Choose a parameter set, run encapsulation and decapsulation, then flip a ciphertext bit.
exhibits.outcome: Shows wire bytes, matching shared secrets, and an altered decapsulation outcome.

exhibits.title: Public and Secret Basis Lens
exhibits.action: Switch between two bases of one lattice and compare decoding trials.
exhibits.outcome: Displays the same dot set through different basis vectors and performance of the simple decoder.
exhibits.limits: The two-dimensional lens is an analogy for harder high-dimensional problems.

exhibits.title: Secret and Public Basis Decoding
exhibits.action: Run 400 off-lattice coordinate-rounding trials under two descriptions of the same lattice.
exhibits.outcome: Contrasts nearest-point success from a short basis with misses from a skewed public basis.
exhibits.limits: Two-dimensional geometry is only an intuition for high-dimensional lattice decoding.

exhibits.title: Toy Secret-Search Scaling
exhibits.action: Select larger toy parameters after a measured tiny-key search.
exhibits.outcome: Projects brute-force keyspace and time growth for the same LWE-style equation under different dimensions.
exhibits.limits: Projected times use a browser-measured or assumed rate, not a real lattice-security estimate.

exhibits.title: Beacon Run Basis Refit
exhibits.action: Play the default six-chart flight game: jump by basis vectors, refit B by adding or subtracting A, collect three beacons, and dock.
exhibits.outcome: Shows that a reversible integer basis change alters available moves and route length while the lattice point set stays fixed.
exhibits.limits: A finite board and route target teach basis geometry, not SVP, CVP, lattice reduction, or ML-KEM attack cost.

exhibits.title: From Eight Dots to High Dimensions
exhibits.action: Compare one-step candidate counts as dimension increases, then read the distinction between the two-dimensional picture and lattice reduction.
exhibits.outcome: Shows why checking 3²−1 nearby candidates by eye does not scale to cryptographic dimensions.
exhibits.limits: The candidate-count analogy is not an ML-KEM security estimate.

exhibits.title: Shortest Vector, Closest Vector, and Module-LWE
exhibits.action: Read the classic view’s behind-the-puzzle explanation of the distorted grid and private dial hint.
exhibits.outcome: Separates an eight-candidate origin search from full SVP, nearest-target CVP, and the noisy modular equations behind ML-KEM.
exhibits.limits: The signal game’s private dial hint is a mechanic and the eight-dot search is not a real lattice attack.

exhibits.title: ATTACK 1: NTT POWER ANALYSIS
exhibits.action: Set secret and ciphertext coefficients, trace count and noise, generate model power traces and run correlation power analysis.
exhibits.outcome: The correlation ranking may distinguish a coefficient as Hamming-weight signal emerges above noise.
exhibits.limits: Power traces are generated by a leakage model, not measured on a device.

exhibits.title: ATTACK 2: FAULT INJECTION ON REJECTION SAMPLING
exhibits.section: ATTACK 2: FAULT INJECTION ON REJECTION SAMPLING
exhibits.action: Run normal and faulted signing batches and then launch recovery from faulty signatures.
exhibits.outcome: The display contrasts rejection behavior and key-recovery evidence under an injected acceptance fault.
exhibits.limits: Faulted signatures and collection are simulated; the experiment does not show physical fault injection.

exhibits.title: ATTACK 3: KYBERSLASH — TIMING SIDE-CHANNEL
exhibits.action: Run vulnerable division timing and the constant-time model side by side.
exhibits.outcome: Shows how data-dependent division can separate timing distributions and how fixed-work arithmetic removes that modeled signal.
exhibits.limits: A timing model, not a benchmark of a deployed ML-KEM implementation.

exhibits.title: ATTACK 4: LOOP-ABORT FAULT ON NONCE EXPANSION
exhibits.section: ATTACK 4: LOOP-ABORT FAULT ON NONCE EXPANSION
exhibits.action: Choose where ExpandMask aborts, inject the software fault, sign and run the in-browser lattice attack.
exhibits.outcome: The nonce strip and dimension plot show surviving coefficients; within the cap, real ring arithmetic and LLL return a candidate secret.
exhibits.limits: Fault injection is simulated; signing is reduced to one polynomial and omits the second validity check. Beyond the browser cap, recovery is modeled rather than executed.

exhibits.title: ATTACK 5: THE BIGGER PICTURE
exhibits.action: Compare the implementation attack mechanisms and read the countermeasures and references.
exhibits.outcome: The recap distinguishes mathematical assumptions from power, fault and timing failures.
exhibits.limits: A synthesis panel; it does not independently test all countermeasures on real devices.

exhibits.title: Drag a lattice basis and decode by rounding
exhibits.action: Choose good or bad basis presets or drag vectors and target.
exhibits.outcome: Exact integer checks show whether bases generate the same lattice and how nearest-plane rounding can miss the closest vector.
exhibits.limits: Two-dimensional bounded examples; nearest-vector search is feasible only at toy size.
exhibits.section: Exhibit 1 · One lattice, many bases — and decoding by rounding

exhibits.title: Compare shortest vector under different bases
exhibits.action: Switch basis and predict whether the shortest lattice vector changes.
exhibits.outcome: Same lattice points retain the same shortest vector despite differing basis descriptions.
exhibits.limits: The page solves small two-dimensional instances, not large cryptographic SVP.
exhibits.section: Exhibit 2 · Good basis, bad basis — the Shortest Vector Problem

exhibits.title: Step Gauss and LLL basis reduction
exhibits.action: Step, run or reset reduction on a skewed basis.
exhibits.outcome: Shows exact size-reduction and swap steps yielding a shorter, more useful basis.
exhibits.limits: Low-dimensional teaching inputs do not imply LLL breaks standard lattice schemes.
exhibits.section: Exhibit 3 · Turning a bad basis good: Gauss and LLL, step by step

exhibits.title: Solve noisy equations and short-kernel challenges
exhibits.action: Try a secret guess against LWE rows or a short nonzero vector against SIS constraints.
exhibits.outcome: Displays row-level residual noise and modular zero checks.
exhibits.limits: Small q and matrices are illustrative, not standard hardness parameters.
exhibits.section: Exhibit 4 · The same gap, spoken in Fq: LWE and SIS

exhibits.title: Encapsulate and tamper with a toy-Kyber ciphertext
exhibits.action: Run seeded key generation, encapsulation and decapsulation; alter the ciphertext and retry.
exhibits.outcome: Displays MLWE arithmetic and a teaching Fujisaki–Okamoto layer with implicit rejection behavior.
exhibits.limits: Tiny parameters and seeded reproducibility are not FIPS 203 ML-KEM or production key generation.
exhibits.section: Exhibit 5 · Standing on the gap: toy-Kyber and toy-Dilithium

exhibits.title: Sign and verify in a toy-Dilithium core
exhibits.action: Sign a message with rejection sampling, verify, then tamper with message or response z.
exhibits.outcome: Displays an MLWE-derived key and signing trace; altered signatures fail verification.
exhibits.limits: Tiny teaching parameters do not implement FIPS 204 ML-DSA.
exhibits.section: Exhibit 5 · Standing on the gap: toy-Kyber and toy-Dilithium

exhibits.title: Visible and Hidden LFSR
exhibits.action: Clock a visible five-stage register and collect bits from a new hidden degree-3–12 register.
exhibits.outcome: The visible transition and hidden output prefix establish the observation available to an attacker.
exhibits.limits: The hidden generator is a deliberately simple LFSR, not a modern stream cipher.

exhibits.title: Berlekamp–Massey Recurrence Fit
exhibits.action: Step through discrepancy updates or analyze up to 1,024 manually entered bits.
exhibits.outcome: The shortest fitted recurrence and candidate continuation are displayed from observed bits.
exhibits.limits: A manually entered sequence has no source generator here, so its prediction cannot be independently verified.

exhibits.title: Freeze and Check a Hidden Forecast
exhibits.action: Freeze 64 predicted bits, compare with the generator continuation, and try ambiguity or early-failure fixtures.
exhibits.outcome: The frozen forecast is evaluated against unseen bits, separating a prefix fit from verified prediction.

exhibits.title: Geffe Combiner Inspection
exhibits.action: Clock three disclosed registers and measure a 466-bit output correlation profile.
exhibits.outcome: The nonlinear selector combines LFSRs while output retains detectable correlations with component streams.

exhibits.title: Hidden Geffe State Recovery
exhibits.action: Start a hidden Geffe session or fixed fixture, run or cancel correlation recovery, and verify a frozen continuation.
exhibits.outcome: A worker searches R1 and R3 states, derives R2 constraints, and checks recovered state separately from output agreement.
exhibits.limits: A failed finite-budget scan is not proof of cryptographic security, and this attack is not claimed against SNOW 3G or ZUC.

exhibits.title: Trivium Initialization and Zero-Round Key Recovery
exhibits.action: Clock Trivium's 288-bit state, measure Berlekamp–Massey profiles and freeze 64-bit forecasts, then compare full initialization with a zero-round key-recovery experiment.
exhibits.outcome: The eSTREAM-vector-checked generator produces measured recurrence fits and forecast checks. A worker uses the public IV and 1,024 output bits to solve 66 equations and test 16,384 candidate keys before a separate hidden-key comparison.
exhibits.limits: The recovery equations target zero initialization, not the specified 1,152-round cipher; this is not a cube attack. Finite-prefix profiles and failed recovery do not certify security.

exhibits.title: Exact Four-Input Boolean Combiner Audit
exhibits.action: Edit any of the 16 outputs, inspect exact algebraic and correlation criteria, then run bounded recurrence, pair-state and single-state counterexamples.
exhibits.outcome: Parity remains linearly predictable, an order-one-resilient table exposes an order-two relation, and an algebraic-immunity-two table still yields its R4 state in the bounded scan.
exhibits.limits: Exactly four inputs are analyzed; Walsh probabilities assume independent uniform bits, while deterministic LFSR agreement is measured separately. The scans cover only 127 states or 105 state pairs, and algebraic immunity two does not exclude every fast algebraic relation.

exhibits.title: Toy-Oracle Cube Sum and Superpoly Recovery
exhibits.action: Exhaust four two-variable public-input cube faces across all eight teaching keys, recover each superpoly, then query three affine maxterms under one hidden toy key and verify the frozen candidate on four disjoint held-out rows.
exhibits.outcome: C12, C13 and C24 form a rank-three system that filters 8 → 4 → 2 → 1 to key 110. C34 remains a valid cube with a quadratic superpoly; dropping C24 leaves 001/110, and flipping C13 recovers 000 before held-outs reject it.
exhibits.section: Sum a cube, recover a superpoly
exhibits.limits: This is a separate three-secret/four-public degree-four toy oracle. Preprocessing enumerates all eight teaching keys; online recovery assumes repeated chosen-public-input queries under one fixed secret. C34 is a valid cube whose quadratic superpoly is not a maxterm and is excluded only from this bounded affine solve. The lesson executes no Trivium state or round and makes no attack or performance claim against reduced-round or full Trivium.

exhibits.title: Historical A5/1 Majority Clocking and Bounded State Completion
exhibits.action: Run the reverse-engineered BGW Kc/COUNT setup, derive the post-key, post-COUNT and post-100 checkpoints, reproduce both 114-bit burst values, predict a pre-clock majority decision, compare regular clocking, then enumerate 4,096 completions of a 52-disclosed/12-hidden post-warm-up state.
exhibits.outcome: An independent transcription agrees at three derived setup checkpoints and reproduces both BGW burst values; the first fixture step advances R1/R2. The bounded route filters to candidate 1425, whose frozen continuation matches 32 disjoint held-out bits before a separate controller-state comparison confirms the state. Sixteen observations leave 11 completions; for this fixture the regular-clock model leaves none after two bits, while corrupted observation 29 selects candidate 1409 before 11 held-out mismatches reject it.
exhibits.limits: The internal cipher definition is the reverse-engineered historical BGW version, not public modern-standard text. The state-completion exercise assumes an aligned 32-bit known keystream and extraordinary disclosure of 52 exact post-100 state bits; its 4,096 raw completions are not proved reachable from Kc setup. It is not a published A5/1 attack, does not recover Kc, processes no radio capture and says nothing about modern cellular encryption.

exhibits.title: Same lattice, different basis
exhibits.action: Change a basis and inspect lattice points and determinant.
exhibits.outcome: Shows two bases generate the same discrete lattice and fundamental area.
exhibits.limits: Low-dimensional visual example, not a cryptographic lattice parameter set.

exhibits.title: Gram–Schmidt stepper
exhibits.action: Advance through orthogonalization of basis vectors.
exhibits.outcome: Displays projections and the orthogonal component used in reduction.
exhibits.limits: Geometric display is low dimensional and does not implement high-dimensional numerical stabilization.

exhibits.title: LLL reduction step by step
exhibits.action: Choose a 2D, 3D or q-ary preset, set delta and step or autoplay size reduction and swaps.
