exhibits.outcome: Shows changed basis, Gram–Schmidt data and short vectors after LLL operations.
exhibits.limits: These are tiny instances for inspecting mechanics, not production lattice cryptanalysis.

exhibits.title: Recover toy LWE secret
exhibits.section: Exhibit 4 - Break a Toy LWE Instance
exhibits.action: Generate small LWE samples, vary n/q/noise/BKZ block size and run reduction; inspect primal embedding cancellation.
exhibits.outcome: Reports whether reduction actually exposes (-s,e,±1), separately from an exhaustive search teaching baseline.
exhibits.limits: Toy BKZ omits projected blocks, pruning and numerical engineering; Kyber-size action reports a bound rather than running a full attack.

exhibits.title: Rough BKZ parameter model
exhibits.action: Move n to compare illustrative block-size slope and published security context.
exhibits.outcome: Highlights why the simple beta formula gives wildly wrong absolute values for ML-KEM-size instances.
exhibits.limits: The formula is a rough toy slope, explicitly not a security estimate or extrapolation to production parameters.

exhibits.title: Merkle–Hellman and Algorithm SV
exhibits.section: Exhibit 6 - Knapsack Trapdoors and the Limits of Worst-Case Hardness
exhibits.action: Generate a validated toy Merkle–Hellman key, encrypt and trapdoor-decrypt selected bits, then give only the public weights, ciphertext and delta to the original Lagarias–Odlyzko Algorithm SV basis and the lab's existing LLL engine.
exhibits.outcome: Independently checked candidate rows recover the selected plaintext on suitable low-density toy instances; a reproducible in-budget counterexample shows that this bounded LLL route can also fail while trapdoor decryption succeeds.
exhibits.limits: Recovers message bits on selected toy instances, not the original or an equivalent trapdoor. It is the unscaled 1985 Algorithm SV embedding, not Shamir's attack or the later Coster variant; failures and the bounded seed sweep establish neither a density threshold nor security, and imply nothing about production lattice schemes.

exhibits.title: Guided reduction challenges
exhibits.action: Set up LLL swap, delta or toy-LWE challenges and test results in the preceding exhibits.
exhibits.outcome: Provides reproducible paths through basis reduction and attack controls.
exhibits.limits: Challenges reuse the toy engines and their limits.

exhibits.title: LMS stateful signing
exhibits.action: Sign multiple messages from a 32-leaf LMS tree and verify a signature.
exhibits.outcome: The next-index counter advances, leaves are consumed, and an authentication path verifies against the root.
exhibits.limits: The small h=5 tree makes exhaustion visible and is a teaching parameter.

exhibits.title: One-time leaf reuse forgery
exhibits.action: Enable forced leaf reuse, sign more than once with it and attempt a forged message.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect revealed one-time key material and whether the forged signature verifies after sufficient reuse.
exhibits.limits: The reuse switch deliberately bypasses the one-time signing rule.

exhibits.title: HSS rollover and capacity
exhibits.action: Sign one message or fill the current Level-2 tree to watch hierarchy rollover.
exhibits.outcome: See the Level-1 tree authenticate a fresh Level-2 public key and the finite capacity counter advance.
exhibits.limits: The hierarchy visualization abstracts full HSS transcript bytes; sizes are given separately.

exhibits.title: LMS and HSS deployment tradeoffs
exhibits.action: Read firmware-signing scenarios and expand the LMS/XMSS/SPHINCS+ comparison table.
exhibits.outcome: Compare state, signature size and signing context across stateful and stateless hash-based signatures.
exhibits.limits: The deployment panel is a sourced narrative and comparison, not an implementation of those systems.

exhibits.title: LMS Merkle Key
exhibits.action: Generate the 1024-leaf LMS key and inspect individual leaf state and root.
exhibits.outcome: Shows T[1] public root and the remaining one-time signing capacity.
exhibits.section: Exhibit 1: Merkle Tree of OTS Keys

exhibits.title: Signing Burns an Index
exhibits.action: Sign firmware twice, unsafely set q, and export secret state.
exhibits.outcome: Shows index consumption and why rollback or clones endanger one-time use.
exhibits.limits: Exported secret state is intentionally unsafe.

exhibits.title: LM-OTS Hash Chains
exhibits.action: Sign message A and compare reachable hash-chain depths needed for message B.
exhibits.outcome: Shows forward-only chain values and blocked positions from a single signature.
exhibits.section: Exhibit 3: Inside One OTS — the Winternitz Chain

exhibits.title: Merkle Authentication Path
exhibits.action: Inspect the path for a signed leaf.
exhibits.outcome: Shows sibling nodes and recomputation of the root compared to T[1].

exhibits.title: Live Reused-Index Forgery
exhibits.action: Choose leaked signatures from rolled-back copies and a target message, then mount the attack.
exhibits.outcome: Constructs a signature from revealed chain values and verifies it against the genuine public key.

exhibits.title: HSS Hierarchy
exhibits.action: Generate a two-level hierarchy and sign a boot manifest.
exhibits.outcome: Shows a root LMS key certifying a leaf-tree key and that tree signing the message.

exhibits.title: When Stateful Signatures Fit
exhibits.action: Follow the decision tree about signature count and reliable state management.
exhibits.outcome: Identifies firmware, boot chains, and controlled signers as fits for LMS/XMSS, and contrasts stateless SLH-DSA for unconstrained signing.

exhibits.title: Make a pair
exhibits.action: Generate an RSA key pair and inspect the public and private-key roles.
exhibits.outcome: The UI shows which key can be shared and which remains private before encryption or signing.
exhibits.limits: Browser lesson uses a controlled teaching workflow; key generation alone does not authenticate the key owner.

exhibits.title: Encrypt a note to you
exhibits.action: Write a note and encrypt under the generated public key.
exhibits.outcome: The ciphertext and byte counter appear, showing that anyone with the public key can lock a note to this key.
exhibits.limits: Encryption does not identify the sender; RSA-OAEP limits payload size and is not a bulk-data channel.

exhibits.title: Open it — and see what opening proves
exhibits.section: Open it — and see what opening proves
exhibits.action: Decrypt with the matching key, try an unrelated key and have a stranger encrypt to the public key.
exhibits.outcome: The correct owner opens both valid ciphertexts while the wrong key fails; sender identity is not established by public-key encryption.
exhibits.limits: Failure of a wrong-key trial is an illustration; ciphertext authenticity requires an additional mechanism.

exhibits.title: The same pair, a different job
exhibits.section: The same pair, a different job
exhibits.action: Sign a message with the private key, verify with the public key and tamper with the message.
exhibits.outcome: Verification succeeds for the intact message and fails after alteration.
exhibits.limits: A verified signature establishes control of the private key only; a separate trust path must bind that key to a person.

exhibits.title: How this demo checks its own results
exhibits.section: How this demo checks its own results
exhibits.action: Review the encryption/signature role comparison and pinned result checks.
exhibits.outcome: The panels summarize the four key jobs and compare known expected cryptographic outcomes.
exhibits.limits: Pinned checks validate examples, not the identity of a key holder or a general implementation audit.

exhibits.title: Race discrete-log algorithms on one target
exhibits.action: Choose a finite field or toy curve, target and method; run solvers under one calibrated operation and time cap.
exhibits.outcome: Reports independently checked exponents, partial leakage, attempts, memory and traces for brute force, BSGS, rho, kangaroo, Pohlig–Hellman and index calculus where applicable.
exhibits.limits: Small groups and capped attempts; a solver timing out is not evidence of security.

exhibits.title: Recover smooth-order exponents digit by digit
exhibits.action: Load smooth modulus, safe-prime or arena fixtures and run Pohlig–Hellman.
exhibits.outcome: Shows prime-power residues, partial leakage when a large factor is skipped, and CRT recombination.
exhibits.limits: Prime factors above the stated digit limit are skipped and reported as partial rather than recovered exponents.

exhibits.title: Compare generic table and walk methods
exhibits.action: Select BSGS, rho or kangaroo over finite-field and curve fixtures; inspect traces.
exhibits.outcome: Displays table crossing, cycle or interval trap and measured operations.
exhibits.limits: Toy curve and groups; interval search requires the exponent to lie in its selected interval.

exhibits.title: Build factor-base relations and solve fresh targets
exhibits.action: Choose bound, precompute relations modulo 1019, then solve a target using them.
exhibits.outcome: Displays matrix rank, elimination and an independently verified individual logarithm.
exhibits.limits: Elementary index calculus is finite-field specific; this is not a number field sieve implementation.

exhibits.title: Forge groups with chosen discrete-log weaknesses
exhibits.action: Choose smooth order, short exponent, small field or toy curve and measure all methods.
exhibits.outcome: Shows which algorithms solve a constructed target under equal budgets.
exhibits.limits: Another method may also succeed; weak toy examples are chosen for comparison.

exhibits.title: Compare field and subgroup size cost curves
exhibits.action: Inspect formula lines and plotted measured browser runs.
exhibits.outcome: Contrasts generic square-root scale with finite-field asymptotic estimates and key-length guidance.
exhibits.limits: NFS is formula only and uses different work units than browser group-operation counts.

exhibits.title: Recover a static exponent using a teaching subgroup oracle
exhibits.action: Submit subgroup elements to a raw exponentiation oracle and follow residue recovery.
exhibits.outcome: Shows actual oracle answers and a reconstructed exponent on bounded groups.
exhibits.limits: The deliberately exposed raw exponentiation oracle is not an authenticated key-exchange protocol; controls and groups are teaching fixtures.

exhibits.title: Sparse-Secret Hint Collapse
exhibits.action: Animate the headline hint-count comparison and change Hamming weight and dimension in the chart.
exhibits.outcome: The C·h·log₂h estimate and n/2 prior baseline move differently, showing the effect of sparsity.
exhibits.limits: These modeled paper-parameter counts are heuristic under the GAA, not a run of lattice reduction.

exhibits.title: Perfect and Approximate Hint Mechanism
exhibits.action: Read the LWE primer, compare perfect and noisy hints, and step through position-search logic.
exhibits.outcome: The worked explanation shows how clean leaked equations reduce uncertainty about a sparse secret.

exhibits.title: Toy Sparse-Secret Recovery
exhibits.action: Choose n, h, and seed; run recovery or sweep weights.
exhibits.outcome: A real sampled LWE instance and hints produce measured support and value costs, then compare the recovered vector with the planted secret and residual equations.
exhibits.section: Run it: recover a real secret from real hints
exhibits.limits: This is a bounded toy-parameter recovery, separate from the paper-scale heuristic estimates.

exhibits.title: Measure the Gaussian Approximation
exhibits.action: Change secret weight or seed and compare 4,000 sampled hint values with a predicted Gaussian and KS critical value.
exhibits.outcome: The chart and Kolmogorov–Smirnov result expose where very sparse distributions depart from the assumption.
exhibits.limits: A single 5% test can reject a true Gaussian by chance; sampled evidence is not a universal theorem.

exhibits.title: Leakage Scenario and Profile Calculator
exhibits.action: Choose a scenario, tune hints per operation and operation count, or paste period-by-period leakage numbers.
exhibits.outcome: The page compares accumulated hints with the selected heuristic threshold and charts periods and peaks.
exhibits.limits: Leak rate is an illustrative user input, not measured hardware leakage; risk verdicts are conditional estimates.

exhibits.title: Self-Check and Known Gaps
exhibits.action: Use the recall prompts and read sources, parameter boundaries, and stated limitations.
exhibits.outcome: The text distinguishes a calculated threshold, toy attack, and unmodeled physical leakage channel.

exhibits.title: CRC corruption versus MAC
exhibits.action: Send accidentally corrupted or deliberately changed payment, repair or force CRC, then submit the same change to an HMAC receiver.
exhibits.outcome: CRC catches accident but an attacker can recompute it; a secret-key HMAC rejects unless the key leaks.
exhibits.limits: A MAC does not encrypt or prevent replay; the key-leak checkbox deliberately removes its secrecy assumption.

exhibits.title: HMAC internals and verification
exhibits.action: Enter key and message, step through inner and outer pad hashes, compare bit changes and verify a candidate tag.
exhibits.outcome: Displays SHA-256 HMAC stages and accepted or rejected tags.
exhibits.limits: Avalanche display alone does not establish authentication security.

exhibits.title: AES-CMAC stages
exhibits.action: Compute, step and verify CMAC over entered bytes.
exhibits.outcome: Shows K1/K2 derivation from AES_K(0), final block treatment and tag verdict.
exhibits.limits: Key and message are educational inputs in the browser; tag security presumes a secret key.

exhibits.title: Poly1305 one-time key reuse
exhibits.action: Compute a tag, reuse one narrowed one-time key for two messages, recover candidates and submit a forged tag.
exhibits.outcome: The original authenticator accepts a forgery under the deliberately reused key.
exhibits.limits: The attack chooses only 16 free r bits for live search; full-size Poly1305 has about 106 free clamped bits and the demonstration is not a general recovery algorithm.

exhibits.title: Raw GHASH field toy
exhibits.action: Compute field products and run fixed-H linearity and recovery on raw single-block toy tags.
exhibits.outcome: Shows T=C·H algebra under XOR and recoverable H for distinct toy blocks.
exhibits.limits: Omits AAD, length block and nonce-derived mask; no complete AES-GCM forgery endpoint. Real one-block full GCM tag differences involve ΔC·H².

exhibits.title: Secret-prefix length extension
exhibits.action: Capture a bare SHA-256 secret-prefix tag, guess secret length, forge an appended message and submit to bare and HMAC receivers.
exhibits.outcome: The bare verifier accepts a correctly padded extension while HMAC rejects.
exhibits.limits: Requires a correct secret-length guess; it attacks a broken MAC construction, not SHA-256 collision resistance.

exhibits.title: Byte-by-byte tag comparison oracle
exhibits.action: Measure comparison timing illustrations and recover selected tag bytes using the longest-prefix signal.
exhibits.outcome: Shows a byte-wise search when an oracle reveals exact matched-prefix length.
exhibits.limits: The oracle directly exposes prefix length as a noise-free stand-in; browser wall-clock samples cannot resolve each byte this way.

exhibits.title: Variable-length raw CBC-MAC forgery
exhibits.action: Acquire one or two valid tags, splice a longer message and compare raw, agreed-length, prefixed-length and CMAC verifiers.
exhibits.outcome: Raw variable-length receiver accepts a forged tag; correctly scoped controls reject, and chaining traces show convergence.
exhibits.limits: Classical splice assumes variable-length messages and ordinary tag queries; fixed-length quantum-query attacks are outside scope.

exhibits.title: PMAC independent AES lanes
exhibits.action: Compute the exact byte-aligned Black–Rogaway 2002 PMAC, inspect Gray-code offsets and lane traces, alter content or position, and compare its dependency waves with CMAC.
exhibits.outcome: Full-byte verification accepts the genuine PMAC tag and rejects content, position and wrong-final-rule controls while exposing the exact AES work and modeled dependency span.
exhibits.limits: Implements byte-aligned messages and full tags only. Dependency waves are not a browser speed benchmark; the ordinary classical-query lesson does not implement Q2 oracle access, under which published attacks show PMAC is not secure.

exhibits.title: Boolean mask shares
exhibits.action: Edit the secret and draw a fresh random mask.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect two XOR shares separately and their recombination to the original byte.

exhibits.title: Masked AES S-box construction
exhibits.action: Switch between fresh and frozen masks, redraw masks and follow masked AES-128 known-answer checks.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect recomputed masked S-box table and matching plain versus masked ciphertext.
exhibits.section: The construction: first-order Boolean masking of AES-128

exhibits.title: Side-channel attack bench
exhibits.action: Choose protection mode, attack method, trace count and target bit; run an attack.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect ranked key guesses and convergence under modeled leakage for DPA, CPA and higher-order combinations.
exhibits.limits: Leakage traces are simulated; no physical device power measurements are taken.
exhibits.section: The bench: same attack, one switch

exhibits.title: Frozen mask failure
exhibits.action: Choose a fixed mask constant and run the distinguisher.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect key ranking and where a fixed mask undermines the intended protection.
exhibits.section: Act 4 — the mask that stopped moving

exhibits.title: What masking costs an attacker
exhibits.action: Select a recorded claim and reproduce the same seeded trace schedule.
exhibits.outcome: Compare traces to stable key-byte disclosure for unprotected, fresh-masked and frozen-mask variants, including second-order attacks and non-disclosure bands.
exhibits.limits: Counts come from a fixed-seed modeled Hamming-weight leakage process, not hardware traces.

exhibits.title: Masking proof-model boundary
exhibits.action: Read the Scope tab, the glitch note and the hardware-side-channel example.
exhibits.outcome: Identify why a probing-model result does not establish real-chip resistance when transient glitches can combine shares; the lab states this boundary without simulating glitches.
exhibits.limits: No physical leakage or glitch experiment is implemented.
exhibits.section: Scope: what is real here, and what is not

exhibits.title: Break the toy cipher
exhibits.action: Choose known-plaintext traffic, rounds, S-box, final-key nibble and approximation; run the attack or use starvation, added-round, and bad-relation presets.
exhibits.outcome: Sixteen candidate counters rank a guessed four-bit last-round subkey with success/failure verdict and screening context.
exhibits.limits: Only an 8-bit toy SPN and a four-bit subkey nibble are attacked; a successful run is not a modern cipher break.

exhibits.title: Inspect the cipher
exhibits.action: Slide an eight-bit plaintext value through the selected SPN.
exhibits.outcome: The encryption walkthrough updates and highlights the pre-final-round state that a nibble guess can partially undo.
exhibits.limits: Eight-bit classroom cipher; the walkthrough is not DES or AES.

exhibits.title: Inspect one S-box leak
exhibits.action: Select an input-mask/output-mask cell in the 16×16 linear approximation table.
exhibits.outcome: A detail view enumerates all sixteen S-box inputs and shows agreement counts and bias for the selected parity equation.
exhibits.limits: The statistics are exact for a four-bit teaching S-box; LAT cells are not direct attack success probabilities.

exhibits.title: Watch the bias compound
exhibits.action: Apply trail rounds one at a time and open the measured-versus-predicted bias detail.
exhibits.outcome: Per-round correlations and predicted aggregate bias shrink; a full-codebook measurement across keys exposes linear-hull reinforcement or cancellation.
exhibits.limits: The lemma assumes independent approximations; real whole-cipher bias can differ, as the panel itself measures.

exhibits.title: How much traffic do you need?
exhibits.action: Run complete attacks over sixty toy keys at several sample sizes, then compare repeated versus distinct known-plaintext sampling.
exhibits.outcome: Tables juxtapose the inverse-square single-counter prediction with measured key-ranking success, duplicate-input counts, Wilson intervals, and finite-population correction.
exhibits.limits: Measurements are over random keys of an 8-bit toy cipher; intervals describe across-key proportions, not guarantees for a key or a real cipher.
exhibits.section: How much traffic do you need?

exhibits.title: The pair-mate attack
exhibits.action: Read the comparison table of differential and linear cryptanalysis on the same toy SPN.
exhibits.outcome: The page contrasts attack access, measured relation and target information for the two cryptanalytic methods.
exhibits.limits: The comparison is explanatory; this section does not run a differential attack.

exhibits.title: Why the Linear Attack Works
exhibits.action: Select links in the mechanism chain from S-box imbalance to a final-round key-guess counter.
exhibits.outcome: The panel connects bias, piling-up and the measured distinguishing signal for the selected settings.
exhibits.limits: The attack is on an 8-bit toy SPN.

exhibits.title: Attack Fidelity and Limits
exhibits.action: Read the real-versus-not checklist for the cipher, LAT, exhaustive mask trail and the scope of key recovery.
exhibits.outcome: The legacy linear attack recovers four final-subkey bits; the differential–linear route ranks a final whitening byte, and neither is full key recovery or evidence about AES or DES.
exhibits.section: What this is, and what it does not prove
exhibits.limits: The differential-linear result is limited to a fixed three-round 8-bit Heys toy and observable whitening material; it does not recover the master key, attack the full four-round toy, reproduce DES, or attack production cryptography.

exhibits.title: Reduced-Round ChaCha Research Context
exhibits.action: Read the linked differential-linear research context.
exhibits.outcome: The note distinguishes paper cost estimates on reduced-round ChaCha from the full 20-round construction and from this toy demo.

exhibits.title: Two masks and a structural zero
exhibits.section: Look at more than one relation
exhibits.action: Choose one of three fixed toy keys and 16, 64, or all 256 distinct plaintexts; compare two mask relations and their joint outcomes with a no-trail pair.
exhibits.outcome: The table counts all four joint outcomes on the same traffic; a no-trail pair has zero full-codebook correlation for every toy round key, though a short sample can look biased.
exhibits.limits: Fixed 8-bit toy SPN. This is a counted two-mask observation and structural-zero example, not a full multidimensional key-recovery attack or an attack on production DES or ChaCha.

exhibits.title: Differential–Linear Composition and Subkey Ranking
exhibits.action: Choose a pair budget and run the fixed three-round differential–linear experiment, then compare its main path with a cancelling control.
exhibits.outcome: The lab computes the prefix DDT and signed suffix paths, measures the real pair statistic, ranks observable final-whitening material and checks the winner on unused pairs when a holdout exists.
exhibits.limits: Fixed three-round 8-bit Heys toy only. The exercise does not recover the 16-bit master key, attack the full four-round toy cipher, reproduce DES, attack production cryptography, or treat its deterministic 512-key sample as a random-population estimate.

exhibits.title: Oil Variables and Whipping Capacity
exhibits.action: Change MAYO parameter set and whipping factor k.
exhibits.outcome: Shows why one UOV-style copy lacks enough oil unknowns and how k copies change the linear system and byte cost.

exhibits.title: MAYO Key Generation
exhibits.action: Choose parameters and optional seed, then generate a compact keypair.
exhibits.outcome: Displays trapdoor and public key structure and sizes.
exhibits.section: Keygen: a needle small enough to shrink the haystack

exhibits.title: Whipped Signing Walkthrough
exhibits.action: Enter a message and step through hashing, vinegar choice, whipping, solving, and assembling a signature.
exhibits.outcome: Shows the unwhipped failure of unknowns, the solvable enlarged system, and verification of the result.
exhibits.section: Sign: watch too few oil variables become enough

exhibits.title: Verification and Forgery Attempts
exhibits.action: Verify a signature, tamper with message or signature, and try forgery controls.
exhibits.outcome: Computes public-map target comparison and reports genuine verifier acceptance or rejection.
exhibits.section: Verify: compute both sides, then try to fool it
exhibits.limits: Failed toy forgery attempts do not establish security of the scheme.

exhibits.title: UOV versus MAYO Byte Tradeoff
exhibits.action: Change historical round-two oil and whipping splits.
exhibits.outcome: Compares public-key and signature sizes as k and o change.
exhibits.section: UOV versus MAYO, by the byte
exhibits.limits: Historical parameters are retained for instruction, not current security guidance.

exhibits.title: Reference Vector and Preconditions
exhibits.action: Replay a shipped parameter-set vector and check parameter preconditions.
exhibits.outcome: Compares derived key/signature bytes with known answers and reports the necessary construction checks.
exhibits.section: The real thing: reference vectors and preconditions, checked here
exhibits.limits: Known-answer tests do not prove security or constant-time behavior.

exhibits.title: Random Guess and Wrong Oil-Space Forgery
exhibits.action: Guess complete signatures, replace the oil space entirely or by one nibble, and compare against the genuine-oil control.
exhibits.outcome: Shows public-map rejection of forged signatures even when altered-oil signing solves an internal linear system; random-guess hit rates are only a baseline.
exhibits.limits: A failed sample is not a security proof; the toy set can be guessed and the random-guess baseline is not the best known attack.

exhibits.title: MAYO Demonstration Boundary
exhibits.action: Read the scope cards identifying implemented signing code, vector tests, unbuilt UOV internals, side channels, and other multivariate candidates.
exhibits.outcome: Separates tested implementation behavior from structural security evidence and from algorithm-family comparisons.
exhibits.section: What this demo does and does not prove
exhibits.limits: The lab does not run cryptanalysis or prove MAYO security; implementation is not constant-time.

exhibits.title: Scramble a toy binary Goppa generator
exhibits.section: 1. Binary Goppa Codes and the McEliece Trapdoor
exhibits.action: Switch between Bob's structured generator G, the row-mixed S·G matrix, and the permuted public Gpub matrix.
exhibits.outcome: Displays the computed toy matrices and explanatory captions showing how obvious visual structure changes under row mixing and column permutation.
exhibits.limits: A GF(16), n=16 toy visual; a random-looking matrix display does not establish indistinguishability or structural-attack resistance of real Classic McEliece keys.

exhibits.title: Toy Goppa encapsulation, Patterson decoding and tampering
exhibits.action: Encapsulate, toggle ciphertext bits or exceed the correction radius, decapsulate with the trapdoor, and run the toy brute-force attacker comparison.
exhibits.outcome: Shows the ciphertext and error weight, Patterson decoding steps and success or failure, shared-secret agreement, and the toy attack's search result; successful decapsulation can key an AES-GCM message round-trip.
exhibits.limits: A n=16, t=2 teaching KEM with toy brute force, not the production Classic McEliece KEM, a practical attack on real parameters, or the 2026 structural preprint's recovery method.

exhibits.title: Classic McEliece Public Key Scale
exhibits.action: Compare the mceliece348864 public key with ML-KEM, RSA and a profile photo; scroll the first 8 KB of a generated illustrative hex dump.
exhibits.outcome: The specified 261,120-byte public key dominates the size chart, while the hex bytes only simulate the specified length.
exhibits.limits: The displayed key bytes are simulated, not a generated production McEliece key.

exhibits.title: Code-Based KEM Tradeoffs and Deployment
exhibits.action: Compare public keys, ciphertexts, archived cycle counts, assumptions and use-case guidance across Classic McEliece, ML-KEM, BIKE and HQC.
exhibits.outcome: The table separates specification size figures from historical benchmark runs and describes contemporary deployment guidance.
exhibits.limits: Cycle counts are archived Round 3 measurements on Haswell, not a same-version current deployment ranking.

exhibits.title: McEliece Cryptanalysis Timeline
exhibits.action: Read the history from the 1978 encryption construction through later Classic McEliece KEM, NIST selection and 2026 research.
exhibits.outcome: The panel distinguishes no known practical production-size break from heuristic structural key-recovery estimates and explains assumption diversity.

exhibits.title: 2 · Build a Tree
exhibits.action: Add or remove leaves, choose presets and inspect the tree root and node hashes.
exhibits.outcome: SHA-256 hashing builds a Merkle root that changes when leaf content changes.
exhibits.limits: A root is only trustworthy when obtained through an authenticated channel.

exhibits.title: 3 · Generate a Proof
exhibits.action: Select a leaf and inspect the sibling path to the displayed root.
exhibits.outcome: The proof includes sibling hashes and positions needed to recompute a membership root.
exhibits.limits: A proof establishes membership relative to a particular root, not the truth of leaf content.

exhibits.title: 4 · Verify a Proof
exhibits.action: Run or step verification, edit the proof, alter the leaf and compare an honest trusted root with a prover-supplied root.
exhibits.outcome: The recomputation trace passes valid paths and rejects inconsistent ones; supplying both proof and root defeats the trust conclusion.
exhibits.limits: A matching root chosen by the same untrusted prover gives no external authenticity guarantee.

exhibits.title: 5 · Why It Scales (Logarithmic Proofs)
exhibits.action: Choose tree sizes up to 4096 leaves and generate an actual proof.
exhibits.outcome: Compares proof path length with full-tree size to illustrate logarithmic growth.
exhibits.limits: This measures proof size in generated teaching trees, not a production log’s operational cost.

exhibits.title: 6 · Security: Why the 0x00 / 0x01 Prefixes Matter
exhibits.action: Run the leaf/node ambiguity attack and compare roots under odd-node duplication.
exhibits.outcome: The exhibits show how domain-separated hashing and specified tree shape avoid structural ambiguities.
exhibits.limits: The crafted cases illustrate specific design pitfalls, not SHA-256 collision discovery.

exhibits.title: 7 · Consistency (Append-Only) Proofs
exhibits.action: Prove a larger tree extends a smaller one, then rewrite, delete or reorder an early entry.
exhibits.outcome: The consistency verification accepts an append-only history and detects selected rewritten histories.
exhibits.limits: Only a trusted old root anchors the append-only claim; a prover can lie if both roots are untrusted.

exhibits.title: 8 · Verify a REAL Certificate Transparency Entry
exhibits.section: 8 · Verify a REAL Certificate Transparency Entry
exhibits.action: Verify a bundled certificate-transparency inclusion proof and flip one certificate bit.
exhibits.outcome: The original leaf validates against the pinned log root; the modified certificate fails recomputation.
exhibits.limits: The fixture and root are pinned; this does not query a live CT log or validate certificate issuance.

exhibits.title: 10 · Recap: The Two Proofs, Side by Side
exhibits.section: 10 · Recap: The Two Proofs, Side by Side
exhibits.action: Compare inclusion and consistency roles and read application examples.
exhibits.outcome: The recap distinguishes membership from append-only history across Bitcoin, Git and CT examples.
exhibits.limits: Context and self-check do not implement the full cited external systems.

exhibits.title: Build a tree, prove inclusion and tamper with a leaf
exhibits.action: Enter 2–16 leaves, build a tree, select a leaf, generate and walk a proof, then tamper.
exhibits.outcome: Shows SHA-256 root changes and recomputation of a logarithmic inclusion path.
exhibits.limits: Proof verification assumes a trustworthy expected root; the demo’s own root is used here.

exhibits.title: Compare odd-leaf conventions and duplicate-transaction malleability
exhibits.action: Switch RFC 6962 promotion and Bitcoin duplication, rebuild and inspect the advanced example.
exhibits.outcome: Shows a duplicate-last-leaf tree ambiguity associated with CVE-2012-2459.
exhibits.limits: The odd-node mode changes only after rebuilding; the vulnerability is structural, not a SHA-256 collision.

exhibits.title: Forge an inclusion proof without leaf/node prefixes
exhibits.action: Switch naive hashing and RFC 6962 prefixes and inspect a forged 64-byte leaf and ordinary verifier result.
exhibits.outcome: Without prefixes the internal-node bytes can be reinterpreted as a leaf, whereas separated hashes reject the forgery.
exhibits.limits: The attack targets a naive tree with overlapping leaf and internal hash input spaces; it is not a SHA-256 collision.
exhibits.section: Section B2: The second-preimage attack, mounted

exhibits.title: Verify a Merkle consistency proof against changing history
exhibits.action: Select append, rewrite, delete or reorder history and inspect reconstructed old and new roots.
exhibits.outcome: Honest append proves continuity; changed earlier entries fail verification even when the new log is larger.
exhibits.limits: The auditor must retain the old trusted root; proof of one log view does not rule out split views.

exhibits.title: Calculate inclusion proof size at varying leaf counts
exhibits.action: Enter leaf count and compare proof-size rows and membership approaches.
exhibits.outcome: Shows logarithmic tree depth and hash counts for Merkle inclusion.
exhibits.limits: Calculator reports size scaling, not actual hashing time or a proof of data availability.
exhibits.section: Section D: Proof Size and Efficiency

exhibits.title: Follow leaf hashes to a root and inclusion path
exhibits.section: Section A: What is a Merkle Tree?
exhibits.action: Read structure, prefix separation and path diagram.
exhibits.outcome: A leaf change propagates to root; a sibling hash per level lets a verifier recompute membership.
exhibits.limits: Four-leaf diagram; live hashing is in Section B.

exhibits.title: Relate Git object IDs to Merkle-style roots
exhibits.action: Read the Git system card.
exhibits.outcome: Changing a file changes its blob, tree and commit IDs through content addressing.
exhibits.limits: Context card; no Git repository is hashed in the lab.

exhibits.title: Relate Bitcoin transaction root to light-client inclusion
exhibits.action: Read the Bitcoin system card.
exhibits.outcome: A block header commits to transactions by Merkle root and SPV checks a logarithmic proof.
exhibits.limits: Context card; no live Bitcoin proof validation.

exhibits.title: Relate Certificate Transparency to signed tree heads
exhibits.action: Read the CT system card.
exhibits.outcome: Signed tree heads and audit proofs commit to append-only certificate history with distinct leaf/node prefixes.
exhibits.limits: Context card; local consistency proof is separate.

exhibits.title: MGM Seal and Open
exhibits.action: Select Magma or Kuznyechik, enter key, ICN, plaintext, and AAD, then seal or alter ciphertext, AAD, or tag before opening.
exhibits.outcome: The receiver verifies the tag before releasing plaintext, so altered inputs are rejected.
exhibits.limits: Teaching implementation in browser memory without constant-time or side-channel guarantees.

exhibits.title: One GHASH Subkey versus Per-Block MGM Coefficients
exhibits.action: Fold authenticated blocks one at a time or show the whole tag computation.
exhibits.outcome: A table contrasts powers of one H in GCM-shaped arithmetic with fresh per-position H_i values in MGM.
exhibits.section: One H, or one H per block
exhibits.limits: The GCM-shaped comparison uses the selected cipher and field; it is not WebCrypto AES-GCM.

exhibits.title: RFC 9058 Intermediate-Value Checks
exhibits.action: Choose an RFC example and run computed values beside the published intermediates.
exhibits.outcome: The table reports agreement for internal counters, blocks, and tags rather than checking only the final tag.

exhibits.title: MGM Nonce-Reuse Keystream Exposure
exhibits.action: Encrypt two messages under one ICN or give the second its own ICN as a control.
exhibits.outcome: Ciphertext XOR and known first plaintext recover the second message when the tuple repeats, even though both tags verify.
exhibits.limits: This panel demonstrates confidentiality loss, not MGM tag forgery.

exhibits.title: 64-Bit versus 128-Bit Usage Bound
exhibits.action: Move a per-key volume slider and inspect Magma and Kuznyechik bound values and TLS rekey table.
exhibits.outcome: The same RFC advantage formula diverges with block size, motivating rekey limits.
exhibits.limits: This is a bound calculation and RFC 9367 table, not an implemented TLS key schedule.

exhibits.title: Magma S-Box Parameter Choice
exhibits.action: Swap two param-Z entries and encrypt the fixed reference block, then restore the standardized table.
exhibits.outcome: Changing the substitution table changes ciphertext despite the same network, key, and block.
exhibits.section: Magma's S-box: a choice the old standard left open
exhibits.limits: The swapped table is hypothetical and is not a validated historical GOST parameter set.

exhibits.title: MISTY1 and KASUMI on one block
exhibits.section: Give both designs the same bytes
exhibits.action: Enter a 128-bit key and 64-bit block, compare encryption or decryption and load an RFC 2994 example.
exhibits.outcome: Shows outputs, round-trip checks and pinned known-answer status for both eight-round implementations.
exhibits.limits: Raw single-block demonstration; no secure mode, authentication or mobile network stack is implemented.

exhibits.title: Inspect changed cipher components
exhibits.section: Eight rounds stayed. The proof boundary did not.
exhibits.action: Select key schedule, FI or FL in paired MISTY1 and KASUMI diagrams.
exhibits.outcome: Explains how linear schedule, modified nonlinear stage and round placement alter the proof boundary.
exhibits.limits: The attack depends on aligned changes rather than one isolated edited component.

exhibits.title: Seven-round related-key quartet
exhibits.action: Choose a pinned right-quartet fixture, run seven-round related-key boomerang stages and perturb one key relation.
exhibits.outcome: Computes KASUMI quartet outcome against a MISTY1 reduced-core control.
exhibits.limits: Requires access to four related-key encryption/decryption oracles and pinned right quartets; this is a reduced seven-round distinguisher, not a full network compromise.

exhibits.title: Full MISTY1 theoretical context
exhibits.section: Full MISTY1 also fell, but only in theory
exhibits.action: Read later attack scope and work-factor context.
exhibits.outcome: Separates theoretical full-round results from the live seven-round experiment.
exhibits.limits: No full MISTY1 attack is executed.

exhibits.title: MLS group membership and messages
exhibits.action: Add, remove or update a member, then send an application message from a leaf.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect epoch changes, TreeKEM path updates and AES-GCM sealed messages in the transcript.
exhibits.limits: Buttons stage and immediately commit proposals; commits and application messages are unsigned in this teaching subset.

exhibits.title: Forward secrecy walkthrough
exhibits.action: Advance a scenario to compare old and new message keys after ratchet and epoch changes.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect that discarded prior keys are unavailable to the current state in the modeled group.
exhibits.limits: The group and delivery service live in one browser process.

exhibits.title: Post-compromise recovery
exhibits.action: Mark a member’s epoch secret exposed, then make a fresh Update and test recovery.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect key rotation after compromise and whether the old secret derives the new epoch material.

exhibits.title: Removed member access
exhibits.action: Remove a leaf and try to open subsequent ciphertext using its snapshot.
exhibits.outcome: See access fail for the removed participant after an epoch-changing commit.

exhibits.title: Post-quantum MLS draft comparison
exhibits.action: Switch among post-quantum MLS draft choices in the comparison panel.
exhibits.outcome: Compare the conceptual changes against the current classical TreeKEM teaching path.
exhibits.limits: The PQ draft panel is explanatory; the interactive group mechanics use X25519.

exhibits.title: MLS versus pairwise ratchets
exhibits.action: Read the Concepts explainer and compare the seven-row X3DH/Double Ratchet versus MLS table.
exhibits.outcome: Contrast pairwise sender work with TreeKEM path updates, epoch schedules and group recovery.
exhibits.limits: Complexity and security rows compare protocol architectures; only the MLS teaching subset runs in this browser.

exhibits.title: MLS group lifecycle tour
exhibits.action: Advance the guided steps through add, send, update, convergence, removal, lockout and compromise recovery.
exhibits.outcome: Watch the same live group state, tree and epoch evolve through the narrated sequence.
exhibits.limits: Tour orchestrates the teaching subset; commits and application messages lack credential signatures.

exhibits.title: Live MLS epoch key schedule
exhibits.action: After an Update, reveal the Key Schedule panel and inspect two input secrets and labelled derived outputs.
exhibits.outcome: See init_secret and TreeKEM commit_secret feed HKDF into epoch, encryption and next-init material.
exhibits.limits: Only eight-byte prefixes of live secrets are shown; application commits are unsigned in this teaching subset.

exhibits.title: TreeKEM convergence proof
exhibits.action: Commit an Update and derive the root secret independently as each member.
exhibits.outcome: Compare ratcheting by the committer against HPKE decryption by other members and match the shared root to the epoch commit_secret.
exhibits.limits: All members execute in one browser process, with an in-memory delivery service.

exhibits.title: MLS membership and churn presets
exhibits.action: Run the one-click add, remove, compromise and five-update churn stories.
exhibits.outcome: Watch real commits alter tree, epoch, narration and key schedule with each chosen scenario.
exhibits.limits: The PCS preset marks compromise; the separate PCS panel performs the healing Update.

exhibits.title: MLS concepts and proposal boundary
exhibits.action: Expand the explanations of forward secrecy, recovery, tree scaling and proposal versus commit.
exhibits.outcome: Distinguish a staged Proposal from the Commit that changes group epoch, and inspect which MLS pieces this teaching subset omits.

exhibits.title: Security Contract and Oracle Scenarios
exhibits.action: Select a deployment scenario and compare its encryption/decryption oracle access.
exhibits.outcome: Shows which assumed adversary model applies and whether forgery queries are available.

exhibits.title: Decryption Oracle Candidate Elimination
exhibits.action: Try the same candidate list without and with a decryption oracle.
exhibits.outcome: Shows ciphertext-only observations leave candidates unresolved while acceptance of forged ciphertext narrows them.
exhibits.limits: Uses a reduced toy instance, not an attack at full HiAE parameters.

exhibits.title: Toy HiAE Seed Recovery and Forgery
exhibits.action: Generate a reduced four-block instance, observe a zero-block keystream, search its small seed space, and query an exposed oracle.
exhibits.outcome: Reports recovered key candidates and accepted forgery only in an oracle-enabled scenario.
exhibits.limits: Exhaustive 16-bit toy seed search is distinct from Hu’s full-size differential technique.

exhibits.title: AESL Differential Step
exhibits.action: Run a fresh differential pair through AESL and inspect active S-box constraints.
exhibits.outcome: Counts DDT solutions and measures one-step candidate reduction against actual output.
exhibits.section: Run the paper's technique — the differential step, measured
exhibits.limits: Runs one AESL call with four active S-boxes, not the full attack or its reported complexity.

exhibits.title: HiAE Security Contract
exhibits.action: Read the model’s adversary conditions and distinguish full HiAE from the reduced toy.
exhibits.outcome: Separates a stated nonce-respecting claim from the extended decryption-oracle setting and shows which state representation the browser simulates.
exhibits.limits: The 4-block toy cannot substantiate a full 256-bit key-recovery complexity.

exhibits.title: HiAE Cryptanalysis and Response
exhibits.action: Review the attack papers and designer response, including the explicit claims each result does and does not establish.
exhibits.outcome: Separates extended-model cryptanalysis, computational cost, and the intended-model security claim.
exhibits.limits: This panel recounts papers; the cited full attack complexities are not executed in the browser.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 1 — The Idea
exhibits.action: Reshuffle three visual secret shares and inspect the partial-view analogy.
exhibits.outcome: The cards illustrate splitting a witness so one hidden view does not directly reveal it.
exhibits.limits: An analogy; it does not by itself establish zero knowledge.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 2 — MPC Party Simulation
exhibits.action: Split a witness, simulate parties, challenge a hidden view and verify revealed views.
exhibits.outcome: The transcript shows commitments, party computations and whether the opened views are consistent.
exhibits.limits: A small educational protocol; one opened round has nonzero soundness error.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 2b — Play a Cheating Prover
exhibits.action: Make one or 100 cheating attempts and compare acceptance counts.
exhibits.outcome: The trial tally illustrates the per-round probability of a malformed witness escaping a partial-view challenge.
exhibits.limits: Finite Monte Carlo runs vary; this toy soundness experiment is not a production parameter estimate.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 3 — Fiat-Shamir Signature
exhibits.action: Run the noninteractive challenge derivation for a message, then modify the message.
exhibits.outcome: The transcript-derived challenge and verification change with the signed message.
exhibits.limits: The demonstration uses small parameters and does not claim standard-level signature security.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 4 — Toy PERK
exhibits.action: Generate a toy PERK keypair, sign and verify a message, and reveal or hide the private permutation.
exhibits.outcome: Shows a different underlying relation, H·π(y)=b, in the same MPCitH wrapper and displays signature-size components.
exhibits.limits: Toy parameters make the relation inspectable; not a production PERK implementation.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 5 — Security Diversity
exhibits.action: Read the alternative hard-problem families and implementation leakage note.
exhibits.outcome: The panel distinguishes the reusable MPCitH proof wrapper from the assumptions and side channels of a chosen instantiation.
exhibits.limits: External leakage research is described as context; FAEST and SDitH are not implemented or attacked here.

exhibits.title: Sign and verify with an oil-and-vinegar trapdoor
exhibits.action: Choose parameter preset and message; generate key, sign, verify, flip a signature byte or edit the message.
exhibits.outcome: Shows vinegar guesses and linear oil solve, then acceptance or rejection under public quadratic equations.
exhibits.limits: Tiny educational parameters do not provide a secure signature scheme.

exhibits.title: Recover balanced oil subspace and forge a signature
exhibits.action: Run the public-key-only attack against balanced and unbalanced toy instances.
exhibits.outcome: Displays measured attack effort and verifier verdict for the forged signature, contrasting parameter choices.
exhibits.limits: Only v=o=3 or 4 balanced toy instances are attacked; this does not scale to deployed UOV parameters.
exhibits.section: Recover the Trapdoor and Forge a Signature

exhibits.title: Inspect the Rainbow cryptanalysis story
exhibits.action: Follow the steps of the documented attack narrative.
exhibits.outcome: Explains why Rainbow’s layered multivariate structure did not survive cryptanalysis.
exhibits.limits: Historical explanation, not an implementation of the Rainbow attack.

exhibits.title: Compare signature sizes and family lineage
exhibits.action: Inspect key/signature size table and oil-and-vinegar family cards.
exhibits.outcome: Shows the large public-key tradeoff and variant history.
exhibits.limits: Table values are illustrative references and do not certify present-day scheme recommendations.

exhibits.title: Weighted MuSig2 Key Aggregation
exhibits.action: Change signer count, make fresh or identical key sets, reverse order, or apply KeySort.
exhibits.outcome: Live BIP-327 coefficients and a small finite-curve view show how weighting changes the aggregate key.
exhibits.section: Why you cannot just add public keys
exhibits.limits: The 7-bit curve picture is a separate teaching analogue of the 256-bit calculation.

exhibits.title: Rogue-Key Attack and Coefficient Defense
exhibits.action: Run a naive last-key cancellation attack, then try the same attack under BIP-327 weighting or enter a candidate rogue key.
exhibits.outcome: A solo BIP-340 signature verifies under naive aggregate addition but the protected construction blocks the same manipulation.
exhibits.section: The attack that broke naive multisig

exhibits.title: One-Nonce Steering and Two-Nonce Defense
exhibits.action: Choose an attacker target aggregate nonce and run one-nonce, two-nonce, and advanced forgery controls.
exhibits.outcome: The experiments expose last-mover steering and why MuSig2 binds two nonce halves with a challenge derived from their aggregate.
exhibits.section: Why two nonces, and not one
exhibits.limits: Some advanced searches use deliberately reduced challenge widths; their cost does not describe a full-width attack.

exhibits.title: Full MuSig2 Signing Session
exhibits.action: Change signers, message, key sorting, or a partial-signature tamper and advance the signing sequence.
exhibits.outcome: The aggregate 64-byte BIP-340 signature verifies after individual partial checks when honest and rejects tampering.
exhibits.limits: All listed signers must participate; nonce storage and timing side channels are outside the browser demonstration.

exhibits.title: BIP-327 Official Vector Checks
exhibits.action: Read live accepting and malformed-input results against specification vectors.
exhibits.outcome: Expected and computed bytes plus rejection reasons provide evidence of protocol logic conformance.
exhibits.section: Checked against the specification’s own bytes
exhibits.limits: Vector agreement does not establish side-channel safety or secure nonce persistence.

exhibits.title: Predict the fourth decimal output
exhibits.action: Apply the public multiply-add recurrence to three shown outputs and enter a fourth guess.
exhibits.outcome: Checks prediction of the entire state exposed by the toy generator.
exhibits.limits: A four-digit toy; its predictability does not characterize every generator.

exhibits.title: Recover java.util.Random state
exhibits.action: Generate two nextInt outputs, search all 65,536 hidden low bits, or run the 2^22 nextDouble first-half search.
exhibits.outcome: Shows actual candidate counts and matching 48-bit states from Java’s LCG formula.
exhibits.limits: Matches Java SE 21 Random’s public recurrence; this is state recovery, not a guess of a weak seed.

exhibits.title: 512-bit truncated LCG lattice
exhibits.section: 3 · Too many hidden bits to enumerate
exhibits.action: Run an instance or 200 multiplier trials using exact 2D reduction and nearest-plane search.
exhibits.outcome: Reports a prediction only when a unique candidate state satisfies the observed truncated outputs.
exhibits.limits: Book-sized illustrative LCG, not a deployed generator; ambiguous recoveries do not yield a prediction.

exhibits.title: Predict one future bit
exhibits.action: Choose toy, Java, 512-bit LCG or RFC 8439 ChaCha20 control and play independent trials.
exhibits.outcome: Displays win rate for this specific predictor and random fallback on unresolved recovery.
exhibits.limits: One predictor’s near-half win rate is not a security proof quantifying over all efficient predictors.

exhibits.title: Looks random but predictable
exhibits.action: Inspect frequency and run counts beside recurrence-based predictions.
exhibits.outcome: Shows why superficial output statistics can coexist with predictable state.
exhibits.limits: Illustrative checks are not NIST SP 800-22 statistical tests.

exhibits.title: Noise pattern selector
exhibits.action: Select among the named handshake patterns and inspect message sequence and properties.
exhibits.outcome: See how the chosen pattern changes DH tokens, identity exposure and handshake transcript.

exhibits.title: Noise handshake walkthrough
exhibits.action: Step each message, inspect token-by-token byte blocks and both parties’ state, and predict hash or key-schedule updates.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect real chained hash, chaining key and cipher-key transitions through the selected handshake.
exhibits.limits: The downloadable session-state JSON contains private keys and secrets; it is a teaching export, not a shareable public transcript.

exhibits.title: Bidirectional transport and rekey
exhibits.action: Encrypt and send in both directions, rekey either sender cipher and start a fresh session.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect ciphertext, authentication and synchronized receive behavior under transport keys.

exhibits.title: Noise misuse experiments
exhibits.action: Run bit flip, static-key swap, nonce reuse, PSK mismatch, replay and after-the-fact key compromise cases.
exhibits.outcome: Compare authentication failures and misuse consequences under the chosen handshake pattern.
exhibits.limits: Some attack effects depend on the selected pattern and whether it uses a PSK.

exhibits.title: Noise pattern comparison
exhibits.action: Select patterns side by side and click property cells.
exhibits.outcome: Compare authentication, forward secrecy, identity hiding and message count with a per-pattern explanation.

exhibits.title: WireGuard packet mapping
exhibits.action: Inspect IKpsk2 tokens and hover labeled initiation and response packet blocks.
exhibits.outcome: Map Noise tokens onto WireGuard packet fields, timestamp replay protection and outside-Noise MACs.
exhibits.limits: The runnable Noise lab uses browser AES-256-GCM and SHA-256; WireGuard uses ChaChaPoly and BLAKE2s.

exhibits.title: Step the modular entropy multiplier
exhibits.section: The modular entropy multiplier, one step at a time
exhibits.action: Press Step the circuit, Step 8 times, or Reset.
exhibits.outcome: The analog-state marker moves through threshold, fold/stretch rule and emitted bit strip; a deterministic seeded model makes adjacent-bit dependence visible.
exhibits.limits: Transcribed simulation from vendor circuit; no connected physical device, and its design rate is not a measured entropy estimate.

exhibits.title: Design rate and assessed estimate
exhibits.section: A design rate is not a measurement
exhibits.action: Compare the device design log2(K) rate with the pinned assessment and driver ceiling.
exhibits.outcome: Separately labeled theoretical and native-tool-on-model figures expose the gap.
exhibits.limits: Native assessment concerns one model-generated million-sample file, not a hardware certification or live calculation.

exhibits.title: Inspect sample bytes
exhibits.action: Select a shipped fixture or local file, choose layout and symbol width, then Analyse.
exhibits.outcome: Worker computes balance, runs, repeated blocks, lag autocorrelation and byte/bit previews.
exhibits.limits: Descriptive statistics are not SP 800-90B entropy estimates; uploaded files stay local and have an input cap.

exhibits.title: Pinned non-IID assessment
exhibits.action: Select a shipped fixture and inspect the minimum, per-bit conversion, branch rule and individual non-IID estimators.
exhibits.outcome: Recorded native SP 800-90B assessment shows the binding estimator and distinctions among bits per sample and bits per bit; custom files show Not Run.
exhibits.limits: No browser estimator for changed/uploaded bytes; a figure applies only to its exact hashed fixture and recorded native run.

exhibits.title: Compare two assessment implementations
exhibits.action: Select one of seven published synthetic inputs.
exhibits.outcome: Pinned NIST-fork and Theseus values for ten estimators, absolute differences and overall minima are displayed with input hashes.
exhibits.limits: Recorded native runs only; six synthetic model seeds are not a confidence interval or hardware entropy claim.

exhibits.title: IID assumption decision
exhibits.action: Select a specified source scenario and reveal the explanation.
exhibits.outcome: Explains that bias can coexist with IID, while memory, drift, and a public alternating rule defeat inferences from balanced histograms.
exhibits.limits: Specified thought-experiment models; the answer is not inferred from a finite statistical test.

exhibits.title: Faults versus reported estimate
exhibits.section: What the faults did to the reported figure
exhibits.action: Compare clean and deliberately faulty model fixtures and inspect estimator-by-estimator differences.
exhibits.outcome: Some faults raise the reported minimum despite other estimators dropping; pinned native results and fixture provenance are shown.
exhibits.limits: Precomputed model fixtures; the browser does not reassess edited/custom files.

exhibits.title: Reproduce predictable counter-hash
exhibits.section: The experiment: a stream everyone can predict
exhibits.action: Regenerate the first 64 bytes from the published SHA-256 counter construction.
exhibits.outcome: Regenerated bytes match a predictable fixture whose pinned assessment looks high, demonstrating sample statistics cannot prove unknown source entropy.
exhibits.limits: SHA-256 computation is real; the high assessment is a pinned native result on a published deterministic file, not a genuine secret entropy claim.

exhibits.title: Output multiplier entropy ledger
exhibits.section: The driver’s sponge, and its output multiplier
exhibits.action: Move outputMultiplier slider and inspect output bits versus fixed input entropy budget and sponge output.
exhibits.outcome: More output bytes dilute the chargeable entropy per output bit while the input budget bar stays fixed.
exhibits.limits: Ledger uses a design/driver ceiling rather than measuring raw hardware entropy; initial sponge input may be a labeled placeholder until model bytes load.

exhibits.title: Before and after conditioning
exhibits.section: The same source, measured before and after conditioning
exhibits.action: Compare pinned raw and conditioned fixture assessments.
exhibits.outcome: The measured per-output-bit number rises after conditioning although the modeled source did not gain entropy.
exhibits.limits: Pinned native measurements of model-generated streams; a high conditioned-output figure cannot establish source entropy.

exhibits.title: Public pad decryption
exhibits.section: A public pad is not a pad
exhibits.action: Enter a message and pad length, then Encrypt, then decrypt.
exhibits.outcome: Real SHA-256-generated public pad and XOR ciphertext recover the message without a secret; short pad reveals an uncovered tail.
exhibits.limits: The pad construction is deliberately public and predictable; this is an insecurity demonstration, not secure OTP use.

exhibits.title: Two-time-pad XOR leak
exhibits.section: Used twice, the pad cancels itself
exhibits.action: Enter two messages and reuse the same pad once.
exhibits.outcome: The two ciphertexts XOR to the XOR of the plaintext prefixes, with the pad canceling.
exhibits.limits: Demo uses a public deterministic pad and the common length prefix; the algebraic cancellation holds for any reused XOR pad.

exhibits.title: From Source Evidence to RBG Construction
exhibits.section: Connect source evidence to RBG construction
exhibits.action: Read the SP 800-90C RBG1, RBG2, RBG3 and RBGC context after the six tabs.
exhibits.outcome: The text connects source health and entropy accounting to construction classes without certifying the browser model.

exhibits.title: Entropy Assessment Scope
exhibits.section: What this lab does not establish
exhibits.action: Read the limits list after the source, sample, assessment, break, conditioning and pad exhibits.
exhibits.outcome: The caveats bound what the in-browser source model, fixtures and assessment can establish.

exhibits.title: Compute exact parity bias with source memory
exhibits.section: Does XOR remove bias when the source remembers?
exhibits.action: Choose independent, repeating or alternating binary sources, initial law and block length; compute exact parity probabilities.
exhibits.outcome: The signed transition kernel exposes dependence missed by multiplying marginal biases, including even/odd behavior, distance from a fair bit and the first-order bound.
exhibits.limits: Analytic homogeneous first-order binary model with declared probabilities; not a hardware measurement, source assessment, independent-block certificate or hidden/unbounded-memory guarantee.

exhibits.title: The XOR reveal
exhibits.action: Encrypt two editable messages under one key and reused nonce, then enter and slide a guessed crib.
exhibits.outcome: See C1 XOR C2 equal P1 XOR P2 and recover matching bytes of the second message without the encryption key.
exhibits.limits: The learner can see and edit both teaching plaintexts; a real attacker needs an accurate guess about one message.
exhibits.section: The XOR reveal — recover a message you were never given

exhibits.title: Same mistake, four outcomes
exhibits.action: Run fresh-versus-reused IV/nonce scenarios for AES-CTR, AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305 and AES-CBC.
exhibits.outcome: Read primitive return values separately from security verdicts and a running table of plaintext exposure, forgery and key recovery; CBC reuse reveals prefix equality while AEAD reuse enables nonce-specific forgery.
exhibits.limits: The scoreboard records the demonstrated scenario and explicitly does not claim recovery of the AES or ChaCha20 encryption key; CBC and CTR supply no authentication.

exhibits.title: CBC: different IVs can still leak
exhibits.action: Run the chosen-plaintext predictable-IV case against a control where plaintext is committed before a fresh IV is drawn.
exhibits.outcome: Observe identical first ciphertext blocks under distinct, predictable IVs when P2=P1 XOR IV1 XOR IV2, compared with the random-IV control.
exhibits.limits: Controlled first-block equality only; no AES key or unknown-plaintext recovery, and no claim of a CBC padding oracle.
exhibits.section: CBC: different IVs can still leak

exhibits.title: Run the AES-GCM mask cancellation on fresh bytes
exhibits.section: AES-GCM: the mask cancels, leaving a polynomial in H
exhibits.action: Open the GCM derivation and press Run it on real bytes and cancel.
exhibits.outcome: See two computed tags, independently derived masks, the recovered GHASH subkey H, and checks that both masks match and the tag-difference equation holds.
exhibits.limits: The worked derivation uses two equal-length single-block ciphertexts and one reused nonce; it recovers H and a nonce-specific tag mask, not the AES key.

exhibits.title: Run the Poly1305 pad cancellation on fresh numbers
exhibits.section: ChaCha20-Poly1305: the one-time key is reused, so (r, s) leaks
exhibits.action: Open the ChaCha20-Poly1305 derivation and press Run it on real numbers and cancel.
exhibits.outcome: See computed tags, the same additive term s derived independently from each, recovered clamped r, and checks of the subtraction identity.
exhibits.limits: The two probes and their tags are constructed for this educational recovery; the ChaCha20 encryption key is not recovered, and the forgery applies under the reused nonce.

exhibits.title: Explore random-nonce collision probabilities
exhibits.section: Random 96-bit nonces and the birthday bound
exhibits.action: Choose a 32-, 64- or 96-bit random nonce space and vary the message-count slider.
exhibits.outcome: Read a recalculated chance of at least one repeat and the approximate message count for a 50 percent collision chance.
exhibits.limits: The code uses the exponential birthday approximation for independent uniformly random nonces; the slider is not a test of any deployed nonce generator or counter persistence.

exhibits.title: Nonce Uniqueness and Threat Model
exhibits.section: What is a nonce, and why does reuse matter?
exhibits.action: Read the opening definition and reused-nonce premise before running the ciphers.
exhibits.outcome: The primer frames mode-specific requirements for keystream and authentication behavior.

exhibits.title: Counters That Rewind
exhibits.action: Read how restored VM snapshots, forks and rolled-back containers repeat a long-lived key’s counter values.
exhibits.outcome: A locally monotonic design can reissue past nonces when its environment rolls back.

exhibits.title: Nonce Misuse Mitigations and Scope
exhibits.section: Fixes, and what this lab is not
exhibits.action: Compare uniqueness requirements and the described AES-GCM-SIV mitigation, then inspect the lab’s explicit limits.
exhibits.outcome: The section distinguishes an RFC 8452 behavior description from a live GCM-SIV implementation and separates authentication-key forgery from AES-key recovery.
exhibits.limits: GCM-SIV is described, not executed in this lab.

exhibits.title: Wider-Block GCM Proposal Context
exhibits.action: Read the draft wGCM research note and current execution boundary.
exhibits.outcome: The text says a longer AES key does not change AES’s 128-bit block and the draft 256-bit-block mode is not run here.

exhibits.title: AES-GCM versus AES-GCM-SIV Nonce Reuse
exhibits.action: Encrypt two editable messages with reused or fresh nonces and run the attack.
exhibits.outcome: Shows AES-GCM plaintext XOR and tag-forgery exposure against misuse-resistant SIV output.
exhibits.section: B — See It Break (Live Attack Demo)

exhibits.title: Keystream Cancellation
exhibits.action: Animate cancellation of a reused GCM keystream.
exhibits.outcome: Shows C1 XOR C2 equal to P1 XOR P2 without a key.

exhibits.title: GHASH Key Recovery and Tag Forgery
exhibits.action: Use the two chosen messages and run the recovered-H attack, then verify a forged tag.
exhibits.outcome: Factors the nonce-reuse equation over GF(2^128), tests candidates, and has real AES-GCM accept the forgery.
exhibits.limits: Known plaintext is needed to construct chosen forged ciphertext; the browser caps messages at 512 bytes for the root search.

exhibits.title: Synthetic IV Derivation
exhibits.action: Edit the SIV plaintext or compare a repeated message with one changed byte.
exhibits.outcome: Shows POLYVAL-derived tag, synthetic CTR IV, and ciphertext change together.
exhibits.section: D3 — Tag-as-IV, Live: plaintext → tag → IV → ciphertext
exhibits.limits: Reusing a nonce under SIV still reveals when plaintext and associated data repeat.

exhibits.title: AEAD Nonce Uniqueness
exhibits.action: Read the per-key nonce rule and inspect a 96-bit nonce example.
exhibits.outcome: Connects AES-GCM security to unique, public nonces and the IV terminology.

exhibits.title: Synthetic-IV Construction
exhibits.action: Trace AES-GCM-SIV from per-nonce keys through POLYVAL, encrypted tag, and the CTR initial block.
exhibits.outcome: Shows why different plaintexts under a repeated nonce use different keystreams, with identical-input equality still visible.
exhibits.limits: This section explains the pipeline; the D3 panel executes a live tag/IV comparison.

exhibits.title: AES-GCM-SIV Per-Nonce Keys
exhibits.action: Follow the counter-plus-nonce AES blocks and truncated halves used for auth and encryption keys.
exhibits.outcome: Shows derivation of a 128-bit authentication key and 256-bit encryption key from a 256-bit master key.

exhibits.title: Encrypted POLYVAL Tag
exhibits.action: Inspect the POLYVAL equation and the AES encryption of its output.
exhibits.outcome: Explains why XOR of two published SIV tags does not expose the linear polynomial in H as the GCM reused-nonce attack does.
exhibits.section: D2 — POLYVAL Authentication (why the cancel trick dies)

exhibits.title: GCM versus GCM-SIV Selection
exhibits.action: Compare nonce coordination, two-pass encryption, and use-case guidance in the tables and scenarios.
exhibits.outcome: Maps assured unique nonces, distributed encryptors, and key storage to different misuse and operational tradeoffs.
exhibits.limits: Guidance is contextual and the table’s status/deployment statements are tied to this pinned source.

exhibits.title: Proposed Wider-Block GCM Boundary
exhibits.action: Read the dated research note distinguishing a proposed 256-bit-block cipher mode from AES-256 and this lab’s implemented modes.
exhibits.outcome: Clarifies that increasing an AES key length does not increase its 128-bit block size or implement the proposal.
exhibits.limits: This pinned note describes a proposal as of October 2026; the lab neither implements wGCM nor establishes its current standards status.

exhibits.title: AES-GCM-SIV Operational Limitations
exhibits.action: Read the limitation list beside the AES-GCM and AES-GCM-SIV selection table.
exhibits.outcome: Identifies the lack of FIPS approval, the need to buffer plaintext before encryption, the second pass, and narrower deployment experience.
exhibits.limits: Status and deployment experience are the claims made by this pinned page, not a live standards or implementation survey.

exhibits.title: Configuration
exhibits.action: Choose leaked MSBs or LSBs, fixed-prefix, nonce reuse or RFC 6979 defender preset, set signatures and generate an ECDSA attack.
exhibits.outcome: The lab signs under the selected nonce condition and displays the signature log and recovery verdict.
exhibits.limits: The compromised nonce conditions are constructed teaching fixtures; RFC 6979 is a control, not a guarantee against every implementation leak.

exhibits.title: Two signatures, no lattice needed
exhibits.action: Run the repeated-nonce preset and inspect the algebra of two signatures sharing k.
exhibits.outcome: The displayed equations recover k and private key directly without lattice reduction.
exhibits.limits: Requires the same effective nonce under one private key and distinct messages; ordinary unique nonces do not expose this simple equation.

exhibits.title: Lattice View
exhibits.action: Inspect signature equations, hidden-number bounds, lattice rows, basis view and projected solution for partial nonce bits.
exhibits.outcome: The reduction attempts candidate-key recovery and verifies candidates against signatures and the public key.
exhibits.limits: Success depends on leak strength, signatures and solver bounds; a projected lattice is a visualization, not a proof of recovery.

exhibits.title: Can this configuration recover the key?
exhibits.section: Can this configuration recover the key?
exhibits.action: Measure a boundary sweep over leaked bits and available signatures.
exhibits.outcome: The feasibility panel compares information floors, practical thresholds and observed recovery probes.
exhibits.limits: Measured probes are finite and configuration-specific; a failure to recover in a sweep is not a general security bound.

exhibits.title: Attack workflow vs. defense
exhibits.action: Read the ECDSA equation, historical cases and paired attack/defense workflow.
exhibits.outcome: The context distinguishes nonce reuse, biased or partially exposed nonces, and deterministic-nonce defenses.
exhibits.limits: Historical discussion is explanatory; this page does not reproduce each cited real-world exploit.

exhibits.title: Generate a classic NTRU teaching keypair
exhibits.action: Generate f and g, retrying when f is not invertible in the two rings.
exhibits.outcome: Displays polynomial inverse steps, public key and private components.
exhibits.limits: Fixed small teaching parameters; not standardized NTRU KEM or deployable encryption.

exhibits.title: Encrypt and decrypt a ternary-encoded message
exhibits.action: Type a message, encrypt, decrypt, then tamper with ciphertext.
exhibits.outcome: Shows message polynomial, blind, ciphertext and decryption intermediates with live algebraic checks.
exhibits.limits: Bare classic NTRU encryption is not authenticated; ciphertext tampering can change or invalidate plaintext.

exhibits.title: Reduce a lattice basis and attack a small NTRU key
exhibits.action: Apply or autoplay reduction steps, then generate a small key and run LLL on its NTRU lattice.
exhibits.outcome: Shows short vectors and whether a reduced vector corresponds to the small private key.
exhibits.limits: The attack runs on deliberately small keys; reducing real secure NTRU parameters is much harder.
exhibits.section: Exhibit 3: The Lattice Perspective — how you would attack NTRU

exhibits.title: Compare NTRU and Kyber constructions
exhibits.action: Inspect the side-by-side construction comparison.
exhibits.outcome: Contrasts NTRU’s ring polynomial approach with Kyber’s module-LWE design.
exhibits.limits: The comparison is explanatory and does not implement or rank production ML-KEM security.

exhibits.title: Trace NTRU adoption and patent history
exhibits.section: Exhibit 5: Historical Impact and Patent Story
exhibits.action: Read the invention, patent, standards and NIST timeline.
exhibits.outcome: Shows NTRU roots in lattice cryptography and compares its standardization path with ML-KEM.
exhibits.limits: Historical context only, not a recommendation of NTRU Classic parameters.

exhibits.title: Library Query Privacy and XOR Scheme
exhibits.action: Read the one-server privacy problem, noncolluding two-server assumption, and XOR query equations.
exhibits.outcome: The walkthrough explains how each server sees a uniformly distributed subset while the two replies combine to recover only the selected item's checked-out bit.
exhibits.limits: The privacy statement assumes uniform independent subset sampling, identical databases, noncolluding servers and a view limited to one protocol query; it excludes transport metadata, logs and collusion.

exhibits.title: Two-Server PIR Query
exhibits.action: Select a catalog item and advance the query walkthrough.
exhibits.outcome: Actual sampled subset queries and independently computed XOR responses recover the selected one-bit checked-out flag; a direct database comparison checks correctness and each computed one-server anonymity set retains all 16 indices.
exhibits.limits: The two servers and their noncollusion are simulated in one browser; the protocol retrieves one bit rather than a catalog record, contacts no network servers, models no transport metadata or logs, and loses privacy if the query shares are combined.

exhibits.title: Communication and Server Tradeoffs
exhibits.action: Inspect the cost table and read the comparison among download-all, the executed basic XOR scheme, cited multi-server PIR bounds, CPIR and research systems.
exhibits.outcome: The section identifies the executed basic scheme's two O(n)-bit queries, separates that cost from better cited PIR constructions, and contrasts information-theoretic and computational assumptions.
exhibits.limits: The advanced communication bounds, CPIR families and research systems are explanatory references; the executed basic XOR and bounded GF(8) routes do not claim those asymptotic or deployment efficiencies.

exhibits.title: Librarian Privacy and Policy Boundaries
exhibits.action: Read the legal landscape, where IT-PIR fits, and honest limitations.
exhibits.outcome: The section connects query confidentiality to operational assumptions without claiming to resolve catalog content or legal policy issues.
exhibits.limits: The legal history is explanatory and not legal advice; PIR does not erase patron identity, timing, network, application or circulation records.

exhibits.title: Robust PIR Fault and Collusion Workbench
exhibits.action: Select a catalog bit, choose honest, unavailable, corrupted or stale behavior independently for five servers, choose one or two query views and run the field arithmetic.
exhibits.outcome: Actual GF(8) unit-vector shares and server dot products form a degree-one Reed-Solomon word; the decoder corrects or refuses within its derived radius, a pinned beyond-bound transcript accepts the wrong bit, one query view retains every target and two distinct views interpolate the one-hot target.
exhibits.section: Robust Shelf: missing and dishonest servers
exhibits.limits: This is a 1-private, 2-out-of-5 linear unit-vector teaching construction over GF(8), not Beimel-Stahl Theorem 5.2, Goldberg's full protocol, Percy++, RAID-PIR or production. The threshold permits twice the Byzantine count plus the unavailable count to be at most three; it supplies no provenance, freshness or privacy against two colluding query recipients.

exhibits.title: OPAQUE protocol map
exhibits.section: Start Here: The Whole Protocol on One Screen
exhibits.action: Follow linked stages from password through OPRF, envelope and 3DH.
exhibits.outcome: Orients the registration and login exhibits by the values each actor learns.
exhibits.limits: Map is explanatory; exact acceptance is established in the following live exhibits.

exhibits.title: Three storage choices after breach
exhibits.section: Exhibit 1: Why Current Password Auth Is Broken
exhibits.action: Simulate a database leak for plaintext, salted hash and OPAQUE record; register first to display the actual stored record.
exhibits.outcome: Contrasts immediately exposed password, offline-checkable hash and authenticated OPAQUE envelope bytes.
exhibits.limits: This overview alone overstates breach resistance if the per-user OPRF key also leaks; Exhibit 4 actually tests offline guesses and finds a weak password.

exhibits.title: Blind and unblind password input
exhibits.section: Exhibit 2: The OPRF — Hiding Password from Server
exhibits.action: Run the OPRF repeatedly with the same password and a fresh blind.
exhibits.outcome: Shows different blinded wire values yet the same client-unblinded result under one server key.
exhibits.limits: The browser runs both roles; it does not reproduce an independent network or guarantee endpoint secrecy.

exhibits.title: Register an authenticated envelope
exhibits.section: Exhibit 3: Registration and the Login Handshake
