exhibits.action: Enter a username and password and register using the real OPRF and envelope construction.
exhibits.outcome: Displays client public key, server masking key and authenticated envelope while the client key is derived from password material.
exhibits.limits: The demo intentionally holds all parties and password in browser memory; its envelope is a particular authenticated format.

exhibits.title: Step through KE1, KE2 and KE3
exhibits.section: Exhibit 3: Registration and the Login Handshake
exhibits.action: Run a three-message login stepper, including a wrong-password control and session-key leakage scenario.
exhibits.outcome: Shows envelope MAC failure for wrong password and mutual authentication/session derivation for a correct run.
exhibits.limits: A browser protocol trace, not production networking; leaking one session key is a controlled experiment.

exhibits.title: Attack the stored OPAQUE record
exhibits.action: After registration, test no-password recovery, actual offline dictionary guesses with stolen per-user OPRF key, cross-user precomputation and forged server KE2.
exhibits.outcome: Wrong guesses fail, the correct weak-password guess authenticates and recovers credentials at a measured scrypt cost; forged static server key is rejected.
exhibits.limits: The true password is intentionally placed last in a tiny dictionary; timings are single-browser measurements with scrypt N=2^15, below recommended production cost.

exhibits.title: OPAQUE deployment context
exhibits.action: Read application and library integration examples.
exhibits.outcome: Describes protocol adoption context and the authentication guarantees the page models.
exhibits.limits: Integration context is illustrative; no vendor system or production client is contacted.

exhibits.title: Access pattern leak versus ORAM
exhibits.action: Inspect a medical-record access scenario and replay it through ORAM.
exhibits.outcome: Compare what encryption hides with what repeated server access reveals, then view randomized path access.

exhibits.title: Path ORAM tree and stash
exhibits.action: Initialize a tree, step random accesses, switch to server view and read or write a block.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect position-map remapping, stash occupancy and legal eviction along accessed paths.
exhibits.limits: A small in-browser tree makes the mechanism observable and does not measure production-scale performance.

exhibits.title: Path ORAM read and write
exhibits.action: Initialize the walkthrough, read block 5, write a value and advance individual steps.
exhibits.outcome: See client stash transitions and server communication at each access step.

exhibits.title: Adversary view and path statistics
exhibits.action: Run twenty random accesses and compare client and server logs.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect the visible server paths and their statistical summary while block identities stay hidden.

exhibits.title: Path ORAM costs and caveats
exhibits.action: Compare plain encrypted storage against Path ORAM and read use-case and security-caveat panels.
exhibits.outcome: See per-access path bandwidth, client stash and position-map costs, plus timing, stash overflow and semi-honest-server boundaries.
exhibits.limits: Counts use the small in-browser tree; production cost and threat models depend on construction and deployment.
exhibits.section: Costs and When ORAM Is Worth It

exhibits.title: Deterministic Equality and Frequency Recovery
exhibits.action: Select department and deterministic AES-GCM-SIV, query encrypted equality, then match ciphertext frequencies to public counts.
exhibits.outcome: Shows authenticated ciphertexts remain queryable and inferred plaintext labels emerge without decryption.
exhibits.limits: Recovery relies on auxiliary frequency data and the selected dataset.

exhibits.title: Order-Preserving Encryption and Rank Attack
exhibits.action: Choose age or salary under toy BCLO OPE, run range/sort queries, then recover from public ranks.
exhibits.outcome: Shows dense ages can align to auxiliary values while sparse salary gaps leave uncertainty.
exhibits.limits: OPE is an 8-bit plaintext to 16-bit ciphertext toy; sparse-gapped recovery is incomplete.

exhibits.title: Order-Revealing Encryption and Tree Recovery
exhibits.action: Select binary CLWW ORE, compare or sort ciphertexts, and run the recovery step.
exhibits.outcome: Shows pairwise comparisons exposing first differing bits and a reconstructed radix tree aligned with public statistics.

exhibits.title: Randomized AES-GCM Control
exhibits.action: Select randomized control and try an equality query or recovery on repeated values.
exhibits.outcome: Shows fresh encryptions of equal values fail ciphertext equality and the distinct ciphertext count is reported.
exhibits.limits: Without a searchable relation this demo cannot offer the same server-side query features.

exhibits.title: Auxiliary Population Sensitivity
exhibits.action: Vary table size and switch matching synthetic, shifted, or mismatched public distributions, then rerun recovery and reveal truth.
exhibits.outcome: The attack score changes or the recovery rejects a support mismatch; comparison with truth shows when statistical side information is inadequate.
exhibits.limits: Synthetic public populations and known row truth are supplied by the teaching dataset; this does not predict success on an arbitrary real database.

exhibits.title: A. What is Oblivious Transfer?
exhibits.action: Read the 1-out-of-2 choice and privacy goal and compare OT flavors and MPC uses.
exhibits.outcome: The explanation distinguishes receiver choice hiding from protecting the unselected message.
exhibits.limits: Introductory explanation, not a proof of an implementation.

exhibits.title: B. The Simplest OT Protocol
exhibits.action: Initialize a sender and select one of two messages as receiver in the curve-based OT workflow.
exhibits.outcome: The selected ciphertext decrypts; the transcript and privacy audit show the sender’s view and what the receiver can open.
exhibits.limits: Teaching adaptation with a simplified KDF and named validation limits; the browser operates both parties.

exhibits.title: C. OT Correctness & Security
exhibits.action: Run correctness check and guess which of two public curve points encodes the choice over repeated DDH-style trials.
exhibits.outcome: The visualizer records guess results while explaining the assumed computational hiding of the choice.
exhibits.limits: A finite guessing game is not a proof of DDH hardness or malicious-party security.

exhibits.title: D1. OT Extension (IKNP 2003)
exhibits.action: Run 128 base OTs, choose 1000 to 100000 transfers, extend and check every output; optionally activate the deliberately malicious receiver.
exhibits.outcome: The matrix view and timing counters show symmetric-work expansion and, in broken mode, recovery of sender secret r and both outputs.
exhibits.limits: Default IKNP path is semi-honest; malicious mode deliberately violates its assumptions, and browser timing is environment-specific.

exhibits.title: E. All-or-nothing disclosure: choose privately
exhibits.action: Choose one archive capsule in a fresh two-message session and attempt the unselected ciphertext with the receiver key.
exhibits.outcome: The selected message decrypts and AES-GCM rejects the other ciphertext under that key; public curve transcript is displayed.
exhibits.limits: One session does not enforce lifetime exclusivity; this is not the original 1986 construction or general 1-out-of-n OT.

exhibits.title: D. OT in the MPC Ecosystem
exhibits.section: D. OT in the MPC Ecosystem
exhibits.action: Read the listed uses of extension in MPC, private set intersection and related systems.
exhibits.outcome: The context connects the measured extension example to protocols that consume many transfers.
exhibits.limits: Context links do not execute the external MPC systems.

exhibits.title: One-time pad: encrypt and decrypt
exhibits.action: Type a message or generate a new random key of equal UTF-8 byte length.
exhibits.outcome: Byte strips display P, K, P XOR K, and exact recovery by ciphertext XOR K.
concepts: key length equals message byte length
exhibits.limits: Correct use requires a secret uniformly random key shared out of band and never reused; key distribution is not modeled.

exhibits.title: Perfect secrecy: every plaintext is possible
exhibits.action: Enter any plaintext with the fixed ciphertext's exact byte length.
exhibits.outcome: The UI derives K=C XOR P and verifies that the same ciphertext decrypts to the chosen plaintext under that key.
exhibits.limits: The algebra shows possible keys; the secrecy guarantee also needs a uniformly random one-use secret pad.
exhibits.section: 2 · Perfect secrecy — every plaintext is possible

exhibits.title: Limits of perfect secrecy
exhibits.action: Shorten an eight-bit pad, inspect all 256 one-byte candidates, compute an exact two-message indistinguishability game, and edit a four-key encryption table.
exhibits.outcome: The grid rules out unreachable messages, exact fractions show an attacker's success, and independent Shannon-condition checks agree or fail for the editable table.
exhibits.limits: These are tiny exhaustive finite spaces, not measured security of a deployed cipher.

exhibits.title: Prior odds and what a ciphertext changes
exhibits.action: Adjust four prior message weights and select a two-bit observed ciphertext.
exhibits.outcome: An exact prior/posterior table contrasts fresh uniform pad, fresh biased pad, and known-plaintext pad reuse.
exhibits.limits: Two-bit exact teaching models; the reuse column is a separate two-encryption known-plaintext attack, not the outcome of a single ciphertext.
exhibits.section: D · Prior odds and what a ciphertext changes

exhibits.title: Two-time pad: key reuse and crib dragging
exhibits.action: Edit two messages, toggle one reused key versus independent fresh keys, drag or nudge a guessed crib, and pin candidates.
exhibits.outcome: With reuse, C1 XOR C2 reveals P1 XOR P2 and the crib workbench reconstructs overlapping bytes in both plaintexts; with separate keys, the cancellation disappears.
exhibits.limits: The XOR attack covers only overlapping keystream bytes; guesses require plausible plaintext context.
exhibits.section: 3 · Two-time pad — the catastrophic key-reuse attack

exhibits.title: Keystream reuse in real ciphers: structural analogy
exhibits.action: Edit two messages encrypted with the same generated stand-in keystream and crib-drag the XOR strip.
exhibits.outcome: The shared keystream cancels, exposing the same P1 XOR P2 reconstruction pattern as the two-time pad.
exhibits.limits: The page does not run ChaCha20, AES-CTR, or AES-GCM; GCM authentication consequences are not demonstrated.
exhibits.section: 4 · Keystream reuse in real ciphers — the same break

exhibits.title: Import two ciphertexts: cryptanalysis playground
exhibits.action: Paste two hex ciphertexts or load a challenge, then slide and pin cribs in the shared workbench.
exhibits.outcome: The overlapping ciphertext XOR strip and candidate plaintext bytes appear; bundled challenges permit an optional instructor reveal.
exhibits.limits: The method helps recover plaintext only when the inputs share keystream bytes; it does not recover a general encryption key.

exhibits.title: Seven-Step One-Time-Pad Walkthrough
exhibits.action: Start the optional walkthrough and move Back or Next through OTP, perfect secrecy and reuse exhibits.
exhibits.outcome: The guide scrolls to relevant panels and prompts an independent-key control against crib dragging.

exhibits.title: Craft padding and probe a CBC oracle
exhibits.action: Set up a CBC session, flip a predecessor byte, and predict whether padding validates.
exhibits.outcome: The genuine PKCS#7 validity bit reveals information without exposing the AES key.
exhibits.limits: The vulnerable server deliberately leaks padding validity; ordinary CBC does not necessarily expose this signal.

exhibits.title: Recover one plaintext byte from oracle queries
exhibits.action: Encrypt a chosen sample and run or stop the byte-recovery loop.
exhibits.outcome: Shows 256 candidate trials, padding-valid responses and the recovered byte.
exhibits.limits: Query count varies with padding collisions and validation checks.
exhibits.section: Single Byte Recovery — The Core Attack

exhibits.title: Recover a full block of CBC plaintext
exhibits.action: Encrypt a sample and step through automated block recovery.
exhibits.outcome: Displays recovered intermediate AES inverse bytes and XOR with previous block to obtain plaintext.
exhibits.limits: The attack requires repeated chosen-ciphertext oracle access.

exhibits.title: Decrypt a multi-block ciphertext through the oracle
exhibits.action: Generate a secret and run the full ciphertext attack.
exhibits.outcome: Recovers plaintext across blocks with displayed query progress.
exhibits.limits: This is a controlled vulnerable oracle and not an attack on an arbitrary external service.

exhibits.title: Run one attack against leaky, silent and EtM servers
exhibits.action: Run the benchmark against three oracle modes.
exhibits.outcome: The leaky oracle yields data, silent observation gives no padding signal, and Encrypt-then-MAC rejects changes before decrypting.
exhibits.limits: Silent-server behavior is modeled as a constant attacker-visible answer; attack code is shared.

exhibits.title: Try tampering with authenticated AES-GCM
exhibits.action: Encrypt with GCM and flip ciphertext data before decryption.
exhibits.outcome: WebCrypto rejects altered ciphertext under the authentication tag.
exhibits.limits: Authenticated encryption requires correct nonce and key management as well as tag checking.

exhibits.title: Connect CBC padding oracles to documented exploits
exhibits.action: Read the attack cards and TLS 1.3 migration context.
exhibits.outcome: Shows explicit error, timing and downgrade channels in CBC deployments and how TLS 1.3 removes CBC suites.
exhibits.limits: Historical cards only; lab attack execution is in panels one through four.

exhibits.title: Compare CBC with Encrypt-then-MAC against AEAD
exhibits.action: Read scenario guidance for new systems, legacy migration, constrained devices and network protocols.
exhibits.outcome: Explains when an interim CBC and MAC composition is discussed and why AEAD is the target design.
exhibits.limits: Static decision table; not a security proof or deployment checklist.

exhibits.title: Generate a Paillier keypair
exhibits.action: Choose a 64–192-bit educational modulus size and generate a keypair in a worker; inspect N, g and the private parameters.
exhibits.outcome: The page computes primes and Paillier key material and displays the resulting modulus bit length, which can be one bit below the nominal selection.
exhibits.limits: These tiny sizes are deliberately factorable and unsuitable for deployment; the page does not model a hardened key generator.

exhibits.title: Factor the educational modulus
exhibits.action: Press Factor N against the generated small modulus and watch a budgeted Pollard rho search.
exhibits.outcome: When factoring succeeds within the budget, the worker reports steps/time, rebuilds the private key and can decrypt a ciphertext made in the preceding section; larger attempts may give up.
exhibits.limits: Success is conditional on tiny educational keys and a fixed search budget; it is not a practical attack on properly sized Paillier.

exhibits.title: Encrypt, repeat and re-randomize a message
exhibits.action: Encrypt a number, encrypt it again with fresh randomness, decrypt the ciphertext, then re-randomize it using only the public key.
exhibits.outcome: Different ciphertexts can decrypt to the same number; the page shows the new ciphertext and the decryption of each stored example.
exhibits.limits: The demonstration uses very small, insecure key sizes; a re-randomization can occasionally return an unchanged ciphertext when the fresh factor is one.

exhibits.title: Multiply ciphertexts to add plaintexts
exhibits.action: Encrypt two inputs or hand in earlier ciphertexts, multiply the ciphertexts modulo N², decrypt the product, and try the modulus-overflow preset.
exhibits.outcome: The product decrypts to (A+B) mod N; the page also actually decrypts a naive integer sum of ciphertexts to show it generally fails and exposes wraparound when A+B reaches N.
exhibits.limits: The plain sum must be kept below N to represent the intended integer; Paillier alone does not authenticate ciphertexts.

exhibits.title: Aggregate encrypted counts with public weights
exhibits.action: Enter counts and optional weights, then aggregate encrypted counts and exponentiate ciphertexts by public weights.
exhibits.outcome: The page decrypts the encrypted sum and weighted sum and compares them with plaintext totals, showing each encrypted weighted contribution.
exhibits.limits: The scenario uses one local decryption key and educational modulus sizes; it is not a distributed private analytics protocol.

exhibits.title: Rewrite an encrypted ballot and compare MAC admission
exhibits.action: Seal a set of 0/1 ballots, select a ballot and a public-key vote boost, then forge and re-tally with the Encrypt-then-MAC check on or off.
exhibits.outcome: Without authentication the forged ciphertext changes the tally despite hiding the original vote; with the MAC check the altered ballot is rejected, and the page shows the effect of dropping it.
exhibits.limits: This locally keyed MAC checks outsider tampering, not whether an authorized voter submitted a valid 0-or-1 plaintext; it is not a full election protocol.

exhibits.title: BLS12-381 Bilinearity Playground
exhibits.action: Move scalars a and b and compare four actual pairing expressions.
exhibits.outcome: All expressions produce the same full G_T field element, exposing the property used in BLS verification.

exhibits.title: Pairing Groups and Properties
exhibits.action: Inspect group roles, nondegeneracy and efficiency, plus BLS12-381 parameters.
exhibits.outcome: The material distinguishes source groups and target field and locates the classical security assumption.
exhibits.limits: Pairing-based schemes shown here have no post-quantum security.

exhibits.title: BLS Sign and Verify with Tamper
exhibits.action: Generate a keypair, sign a message, verify both pairing values, then alter the signature.
exhibits.outcome: The same G_T value establishes a valid signature; tampering yields mismatch or rejection.

exhibits.title: Same-Message Signature Aggregation
exhibits.action: Generate 2–100 signer keys, sign one message, aggregate signatures, and verify.
exhibits.outcome: One aggregate signature and one aggregate key verify with two pairings independent of signer count in this same-message setting.
exhibits.limits: The two-pairing result assumes all signers sign the same message and the key set is protected against rogue keys.

exhibits.title: Rogue-Key Forgery and Proof of Possession
exhibits.action: Forge against naive aggregate keys and then apply the proof-of-possession defense.
exhibits.outcome: A last mover cancels an honest public key so a solo signature passes naive aggregate verification; the defended path rejects it.
exhibits.limits: Naive aggregation is deliberately insecure; different-message signing is explained separately and loses constant pairing count.

exhibits.title: Pairing Deployments and Size Comparison
exhibits.action: Read Ethereum and Zcash use cases and compare public-key, signature, and verification sizes.
exhibits.outcome: The table frames why aggregation can reduce signature bandwidth despite pairing verification cost.

exhibits.title: Four classical PAKE handshakes
exhibits.action: Run Honest run, Wrong password, or Step one message in SRP-6a, then Go deeper to unlock J-PAKE, CPace and Dragonfly.
exhibits.outcome: Peer scratchpads and wire messages show derived session-key fingerprints; matching confirmed keys turn green, wrong-password handshakes fail.
exhibits.limits: Hand-rolled educational browser engines are not constant-time or production authentication; all four runnable engines are classical.

exhibits.title: Register SRP verifier
exhibits.action: Type a throwaway password and Register {salt, v}, then run the SRP handshake.
exhibits.outcome: Server stores a salt and derived verifier while the demo shows the password staying in the client scratchpad.
exhibits.limits: Demo inputs are shown on screen; do not enter real credentials; an SRP verifier can enable offline guessing after breach.

exhibits.title: Stolen SRP verifier dictionary attack
exhibits.action: After a handshake, open Server breach and run the offline grind with optional candidate guesses.
exhibits.outcome: Real modular exponentiation recomputes verifiers and reports a match if the password is in the tested list; passive transcript scan is shown separately.
exhibits.limits: Finite browser wordlist and local throughput are not a GPU benchmark; literal transcript scan is not a proof of PAKE security.

exhibits.title: On-path transcript inspection
exhibits.action: Open On-path observer after a handshake and inspect raw wire fields and literal-encoding audit.
exhibits.outcome: The visible transcript contains public fields and no recognized literal password encoding in the scanned forms.
exhibits.limits: Scanning strings for literal password encodings is a backstop, not proof that no offline password test exists.

exhibits.title: Curated message tampering
exhibits.action: Go deeper, choose a curated wire-field modification, and run the exchange.
exhibits.outcome: The receiving engine aborts or confirmation fails at the affected step, with a visible reason.
exhibits.limits: Curated single-field mutations only; not a comprehensive adversarial security proof.

exhibits.title: Dragonfly iteration-count leak
exhibits.action: Choose password candidates in the legacy versus fixed-work graph.
exhibits.outcome: Modeled hunting-and-pecking iteration counts vary for legacy early exit and flatten under the fixed-work teaching variant.
exhibits.limits: Modeled iteration count, not measured browser timing; flat count addresses one historical signal, not cache/branch/field-arithmetic leakage or modern SAE hash-to-element.

exhibits.title: PAKE family property matrix
exhibits.action: Compare rows for balanced versus augmented server storage, rounds, construction and standardization.
exhibits.outcome: Matrix places runnable classical families and reference-only OPAQUE side by side with status and deployment context.
exhibits.limits: Reference rows are not runnable implementations; status is sourced from data table and may change over time.

exhibits.title: Post-quantum PAKE boundary
exhibits.action: Read the architecture note and source links.
exhibits.outcome: Explains that runnable group-based PAKE engines are classical and that KEM/password encoding extension remains unimplemented.
exhibits.limits: No post-quantum PAKE engine is implemented; model-conditional preprint discussion does not establish a practical break of the classical demos.

exhibits.title: Select and retrieve a book privately
exhibits.action: Choose a book, create two XOR-related query masks, inspect each server’s XOR response and reconstruct the record.
exhibits.outcome: Shows correct target recovery while each individual uniform mask hides the index.
exhibits.limits: Both servers and the whole database live in the same tab; there is no actual privacy trust boundary or network.

exhibits.title: Join both query masks
exhibits.action: Make the two simulated servers collude after a retrieval.
exhibits.outcome: XORing their query masks reveals the selected book index.
exhibits.limits: The privacy property requires separate operators and delivery paths; the tab itself knows the selected index.

exhibits.title: Naive versus private query
exhibits.action: Toggle ordinary direct query and two-server PIR query views.
exhibits.outcome: Compares which server can identify the requested record.
exhibits.limits: Conceptual comparison of locally simulated servers, not an external privacy service.

exhibits.title: Square-root matrix PIR scaling
exhibits.action: Move catalog-size slider and inspect linear-mask versus matrix-layout communication estimates.
exhibits.outcome: Displays O(N) mask length versus an illustrative O(√N) column-mask and row-response layout.
exhibits.limits: The live eight-book protocol still sends an N-bit mask; the square-root scheme is explained and projected, not executed.

exhibits.title: Deterministic site password derivation
exhibits.action: Enter master passphrase, service, username, version and character policy, then derive a password.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect derived password and pipeline status for PBKDF2, HMAC-DRBG and unbiased character mapping.
exhibits.limits: Composition estimates are ceilings, not measured human passphrase entropy.

exhibits.title: Derivation invariants
exhibits.action: Run the proof control for identical inputs, incremented version and changed service.
exhibits.outcome: Compare four derived outputs for determinism, version rotation and service separation.

exhibits.title: Entropy cap display
exhibits.action: Adjust passphrase assumptions and password length, or load a weak preset.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect the lower of passphrase-composition and seed ceilings versus output-space ceiling.
exhibits.limits: Actual passphrase entropy depends on how it was selected and is not observed by the app.
exhibits.section: The entropy cap — the central lesson

exhibits.title: Offline master-passphrase guessing
exhibits.action: Supply candidate master passphrases and run full derivations against observed site credentials.
exhibits.outcome: See guesses tried and whether a candidate produces credentials consistent with the target.
exhibits.limits: A bounded wordlist experiment cannot prove the master passphrase is unguessable.
exhibits.section: Break it — crack the master passphrase

exhibits.title: Modulo bias comparison
exhibits.action: Inspect generated bytes and character mapping results.
exhibits.outcome: Compare biased modulo selection against rejection sampling that discards out-of-range byte values.
exhibits.section: Seeing modulo bias — and watching it vanish

exhibits.title: HMAC-DRBG internal state walkthrough
exhibits.action: Derive a password and expand the HMAC-DRBG state machine panel.
exhibits.outcome: Follow truncated K and V snapshots, the HMAC transition and the count of generated and rejected bytes for the actual derivation.
exhibits.limits: Only truncated state fingerprints appear in the DOM; full internal state depends on the master secret.

exhibits.title: The Chain
exhibits.action: Select the root, intermediate, or leaf certificate.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect subject, issuer, validity, key and signature details and see which private key signs which certificate.
exhibits.limits: JSON-serialized teaching certificates with WebCrypto signatures, not ASN.1/DER X.509 or complete RFC 5280 path validation.

exhibits.title: Chain Validation and Revocation Evidence
exhibits.action: Run validation; tamper a node, choose missing/current/stale/wrong-signer OCSP evidence, and switch revocation policy.
exhibits.outcome: Read per-link signature checks and an overall trust verdict; a signed but stale good response or missing evidence changes the policy decision without changing certificate signatures.
exhibits.limits: OCSP is directly issuer-signed JSON in this toy; no OCSP wire protocol or complete TLS revocation policy.

exhibits.title: Trust Stores
exhibits.action: Switch among Browser, OS and Application store tabs.
exhibits.outcome: Compare accepted and rejected verdicts for the same signed chain depending on whether its root is a chosen trust anchor.
exhibits.limits: Illustrative in-memory stores, not queries to the visitor's actual browser or operating-system trust store.

exhibits.title: Certificate Transparency
exhibits.action: Submit certificate entries, request inclusion and consistency proofs, select a tree leaf, or simulate misissuance.
exhibits.outcome: See the Merkle tree, SCT entry, proof verification status and misissuance monitor; proof readouts are invalidated when the log grows.
exhibits.limits: A browser-local simulated CT log and monitor; inclusion makes issuance visible but does not prove it was authorized or revoke a certificate.

exhibits.title: CA Compromise
exhibits.action: Select an uncompromised, intermediate-compromised or root-compromised scenario.
exhibits.outcome: Observe a distrusted subtree and the distinction between still-valid signatures and policy distrust.
exhibits.limits: A selected compromise flag models trust policy; it does not actually steal a CA key or issue a real certificate.

exhibits.title: PQ Migration
exhibits.action: Switch among P-256, ML-DSA and hybrid signature footprint tabs.
exhibits.outcome: Compare live-chain P-256 signature size with FIPS 204 reference ML-DSA sizes and a hybrid estimate.
exhibits.limits: Only P-256 is measured live; ML-DSA is a published reference size, not a generated browser signature; no hybrid certificate is constructed.

exhibits.title: Unauthorized Certificate Issuance
exhibits.section: Certificate issuance: where trust can fail
exhibits.action: Read the registry-hijack case study and connect it to validation and Certificate Transparency.
exhibits.outcome: A signed unauthorized certificate can authenticate an attacker who controls its private key and redirected traffic; logging makes issuance visible for response.
exhibits.limits: The case study is narrative context; no registry hijack or TLS handshake is simulated.

exhibits.title: X.509 Semantics Versus Wire Format
exhibits.section: Scope — what this lab does and does not model
exhibits.action: Read the scope matrix for real cryptography, modeled chain validation and omitted parsing.
exhibits.outcome: The lab signs and checks semantic certificate data using JSON rather than DER and does not model ASN.1 parser vulnerabilities.

exhibits.title: Point Addition and Attack Clock
exhibits.action: Switch published resource estimates, toggle primed start, and choose a clock input for an on-spend race.
exhibits.outcome: Computes time and race probabilities from stated assumptions and displays per-operation cost shares.
exhibits.limits: These are paper assumptions and lab derivations, not a running quantum attack.

exhibits.title: In-Place Multiplication Dialog
exhibits.action: Run and step an arithmetic dialog on the secp256k1 or small demo field, then measure random inputs and adjust budget.
exhibits.outcome: Shows reversible recorded Euclidean steps, cost tradeoffs, and boundary reduction behavior.
exhibits.limits: Truncated-comparison approximation errors in the cited algorithms are not simulated here.

exhibits.title: Finite Test Set and Nonce Grinding
exhibits.action: Change test count, draw bound and confidence, then grind a demo-scale nonce to seek a clean validation draw.
exhibits.outcome: Shows a statistical failure ceiling and that repeated chosen draws may miss a persistent defect.
exhibits.limits: The demo does not submit a circuit; a clean draw is not an all-inputs correctness proof.

exhibits.title: Proof Pipeline and Checker Trust
exhibits.action: Step a commitment/proof pipeline, then toggle toy CCX aliasing and its checker before running forward and reverse operations.
exhibits.outcome: Shows a check can accept an irreversible operation if operand constraints are missing, while a corrected check rejects it.
exhibits.limits: The CCX stepper is a small classical toy; no Groth16 proof or quantum circuit is generated.

exhibits.title: Quantum Addition Operating-Point Ledger
exhibits.action: Open the source-row ledger and compare logical qubits, non-Clifford operations, correctness, and operand interfaces.
exhibits.outcome: Shows why reported arithmetic variants and separate proof thresholds cannot be treated as interchangeable hardware estimates.
exhibits.limits: Source claims, approximations, and lab derivations are distinguished; no quantum circuit or hardware is run.

exhibits.title: Pseudo-Mersenne Reduction Boundary
exhibits.action: Toggle between overflow and x+y=p cases in the field-reduction subpanel.
exhibits.outcome: Shows that checking only a 256-bit carry misses exact equality to p, so a separate boundary operation is needed.
exhibits.section: Why a small constant replaces a large subtraction
exhibits.limits: The full-precision calculation does not simulate truncated-comparison or carry-propagation errors of the quantum algorithms.

exhibits.title: ECDSA.Fail Nonce Selection and Statistical Limits
exhibits.action: Read the paper-mechanism panel, clean-draw probability, zero-failure discussion, and two accounts of nonce hunting.
exhibits.outcome: Distinguishes an approximate circuit passing selected tests from all-input exactness and separates measured per-call failure from a full Shor success claim.
exhibits.limits: Competing source accounts are presented without adjudication; the demo grind is not a circuit submission.

exhibits.title: Post-Commitment Randomness for Circuit Tests
exhibits.action: Read the verifier-seed and public-beacon alternatives after the commitment.
exhibits.outcome: Shows how removing prover choice of test-set draw changes the modelled multiplicity from G attempts to one fixed draw.
exhibits.limits: The G=1 model assumes a fixed commitment and no selective restart; neither mitigation is implemented as a deployed verifier.

exhibits.title: Commitment Serialization and Proof Statement
exhibits.action: Step the proof pipeline and inspect the v1-versus-v2 hash discussion.
exhibits.outcome: Explains that cryptographic commitment binds serialized circuit bytes and why equivalent behavior need not yield the same hash.
exhibits.limits: The paper’s full proof and private circuit are described; this panel does not generate their Groth16 proof.

exhibits.title: Groth16 Attestation Assumption
exhibits.action: Read the caveat about the proof wrapper around a claimed quantum resource estimate.
exhibits.outcome: Identifies pairing-based soundness assumptions as separate from correctness of the checker and the underlying circuit.
exhibits.section: The attestation has its own assumptions
exhibits.limits: The discussion does not demonstrate a quantum break of the proof system.

exhibits.title: Information Leaked by Proof Existence
exhibits.action: Read the disclosure panel about announcing a hidden result and proving its possession.
exhibits.outcome: Shows that revealing existence and ownership can create search incentives and coercion risk despite zero-knowledge of the secret.
exhibits.section: Disclosure without details still discloses something
exhibits.limits: The disclosure risks are arguments drawn from cited commentary, not quantified or demonstrated attacks.

exhibits.title: Optional Magic-State Factory Estimate
exhibits.action: Open the optional factory estimate and inspect its operation-to-T-state and cycle-time assumptions.
exhibits.outcome: Derives a T-state rate and two illustrative factory-qubit counts from source operation and time figures plus explicitly labeled lab assumptions.
exhibits.limits: The source paper does not state the four-T-states-per-Toffoli conversion; the factory-qubit calculation is a lab derivation, not a demonstrated machine.

exhibits.title: MAC Playground
exhibits.action: Generate a one-time key, enter a message, compute its Poly1305 tag and verify the original or altered message or tag.
exhibits.outcome: The original passes while message or tag tampering fails.
exhibits.limits: Poly1305 requires a fresh one-time (r,s) key per message; standalone MACs do not encrypt data.

exhibits.title: Polynomial Stepper
exhibits.action: Show the per-block polynomial arithmetic and clamped r for the current message and key.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect 16-byte blocks, appended bit, modular accumulator and final tag construction.
exhibits.limits: A readable arithmetic trace, not a constant-time implementation audit.

exhibits.title: Forge a Tag by Reusing One Key
exhibits.section: Forge a Tag by Reusing One Key
exhibits.action: Authenticate two chosen short messages with one key, recover candidate one-time key values and forge a tag on a third message.
exhibits.outcome: The forged tag passes verification under the reused key once a valid candidate is recovered.
exhibits.limits: The worked algebra constrains message shape; reuse is the vulnerability, not a general attack with properly unique keys.

exhibits.title: Poly1305 Notes
exhibits.action: Switch among what Poly1305 is, the math and constant-time verification notes.
exhibits.outcome: Explains MAC scope, field arithmetic and timing-safe tag comparison.
exhibits.limits: Narrative notes do not measure timing behavior.

exhibits.title: Commit to a polynomial in one BLS12-381 group element
exhibits.action: Choose polynomial and commit against a generated structured reference string.
exhibits.outcome: Displays KZG commitment, degree and time independent of polynomial coefficient count in commitment size.
exhibits.limits: Binding non-hiding teaching commitment; the setup trapdoor must remain unknown.
exhibits.section: Commit — one group element, whatever the degree

exhibits.title: Open and verify a polynomial evaluation
exhibits.action: Set point z and claimed y, then prove and verify or try incorrect claims.
exhibits.outcome: Shows quotient division and pairing check; wrong evaluation yields a nonzero remainder and fails.
exhibits.limits: One opening at a time in coefficient basis; this is not a production batch verifier.
exhibits.section: Open and verify — why the division has to come out exactly

exhibits.title: Audit a ceremony and exploit retained trapdoor
exhibits.action: Run participant contributions, retain their factors, audit the transcript and forge an opening using recovered tau.
exhibits.outcome: The public algebraic transcript checks pass while retained factors reconstruct the trapdoor and make a false opening verifiable.
exhibits.limits: One browser acts as every contributor; the result demonstrates what transcript checks cannot prove about erasure, not an attack on a real ceremony.
exhibits.section: Toxic waste — an all-green transcript over a completely dishonest ceremony

exhibits.title: Show an unenforced degree bound
exhibits.action: Run a high-degree commitment with or without the shifted-commitment degree check.
exhibits.outcome: Opening equations still agree, while the extra pairing relation enforces the intended maximum degree.
exhibits.limits: Missing degree checks do not by themselves break evaluation binding.

exhibits.title: Commit the same polynomial with KZG, IPA and FRI
exhibits.action: Run three commitment and opening schemes against the same polynomial.
exhibits.outcome: Shows measured sizes and local timings alongside scheme-specific assumptions.
exhibits.limits: FRI soundness figure is heuristic with teaching parameters; implementation timings are not production benchmarks.

exhibits.title: Explain why Groth16 has no swappable commitment layer
exhibits.section: Why Groth16 is not on this list
exhibits.action: Read Act 7 claims and the universal versus per-circuit ceremony contrast.
exhibits.outcome: Contrasts layered polynomial IOP and commitment systems with Groth16 circuit-bound QAP reference strings.
exhibits.limits: Conceptual comparison; this act does not implement Groth16 proving.

exhibits.title: Construct two false openings that cancel in a batch
exhibits.section: The last challenge: when two false openings cancel
exhibits.action: Compare honest openings with public-SRS proofs chosen after the batching challenge, then bind both proof points into the challenge.
exhibits.outcome: Individual false openings reject; the premature weighted pairing accepts them and the proof-bound challenge rejects this construction.
exhibits.limits: Two-opening counterexample, not the full PLONK exploit, a trapdoor recovery, or a general security proof for the repaired control.

exhibits.title: Correlation Power Analysis: recover an AES key byte
exhibits.section: Break it yourself: pull an AES key byte out of the noise
exhibits.action: Change the trace-count and noise sliders, choose a reproducible seed, and run the key-byte correlation attack.
exhibits.outcome: Plots the correlation scores for 256 key-byte guesses, the true byte's rank, and whether the simulated leakage lets the attack recover byte 0; can freeze and export the result.
exhibits.limits: The AES and correlation are computed, but power traces are generated by a model; this is not a measured attack on a chip or on browser timing.

exhibits.title: First-order CPA against masking, shuffling, and hiding
exhibits.section: Defended, defeated, or just more expensive?
exhibits.action: Select none, Boolean masking, shuffling, or added noise and click Attack the defended chip.
exhibits.outcome: Regenerates 4,000 simulated traces, reruns the same CPA, and shows a rank and verdict for the chosen defense.
exhibits.limits: The masking result concerns this first-order leakage model and first-order CPA only; the page names but does not implement a second-order attack or prove hardware resistance.

exhibits.title: Hypothetical AES table-lookup cache-line leak
exhibits.section: What a table lookup can reveal through a cache line
exhibits.action: Enter a known plaintext byte and compare a secret-indexed table lookup with uniform access across all cache lines.
exhibits.outcome: Highlights the idealized observed lines and reports the number of key-byte guesses consistent with each observation.
exhibits.limits: A one-byte perfect-observation model with a hypothetical T-table and 64-byte lines; no cache timing is measured, and the lab's JavaScript AES uses a different S-box layout.

exhibits.title: Single-Trace Simple Power Analysis
exhibits.action: Enter a secret exponent and capture a modeled square-and-multiply trace.
exhibits.outcome: Different square and multiply operations expose the exponent bits in one simulated trace and a step table.
exhibits.limits: The BigInt exponentiation runs locally; the power trace is modeled rather than captured.

exhibits.title: Noise versus CPA Trace Budget
exhibits.action: Run the sweep of measurement noise levels and inspect trace counts to key-byte recovery.
exhibits.outcome: The plotted budget rises as a weaker correlation requires more traces.
exhibits.limits: A synthetic leakage model does not predict the exact budget for a real chip.

exhibits.title: Jitter, Resynchronization and Re-Attack
exhibits.action: Jitter the synthetic traces, then cross-correlate them to resynchronize and run the same attack.
exhibits.outcome: Initial misalignment suppresses the CPA peak while the alignment pass restores it.

exhibits.title: Differential versus Correlation Power Analysis
exhibits.action: Race difference-of-means DPA against Hamming-weight Pearson CPA on the same synthetic measurements.
exhibits.outcome: The panel reports the trace count at which each statistic first ranks the true key byte highest.

exhibits.title: Run CPA on a Trace CSV
exhibits.action: Import a trace-per-row CSV with plaintext byte and power samples or download and re-import the supplied example.
exhibits.outcome: The same Pearson correlation ranks key-byte candidates in user-provided data.
exhibits.limits: Raw import omits alignment and point-of-interest selection normally needed for hardware traces.

exhibits.title: Real Cipher and Simulated Leakage Boundary
exhibits.action: Inspect the list of real AES and statistics versus modeled leakage and omitted hardware attacks.
exhibits.outcome: The section limits results to the stated Hamming-weight model and first-order CPA behavior, with no specific-device vulnerability claim.

exhibits.title: Constraint-Based PQ Shortlist
exhibits.action: Choose KEM or signature role, minimum category, wire budget, workload, and environment flags.
exhibits.outcome: The page shortlists schemes from parameter sets actually derived in the browser and gives reasoned exclusions and caveats.
exhibits.limits: The shortlist covers locally supported schemes and cannot decide security or deployment suitability on size and local timing alone.

exhibits.title: Derived Algorithm Size Matrix
exhibits.action: Inspect or request more schemes and compare key, ciphertext, and signature lengths.
exhibits.outcome: Measurements come from live library buffers and operations, with status and failures visible per row.
exhibits.section: Every figure, derived in your browser
exhibits.limits: Only algorithms available in the installed browser library are measured; HQC is outside the local shortlist.

exhibits.title: TLS Handshake Byte Breakdown
exhibits.action: Choose derived KEM and signature values and inspect four PQ-dependent TLS 1.3 buffers and hybrid overhead.
exhibits.outcome: The table totals public key, ciphertext, verification key, and signature bytes rather than modeling a complete handshake.
exhibits.section: PQ-dependent bytes in a TLS 1.3 handshake
exhibits.limits: The panel excludes non-PQ protocol framing and network behavior.

exhibits.title: Local PQ versus Classical Benchmark
exhibits.action: Run keygen, encapsulation or signing, and verification samples for supported schemes and baselines.
exhibits.outcome: Measured distributions appear beside environment details and a take-away run.
exhibits.limits: Local browser timings are not a general performance ranking.

exhibits.title: Verify a Claimed Size
exhibits.action: Enter a size claim and ask the running library for the corresponding buffer.
exhibits.outcome: The interface tests a common misquote against actual derived values and reports agreement or mismatch.

exhibits.title: Pinned Comparison Tray and Risk
exhibits.action: Pin schemes and inspect side-by-side evidence, common misquotes, implementation risk, and caveats.

exhibits.title: Limited-Use SLH-DSA Draft Note
exhibits.action: Read the separate draft reference and evidence boundary.
exhibits.outcome: The panel separates draft limited-use proposals from standardized scheme measurements.

exhibits.title: Explore five post-quantum families
exhibits.action: Select lattice, code, hash, multivariate or isogeny family, then switch between overview, math, notable cryptanalysis and primary-source tabs.
exhibits.outcome: The page displays sourced representative schemes, status, assumptions, tradeoffs and dated research summaries; it warns when an individual scheme was broken rather than declaring an entire family broken. The hash-based view distinguishes mathematical assumptions from implementation leakage, citing the October 2026 SLH-DSA-SHAKE power-analysis preprint with its physical-access condition.
exhibits.limits: This explorer displays authored research/status summaries. It does not execute cryptanalysis, test all schemes, or turn its heuristic standardisation confidence score into a measured security quantity.

exhibits.title: Compare sizes across families
exhibits.action: Switch between public-key, secret-key, and ciphertext/signature metrics for representative parameter sets.
exhibits.outcome: Plots source-data byte counts on a log2 scale, making relative size tradeoffs visible.
exhibits.limits: Bars are representative parameter values and some entries approximate; verify any deployment selection against the named scheme specification. No key pair or ciphertext is generated by this chart.

exhibits.title: Calculate textbook information-set decoding work
exhibits.section: ISD Work: Prange Attack Cost for Code Parameters
exhibits.action: Use Classic McEliece presets or change code length n, dimension k, and error weight t.
exhibits.outcome: Recomputes Prange success probability and expected log2 work using binomial ratios, plus an illustrative half-exponent quantum scaling and category-floor comparison.
exhibits.limits: This computes a textbook cost formula, not a real key-recovery attack or an overall scheme security estimate. Modern ISD, memory tradeoffs and structural attacks are not modeled.

exhibits.title: Generate and verify a Lamport one-time signature
exhibits.action: Generate a 256-bit-width Lamport keypair, sign a chosen message, verify it, then edit the message and verify again.
exhibits.outcome: WebCrypto SHA-256 commitments produce a real one-time signature; the page shows which private halves are revealed and rejects a signature after message tampering.
exhibits.limits: This is a plain one-time Lamport scheme, not an implementation of standardized SLH-DSA, XMSS or LMS.

exhibits.title: Reuse a Lamport key and forge at toy digest width
exhibits.section: Now actually forge one — at a toy width
exhibits.action: Sign a second message under the same key to inspect leaked secret halves; choose a 12-, 16-, or 20-bit toy digest and run a covered-message forgery.
exhibits.outcome: The browser derives key material from two observed signatures, searches SHA-256 candidates at the truncated width, and feeds a forged signature to the same verifier, with a negative control for an uncovered message.
exhibits.limits: The successful forgery is deliberately restricted to 12–20 digest bits; the full-width two-signature forgery grind remains out of reach in this browser lab. It is not a break of SLH-DSA.

exhibits.title: Estimate post-quantum TLS handshake bytes
exhibits.action: Choose a KEM and signature, vary intermediate certificate count, toggle the classical hybrid, or load presets.
exhibits.outcome: Recalculates segmented public-key, ciphertext and signature byte totals and their ratio to an X25519 and ECDSA baseline; broken selections open a research and sibling-lab explanation.
exhibits.limits: A sum of selected component sizes, not a real TLS handshake, interoperability run, or complete wire-size measurement. Broken schemes are retained for comparison only.

exhibits.title: Move a 2D lattice basis and trace its reduction
exhibits.action: Drag basis vectors or choose presets, then run one Lagrange–Gauss step or reduce to a fixed point.
exhibits.outcome: The SVG and readouts update lattice points, shortest nonzero vector, determinant, orthogonality defect and a step-by-step reduction trace.
exhibits.limits: The exercise is exact two-dimensional geometry; it does not solve Module-LWE, run BKZ on production parameters, or estimate a concrete quantum attack.

exhibits.title: Read the head-to-head family comparison
exhibits.action: Pin representative schemes in the explorer and compare the resulting highlighted family rows.
exhibits.outcome: The table shows each family's hard problem, available KEM or signature role, public-key range among listed schemes and stated maturity.
exhibits.limits: Rows summarize authored scheme data; a family-level status or smallest-to-largest key range is not a security proof for each candidate.

exhibits.title: Trace the dated post-quantum history timeline
exhibits.action: Read the timeline of discoveries, attacks and standards milestones.
exhibits.outcome: Shows dated authored milestones from McEliece through the 2024 FIPS publications, with scheme breakages distinguished from family-wide claims.
exhibits.limits: A curated historical summary, not an automatically refreshed standards feed or implementation.

exhibits.title: Compare approximate library support
exhibits.action: Read the scheme-by-library matrix and its shipped, experimental and planned legend.
exhibits.outcome: Displays an authored snapshot of support across selected libraries and warns readers to verify each current changelog.
exhibits.limits: Approximate mid-2026 authored support table; it is neither a live package inventory nor an interoperability or security test.

exhibits.title: Explore conditional KEM and signature recommendations
exhibits.action: Choose whether a KEM, signature or both are needed, then prioritize a NIST primary, diversity, output size or public-key size.
exhibits.outcome: An authored rule table shows a scheme combination, rationale, caveats and a link to try the selection in the byte calculator.
exhibits.limits: Fixed educational recommendations are not live standards decisions or deployment approval; protocol, threat model and library support require independent review.

exhibits.title: Explore quantum threat and migration context
exhibits.action: Switch among Shor, harvest-now-decrypt-later, lattice selection, hybrids and NIST categories tabs.
exhibits.outcome: Reads conditional risk explanations, a sourced RSA-2048 quantum resource-estimate comparison, and a table that keeps quantum-depth thresholds separate from classical gates.
exhibits.limits: The resource figures are conditional estimates from separately dated papers, not a quantum factoring demonstration, a universal minimum, or a Q-Day forecast.

exhibits.title: Read post-quantum terms and definitions
exhibits.action: Browse the glossary terms used throughout the comparison.
exhibits.outcome: Displays short authored definitions for the cryptographic jargon and points back to the representative family sources.
exhibits.limits: The glossary is an explanatory reference, not a runnable construction or formal security definition.

exhibits.title: Read four closing post-quantum takeaways
exhibits.section: If You Remember Only Four Things
exhibits.action: Read the final four-part summary after the interactive sections.
exhibits.outcome: Recaps current primary lattice standards, code and hash diversity, specific broken finalist schemes, and hybrid migration.
exhibits.limits: A dated educational summary, not an implementation, a security proof, or a live standards feed.

exhibits.title: Inventory and Mosca inequality
exhibits.section: Step 1 — Are you already late? (Inventory & Mosca)
exhibits.action: Load a sample enterprise, government or finance inventory and change assumed quantum arrival and migration duration.
exhibits.outcome: Computes an HNDL planning score only for explicitly inventoried classical key-establishment or public-key encryption paths; separately explains signature migration urgency.
exhibits.limits: Inventories, CRQC year and migration time are illustrative; a signing key alone does not establish recorded-traffic decryption exposure.

exhibits.title: Milestones and deadline sequencing
exhibits.action: Adjust deadline and readiness assumptions while comparing published milestones.
exhibits.outcome: Shows migration sequence and a model-derived doom meter beside read-only source events.
exhibits.limits: The modeled schedule and meter are scenario outputs, not official deadlines.

exhibits.title: Composite-style certificate and tamper
exhibits.section: Steps 2 & 3 — The fix and its cost (Hybrid certificate)
exhibits.action: Switch classical, hybrid and pure-PQ views, inspect measured ECDSA-P256/ML-DSA-65 bytes and tamper with either signature or certificate body.
exhibits.outcome: Shows both signatures required by the teaching AND verifier and the payload size cost.
exhibits.limits: Uses a JSON body and modeled X.509 envelope, not DER or an interoperable certificate chain; backward-compatible policy needs explicit downgrade protection.

exhibits.title: Canary fleet rollout
exhibits.section: Step 5 — How to deploy safely (Fleet rotation)
exhibits.action: Set canary share, monitoring window, rollout stages and injected failure, then run rotation.
exhibits.outcome: Displays per-server state and automatic rollback after monitoring failures.
exhibits.limits: Simulated fleet and failures; no server configuration or certificates are deployed.

exhibits.title: Verify modeled cryptography
exhibits.section: Prove it — verify the cryptography yourself
exhibits.action: Run the page’s signature and certificate verification suite.
exhibits.outcome: Displays checks and failures for generated keys and tampered forms.
exhibits.limits: Passing selected tests is not a complete certificate implementation audit.

exhibits.title: Full Handshake, Live
exhibits.action: Step or auto-play through the client and server exchange; Reset generates fresh values.
exhibits.outcome: Displays the serialized hybrid ClientHello and ServerHello, independently computed 64-byte ML-KEM-768 || X25519 secrets, and their match result.
exhibits.limits: Both TLS peers run inside the browser; this is an educational simulation of hello exchange and key schedule, not a production TLS stack or a network TLS connection.

exhibits.title: Why Hybrid?
exhibits.action: Read the threat scenarios and which component still protects the connection.
exhibits.outcome: A static table shows the intended hedge if one component's security assumption fails; no attacker or downgrade is executed.
exhibits.limits: Static threat scenarios are simplified conditional claims, not a tested security proof or a demonstration of Shor's algorithm.

exhibits.title: Building the Hybrid Secret
exhibits.action: Inspect the per-run ML-KEM and X25519 secret previews and press Reset to regenerate the exchange.
exhibits.outcome: Shows ML-KEM || X25519 in RFC 10024 order entering the TLS 1.3 HKDF key schedule, with actual handshake and traffic secret previews.
exhibits.limits: The previews come from real local computations; no finished TLS record protection or remote peer is shown.

exhibits.title: Size and Compute Impact
exhibits.action: Compare the current hybrid and classical hello sizes and locally timed key exchange operations; Reset refreshes the measurement.
exhibits.outcome: Shows measured byte counts, best-of-samples CPU timings and an approximate 1500-byte MTU visual.
exhibits.limits: CPU measurements are local microbenchmarks, not network latency or portable performance rankings. The MTU graphic uses a typical boundary; it does not simulate packets or middleboxes.

exhibits.title: Wire Format Inspector
exhibits.action: Enable Show wire bytes and select the named group, X25519, or ML-KEM byte region.
exhibits.outcome: Highlights computed offsets in the actual serialized ClientHello generated by the local exchange, eliding the large middle of the ML-KEM share.
exhibits.limits: Inspector shows a locally serialized teaching ClientHello, not packets captured from a live TLS connection.

exhibits.title: Deployment Reality
exhibits.action: Read the dated deployment note and the linked IETF group identifier.
exhibits.outcome: Displays adoption context and a source link for RFC 10024's X25519MLKEM768 group 0x11EC.
exhibits.limits: Adoption figure is explicitly dated mid-September 2025; this panel measures no live deployment.

exhibits.title: Build a PQXDH transcript
exhibits.action: Step through Bob's signed prekey bundle, Alice's four X25519 Diffie-Hellman terms and ML-KEM encapsulation, initial-message delivery, and independent Bob derivation.
exhibits.outcome: The browser computes five secret components and an HKDF-SHA-512 session key, measures wire fields, verifies the AES-GCM initial message, and compares Alice's and Bob's keys byte for byte.
exhibits.limits: This is a browser teaching profile of Signal's PQXDH Revision 3, using separate strict Ed25519 signatures and standardized ML-KEM-1024 in place of the revision's XEdDSA and Kyber example. It is not wire-compatible with libsignal; no quantum algorithm runs here.

exhibits.title: Grant curve and lattice breaks to an adversary model
exhibits.section: Open the boxes the model grants
exhibits.action: Complete the handshake, grant the model all X25519 private keys with Curve break, then optionally grant it the ML-KEM secret with Lattice break.
exhibits.outcome: With only the curve grant, it recomputes four DH outputs but lacks the KEM secret and cannot rederive the session key; with both grants, it derives the same session key.
exhibits.limits: The model directly hands private values to the adversary. It neither runs Shor's algorithm nor breaks ML-KEM, and does not prove the security of a deployed implementation.

exhibits.title: Corrupt a prekey signature or ML-KEM ciphertext
exhibits.action: Run the prekey-signature corruption and KEM ciphertext-bit-flip controls on fresh handshakes.
exhibits.outcome: Alice aborts on a bad PQ prekey signature before the handshake; after KEM ciphertext tampering, Bob's first AES-GCM authentication rejects the message.
exhibits.limits: These controlled failure cases are not a chosen-ciphertext security proof or exhaustive malformed-input analysis.

exhibits.title: Exhaust one-time PQ prekeys
exhibits.action: Enable Reuse last-resort key and run two Alice handshakes against the same fallback public key.
exhibits.outcome: The panel checks that the same last-resort PQ prekey identifier served both sessions while their encapsulated shared secrets differ.
exhibits.limits: Reusing the fallback public key does not by itself reveal either session key; the page conditions future compromise on recovering the retained private key and other needed inputs.

exhibits.title: Test authentication and post-compromise healing limits
exhibits.section: Two green handshakes, two missing guarantees
exhibits.action: Substitute a signed bundle under granted classical identity secrets, then compromise and ratchet a completed session with Curve break on or off.
exhibits.outcome: The first model confirms a valid classical signature can accompany adversary control of the initial message; the reduced X25519 ratchet refreshes roots for honest peers, but a curve-break grant can let the adversary follow those roots.
exhibits.limits: This reduced DH-root update is not full Double Ratchet, SPQR or Triple Ratchet; the adversary is explicitly granted secrets rather than running a quantum recovery algorithm.

exhibits.title: X3DH to PQXDH Byte-Level Diff
exhibits.action: Open the transcript diff and implementation-profile disclosures.

exhibits.section: X3DH becomes PQXDH at one boundary
exhibits.limits: Separate Ed25519 signatures replace specified XEdDSA; final ML-KEM and Kyber Round 3 are not wire-compatible.

exhibits.title: Pinned PQXDH Protocol Record
exhibits.action: Inspect the protocol revision, KAT provenance and primary source links.
exhibits.outcome: The source record places the live checks beside the PQXDH specification and the newer post-quantum ratchet context.

exhibits.title: Miller–Rabin square chain
exhibits.action: Enter a candidate and base, inspect and step the modular-square chain.
exhibits.outcome: A witness proves compositeness; an exhausted chain without a witness is only a probable-prime result.
exhibits.section: Find a reason this number is not prime

exhibits.title: Exact Fermat and strong-liar census
exhibits.action: Choose a composite and count every base.
exhibits.outcome: Compare Fermat liars, Miller–Rabin strong liars and the unit-group denominator, including the n=9 exception.

exhibits.title: Fixed-base pseudoprime challenge
exhibits.action: Run published fixed prime-base lists against strong pseudoprimes, then sample 100 fresh random bases.
exhibits.outcome: Observe a composite passing a bounded fixed list despite random bases revealing witnesses.
exhibits.limits: The deterministic guarantee applies only below its strict proven bound.
exhibits.section: A fixed list is only as good as its proven range

exhibits.title: Probable-prime generation
exhibits.action: Choose candidate size and number of runs, then generate and measure candidates.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect sieve counts, Miller–Rabin rounds, timing and the distinction between proved small primes and probable large ones.
exhibits.limits: The 1024-bit teaching path is not a FIPS-conformant RSA key generator or a primality certificate.
exhibits.section: How many candidates until a prime?

exhibits.title: Toy composite liar-fraction search
exhibits.action: Enumerate all odd composites and bases under a selected small cap.
exhibits.outcome: Plot exact strong-liar fractions among units and find quarter-bound cases.
exhibits.section: Where do the worst liar fractions occur?

exhibits.title: 1024-bit FIPS-shape probable prime generation
exhibits.action: Run the separate 1024-bit generation tab for one or three candidate searches.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect candidates tried, sieve count, measured browser timing and five Miller–Rabin rounds per accepted probable prime.
exhibits.limits: Teaching shape only: no validated DRBG, RSA exponent or p−q constraints, and no primality certificate.

exhibits.title: Prove a small prime with a recursive certificate
exhibits.action: Generate a Lucas–Pratt certificate for a candidate up to 1,000,000, edit or paste its JSON, and run an independent recursive verifier.
exhibits.outcome: A complete factor tree and full-order modular witness prove primality; changing a factor, subproof, or witness makes verification fail.
exhibits.limits: Generation uses trial division and is capped at 1,000,000; verification checks the supplied proof without factoring or calling the generator. It does not certify the separate 1024-bit probable-prime output or implement ECPP/AKS.

exhibits.title: Private VOPRF token issuance and redemption
exhibits.section: A receipt with no name on it
exhibits.action: Keep Private issuance selected; issue a token, redeem it at the origin, and compare the issuer and origin ledgers.
exhibits.outcome: The client verifies a P-384 DLEQ proof, finalizes a type-0x0001 token, the origin checks its authenticator and fresh nonce, and the collusion check reports no computable equality match for a properly blinded request.
exhibits.limits: All roles and the issuer secret run in one local browser session; no HTTP transport, attester, rate limiting, global key-consistency protocol, batched issuance or production service is implemented.

exhibits.title: Remove blinding and link issuance to redemption
exhibits.action: Choose BROKEN: remove blinding, issue the token, redeem it, then try to link the ledgers.
exhibits.outcome: Sets the blinding scalar to one; the issuer-observed raw input point equals the point derived from the redeemed token, and the UI draws one computed link and an alarm verdict.
exhibits.limits: An intentional local broken mode demonstrating direct point equality; it does not model probabilistic tracking, network metadata or a deployed Privacy Pass service.

exhibits.title: Link otherwise valid tokens by per-client issuer keys
exhibits.action: Choose BROKEN: per-client published key, select a roster size of two, three or four clients, issue and redeem their tokens, then link ledgers.
exhibits.outcome: Each client verifies a valid DLEQ proof under its own published key and redeems; the UI counts distinct key-ID buckets and draws one link per client partition.
exhibits.limits: A fixed local roster of two to four synthetic clients; valid per-client proofs alone do not establish that all clients saw the same globally published key.

exhibits.title: Reject an issuer response under an unpublished key
exhibits.action: Choose BROKEN: unpublished issuer key and click Issue token.
exhibits.outcome: A careful client verifies the DLEQ proof against the trusted published key and aborts before finalization; the page separately shows that a careless client's token would be refused by the origin configured with that trusted key.
exhibits.limits: The rogue issuer and careless client are intentionally local counterfactuals; this demonstrates checking the already trusted key, not global key-distribution or key-consistency infrastructure.

exhibits.title: Compare the other Privacy Pass token type and its RSA-oracle exposure
exhibits.section: The Other Token Type: Blind RSA and √eNFS (2026)
exhibits.action: Read the side-by-side discussion of VOPRF type 0x0001 and Blind RSA type 0x0002, the attack cost distinction, mitigations and this lab's scope.
exhibits.outcome: The page identifies Blind RSA as publicly verifiable, separates a measured 1024-bit result from a 2048-bit extrapolation, and explains why this VOPRF implementation is not an RSA signing oracle.
exhibits.limits: This is a source-linked explanation only. The lab implements type 0x0001 VOPRF; it does not issue Blind RSA tokens or run the cited RSA attack.

exhibits.title: Inspect the Privacy Pass wire values and scope
exhibits.section: Inspect the real wire values and scope
exhibits.action: Issue a token and open the expandable wire-values and scope panel.
exhibits.outcome: See the published P-384 key and token key ID, the generated TokenRequest, TokenResponse and Token encodings, official test-vector counts, and the protocol pieces this local session omits.
exhibits.limits: Displayed encodings come from the one-session VOPRF path. The test-vector count refers to project tests; this panel does not itself run an interop suite or implement HTTP transport.

exhibits.title: Prio3 Report Preparation
exhibits.action: Choose a count or bounded sum measurement, split a report, and prepare each aggregator share.
exhibits.outcome: Shows two envelopes, verifier shares, and the validity decision from real field/proof code.
exhibits.limits: Two-aggregator teaching implementation without DAP transport or constant-time guarantees.

exhibits.title: Collector Tally
exhibits.action: Add accepted reports and compare the unsharded total with a separately computed plain sum.
exhibits.outcome: Shows private input shares combine into an aggregate output.
exhibits.limits: No differential privacy is added to the aggregate.

exhibits.title: Invalid and Replayed Report Tests
exhibits.action: Try out-of-range salary, damaged proof share, and repeated report controls.
exhibits.outcome: Shows proof rejection of invalid input and corruption; replay passes proof preparation but is refused by a separate nonce registry.
exhibits.limits: Replay protection is outside the VDAF proof.

exhibits.title: Aggregator Collusion
exhibits.action: Toggle collusion and put both report envelopes in one view.
exhibits.outcome: Shows combined input shares reveal the encoded measurement.
exhibits.section: Put both envelopes on one desk

exhibits.title: Valid Lie and Single-Report Leakage
exhibits.action: Run well-formed false-report and one-report fixtures.
exhibits.outcome: Shows a valid circuit proof cannot attest real-world truth or hide a one-person public total.
exhibits.section: What a valid proof cannot prove

exhibits.title: Prio3 Reference Vector Checks and Scope
exhibits.action: Read the pinned-evidence panel and compare runtime Count and bounded Sum output shares to reference vectors.
exhibits.outcome: Reports three known-answer checks and identifies implemented Field64, TurboSHAKE128, FLP, and Prio3 components.
exhibits.limits: The vector panel does not test differential privacy. The lab provides no DAP transport, production differential-privacy deployment, additional aggregator count, or production hardening; vector agreement does not prove security.

exhibits.title: Exact-Release Differencing
exhibits.action: Run two equal-size twelve-slot Prio3Sum queries, replace one bounded slot with zero, and subtract the exact totals.
exhibits.outcome: Shows the difference equals Lane's clamped, floor-quantized contribution even though each aggregator sees only its own shares.
exhibits.limits: This is a deliberately insecure exact-release control. It preserves cohort size and demonstrates output differencing; it does not claim Prio3 hides released totals.

exhibits.title: Participant-Contributed Noisy Release
exhibits.action: Choose an honest/corrupt, dropout, collusion, output-cap, or repeat scenario, then commit one cohort and attempt one release.
exhibits.outcome: Releases one collector-visible noisy Prio3Sum only when the bounded trust and delivery conditions hold; every listed failure path releases no aggregate.
exhibits.limits: The bounded claim assumes non-colluding aggregators, externally authenticated sender-to-slot bindings, independent honest randomness, at least six honest noise contributors, complete delivery and one accounted release. The browser supplies no durable atomic ledger, DAP transport or production attestation.

exhibits.title: Differential-Privacy Trust Boundary Comparison
exhibits.action: Compare central, local, this distributed lesson, and shuffle DP while opening the separate collector and omniscient teaching views.
exhibits.outcome: Separates who sees inputs, where noise is trusted, the advertised activation and cap accounting, and which collusion or threshold failures invalidate the release claim.
exhibits.limits: Only the bounded distributed route is implemented here. Central, local and shuffle DP are comparison rows; the lab implements no shuffler or amplification theorem, and the per-client trace is explicitly not collector-visible.

exhibits.title: Compute visible-abort and retry privacy transcripts
exhibits.action: Choose a one- through three-attempt cap and compute exact neighboring probabilities for an ordinary release, one visible selective abort, publication conditioned on success, capped fresh retries and an independent-abort control.
exhibits.outcome: Shows exact neighboring probabilities for every complete public transcript, each mechanism's tight likelihood-ratio envelope, the conditioned distribution's delta at the original ratio, stopping conditions and separate public, aborter-only and teaching views.
exhibits.section: Who sees an abort changes the mechanism
exhibits.limits: A separate exact finite additive-noise model motivated by CL084, not an attack on the S04 construction or a claim that every abort violates differential privacy. The omniscient distribution ledger is teaching-only; a public observer does not see rejected candidate values.

exhibits.title: Run the search
exhibits.action: Choose a protocol and run the finite-state symbolic attacker search.
exhibits.outcome: The checker reports an attack trace or no attack within its configured bound, with explored-state diagnostics.
exhibits.limits: Perfect cryptography and bounded sessions are assumed; no-attack-in-bound is not a computational or implementation-security proof.

exhibits.title: One attacker, two conversations
exhibits.action: Run Needham-Schroeder Public Key and its Lowe identity-field fix, then step the attacker’s two-session trace.
exhibits.outcome: The original admits an impersonation relay, while the added responder identity blocks unification in the repaired model.
exhibits.limits: The verdicts are relative to the modeled messages, equational theory and finite search bound.

exhibits.title: Each protocol, its goal, its verdict
exhibits.section: Each protocol, its goal, its verdict
exhibits.action: Compare naive Diffie-Hellman with signed shares through the same symbolic search.
exhibits.outcome: An unauthenticated substitution reaches the attacker goal; signed shares block it in the modeled trust setting.
exhibits.limits: Signature identities are trusted in the model; the checker does not validate PKI or cryptographic implementations.

exhibits.title: How the search actually works (for the curious)
exhibits.section: How the search actually works (for the curious)
exhibits.action: Step the trace, inspect attacker knowledge and named derivation rules, and open the expert details.
exhibits.outcome: Every learned symbolic term is tied to a rule such as forwarding, decryption with a held key or construction.
exhibits.limits: The only modeled algebraic equality is the chosen DH shared key; no XOR or broader equational theory is handled.

exhibits.title: Seal messages under four authenticated-encryption compositions
exhibits.action: Enter two messages, optionally match them, then seal under MtE, EtM, E&M and AES-GCM.
exhibits.outcome: Compares packet layout, order of checks and equality behavior.
exhibits.limits: Four constructions illustrate composition, not a universal security proof for every implementation.
exhibits.section: Exhibit 1 — The Four Orders, Side by Side

exhibits.title: Recover bytes against a decrypt-before-authenticate seam
exhibits.action: Run the padding oracle attack on the lab’s vulnerable CBC composition.
exhibits.outcome: Displays oracle queries and decrypted bytes from observable padding behavior.
exhibits.limits: The oracle is deliberately leaky; attack success depends on a visible padding response.

exhibits.title: Recover a tag through a modeled timing signal
exhibits.action: Run tag recovery using only timing observations.
exhibits.outcome: Shows character-by-character timing evidence and recovered tag.
exhibits.limits: Timing is simulated in the browser; it is not a real remote network timing attack.
exhibits.section: Exhibit 3 — The Clock Never Lies: Timing Side-Channels

exhibits.title: Recover a secret through compress-then-encrypt length
exhibits.action: Run the length-only recovery or choose a new secret.
exhibits.outcome: Chosen text changes compressed ciphertext lengths, enabling the demo to infer secret bytes.
exhibits.limits: Controlled compression setup; real exploitability depends on attacker input placement and shared compression context.

exhibits.title: Step historical TLS composition changes
exhibits.action: Step or play through TLS version cards.
exhibits.outcome: Shows how successive designs addressed padding, MAC ordering and AEAD use.
exhibits.limits: Historical explanation, not a live TLS stack or deployment inventory.
exhibits.section: Exhibit 5 — How TLS Learned This Lesson

exhibits.title: Evaluate a proposed composition design
exhibits.action: Set protocol choices and evaluate the design.
exhibits.outcome: Displays rule-based findings for authentication, ordering and side-channel exposure.
exhibits.limits: A teaching checklist cannot establish formal protocol security.

exhibits.title: Contact Discovery Privacy Problem
exhibits.action: Read the contacts scenario and leakage boundary of ordinary list upload.
exhibits.outcome: The introduction motivates finding an intersection while limiting what each party learns.

exhibits.title: DH-PSI Step Walkthrough
exhibits.action: Step through hashing emails to ristretto points, each party’s scalar multiplication, commutation, and matching.
exhibits.outcome: A byte-level sequence shows why both paths to a shared item yield the same doubly blinded point.

exhibits.title: Custom-Set DH-PSI or OPRF-PSI
exhibits.action: Enter Alice and Bob sets and run either three-round DH-PSI or OPRF-PSI.
exhibits.outcome: The browser computes the intersection and protocol trace using real ristretto group operations.
exhibits.limits: Both roles run in one browser; this is not a networked malicious-secure deployment.

exhibits.title: Five PSI Misuse Experiments
exhibits.action: Run set-size inflation, small-domain enumeration, scalar reuse, malformed-point validation, and a lying OPRF publisher.
exhibits.outcome: Each result surfaces what the base protocol leaks or fails to bind, including protocol-level rejection of bad points.
exhibits.section: What Can Go Wrong — Attack Simulations
exhibits.limits: The malicious-party cases illustrate missing checks; the main protocol assumes semi-honest parties.

exhibits.title: Canonical Vectors and Wire Transcript
exhibits.action: Recompute fixed-seed test vectors and inspect each serialized ristretto point on the wire.
exhibits.outcome: The reproducible fixture supports byte-exact comparison with the real group implementation.
exhibits.limits: The fixed scalars and disabled shuffling in this reference oracle are not a secure execution mode.

exhibits.title: Local Benchmarks and DDH Byte Test
exhibits.action: Measure hash-to-point, scalar multiplication, and PSI runs, then bin bytes from 5,000 blinded outputs.
exhibits.outcome: Local timings and chi-square output provide implementation diagnostics and a limited empirical distribution check.
exhibits.limits: A byte-frequency test does not prove DDH pseudorandomness or malicious security.

exhibits.title: Deployments, Security Sketch, and Comparison
