exhibits.action: Read semi-honest simulator intuition, deployment examples, and protocol comparison.
exhibits.outcome: The prose states the DDH security assumption and explicit limits on timing, side channels, and malicious behavior.

exhibits.title: Guided beacon verification story
exhibits.action: Follow a short verify, tamper, operator-knowledge and threshold contrast.
exhibits.outcome: Connects hash integrity to authenticity, unpredictability and unique threshold output.
exhibits.limits: A guided route through pinned data and local toy threshold shares, not a live beacon service.

exhibits.title: Recompute a NIST pulse
exhibits.action: Choose a pinned pulse, switch 4- versus 8-byte length prefixes and flip a localRandomValue bit.
exhibits.outcome: Byte map and SHA-512 comparison show matching deployed serialization or failure under changed bytes.
exhibits.limits: Pinned public pulses; 8-byte draft text differs from the deployed 4-byte prefix behavior.

exhibits.title: Rewrite a NIST pulse
exhibits.section: Act 2 · Walk the chain, then rewrite history
exhibits.action: Rehash a modified pinned pulse and inspect links, precommitments and RSA signatures.
exhibits.outcome: The edited pulse may self-hash but independent chain and signature checks flag the rewrite.
exhibits.limits: The attacker lacks NIST’s signing key; fixture history is not a live network feed.

exhibits.title: Short path across old pulses
exhibits.section: Act 3 · Skip from a month ago to now
exhibits.action: Drop an intermediate pulse from a pinned skiplist path.
exhibits.outcome: Shows whether each hop has a valid previous/hour/day/month/year link and separate self-hash checks.
exhibits.limits: A consistent path proves linkage to a trusted anchor, not authorship by itself.

exhibits.title: Check NIST authorship and limits
exhibits.section: Act 4 · Who vouches for the pulse?
exhibits.action: Choose pinned cases and inspect certificate ID, pulse hash, precommitment and RSA signature verification.
exhibits.outcome: Shows origin verification when it passes, a mismatched rotation case, and a fully verified value known to the operator before release.
exhibits.limits: Certificate chain signature and trust anchor are not verified here; a valid pulse cannot prove operator unpredictability.

exhibits.title: Newest pinned NIST signature finding
exhibits.action: Read independently checked hash, chain, precommitment, named certificate and signature results.
exhibits.outcome: Reports whether the pinned pulse’s origin can be verified with its named certificate.
exhibits.limits: Pinned observation is date-specific; failed verification is not evidence that the operator or chain is compromised.

exhibits.title: Verify drand BLS round
exhibits.action: Choose pinned chained or unchained rounds, alter claimed round or prior signature, and inspect pairing and randomness.
exhibits.outcome: Shows pairing accept/reject, SHA-256(signature) consistency and continuity to previous or genesis value.
exhibits.limits: Uses captured rounds, not live drand; a valid signature relies on a trusted pinned group key.

exhibits.title: Toy threshold signer quorums
exhibits.section: Act 6 · Why a threshold makes the output unique
exhibits.action: Select signers, combine partial signatures and repeat with a different quorum or fresh shares.
exhibits.outcome: Shows every valid 3-of-5 quorum produces one identical group signature for the round while below-threshold sets fail.
exhibits.limits: Local toy dealer controls all shares; it is not drand’s distributed key-generation network.

exhibits.title: NIST and drand property table
exhibits.section: What you can and cannot check, side by side
exhibits.action: Follow checks behind tamper, unpredictability, uniqueness, verifiability and liveness rows.
exhibits.outcome: Summarizes observed/pinned checks and distinct operational assumptions.
exhibits.limits: Some property judgments are conditional or partial, not cryptographic proofs of real-world liveness or future honesty.

exhibits.title: Beam-splitter source model
exhibits.section: A beam-splitter QRNG — unpredictable by physics, imperfect by engineering
exhibits.action: Set detector mismatch and persistence, emit another stream, or stick detector B.
exhibits.outcome: Raw click bits and measured detector balance change; downstream entropy, extractor, and health panels update.
exhibits.limits: Photons are simulated using browser cryptographic randomness; this is not a connected physical QRNG or a source validation.

exhibits.title: Shannon versus min-entropy
exhibits.section: Shannon says “99.7% random.” Min-entropy says otherwise.
exhibits.action: Change source mismatch or persistence and inspect the live chart and attacker-work display.
exhibits.outcome: Measured Shannon and bias-based min-entropy diverge; a configured-model most-likely-path bound supplies the correlated block accounting.
exhibits.limits: Per-bit bias formulas assume independent bits; the correlated attacker-work figure depends on this synthetic source model, not an assessed hardware source.

exhibits.title: Von Neumann debiasing
exhibits.section: Von Neumann debiasing: perfect balance, brutal cost, wrong assumption
exhibits.action: Step bit pairs, run the rest, then make the source 80% streaky.
exhibits.outcome: See 01/10 kept, equal pairs discarded, throughput and output balance; a first-order predictor may expose dependence after debiasing.
exhibits.limits: Real pair processing on a simulated bitstream; first-order predictor is a diagnostic, not proof of unpredictability.

exhibits.title: Seeded Toeplitz extraction
exhibits.section: Toeplitz extraction — trading quantity for uniformity, with a receipt
exhibits.action: Set output length, draw a fresh seed, and extract; try exceeding the model min-entropy budget.
exhibits.outcome: A real GF(2) Toeplitz matrix-vector product displays output, seed/matrix, first-row parity, and Leftover Hash Lemma distance bound; a latched health alarm blocks extraction.
exhibits.limits: Input is simulated and k comes from its configured model; Toeplitz is not listed as a vetted SP 800-90B conditioning component; the displayed policy thresholds are teaching choices.

exhibits.title: Continuous RCT/APT monitor
exhibits.section: SP 800-90B health tests — because a dead source outputs a beautiful constant
exhibits.action: Stick and repair the detector, then explicitly recommission after an alarm.
exhibits.outcome: Continuous Repetition Count and Adaptive Proportion monitors show cutoffs, failures, and a latched boundary that blocks extractor input.
exhibits.limits: Health tests act on synthetic emissions and are tripwires for specified failures, not entropy estimators or source certification.

exhibits.title: Health-test threshold workshop
exhibits.section: The source has failed. Will your monitor notice?
exhibits.action: Choose failure mode and RCT/APT cutoffs or window, then test the setting.
exhibits.outcome: Reproducible trials report detection, pre-failure alarms, misses, median delay, and an analytical IID APT window false-alarm probability.
exhibits.limits: Small, fixed-seed synthetic trials; manual thresholds require source-specific deployment justification and do not alter the commissioned monitor above.

exhibits.title: Seal a threshold vault box
exhibits.action: Select a box, enter a secret and three keyholder passwords, then seal.
exhibits.outcome: The pipeline encrypts under AES-256, splits its key 2-of-3, wraps shares with SMAUG-T and signs the container with HAETAE.
exhibits.limits: The included signature public key is unauthenticated and cannot by itself establish who sealed the box.

exhibits.title: Two-keyholder vault opening
exhibits.action: Supply any two correct keyholder passwords to open a sealed box, and try invalid or missing shares.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect signature verification, KEM decapsulation, share reconstruction and authenticated decryption status.

exhibits.title: Tampered container test
exhibits.action: Run the panel’s tamper check against a throwaway copy of the sealed container.
exhibits.outcome: The changed container fails at signature verification before share recovery.
exhibits.limits: Successful verification under an embedded replaceable key is not external signer authentication.

exhibits.title: Portable vault container
exhibits.action: Export or import a sealed vault file and reset the demo state.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect persistence and restoration of serialized sealed boxes.

exhibits.title: Classical versus post-quantum vault key exchange
exhibits.action: Toggle the two explanatory cases alongside the SMAUG-T pipeline.
exhibits.outcome: Compare harvest-now-decrypt-later risk for an RSA/ECDH hypothetical with the intended lattice-KEM threat model.
exhibits.limits: Static explanations; the lab does not run an RSA/ECDH comparison or quantum attack.

exhibits.title: Vault primitive choices and failure cards
exhibits.action: Expand the quick decision rules and four failure-scenario cards.
exhibits.outcome: Compare authenticated storage, threshold sharing, post-quantum KEM and signature roles with nonce, threshold, key-authentication and classical-only failure modes.
exhibits.limits: These are static teaching cards, not live experiments on each failure mode.
exhibits.section: Go deeper — when to use each primitive

exhibits.title: Korean PQC origin and browser parameter sets
exhibits.action: Read the Research Origin panel and compare the browser pair with the repository CLI settings.
exhibits.outcome: Identify SMAUG-T as the KEM, HAETAE as the signature, and the lower browser parameter sets used for load speed.
exhibits.limits: The panel names parameter choices and research provenance; it does not benchmark attack costs.

exhibits.title: Classical and Hybrid Session Setup
exhibits.action: Select simplified X3DH or hybrid ML-KEM-1024 setup and start the session; optionally alter KEM ciphertext.
exhibits.outcome: Shows verified prekey handshake terms and a shared root before the classical message ratchet begins.
exhibits.limits: Hybrid setup seeds the classical Double Ratchet; the page does not implement SPQR or continuous post-quantum ratcheting.

exhibits.title: Live Double Ratchet Conversation
exhibits.action: Send custom or sample messages between Alice and Bob and inspect key state and wire data.
exhibits.outcome: Shows message encryption/decryption, advancing chain keys, and new DH root keys on response.

exhibits.title: Signed Prekey Tamper Check
exhibits.action: Try the man-in-the-middle control on session setup.
exhibits.outcome: Shows prekey signature verification reject substituted key material.

exhibits.title: Skipped Message Keys
exhibits.action: Generate five messages and deliver them in a changed order.
exhibits.outcome: Shows Bob storing skipped message keys and consuming them when late packets arrive.

exhibits.title: Compromise Point Explorer
exhibits.action: Run the forward-secrecy demo and move the compromise point.
exhibits.outcome: Shows which deleted earlier message keys are unavailable from later state.
exhibits.section: Forward Secrecy — Why Past Messages Stay Safe

exhibits.title: Classical DH Break-In Recovery
exhibits.action: Compromise Bob’s current state, send a fresh Alice message, and complete Bob’s DH ratchet.
exhibits.outcome: Shows recovery from a snapshot compromise after fresh DH input.
exhibits.limits: This models classical recovery only; the hybrid handshake alone offers no quantum post-compromise healing.

exhibits.title: Symmetric and DH Ratchet Key Timeline
exhibits.action: Send messages and switch to Ratchet State to inspect per-message key derivations and DH root-key transitions.
exhibits.outcome: Marks a new root and chain at each direction-change ratchet and one-use message keys as the chain advances.
exhibits.limits: Timeline is drawn from local session state; no external network or contacts.

exhibits.title: Hybrid Setup versus Continuous PQ Ratcheting
exhibits.action: Read the comparison of classical and hybrid startup with Triple Ratchet during a conversation.
exhibits.outcome: Separates one-time ML-KEM-1024 input at session setup from later classical-only DH recovery and describes continuous PQ refresh as a distinct, unbuilt construction.
exhibits.section: How this compares with current Signal
exhibits.limits: SPQR and Triple Ratchet are reading-only; this lab does not offer post-quantum healing after state compromise.

exhibits.title: Classical X3DH Setup and KDF Deviation
exhibits.action: Read the four-DH classical setup, signed and one-time prekeys, and the explicit omitted-prefix note.
exhibits.outcome: Explains why the demo’s bare HKDF of four DH outputs differs from spec-conformant X3DH domain separation and wire compatibility.
exhibits.limits: The demo’s classical KDF omits the F prefix and cannot interoperate with real X3DH or libsignal.

exhibits.title: Chain Key Convergence Check
exhibits.action: Exchange messages and inspect whether Alice’s sending chain and Bob’s receiving chain, and their reverse direction, independently match.
exhibits.outcome: The page compares chain-key state across both parties after ratchet steps, illustrating shared derivation without transmitting those keys.
exhibits.limits: A local browser exchange between simulated parties, not Signal’s current production protocol.

exhibits.title: 1 · The Relay
exhibits.action: Switch BBS98 or AFGH, encrypt to Alice, issue rk, transform through the proxy and decrypt as Bob; try corrupt rk, misroute or decrypt after the hop as Alice.
exhibits.outcome: A live exponent ledger and persistent proxy journal show what changes, who opens the result and which malformed paths refuse.
exhibits.limits: Teaching adaptation of AFGH to Type-3 BLS12-381; neither scheme here is CCA2-secure and session keys are not production-managed.

exhibits.title: 2 · Collusion
exhibits.action: Let Bob and the proxy pool their values under each scheme, then use any recovered secret.
exhibits.outcome: BBS98 exposes Alice’s scalar through division of rk and Bob’s scalar; the tested AFGH path does not reveal it.
exhibits.limits: AFGH resistance is demonstrated only for these attacks; the theorem’s security reduction is not reproduced.

exhibits.title: 3 · One Hop
exhibits.action: Relay Alice’s ciphertext through Bob, Carol and Dave, compose proxy keys and try wrong-level decryption.
exhibits.outcome: BBS98 supports transitive multi-hop and unissued composed delegations, whereas AFGH reaches a target-group level that cannot hop again.
exhibits.limits: The consequences arise from the implemented group shapes; policy authorization is separate from the cryptographic ability to compose.

exhibits.title: 4 · Delegation Graph
exhibits.action: Add delegation edges and inspect the persistent proxy journal and graph.
exhibits.outcome: The panel shows which edges were issued and how allowed transforms relate to stored proxy keys.
exhibits.limits: The journal persists only within the browser session and is not an external audit log.

exhibits.title: 5 · Un-delegate
exhibits.action: Attempt to remove delegation and then rotate keys through the provided workflow.
exhibits.outcome: Shows why withdrawing a proxy rk alone cannot erase already transformed ciphertext access.
exhibits.limits: Existing recipient knowledge and copied ciphertexts cannot be made secret again by deleting a relay key.

exhibits.title: 6 · Vectors
exhibits.action: Run the published primitive vectors, independent self-checks and hand-checkable BBS98/AFGH transcription checks.
exhibits.outcome: The three groups are reported separately so scheme checks are not confused with external known-answer vectors.
exhibits.limits: BBS98 and AFGH have no published standard vectors; self-checks and hand-derived examples are not independent cryptographic audits.

exhibits.title: Advance an epoch while retaining the same secret
exhibits.action: Advance a 3-of-5 sharing and inspect old and new shares and full dealing audit.
exhibits.outcome: Each share changes while the reconstructed secret and public key remain equal.
exhibits.limits: One browser simulates custodian channels and exposes secret audit state for pedagogy.
exhibits.section: 1 · Turn the epoch — same secret, brand-new shares

exhibits.title: Step through the zero-constant reshare mechanism
exhibits.action: Step, reroll or run the small-field arithmetic.
exhibits.outcome: Shows participants adding zero-constant polynomial evaluations, preserving the intercept.
exhibits.limits: Small GF(1019) numbers are for legible arithmetic, not secure parameterization.
exhibits.section: 2 · The whole trick — a polynomial pinned to zero

exhibits.title: Compare mobile theft across five epochs
exhibits.action: Choose which custodians are copied each epoch and run with or without resharing.
exhibits.outcome: Stale shares from different epochs fail to reconstruct the same key, while accumulating one fixed generation can expose it.
exhibits.limits: The adversary schedule is a model; guarantees assume proper erasure and fewer than t exposures per epoch.
exhibits.section: 3 · The mobile adversary — why resharing exists

exhibits.title: Try reconstructing with shares from mixed epochs
exhibits.action: Select old and new shares and reconstruct.
exhibits.outcome: Shows cryptographic interpolation and a separate security verdict when shares come from incompatible epochs.
exhibits.limits: A numeric interpolation result from mixed shares is not the original secret.
exhibits.section: 4 · Break it yourself — mix the epochs

exhibits.title: Detect a nonzero refresh contribution
exhibits.action: Run a verified reshare with a dishonest dealer and inspect the unchecked counterfactual.
exhibits.outcome: Feldman commitments flag a nonzero constant; the no-check variant silently changes the secret.
exhibits.limits: Counterfactual intentionally suppresses verification to exhibit the failure.
exhibits.section: 5 · The dealer who lies — Feldman catches a nonzero constant

exhibits.title: Reshare 3-of-5 into 4-of-7 membership
exhibits.action: Run committee and threshold rotation.
exhibits.outcome: Checks the same public key with new shares and enforces the new 4-of-7 threshold.
exhibits.limits: Local simulation does not establish secure transport, identity or share erasure across real custodians.

exhibits.title: Squares and Roots Modulo a Prime
exhibits.action: Choose a small prime and value, find modular roots, and square them back.
exhibits.outcome: The trace and residue table show which nonzero values are quadratic residues and how roots come in ± pairs.
exhibits.section: Half of the nonzero values are squares

exhibits.title: Jacobi +1 Challenge
exhibits.action: Draw a challenge for a small composite modulus, guess its class, then reveal factors and full grid.
exhibits.outcome: The public +1 symbol admits both square and pseudosquare classes that the factors distinguish.
exhibits.limits: The toy moduli 77 and 437 are too small to provide security.

exhibits.title: Goldwasser–Micali Bit Encryption
exhibits.action: Enter bits, encrypt twice, decrypt, and multiply a ciphertext by a public pseudosquare.
exhibits.outcome: The current run reports whether repeated randomized encryptions differ; decryption recovers the bits, and ciphertext multiplication flips a bit without an integrity check.
exhibits.section: One encrypted group element per bit
exhibits.limits: The small shared modulus is a teaching fixture and must not be used as a real key.

exhibits.title: Rabin Four Roots and One-Bit Construction
exhibits.action: Choose redundancy or canonical-root decryption, encrypt and decrypt, and open the randomized one-bit variant.
exhibits.outcome: The four modular roots reveal why decryption needs a disambiguation rule; the one-bit form demonstrates its different CPA claim.
exhibits.section: Squaring is easy. Which root was the message?
exhibits.limits: Redundancy is not a chosen-ciphertext security proof; the one-bit construction claims CPA security under its assumptions only.

exhibits.title: Rabin Chosen-Ciphertext Factor Recovery
exhibits.action: Send x² to either oracle rule or measure 100 random queries, then compute gcd from an unexpected root.
exhibits.outcome: The canonical-root rule can disclose a factor; redundancy refusals and accidental toy matches are reported separately.
exhibits.section: Ask for one root. Recover the factors.
exhibits.limits: An oracle refusal stops that query, not all attacks; the toy redundancy and key sharing with Goldwasser–Micali are pedagogical.

exhibits.title: BBS Bits and the Blum–Goldwasser Rewind
exhibits.action: Encrypt a bit string with a fresh or reproducible unit seed, inspect the repeated-squaring stream, rewind the transmitted final state with the factors, and run disclosure, reuse, malleability and validity controls.
exhibits.outcome: The current run exposes both BBS/HAC bit indexing and a factor-assisted Blum–Goldwasser round trip, while the negative controls derive their leaks or failures from the actual state and ciphertext.
exhibits.section: One group element carries the whole message
exhibits.limits: Toy moduli and manually selected short cycles are not security evidence. The implementation follows HAC 8.56 indexing and prime conditions, treats a short final block as a teaching adaptation, and provides neither authentication nor a BBS credential-signature scheme.

exhibits.title: One-way impossibility and the return
exhibits.section: Impossible one way. Certain on the round trip.
exhibits.action: Step a surprising substitution difference through the one-way and round-trip checks.
exhibits.outcome: Shows a zero one-way transition alongside a nonzero round-trip count measured for the selected S-box.
exhibits.limits: This is a toy eight-bit cipher and one S-box switching layer.

exhibits.title: Inspect the teaching SPN
exhibits.action: Read the small SPN structure and choose the substitution table shared by every measurement.
exhibits.outcome: Changing the S-box recomputes all attack panels against the selected cipher.
exhibits.limits: An eight-bit block and 16-bit key permit exhaustive teaching measurements, not production security.

exhibits.title: Measure a single differential trail
exhibits.action: Select round count and substitution table, then count a chosen output difference from actual encryptions.
exhibits.outcome: Plots measured trail decay as the cipher rounds grow.
exhibits.limits: Finite tiny domains are enumerated; rates do not extrapolate into modern cipher security.

exhibits.title: Find an impossible transition
exhibits.action: Set input and output differences and rounds, then test the absence of the transition over sampled or exhaustive keys.
exhibits.outcome: Displays zero and nonzero event counts with the measured scope of the claim.
exhibits.limits: A zero in a sampled run alone is not a proof across all keys.

exhibits.title: Eliminate final subkey guesses
exhibits.section: Eliminating keys with an event that cannot occur
exhibits.action: Choose input-difference sets and three or four rounds, run the sieve or randomize its hidden key.
exhibits.outcome: Shows surviving eight-bit final subkeys and whether the true subkey stays in the set.
exhibits.limits: Searches a small eight-bit final subkey, not a production cipher key.

exhibits.title: Measure returning quartets
exhibits.section: The boomerang: two short trails instead of one long one
exhibits.action: Run forward and backward text quartets across selected key samples and inspect measured return rates.
exhibits.outcome: Contrasts actual returns with the independent-trail estimate and the random-return baseline.
exhibits.limits: The browser acts as both encryption and decryption oracle for a toy cipher; estimates rely on independence assumptions.

exhibits.title: Walk and tabulate the boomerang switch
exhibits.section: The switch, where the estimate breaks
exhibits.action: Choose a switch case and split round, step through a real quartet, and compare DDT with BCT over all middle states.
exhibits.outcome: Shows where one-way trail estimates diverge from measured round-trip connectivity.
exhibits.limits: BCT covers one substitution layer; this page does not model a multiple-round Murphy incompatibility example.

exhibits.title: Historical examples and scope
exhibits.action: Read cited Skipjack, IDEA, COCONUT98 and related-key AES attack context.
exhibits.outcome: Connects impossible-event and boomerang ideas to historical published targets.
exhibits.limits: Historical attacks are described here, not implemented against those real ciphers.

exhibits.title: Ring signing and anonymity view
exhibits.action: Choose ring size and signer, sign a message, switch between signer and verifier views and tamper with the signature or message.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect verifier acceptance and why the public ring transcript does not identify the private-key holder.

exhibits.title: Linkable ring spends
exhibits.action: Submit two spends to a ledger with selectable signers.
exhibits.outcome: Compare key images and detect repeat use of the same signer without revealing the signer’s ring index.
exhibits.limits: The ledger is an in-browser model, not a cryptocurrency network.

exhibits.title: Ring size versus timing
exhibits.action: Run a timing sweep across ring sizes 2 through 11.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect signing and verification cost as the anonymity set grows.
exhibits.limits: Browser timing is local and dependent on machine conditions.

exhibits.title: Group credential and manager opening
exhibits.action: Sign as a selected member under an issued credential, verify the signature and ask the manager to open it.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect real ECDSA checks and the manager’s mapping from stable credential ID to member; a verifier can link repeat uses of the same handle.
exhibits.limits: The credential ID and member public key are carried in the signature, so this teaching construction is publicly linkable and does not provide full group-signature anonymity.

exhibits.title: Ring privacy in real-world systems
exhibits.action: Read the Monero, Zcash and Bitcoin comparison with linked scheme literature.
exhibits.outcome: Distinguish Monero-style linkable ring spends from shielded zero-knowledge proofs and transparent transaction graph analysis.
exhibits.limits: These are descriptive ecosystem cards; no blockchain is queried.

exhibits.title: Toy RSA Key Generation
exhibits.action: Choose primes p and q and exponent e, then generate a key.
exhibits.outcome: Shows n, Euler totient, coprimality, and modular inverse d step by step.
exhibits.section: 2 · Generate a key, step by step
exhibits.limits: Small chosen primes are for arithmetic instruction, not secure keys.

exhibits.title: Textbook RSA Round Trip
exhibits.action: Enter a short ASCII message, encrypt and decrypt, and compare exponentiation traces.
exhibits.outcome: Displays integer encoding, repeated squaring, and the recovered message.
exhibits.limits: Textbook RSA is deterministic and lacks OAEP padding.

exhibits.title: Toy RSA Signature
exhibits.action: Sign a message and optionally tamper with it before verification.
exhibits.outcome: Shows toy-hash representative and signature verification mismatch for changed messages.
exhibits.limits: Uses a toy FNV-1a hash, not secure RSA-PSS.

exhibits.title: Factoring the Small Modulus
exhibits.action: Factor the generated small n and reconstruct d.
exhibits.outcome: Recovers primes and decrypts with the reconstructed private exponent.
exhibits.limits: The 2048-bit timing is projected; its factor button is disabled.

exhibits.title: Textbook versus RSA-OAEP
exhibits.action: Encrypt the same message repeatedly under textbook RSA and WebCrypto RSA-OAEP, then inspect malleability.
exhibits.outcome: Shows deterministic raw ciphertext and randomized OAEP ciphertext, plus multiplicative textbook manipulation.

exhibits.title: RSA Trapdoor and Key Roles
exhibits.action: Inspect the multiplication/factoring diagram and public/private key cards.
exhibits.outcome: Introduces n=pq, public encryption or verification, and private decryption or signing.
exhibits.limits: The small-key live exercises elsewhere are educational and do not represent the cost of factoring a 2048-bit key.

exhibits.title: RSA Exponent Round Trip
exhibits.action: Generate a key and inspect the computed encryption/decryption flow and modular clock.
exhibits.outcome: Shows c=m^e mod n and recovery by d, illustrating why the exponents undo each other for the displayed message.
exhibits.section: 3½ · The round trip, in one picture

exhibits.title: New to public-key crypto? Start here.
exhibits.section: New to public-key crypto? Start here.
exhibits.action: Read the padlock analogy and glossary, then the closing implications for deployed RSA and quantum migration.
exhibits.outcome: The framing explains public and private keys, the factoring trapdoor, padding choices and why deployed systems need migration planning.
exhibits.limits: An analogy and deployment context, not a new RSA security or timeline estimate.

exhibits.title: Textbook RSA
exhibits.action: Generate tiny or larger teaching RSA parameters, encrypt/decrypt an integer message and try trial division on the tiny modulus.
exhibits.outcome: The page traces n, e, d and the trapdoor arithmetic; the tiny modulus factors, and repeating an unpadded encryption yields identical ciphertext.
exhibits.limits: Toy RSA and 512-bit example are not secure; unpadded textbook RSA is deterministic and malleable.

exhibits.title: RSA-OAEP: Secure Encryption
exhibits.action: Generate RSA-2048 or RSA-4096 WebCrypto keys, encrypt twice, inspect OAEP encoding and decrypt.
exhibits.outcome: Identical plaintexts produce different randomized ciphertexts, with OAEP mask-generation and padding displays.
exhibits.limits: OAEP protects message confidentiality under assumptions and correct use; it does not authenticate a sender or support arbitrarily large messages.

exhibits.title: RSA-PSS: Secure Signatures
exhibits.action: Generate a signing key, sign a message and verify original and tampered variants; inspect PSS encoding and compare v1.5.
exhibits.outcome: The valid signature passes, while the changed message fails verification.
exhibits.limits: Verification binds bytes to a private key, not a real-world identity without key authentication.

exhibits.title: Small Exponent Attack — Håstad Broadcast
exhibits.action: Choose vulnerable e=3 unpadded broadcast or the OAEP contrast, encrypt one message to three recipients and reconstruct with CRT plus cube root.
exhibits.outcome: The vulnerable configuration reveals the message without factoring recipient moduli; randomized padding disrupts the simple relation.
exhibits.limits: Requires the same small integer message under distinct moduli with no proper randomized padding; e=3 by itself is not the flaw.

exhibits.title: Bleichenbacher PKCS#1 v1.5 Oracle
exhibits.action: Set up small RSA, query padding conformity and run adaptive search automatically or answer oracle queries by hand.
exhibits.outcome: The interval narrowing and query trace recover the padded message through a validity oracle.
exhibits.limits: This intentionally exposes a padding-validity signal over a small modulus; properly designed deployments must avoid distinguishable decryption failures.

exhibits.title: Oracle Without Factoring — √eNFS (2026)
exhibits.action: Verify the brief’s pinned mathematical constants and try the toy raw-oracle malleability piece.
exhibits.outcome: The page separates a reported paper-scale precomputation argument from executable arithmetic checks and a teaching-size oracle relation.
exhibits.limits: The page does not execute number-field sieve precomputation or factor production moduli; paper claims are presented as sourced context.

exhibits.title: RSA vs ECC vs Post-Quantum
exhibits.action: Compare key sizes and run the one-megabyte hybrid-encryption timing example.
exhibits.outcome: The panel contrasts public-key operations with bulk symmetric encryption and lists dated algorithm properties.
exhibits.limits: Browser timing and dated comparison tables are illustrative, not hardware-independent benchmarks or current deployment advice.

exhibits.title: Side-by-Side — Textbook vs OAEP, Same Plaintext, Twice Each
exhibits.section: Side-by-Side — Textbook vs OAEP, Same Plaintext, Twice Each
exhibits.action: Encrypt the same input twice under textbook RSA and OAEP, then inspect the pitfalls panel.
exhibits.outcome: The comparison makes deterministic ciphertext equality visible beside randomized OAEP output.
exhibits.limits: A repeat-input example illustrates a concrete weakness; it is not a complete security proof for OAEP.

exhibits.title: Recover a known-prefix RSA message suffix
exhibits.action: Set suffix width, key size and lattice parameters; run the public-only attack and inspect LLL trace.
exhibits.outcome: A short integer root is certified and checked against the original e=3 textbook-RSA ciphertext.
exhibits.limits: Toy public RSA construction without padding; sufficient bounds do not imply failures beyond them are secure.

exhibits.title: Factor RSA with high bits of the larger prime
exhibits.action: Switch to factor scenario, choose leaked high-bit hint and unknown width, then run lattice reduction.
exhibits.outcome: Checks recovered prime low bits and exact factor multiplication against N.
exhibits.limits: Conditional on the larger-prime model and sufficiently small missing part; key-generation and attack are bounded.

exhibits.title: Recover a small RSA private exponent using convergents
exhibits.action: Switch to Wiener scenario and run exact continued fractions of e/N.
exhibits.outcome: Displays candidate convergents and accepts only one reconstructing valid factors and passing public checks.
exhibits.limits: A miss or resource limit is not evidence of security; theorem guarantee has explicit prime and exponent assumptions.

exhibits.title: One Ciphertext, Two Verified Messages
exhibits.action: Forge for two keys, regenerate keys, or flip a ciphertext byte.
exhibits.outcome: WebCrypto AES-GCM accepts one crafted ciphertext and tag under different keys with different plaintext; tampering still fails integrity.
exhibits.limits: This is a controlled two-key construction, not a claim that AES-GCM fails ordinary per-key ciphertext integrity.

exhibits.title: Two Images from One Ciphertext
exhibits.action: Forge and render two image payloads from a shared ciphertext.
exhibits.outcome: Different valid keys authenticate and open distinct pictures from the same envelope.

exhibits.title: Why Two Arbitrary Messages Do Not Fit
exhibits.action: Try to force two chosen messages at the same offset.
exhibits.outcome: The derived keystream constraint exposes one degree of freedom per offset; separate offsets permit the actual construction.
exhibits.section: The catch: why not two arbitrary messages?

exhibits.title: GF(2^128) Forgery Derivation
exhibits.action: Set up and solve the linear system step by step.
exhibits.outcome: The finite-field computation constructs the tag agreement that makes the two interpretations verify.
exhibits.section: The math, one step at a time

exhibits.title: Blind Moderator Scenario
exhibits.action: Send the constructed report to moderation.
exhibits.outcome: The different key holder and reviewer views show how valid tags can support incompatible interpretations.
exhibits.section: Why it matters: the blind moderator

exhibits.title: Committing Construction Controls
exhibits.action: Run the two-key counterexample and ordinary controls under a key-binding fix.
exhibits.outcome: The fixed construction binds key identity so the ambiguity is detected while regular single-key operations remain valid.
exhibits.section: The fix: commit to the key

exhibits.title: AEAD Scope and Limits
exhibits.action: Read the comparison of affected AEAD designs and the explicit non-goals.
exhibits.outcome: The panel separates ciphertext integrity from key commitment and names which constructions carry the issue.

exhibits.title: Choose known plaintext pairs
exhibits.action: Pick a four-round fixture, one-round equivalent-key fixture or random cipher, and vary rounds and observed pairs.
exhibits.outcome: Shows public plaintext-ciphertext observations, withheld checks and a separately revealed original key.
exhibits.limits: The 8-bit block and 16-bit key are deliberately exhaustible; withheld checks exist in browser memory.

exhibits.title: Trace example encryption
exhibits.action: Enter a visible example key and plaintext to inspect each XOR, S-box and permutation step.
exhibits.outcome: Displays direct cipher round states independent of the hidden experiment key.
exhibits.limits: The visible trace key is a teaching input, not the secret key selected for the attack.

exhibits.title: Inspect SAT circuit and clauses
exhibits.action: Select a gate and inspect its Boolean clauses; download the base DIMACS formula.
exhibits.outcome: Shows actual CNF variable and clause structure sent to the local solver.
exhibits.limits: A Boolean encoding of a toy SPN, not a proof that SAT is efficient against modern ciphers.

exhibits.title: Find consistent keys with CaDiCaL
exhibits.action: Find one or another model, continue enumeration in batches, or check a supplied hex key.
exhibits.outcome: Returns keys satisfying observed pairs and checks every returned model against direct encryption.
exhibits.limits: Runs in a browser worker with a 30-second interaction timeout and at most 512 new keys per enumeration click.

exhibits.title: Compare exhaustive candidate set
exhibits.action: Scan all 65,536 master keys against the same observations.
exhibits.outcome: Counts and compares keys found by exhaustive search and solver enumeration.
exhibits.limits: Tiny key space makes exhaustive comparison practical here.

exhibits.title: Verify candidate beyond observations
exhibits.action: Select a solver result and test observed pairs, withheld pairs, all 256 outputs and key identity.
exhibits.outcome: Distinguishes fitting observations from matching the encryption function and original master key.
exhibits.limits: Passing sampled withheld checks does not prove identity; even full function equality may leave different one-round key bits.

exhibits.title: Time SAT and exhaustive search
exhibits.action: Choose first-match or complete-set task, then run five measured trials and warmups per method.
exhibits.outcome: Displays median, range, stage timing and environment for CaDiCaL and exhaustive workers.
exhibits.limits: Results depend on machine and browser; a trial times out at 30 seconds and no universal speed claim follows.

exhibits.title: BIP-340 sign and verify
exhibits.action: Enter a private scalar and message, sign, inspect commitment/challenge/response and flip a message byte.
exhibits.outcome: See a valid 64-byte signature and failure of the same signature against altered message bytes.

exhibits.title: Public verification workbench
exhibits.action: Paste public key, signature and message or load a preset, then verify.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect staged acceptance or the precise rejection cause without a private key.

exhibits.title: Schnorr verification equation
exhibits.action: Step through a generated signature and its verifier equation.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect scalar and elliptic-curve point relationships in the BIP-340 check.

exhibits.title: Nonce reuse key recovery
exhibits.action: Sign two different messages with the same nonce and run algebraic recovery.
exhibits.outcome: Two valid signatures reveal the private scalar, checked against the signing key.

exhibits.title: BIP-340 vector table
exhibits.action: Run official acceptance and rejection vectors and load a row in the workbench.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect each computed verification outcome and exact stage for negative rows.

exhibits.title: Schnorr linearity
exhibits.action: Sign separately and combine the contributions.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect an aggregate signature and its verifier result.
exhibits.limits: This textbook full-point example naively adds nonces and is vulnerable to rogue-key and Wagner-style attacks; it is not deployable multisignature aggregation.

exhibits.title: Toy LWE Equation
exhibits.action: Resample a tiny matrix, ternary secret, and error vector.
exhibits.outcome: Computes and displays b=A·s+e mod q.
exhibits.limits: n=8 toy arithmetic illustrates structure, not full Scloud+.

exhibits.title: Ternary Secret Sampling
exhibits.action: Animate or instantly sample a fixed-weight ternary vector.
exhibits.outcome: Displays +1, -1, and zero distribution and compares secret structures.

exhibits.title: BW32 Error-Correction Explorer
exhibits.action: Encode a 5-bit message, add adjustable noise, decode, and run 100 trials.
exhibits.outcome: Shows recovered value and changing success rates near the correction boundary.

exhibits.title: Scloud+ Key Generation
exhibits.action: Choose a parameter set and run staged key generation.
exhibits.outcome: Displays public matrix derivation, sampled secret/error, computed B, hash, byte sizes, and elapsed time.
exhibits.limits: The lab compares measured demo sizes with specification figures; it is a teaching implementation.

exhibits.title: Encapsulation, Decapsulation, and Tamper
exhibits.action: Run full KEM round trip, then flip ciphertext bytes and decapsulate again.
exhibits.outcome: Shows matching secrets on valid input and FO re-encryption mismatch with implicit rejection on tampering.

exhibits.title: Scloud+ versus FrodoKEM and ML-KEM
exhibits.action: Select a security level to compare key and ciphertext sizes and assumptions.
exhibits.outcome: Displays tabular and graphical specification tradeoffs.
exhibits.limits: Specification comparisons are distinct from the browser implementation’s measurements.

exhibits.title: Small-Parameter KEM Walkthrough
exhibits.action: Step through a fresh toy key generation, encapsulation, decapsulation, tamper, and FO check.
exhibits.outcome: Shows shared-secret agreement and implicit rejection on altered ciphertext with visible small vectors.
exhibits.limits: n=16 and four-byte output secret are visible toy parameters, not deployment security.

exhibits.title: Unstructured LWE KEM Design
exhibits.action: Read the plain-language comparison of LWE assumptions, ternary secrets, and Barnes-Wall coding.
exhibits.outcome: Places Scloud+ alongside FrodoKEM and ML-KEM and distinguishes assumption conservatism from evidence gathered through review.

exhibits.title: Structured versus Unstructured Lattice Assumptions
exhibits.action: Read both sides of the structure tradeoff and the examples of attack research.
exhibits.outcome: Separates a reduction gap in related ideal-lattice problems from an actual ML-KEM break and explains the size-versus-scrutiny choice.
exhibits.section: Structured vs Unstructured: The Real Trade-off
exhibits.limits: These are arguments and research summaries, not live attacks or a proof one scheme is universally safer.

exhibits.title: Demo Timing and Published Cycle Counts
exhibits.action: Set a parameter level and run repeated browser keygen, encapsulation, and decapsulation, then inspect same-platform published Scloud+/FrodoKEM figures.
exhibits.outcome: Shows browser mean timings separately from paper cycle counts.
exhibits.limits: Simplified JavaScript timings are relative feel only and cannot be compared numerically to the published CPU cycle chart.

exhibits.title: Public Scrutiny and KEM Confidence
exhibits.action: Compare open review records and inspect why implementation side channels differ from mathematical breaks.
exhibits.outcome: Explains why a sound ingredient list or author analysis does not replace independent review of a specific construction.
exhibits.limits: Review comparison and status are pinned to the source snapshot, not a current deployment endorsement.

exhibits.title: Build the encrypted index
exhibits.action: Choose a keyword and step or build its encrypted posting rows.
exhibits.outcome: Displays real HMAC-derived tokens and addresses, AES-GCM-encrypted postings and the server’s stored hex rows.
exhibits.limits: Static small index of 24 documents and 14 keywords; keys are session-only and the client/server are objects in one browser.

exhibits.title: Search it — and watch what the server learns
exhibits.section: Search it — and watch what the server learns
exhibits.action: Search a keyword, run all keywords once or clear the server log.
exhibits.outcome: The server returns matching encrypted documents from tokens and logs repeated tokens, result sizes and document identities.
exhibits.limits: The server learns prescribed leakage; this lab does not hide search or access patterns, nor model network metadata.

exhibits.title: Can the server lie about the answer?
exhibits.section: Can the server lie about the answer?
exhibits.action: Choose an honest answer, omission, fabrication or stale replay and test it against the client-retained checkpoint.
exhibits.outcome: Distinguishes per-record AES-GCM authenticity from completeness and freshness of the answer as a whole.
exhibits.limits: Static teaching checkpoint only; assumes a trusted client-retained current snapshot id, expected count and exact encrypted-answer digest, not a general verifiable-SSE protocol.

exhibits.title: What the pattern alone reveals
exhibits.action: Observe a realistic round of queries and inspect charts derived solely from the server log.
exhibits.outcome: The views show token repetition, result volumes, touched documents and overlaps without exposing keys.
exhibits.limits: Pattern richness by itself does not prove inversion; the attack needs external background statistics.

exhibits.title: Break it: turn the access pattern back into queries
exhibits.section: Break it: turn the access pattern back into queries
exhibits.action: Run volume matching and simulated-annealing co-occurrence attacks, varying synthetic statistic jitter.
exhibits.outcome: The attack estimates token-to-keyword mappings from observed logs and auxiliary corpus statistics without cryptographic keys.
exhibits.limits: Exact statistics favor the adversary; jitter is synthetic, and recovery varies with corpus and observation count.

exhibits.title: Your turn: you are the server
exhibits.section: Your turn: you are the server
exhibits.action: Guess token labels from result sizes and overlap, check answers or ask the machine to solve.
exhibits.outcome: The challenge compares human inferences to the same attacker inputs and scoring as the automatic exhibit.
exhibits.limits: A 14-token challenge does not establish recovery rates for an arbitrary real deployment.

exhibits.title: SSE, ORAM, FHE — what each one costs and what each one hides
exhibits.section: SSE, ORAM, FHE — what each one costs and what each one hides
exhibits.action: Compare leakage and work in SSE, ORAM and FHE; time 50 local SSE searches.
exhibits.outcome: The table relates access hiding to compute and state costs alongside the one measured browser search path.
exhibits.limits: Only SSE is timed locally; ORAM and FHE rows are conceptual, not executable implementations.

exhibits.title: Two-keyword AND — naïve SSE versus bounded OXT
exhibits.section: Two-keyword AND — naïve SSE versus bounded OXT
exhibits.action: Enter exactly two indexed keywords joined by AND, compare two actual isolated SSE searches with the bounded OXT route, run five controlled trace pairs and inspect the derived fixed-volume Path ORAM cost.
exhibits.outcome: Both routes return the same plaintext intersection while exposing different measured query volumes, posting-list boundaries, exact ristretto255 membership tests, repeated stags, conditional candidate-point equality and final access patterns.
exhibits.limits: Static two-known-distinct-keyword teaching adapter only: no OR, NOT, parentheses, longer formulas, dynamic or multi-user search, transfer of the full OXT theorem, active-server soundness, completeness, freshness or hardened constant-time behavior. Exact XSet membership removes probabilistic-filter false positives only for honest execution. The Path ORAM table is arithmetic for a separate non-colluding semi-honest storage server, not an ORAM implementation or concealment of the OXT transcript.

exhibits.title: Public-key search — and the trapdoor dictionary attack
exhibits.section: Public-key search — and the trapdoor dictionary attack
exhibits.action: Generate a recipient key, build randomized tags with only its public key, issue and repeat a trapdoor, scan every tag and run included, absent and zero-guess dictionary bounds.
exhibits.outcome: Executes the Type-3 BLS12-381 PEKS equation and shows randomized pre-query tags, deterministic repeated trapdoors, full-scan matches and bounded public-Test keyword recovery.
exhibits.limits: Algebra-preserving Type-3 teaching adaptation only: no transfer of the original symmetric-pairing proof, standardized GT encoding, exact 128-bit claim, body encryption, sender authentication, tag/body binding, completeness, freshness, production isolation, hardened side-channel behavior or post-quantum security; a bounded miss proves only that tested candidates did not pass.

exhibits.title: Fuzzy search — typo recovery leaks a neighborhood
exhibits.section: Fuzzy search — typo recovery leaks a neighborhood
exhibits.action: Enter one bounded ASCII word, choose edit threshold 0, 1 or 2, and compare the existing exact SSE query with three separately built deletion-gram index alternatives.
exhibits.outcome: Real HMAC trapdoors and encrypted candidate rows expose index, query and response costs; client-side Levenshtein filtering derives candidate and final-document error rates, while retained opaque bundles demonstrate a known-anchor neighborhood link unavailable from unequal exact tokens.
exhibits.limits: Bounded exact-map teaching adaptation over 14 ASCII keywords and 24 documents at d=0,1,2; not the paper's trie or performance evaluation, LSH, semantic or ranked search, transposition distance, dynamic or multi-user EFSE, a transferred theorem, a malicious-server result proof or a claim about every fuzzy-search construction.

exhibits.title: What is real here, what is scaled down, and what is not proved
exhibits.section: What is real here, what is scaled down, and what is not proved
exhibits.action: Read the scope panel and introductory glossary.
exhibits.outcome: It labels real WebCrypto, pairing, ristretto255 and fuzzy-search operations, the scaled corpus and stores, exact-statistics controls, the bounded OXT, Type-3 PEKS and deletion-gram adaptation boundaries, and excluded dynamic or volume-hiding schemes.
exhibits.limits: No claim is made about the security of AES-GCM or HMAC themselves, all searchable-encryption designs, transfer of the full OXT theorem, original PEKS proof or fuzzy-search paper proof, standardized GT bytes, active-server completeness or freshness, production role isolation, executed ORAM, arbitrary plaintext recovery, or security after a bounded dictionary miss.

exhibits.title: Write and read a 16-sector XTS volume
exhibits.action: Edit sector text and follow block encryption, tweak ladder and readback.
exhibits.outcome: Shows XTS-AES blocks, sector-number tweak progression and exact decrypted text.
exhibits.limits: Short padded ASCII sectors are pedagogical; XTS provides confidentiality without authentication.

exhibits.title: Flip stored ciphertext and read without an error
exhibits.action: Alter a ciphertext bit in a selected block and read the sector.
exhibits.outcome: One decrypted block changes, while XTS reports no integrity failure.
exhibits.limits: The page’s own write log knows expected content; a real XTS-only driver lacks it.

exhibits.title: Copy a ciphertext block or restore an old sector
exhibits.action: Relocate a block, copy a whole sector elsewhere, or restore an earlier image.
exhibits.outcome: Shows tweak-dependent corruption on relocation and a clean but stale plaintext on rollback, with no XTS error.
exhibits.limits: Attacker needs ciphertext write access; anti-replay needs a trusted version anchor outside the volume.
exhibits.section: Move it, or put it back

exhibits.title: Compare encrypted disk images without the key
exhibits.action: Write or roll back sector values, then take and compare encrypted images.
exhibits.outcome: Unchanged and repeated blocks reveal equality patterns to an observer without decryption.
exhibits.limits: How revealing a pattern is depends on underlying plaintext structure and observation opportunity.
exhibits.section: Watermarking: reading the disk with no key at all

exhibits.title: Compare XTS, AES-GCM and versioned storage
exhibits.action: Run a matrix of nine changes under XTS and integrity-enabled constructions.
exhibits.outcome: Shows XTS’s absence of tamper failure versus authenticated bad-tag results and a separate stale-version check.
exhibits.limits: The trusted version store is modeled as JavaScript state; real anti-rollback requires protected external storage.
exhibits.section: What integrity would actually buy you

exhibits.title: Compare EME2 and XTS data-unit diffusion
exhibits.action: Choose data-unit size and a tamper experiment, then compare changed-byte maps under both modes.
exhibits.outcome: EME2 diffuses changes across more blocks than XTS in observed runs; neither detects a malicious edit.
exhibits.limits: Changed-byte counts are run-specific; wide-block diffusion is not an authentication tag.
exhibits.section: EME2: see a change spread across a data unit

exhibits.title: Two-Passphrase Container Creation
exhibits.action: Enter real and decoy messages with separate passphrases, choose a fixed container size, then create and download.
exhibits.outcome: Rust/WASM derives keys with Argon2id, encrypts both slots, and writes a padded random-looking container.
exhibits.limits: The passphrases must differ and both plaintexts must fit the chosen 4–32 KiB container.

exhibits.title: Argon2id Cost Tuning
exhibits.action: Adjust memory, iterations, and parallelism, inspect local derivation timing, and restore defaults.
exhibits.outcome: The estimate translates a measured run into a rough first-attacker guess cost.
exhibits.limits: The headerless container has no per-container salt; globally fixed role salts allow a reusable precomputed dictionary, so only passphrase entropy protects against that reuse.

exhibits.title: Container Map and Attacker View
exhibits.action: Watch two message slots written into a random-looking container and switch to the attacker-visible map.
exhibits.outcome: The visual compares construction stages with the final opaque bytes and shows slot positions only as a teaching reveal.
exhibits.limits: A format-aware attacker can authenticate the public role domains; the UI’s hidden labels do not give role privacy.

exhibits.title: Decoy Passphrase Coercion Scenario
exhibits.action: Open the just-created container with the decoy passphrase and separately with the real passphrase.
exhibits.outcome: The same file yields different authenticated plaintexts while the decoy disclosure does not reveal the other independently chosen password.
exhibits.limits: The disclosed passphrase’s real/decoy role can be classified offline; no claim of role privacy or safety under broader coercion is supported.

exhibits.title: Upload and Open Vault
exhibits.action: Upload a container, enter a passphrase and creation parameters, then decrypt or clear the displayed message.
exhibits.outcome: A correct passphrase authenticates its slot and recovers only that message; invalid files or guesses report failure.
exhibits.limits: The headerless format does not store Argon2id settings; the opener needs the creation parameters.

exhibits.title: Deniability Model and Limitations
exhibits.action: Read the two-passphrase model, role test, container format, and threat caveats.
exhibits.outcome: The dialog distinguishes two valid openings from guarantees the format cannot make about coercion, deletion traces, or password correlation.

exhibits.title: Step through secret sharing
exhibits.action: Advance an illustrated lesson with short checks of threshold and key-custody concepts.
exhibits.outcome: Explains threshold reconstruction, polynomial shares and the distinction between sharing keys and encrypting files.
exhibits.limits: Teaching questions are conceptual; numerical proof is in the other tabs.

exhibits.title: Generate and reconstruct shares
exhibits.action: Set secret text and t-of-n threshold, generate serialized shares, and submit enough shares for reconstruction.
exhibits.outcome: Displays a changing vault lock, share values, polynomial metadata and reconstructed secret.
exhibits.limits: All shares are generated and shown in one browser session; the page does not distribute them to independent custodians.

exhibits.title: Animate a sharing polynomial
exhibits.action: Configure a finite-field polynomial, generate shares and animate point interpolation.
exhibits.outcome: Shows sampled share points and the Lagrange interpolation steps at zero.
exhibits.limits: Small display field is illustrative; animation is not a custody protocol.

exhibits.title: Test fewer than threshold shares
exhibits.action: Propose a secret consistent with t-minus-one revealed shares and check it.
exhibits.outcome: Illustrates that every candidate field secret remains possible with insufficient shares.
exhibits.limits: The theorem assumes independent uniform coefficients and proper field and share handling.

exhibits.title: Generate and stack visual shares
exhibits.action: Edit a binary source, generate two fresh-pattern shares, stack them with Boolean OR, compare XOR and run exact distribution and negative controls.
exhibits.outcome: Shows white same-pattern and black complementary-pattern blocks, derives four-subpixel expansion and one-half relative contrast, and proves identical complete one-share distributions by enumeration.
exhibits.limits: Binary 2-of-2 teaching construction only; it assumes exact alignment, has no authenticity or printing and optical model, and retains the source and both shares in one browser.

exhibits.title: Encrypt data and share AES key
exhibits.action: Encrypt a message under a new AES-256-GCM key, split the key into t-of-n shares, and paste shares to decrypt.
exhibits.outcome: Shows authenticated decryption on enough valid shares and failure with wrong key, IV or ciphertext.
exhibits.limits: The browser holds all shares and key; there are no custodians, authenticated share formats or operational ceremonies.

exhibits.title: Classify share and decryption failures
exhibits.action: Trigger malformed share, too-small field, corrupted digit, wrong AES IV and wrong key share cases.
exhibits.outcome: Separates format and mathematical rejection, silent wrong-secret reconstruction and GCM authentication failure.
exhibits.limits: Plain x:y:p shares have no integrity mechanism; AES-GCM catches wrong keys only when used to decrypt.

exhibits.title: Applications and Adi Shamir history
exhibits.action: Read key ceremony, threshold signature and MPC contexts, then browse Adi Shamir contributions.
exhibits.outcome: Connects sharing to custody and cryptographic history without running those external systems.
exhibits.limits: Application examples are narrative, not integrations with deployed HSMs or threshold signers.

exhibits.title: Shamir sharing and reconstruction
exhibits.action: Split a secret into n shares, select fewer or at least k, reconstruct and use the result as an HMAC key.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect interpolation output and the recovered secret appearing in one machine’s memory at threshold.
exhibits.limits: Shamir recovers raw bytes and uses HMAC here; it is not the same signature primitive as FROST.

exhibits.title: FROST threshold signing
exhibits.action: Distribute shares, generate round-one commitments, select signers and combine round-two partials.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect a standard Ed25519 signature that verifies at threshold without reconstructing the private key.

exhibits.title: Run both and compromise a machine
exhibits.action: Run Shamir and FROST side by side, then trigger the compromise control.
exhibits.outcome: Compare key-in-memory status and consequences of compromise in the two paths.

exhibits.title: Threshold compromise scenarios
exhibits.action: Move the stolen-share slider, simulate interception during reconstruction and compromise one FROST participant.
exhibits.outcome: Compare subthreshold exposure, the reconstruction window and a one-share signature attempt.

exhibits.title: Shamir versus FROST comparison
exhibits.action: Expand the seven-row side-by-side table after running both paths.
exhibits.outcome: Compare what is shared, reconstruction, output, attack surface, use case and protocol complexity.

exhibits.title: When to use Shamir or FROST
exhibits.action: Read the decision and pitfalls cards for each approach.
exhibits.outcome: Distinguish static secret recovery from distributed signing, and compare combiner, online-round and nonce risks.

exhibits.title: Key exposure timeline
exhibits.action: Inspect the two signing timelines from split secret to output.
exhibits.outcome: Locate the reconstruction and signing window when Shamir exposes a whole secret, versus FROST rounds using shares.

exhibits.title: Adaptive corruption research boundary
exhibits.action: Read the source-linked adaptive-security panel and parameter examples.
exhibits.outcome: Distinguish static from adaptive corruption, the 2025 proof baseline, and the October 2026 canonical-point 488/173 attack versus the adversarial-point 228/114 subset-search measurement.
exhibits.limits: Distinct attack models: the 228/114 result measures successful subset search, not end-to-end browser compromise. The panel executes no adaptive attack or proof; the lab uses a deliberately nonconformant binding transcript.
exhibits.section: Adaptive corruption: what this lesson does and does not show

exhibits.title: Encrypted Selection Vector
exhibits.action: Pick a book, inspect the BFV ciphertext sent for every shelf position and guess which one hides the selected bit.
exhibits.outcome: Shows independently randomized encryptions of zero and one while the modeled server receives no plaintext index.
exhibits.section: The Server's View / What you send
exhibits.limits: This is the direct one-hot path in a local, single-server honest-but-curious model; it does not prove RLWE hardness or deployment privacy.

exhibits.title: Homomorphic Shelf Fold
exhibits.action: Step one, eight or all remaining records through the encrypted-selector fold.
exhibits.outcome: Displays the accumulated ciphertext, measured invariant-noise budget and decrypted selected record after every record has been scanned.
exhibits.section: Homomorphic Selection / The homomorphic inner product
exhibits.limits: The server performs a full schoolbook record scan; the teacher-side noise meter uses the secret key and true record, which a deployed client would not possess.

exhibits.title: Reused Encryption Randomness
exhibits.action: Reuse one encryption-randomness pair, run the same distinguisher against fresh and broken queries and compare its accuracy.
exhibits.outcome: Shows identical zero ciphertexts expose the encrypted one in the deliberately broken mode while fresh-query guesses stay at chance.
exhibits.section: The Server's View / Break it yourself
exhibits.limits: The randomness-reuse mode is explicitly broken, off by default and is not the protocol's honest path.

exhibits.title: Noise and Failure Lab
exhibits.action: Change the modulus, record width and shelf size, retrieve, then exercise each named boundary-failure input.
exhibits.outcome: Shows the measured decryption budget, impossible coefficients, record-tag result and four reachable failure codes.
exhibits.section: Noise Exhaustion / Push it until it breaks
exhibits.limits: The HES 2018 row is used only for its modulus-bit ceiling; its discrete-Gaussian security estimate is not transferred to the lab's centered-binomial error or JavaScript implementation.

exhibits.title: Single-Server versus Two-Server PIR
exhibits.action: Run BFV and two-server XOR retrieval over identical records, then let the two XOR servers collude.
exhibits.outcome: Measures serialized traffic and browser timings for both routes and recovers the target index when the XOR servers compare masks.
exhibits.section: One Server vs Two / Run both protocols over the same shelf
exhibits.limits: Both protocols run as objects in one browser; their local timings are not network or production benchmarks.

exhibits.title: Byte-to-Polynomial Record Encoding
exhibits.section: The Shelf / Pick a book / How a record becomes a polynomial
exhibits.action: Open the selected record's byte-to-coefficient packing disclosure and change the record size.
exhibits.outcome: Shows two four-bit coefficients per byte in plaintext modulus 17, leaving coefficient 16 as a decoding-failure sentinel while wider records consume more noise budget.
exhibits.limits: This packing is shared by the direct and compressed paths, but is specific to this bounded teaching implementation and is not a general BFV or PIR wire format; coefficient 16 and the record tag detect decode failure, not malicious-server dishonesty.

exhibits.title: BFV Coefficient Decryption Trace
exhibits.section: Homomorphic Selection / Open the decryption identity for one coefficient
exhibits.action: Fold more records and open the current accumulator's coefficient-level decryption trace.
exhibits.outcome: Displays c0+c1·s, Delta times the expected message, residual error, the half-Delta correctness ceiling and the decoded coefficient.
exhibits.limits: The trace examines one coefficient using the secret key and expected plaintext; it does not establish deployment security.

exhibits.title: Network Observer Metadata Log
exhibits.section: What It Does Not Hide / What a network observer sees
exhibits.action: Issue random and repeated book queries, then compare serialized upload and response sizes with the observer timestamps.
exhibits.outcome: Shows fixed query and response sizes within one parameter set while request occurrence, timing, count and rate remain visible.
exhibits.limits: The parties and observer are objects in one browser; client identity, routing and real network timing are not measured.

exhibits.title: PIR Security Boundaries and Decryption Feedback
exhibits.section: What It Does Not Hide / Honest scope
exhibits.action: Read the hidden-versus-visible table, implementation boundary and dated decryption-feedback research note.
exhibits.outcome: Separates index privacy from integrity and traffic metadata, names the compressed path's circular-security assumption and scopes the cited IND-CPA-D attacks.
exhibits.limits: The cited BFV/BGV research concerns particular configurations and feedback conditions; the lab does not reproduce those attacks or prove this configuration vulnerable.

exhibits.title: Compressed Query Expansion
exhibits.section: Compressed Query / Four encrypted blocks in, sixty-four encrypted selectors out
exhibits.action: Run direct and compressed retrieval for one fixed-catalog record, then inspect the expansion, cost, noise and discarded one-response ledgers.
exhibits.outcome: Expands four serialized ciphertext blocks into 64 encrypted selectors with Galois key switching; the selected response agrees with direct retrieval and the independently built tagged record while the other three decrypt to zero, and the panel accounts for setup, traffic, fixed responses, record products and switching work.
exhibits.limits: This bounded path uses four 16-selector blocks at q = 2^27 - 39, scans all 64 records and returns four responses under an honest-but-curious model and circular-security assumption. The SHA-256 tag detects decode failure only, the summed response is discarded because its margin is sample-dependent, and the lab does not implement SealPIR multidimensional recursion, sublinear server work or malicious-server integrity.

exhibits.title: Stateful Preprocessing PIR
exhibits.section: Stateful PIR / Run the bounded stateful lesson
exhibits.action: Preprocess the fixed shelf, retrieve and repeat a record, inspect recovery and refresh, then lose state, change the database and rebuild the invalidated epoch.
exhibits.outcome: Streams the actual database into private parity state, sends an eight-byte fixed-shape request, probes and XORs eight records into one 512-byte response, refreshes the consumed hint and derives separate setup, state, wire, probe, update and crossover costs from the executed session.
exhibits.limits: This is a fixed N = 64, B = 512, Q = 33 Piano-style teaching adaptation with client-specific linear setup and retained state larger than the database, not Piano's theorem, reference wire format, benchmark or asymptotic regime. The server has no derived ProcessDB artifact. The scoped availability bound covers primary-hint misses only; hashes do not authenticate freshness, and dynamic updates, malicious-server integrity or privacy, availability, traffic hiding, ORAM, multi-client sharing, hardened storage and crash consistency remain outside the lesson.

exhibits.title: What is Shor's Algorithm?
exhibits.action: Read the factoring, cryptography and period-finding introduction before running the small-number model.
exhibits.outcome: It frames factoring as period finding and distinguishes the theoretical quantum algorithm from the browser demonstration.
exhibits.limits: The intro is conceptual; the resource estimates and live simulator have separate scopes below.

exhibits.title: Run Shor’s Algorithm
exhibits.action: Choose an integer up to 9999 or a preset, run the staged factoring simulation and inspect retries.
exhibits.outcome: Prechecks, random base, order, QFT frequency, continued fractions and gcd post-processing appear in the step log and visualizations.
exhibits.limits: A classical simulator for small N, not a quantum computer or feasible RSA-2048 factoring run.

exhibits.title: Period table and QFT visualization
exhibits.action: Inspect modular-period tables, phase-wheel or probability views and the measured frequency sample.
exhibits.outcome: The chart shows how peaks near multiples of Q/r lead to a recovered period when continued fractions succeed.
exhibits.limits: The displayed QFT distribution is mathematically computed and truncated for visualization; no quantum measurement is performed.

exhibits.title: RSA impact calculator
exhibits.action: Read factoring complexity and dated quantum resource estimates alongside the ECC and resistant-family explanations.
exhibits.outcome: The panel contrasts classical and ideal quantum scaling and situates Shor’s threat to RSA and elliptic-curve discrete logs.
exhibits.limits: Resource estimates are dated assumptions and not predictions that current hardware can break deployed RSA.

exhibits.title: Sign a JSON byte string and reserialize it in transit
exhibits.action: Advance the producer-signature, gateway and receiver verification steps.
exhibits.outcome: Ed25519 rejects the reserialized bytes even though parsed JSON meaning remains the same.
exhibits.limits: The signature primitive holds; the failure is incompatible serialization between parties.

exhibits.title: Compare alternate JSON encodings under JCS
exhibits.action: Edit JSON variants and toggle canonicalization.
exhibits.outcome: Displays byte differences and signature verification behavior for raw versus canonicalized payloads.
exhibits.limits: JCS fixes representation only for its supported JSON data model and profile.

exhibits.title: Reorder keys before verifying a signed object
exhibits.action: Run the key-order stage with JCS off and on.
exhibits.outcome: Raw JSON byte order breaks signature equality; canonical key ordering restores a shared representation.
exhibits.limits: Canonicalization must happen consistently on signer and verifier sides.

exhibits.title: Compare composed and decomposed Unicode strings
exhibits.action: Compare Unicode spellings and JCS results.
exhibits.outcome: Different UTF-8 bytes remain distinct even when text appears equivalent.
exhibits.limits: JCS does not normalize Unicode; applications need an explicit semantic policy.

exhibits.title: Exploit first-wins versus last-wins JSON parsing
exhibits.action: Run the duplicate-key stage with differing parser policies.
exhibits.outcome: A signature can validate a byte string while components disagree about the chosen duplicate value; strict rejection closes the ambiguity.
exhibits.limits: Canonical serialization cannot resolve an ambiguous input that should be rejected before signing or use.

exhibits.title: Compare numeric spellings and canonical bytes
exhibits.action: Test number spellings under raw and JCS paths.
exhibits.outcome: Displays signatures and parser meaning across lexical variants.
exhibits.limits: Applications needing exact integers outside the JSON number profile require a deliberate encoding policy.

exhibits.title: Choose which bytes an application signs
exhibits.action: Compare raw, parsed, canonicalized or envelope-bound signature scopes.
exhibits.outcome: Shows which changes verification detects and where semantic interpretation escapes the signed boundary.
exhibits.limits: Cryptographic validity alone does not prove the intended application meaning was signed.

exhibits.title: Five-Hospital Private Total
exhibits.action: Compare centralized collection with the stated Shamir-based total-only goal.
exhibits.outcome: The first exhibit frames each hospital’s count as private and the sum as the intended output.
exhibits.section: Five hospitals. One question. Zero data sharing.

exhibits.title: Lock Hospital Counts
exhibits.action: Enter and lock five enrollment counts before advancing.
exhibits.outcome: The committed teaching inputs flow into each hospital’s own sharing computation.
exhibits.section: Each hospital enters its enrollment count.

exhibits.title: Generate Threshold Shares
exhibits.action: Inspect the five polynomial shares generated for every hospital and the small finite-field curve illustration.
exhibits.outcome: The Rust/WASM core creates random degree-two Shamir shares; any three points reconstruct one secret while two leave it hidden over the field.
exhibits.section: Each hospital splits its secret into shares.
exhibits.limits: The GF(97) graph is a toy illustration separate from the core GF(2^61−1) arithmetic.

exhibits.title: Share Distribution Matrix
exhibits.action: Inspect each sender-to-recipient share route in the five-by-five matrix.
exhibits.outcome: Every hospital receives one evaluation from every input owner and can form a local aggregate share.
exhibits.section: Each hospital receives one share from every other.
exhibits.limits: All parties are modeled in one browser; there is no network transport.

exhibits.title: Local Sums and Lagrange Reconstruction
exhibits.action: Choose which hospital local sums to combine and inspect the interpolation and total.
exhibits.outcome: Any three local sums reconstruct the same overall enrollment count without reconstructing a named hospital’s count.
exhibits.section: Local sums computed. Total reconstructed. No secret revealed.

exhibits.title: Colluding Hospitals Threshold
exhibits.action: Select a coalition of hospitals and inspect what it can reconstruct about an excluded member.
exhibits.outcome: Two colluders’ shares leave every field secret possible; three shares uniquely recover the target count.
exhibits.limits: The public enrollment range itself leaks a constraint even when two shares do not determine the exact count.

exhibits.title: Run the Simon circuit
exhibits.action: Choose target and 4-to-6-bit width, measure one round or run to verdict, and optionally reveal the held secret.
exhibits.outcome: Shows oracle query count, independent equations and verified period or proof of no nonzero period.
exhibits.limits: Runs full classical statevector simulation, not quantum hardware; oracle truth table is precomputed.

exhibits.title: Inspect amplitudes and cancellation
exhibits.section: Why at least half the answers vanish
exhibits.action: Click input and output grid cells after a measurement to inspect amplitudes and phase arithmetic.
exhibits.outcome: Shows destructive interference of forbidden outcomes and selected cell interpretation.
exhibits.limits: Tiny statevectors and real-valued amplitudes are simulated on a classical machine.

exhibits.title: Solve period equations
exhibits.section: The equations, and what they pin down
exhibits.action: Collect outcomes and inspect row reduction, rank and still-possible periods.
exhibits.outcome: A rank of n-minus-one isolates the nonzero period; full rank diagnoses the injective control.
exhibits.limits: A candidate is checked against the complete tiny truth table before being reported.

exhibits.title: Measure classical and simulated quantum queries
exhibits.action: Run repeated collision searches and full Simon rounds on fresh target instances at several widths.
exhibits.outcome: Reports mean oracle queries and labels birthday versus exhaustive classical behavior appropriately.
exhibits.limits: Does not measure quantum gate costs or wall-clock advantage; all runs execute classically at toy widths.

exhibits.title: Contrast quantum algorithm threats
exhibits.section: Grover, Simon, Shor — three different threats
exhibits.action: Read comparison of search, hidden-period and factoring settings.
exhibits.outcome: Distinguishes quantum query access and affected primitive classes.
exhibits.limits: The comparative family section is explanatory; only Simon is simulated here.

exhibits.title: Inspect target constructions and breaks
exhibits.action: Switch Even-Mansour, CBC-MAC and no-period control; read Feistel and slide attack context.
exhibits.outcome: The live two targets check recovered key or forged tag; other named attacks are described.
exhibits.limits: Only Even-Mansour and CBC-MAC breaks are implemented, with tiny primitive sizes and Q2 oracle assumption.

exhibits.title: Kuznyechik round by round
exhibits.action: Choose a round and step through its transformations.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect the S, L and key XOR intermediate states of the Russian block cipher.

exhibits.title: Published Kuznyechik vectors
exhibits.action: Run RFC 7801 encrypt/decrypt vectors and inspect intermediate states.
exhibits.outcome: See computed results compared with published expected ciphertext and round states.
exhibits.section: The whole cipher, against the published vectors

exhibits.title: S-box reconstruction and diff
exhibits.action: Generate the candidate algebraic pi table and compare all bytes to the reference table.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect match/mismatch cells and count exact byte differences.
exhibits.limits: A matching reconstruction is mathematical evidence about a table, not proof of deliberate design motive.

exhibits.title: Historical claim and probability scale
exhibits.action: Inspect the record, toggle the probability scale and read the scope of the reconstruction.
exhibits.outcome: Compare stated provenance with the computed structural match and an illustrative random-permutation probability.
exhibits.section: What the rebuild does, and does not, establish

exhibits.title: S-box design record and prior art
exhibits.action: Read the dated source-linked statements and three published decompositions of Kuznyechik pi.
exhibits.outcome: Separate a mathematical match from the designers’ stated provenance and the chronology of earlier structural descriptions.
exhibits.limits: The historical record does not establish design intent from table equality.
