exhibits.title: Structural match versus backdoor claim
exhibits.action: Inspect the reality-check shape condition and the source-linked absence of a demonstrated attack.
exhibits.outcome: See why the identified output-side structure alone does not satisfy the cited planted-weakness criterion.
exhibits.limits: This explanatory panel does not prove an attack or a benign design motive.

exhibits.title: SM2 Curve and Published Vectors
exhibits.action: Inspect curveSM2 parameters and run Annex A and C reference checks.
exhibits.outcome: Matches signature and ciphertext components byte for byte before unlocking the other panes.
exhibits.section: Build the specified curve before trusting the exhibit

exhibits.title: SM2 Identity-Bound Signature
exhibits.action: Enter an identity and message, build ZA and sign, then verify.
exhibits.outcome: Shows identity digest feeding the signature and retires output when inputs change.
exhibits.section: The identity enters the hash before the message

exhibits.title: SM2 Ciphertext Byte Orders
exhibits.action: Encrypt once, serialize as C1C3C2 or C1C2C3, and feed each to chosen decoder order.
exhibits.outcome: Shows correct round trips and explicit mismatch failure from interpreting identical components in a different order.
exhibits.section: Encrypt once, regroup the same components

exhibits.title: SM2 Signing Nonce Reuse
exhibits.action: Deliberately sign two different messages with the same k and recover d.
exhibits.outcome: Both signatures verify while equations reconstruct the victim private scalar and public key.
exhibits.section: Reuse one signing nonce and recover the private key
exhibits.limits: Nonce reuse is isolated to broken mode.

exhibits.title: SM2 in ShangMi TLS 1.3 Profile
exhibits.action: Inspect RFC 8998’s listed signature scheme, curve, and SM4 suites.
exhibits.outcome: Places SM2 signing in a named TLS profile while delineating this lab’s narrower implementation.
exhibits.limits: TLS, SM2 key exchange, SM4, and SM3 internals are not implemented here.

exhibits.title: Parameters, and the SM3 layer
exhibits.action: Run SM3, H1, H2 and KDF checks against pinned standard vectors before the other steps.
exhibits.outcome: The panel reports byte-for-byte matches and an intentionally wrong control that must fail.
exhibits.limits: These checks validate named examples; they do not audit the whole cryptographic implementation.

exhibits.title: Extract an identity key, and watch the inversion
exhibits.section: Extract an identity key, and watch the inversion
exhibits.action: Extract an SM9 identity key and force the t1=0 edge case.
exhibits.outcome: The displayed field inversion, group point and refusal path show how the KGC issues a key or rejects a degenerate value.
exhibits.limits: The KGC knows the master secret and can issue keys for identities; this is key escrow by design.

exhibits.title: Sign, exchange and encrypt against the annexes
exhibits.section: Sign, exchange and encrypt against the annexes
exhibits.action: Run pinned and fresh SM9 signatures, test eight rejection cases and deliberately use a wrong H1.
exhibits.outcome: Annex A signature values and verification verdicts are compared with negative-control behavior.
exhibits.limits: Pinned annex agreement tests a fixed example; fresh runs rely on the same implementation.

exhibits.title: SM9 exchange and encryption annexes
exhibits.action: Run Annex B key exchange, Annex C encapsulation and Annex D encryption modes.
exhibits.outcome: The protocol pane compares derived secrets, ciphertexts and standard annex values.
exhibits.limits: These are browser demonstrations of specified examples, not an interoperable production service.

exhibits.title: See what the KGC can do with the same two lines
exhibits.section: See what the KGC can do with the same two lines
exhibits.action: Have the KGC derive a decryption key to read a message and a signing key to sign as another identity.
exhibits.outcome: Both operations use standard verification paths to display the authority’s escrow and impersonation capability.
exhibits.limits: The ability follows from centralized key issuance; no independent identity authentication prevents the KGC in this model.

exhibits.title: The break, and the divergence
exhibits.action: Sign two distinct messages under one nonce, recover an identity signing key and forge another signature; test same-message reuse refusal.
exhibits.outcome: The attack recovers a secret and validates a forged signature under the affected identity.
exhibits.limits: Requires a reused nonce and distinct messages; normal fresh nonces do not trigger the same equation.

exhibits.title: Run Annex B at both hid values
exhibits.section: Run Annex B at both hid values
exhibits.action: Run the key exchange with both published hid conventions.
exhibits.outcome: The pane shows distinct derived keys from otherwise matching inputs, documenting an interoperability divergence.
exhibits.limits: An interoperability mismatch is distinct from key recovery; the lab labels the conflicting source texts.

exhibits.title: Solve and tamper with a cubic R1CS circuit
exhibits.action: Adjust witness x, inspect wire constraints and forge an intermediate wire.
exhibits.outcome: Computed arithmetic constraints show whether the witness satisfies x cubed plus x plus five.
exhibits.limits: Transparent playground exposes the witness; it teaches constraints rather than proving zero knowledge.

exhibits.title: Generate and verify a browser Groth16 proof
exhibits.action: Set x, generate proof, verify, then tamper with public output.
exhibits.outcome: snarkjs produces and checks a BN254 proof for the cubic circuit and reports observed proof size.
exhibits.limits: Static proving artifacts have unverified original ceremony provenance; small output range reveals x, so this demo is not witness-private.

exhibits.title: Prove an unintended assignment, then repair the relation
exhibits.section: A Valid Proof Can Prove the Wrong Application Claim
exhibits.action: Select public a and b, compare intended Boolean XOR with equation-only and bit-constrained Circom relations, generate and verify each real Groth16 path, then swap proof elements as an ordinary-tampering control.
exhibits.outcome: Both relations accept legitimate binary XOR rows; for a=b=2 the weak relation verifies an unmodified proof with public signals [r-4,2,2], while the repaired circuit's in-relation bit constraints prevent proof generation; swapped proof elements are rejected.
exhibits.limits: Bounded adaptation of Kolozyan et al., ePrint 2025/2120 revision 7, especially Sections 2.1-2.3 and 3.2.3. It executes two tiny public-input Circom/Groth16 relations over the BN254 scalar field with single-party demo proving material whose toxic-waste destruction is unverified. It demonstrates one explicit XOR computation/constraint mismatch and repair; it does not implement CCC-Check, reproduce Section 5, generalize detection, establish universal circuit correctness, or treat a browser input check as a relation repair.

exhibits.title: Compare circuit-specific and universal setup
exhibits.action: Inspect the same-circuit workflows and comparison table.
exhibits.outcome: Contrasts Groth16 per-circuit and PLONK universal trusted setup and proof tradeoffs.
exhibits.limits: PLONK panel is explanatory; it does not generate a PLONK proof.
exhibits.section: Groth16 vs PLONK on the Same Circuit

exhibits.title: Run toy powers-of-tau ceremony and forged KZG opening
exhibits.action: Run ceremony contributions and compare an honest opening to a false opening forged with leaked tau.
exhibits.outcome: Toy field verifier accepts the forged claim when the setup secret is known.
exhibits.limits: This KZG visualizer uses a tiny F17 scalar field and modeled pairing relation; it is separate from the real Groth16 panel.

exhibits.title: Simulate a Groth16 per-circuit ceremony
exhibits.action: Run the ceremony visualizer and follow participant contributions.
exhibits.outcome: Illustrates the one-honest-deletion assumption and why phase 2 must be repeated for each circuit.
exhibits.limits: Animation is conceptual; separate toy field ceremony in Exhibit 5 and real Groth16 uses shipped demo keys.

exhibits.title: Distinguish universal SRS backends and PLONK variants
exhibits.action: Read universal SRS examples and original PLONK, custom-gate, lookup and Halo2 backend notes.
exhibits.outcome: A universal bound serves multiple circuits, while KZG and IPA choices change ceremony needs.
exhibits.limits: The PLONK bytes are filler; no PLONK prover artifacts ship in this build.

exhibits.title: Map SNARK statements to production use cases
exhibits.action: Read examples for shielded spending, rollup execution, private membership and OAuth identity.
exhibits.outcome: Each context names a private witness or computation certified by a succinct public proof.
exhibits.limits: Context cards; examples are not run against those production services.

exhibits.title: Check circuit and setup distinctions
exhibits.action: Answer five questions and inspect per-answer explanations and score.
exhibits.outcome: Reinforces core circuit, setup and proof distinctions.
exhibits.limits: Instructional quiz; no cryptographic proof.

exhibits.title: Balanced and Augmented PAKE Login
exhibits.action: Register one password under SPAKE2 and SPAKE2+, then run honest logins on both.
exhibits.outcome: Both real group handshakes agree on keys, while server storage differs between balanced and augmented forms.
exhibits.section: A good day: the two look identical

exhibits.title: M and N Password Mask Walkthrough
exhibits.action: Step through a genuine DH share, password blinding, wire value, unmasking, and matching key.
exhibits.outcome: The five-stage view links SPAKE2’s public masked points to shared secret derivation.

exhibits.title: Nothing-Up-My-Sleeve Mask Points
exhibits.action: Inspect public M and N point derivations and the discrete-log independence requirement.
exhibits.outcome: The panel distinguishes fixed safe generators from an attacker-chosen point with a known relation.
exhibits.section: Why M and N are nothing-up-my-sleeve

exhibits.title: Database Compromise Comparison
exhibits.action: Steal balanced and augmented server records and run the candidate attack against the latter.
exhibits.outcome: The stolen SPAKE2 password-equivalent logs in immediately; SPAKE2+ verifier data resists direct login but permits offline dictionary checking.
exhibits.section: The bad day: steal the database
exhibits.limits: Augmented PAKE limits direct credential reuse after a server breach; low-entropy passwords can still be guessed offline.

exhibits.title: SPAKE2, SPAKE2+, and OPAQUE
exhibits.action: Read the side-by-side server-record and breach comparison.
exhibits.outcome: The section distinguishes balanced, augmented, and OPRF-based PAKE tradeoffs.

exhibits.title: Matter and Thread Commissioning
exhibits.action: Read how SPAKE2+ uses a QR or setup code for device onboarding.
exhibits.outcome: The application context separates local commissioning credentials from a reusable account password.
exhibits.section: You already run this: Matter / Thread

exhibits.title: SPAKE Known-Answer Checks
exhibits.action: Inspect specification-oriented vectors and primitive checks.
exhibits.outcome: The panel provides known-answer evidence for handshake arithmetic used elsewhere in the lab.

exhibits.title: Add authenticated shares locally
exhibits.action: Share two values among three parties and add their value and MAC shares.
exhibits.outcome: Displays reconstructed sum and demonstrates no online message is needed for linear sharing operations.
exhibits.limits: One local browser holds every party share and the dealer state.

exhibits.title: Multiply with a Beaver triple
exhibits.section: Multiplication needs a trick: the Beaver triple
exhibits.action: Step through a preprocessed triple, masked d and e openings, local combination and final authenticated result.
exhibits.outcome: Displays exact field arithmetic, MAC checks and triple consumption.
exhibits.limits: A trusted browser dealer generates triples rather than distributed SPDZ preprocessing.

exhibits.title: Attack a reused triple
exhibits.section: Multiplication needs a trick: the Beaver triple
exhibits.action: Reuse the spent triple or use a fresh one in a second multiplication.
exhibits.outcome: Shows masked-opening relationships leak input information when one-time triple masks repeat.
exhibits.limits: Controlled attack on one local teaching transcript.

exhibits.title: Attack an unauthenticated opening
exhibits.section: Multiplication needs a trick: the Beaver triple
exhibits.action: Lie during the d opening and compare a checked path with a path that skips its MAC check.
exhibits.outcome: Shows how a wrong product can still carry a valid final MAC when the opening was not authenticated.
exhibits.limits: The unsafe path deliberately omits a required protocol check.

exhibits.title: Cheat against MAC off and on
exhibits.section: Cheat, and let the MAC check catch you
exhibits.action: Alter a party value share and optional MAC share, then open under semi-honest and SPDZ checks.
exhibits.outcome: Rejects ordinary cheating, while a precisely adjusted MAC can forge if the globally shared key is disclosed.
exhibits.limits: The dealer reveals alpha in this local demo, enabling a forgery that properly secret-shared alpha prevents.

exhibits.title: Commit before opening check shares
exhibits.section: Cheat, and let the MAC check catch you
exhibits.action: Send an attacker check share last and compare unordered messages with commit-then-open ordering.
exhibits.outcome: Shows adaptive cancellation accepts a forged value without commitments and rejects it with them.
exhibits.limits: Single-value teaching check; production SPDZ batches and randomizes checks.

exhibits.title: Bank offline triples
exhibits.section: Offline vs online: why SPDZ is deployable
exhibits.action: Deal a batch into a shared bank and spend triples in multiplication panels.
exhibits.outcome: Displays dealt, consumed and remaining counts while the online circuit draws from the bank.
exhibits.limits: The expensive distributed triple generation is modeled as instant trusted-dealer output.

exhibits.title: Compute variance from secret shares
exhibits.action: Run a three-input variance circuit using four banked triples and inspect opened masks and final check.
exhibits.outcome: Returns a MAC-checked aggregate or abort while individual hospital inputs remain shared.
exhibits.limits: Three parties are represented in one browser; no actual hospitals or network privacy boundary.

exhibits.title: Compare consistent and shifted MAC-key contexts
exhibits.section: When abort becomes a privacy oracle
exhibits.action: Choose a hidden bit and corrupt-party guess, then run the same authenticated-share request against a key-bound alpha mask and a deliberately shifted beta=alpha+Delta mask/check context.
exhibits.outcome: Computes the public blind opening, unmasked residual, fresh-nonzero-mu masked value and accept/abort result; the Off-Key route recovers the input or tests the promised bit while the same-context and ordinary-corruption controls do not leak it.
exhibits.limits: A three-party trusted-dealer algebraic adaptation of CL079 with one unbatched opening and mu sampled from the nonzero field. It does not reproduce two-party distributed preprocessing, the full private-affine circuit, persistence, batching, concurrency or any evaluated framework. The omniscient audit is not attacker-visible.

exhibits.title: Generate, sign, verify and tamper with real SLH-DSA
exhibits.action: Select one of four SHA-2 SLH-DSA parameter sets, generate a keypair and sign a message, then verify and flip a bit in the signature or message.
exhibits.outcome: Runs noble's keygen/sign/verify, displays measured times and key/signature lengths, and shows verifier acceptance or tamper rejection.
exhibits.limits: Only four SHA-2 parameter sets (128f/128s/256f/256s) are wired; the expandable mechanism diagram is illustrative and is not parsed from the library's actual signature.

exhibits.title: Forge a scaled WOTS+ signature after one-time key reuse
exhibits.section: Forge it yourself — complete WOTS+, checksum included
exhibits.action: Generate the eight-chain teaching key, sign one message and try the forgery search, then sign a different message under the same key and retry.
exhibits.outcome: Counts candidate messages that clear message chains and those blocked by checksum chains; when a reachable new message is found, derives the forged signature by forward hashing and asks the unmodified WOTS+ verifier whether it passes.
exhibits.limits: Complete checksum-chain logic at a deliberately reduced 24-bit digest; rare digest collisions are identified separately, and a finite candidate budget does not guarantee a forgery on every run. This is not a practical break of full-width FIPS 205 WOTS+.

exhibits.title: Compute FORS indices and a reduced forest
exhibits.action: Select a SHA-2 SLH-DSA parameter set, enter a message and click Compute FORS.
exhibits.outcome: Displays the real parameter widths from noble's PARAMS, computes k digest indices via base_2b, hashes reduced trees containing the selected leaves, and visualizes their roots and derived teaching public key.
exhibits.limits: A parallel pedagogical reconstruction, not the internals of the noble signature just produced. The drawn trees stop at height min(a,4), the randomizer and seed are deterministic demo values, and hash-domain details are simplified.

exhibits.title: Test the boundary of independently signed messages
exhibits.action: Add signed messages, verify all, then change message bytes, edit the unsigned author/time, reorder or remove entries, or replace a key and re-sign.
exhibits.outcome: Rechecks the per-entry SLH-DSA signatures and reports whether the present message bytes verify under each supplied key; the exercises show changed bytes fail while unsigned metadata and collection changes can leave remaining signatures valid.
exhibits.limits: The historical Ledger label does not indicate an authenticated append-only ledger: each entry supplies its own key; author, time, ordering, completeness and trusted identity binding are unsigned. Key replacement with re-signing is not a forgery under the original key.

exhibits.title: SHA-256 Merkle Authentication Path
exhibits.action: Build a tree with 4, 8 or 16 leaves, select a leaf and verify its path.
exhibits.outcome: The computed path recombines sibling hashes to reach the root.
exhibits.limits: The small tree teaches authentication paths, not full FIPS 205 signing.

exhibits.title: WOTS+ Chain Point Exposure
exhibits.action: Generate four hash chains, sign a nibble on one chain and derive a later point from the revealed value.
exhibits.outcome: Reusing a one-time chain reveals a forward-computable point but this checksum-free illustration alone is not a complete signature forgery.
exhibits.limits: The separate complete WOTS+ panel supplies checksum chains and a full forgery.

exhibits.title: XMSS Hypertree and Signature Size
exhibits.action: Select a parameter set and render the d-layer XMSS schematic and size breakdown.
exhibits.outcome: The highlighted route shows FORS output being signed up the tree to the public root.
exhibits.limits: The topology uses real parameter counts but drawn triangles are schematic.

exhibits.title: FORS Few-Time Collision Tolerance
exhibits.action: Sign two messages with the same key, compare index vectors, then estimate a reuse margin for N signatures.
exhibits.outcome: The panel contrasts gradual FORS leaf exposure with one-time WOTS+ reuse.
exhibits.section: Collision Tolerance — Why FORS Degrades Gracefully
exhibits.limits: The margin is illustrative, not a security proof; real SLH-DSA randomizes R per signature.

exhibits.title: Hash-Based Mathematical Assumptions and Implementation Leakage
exhibits.action: Read the hash-function assumptions, Grover impact and implementation-leakage note, then follow the primary source for SLH-DSA-SHAKE power analysis.
exhibits.outcome: Distinguishes mathematical assumptions from physical power leakage and the SHAKE research target from this SHA-2 browser implementation.
exhibits.limits: The cited October 2026 preprint requires physical power measurements. The lab does not reproduce the microcontroller experiment; the paper does not establish vulnerability of this SHA-2 browser engine.

exhibits.title: Signature Scheme Sizes and Local Signing Speed
exhibits.action: Compare SLH-DSA parameter signatures with RSA and ML-DSA and inspect session signing-speed bars.
exhibits.outcome: The table exposes the signature-size cost of the hash-based choice alongside browser timings.
exhibits.limits: Timing is local and not a controlled cross-algorithm benchmark.

exhibits.title: Draft Limited-Use Signature Budget
exhibits.action: Set daily signatures, years and independently managed keys and inspect the proposed lifetime-limit calculation.
exhibits.outcome: The calculator estimates whether use would exceed a draft 2²⁴-signature-per-key cap.
exhibits.section: Draft SLH-DSA tradeoff: signatures per key
exhibits.limits: The cited limited-use parameter sets remain draft; the signer above uses existing FIPS 205 sets.

exhibits.title: Build a Sphinx packet
exhibits.action: Enter a message, construct a three-mix path and step through layers from the inside out.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect derived per-hop secrets, fixed-size routing block and MAC in the forward packet.

exhibits.title: Peel one mix hop
exhibits.action: Create a packet and advance one mix at a time.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect routing-block changes, per-hop MAC checks and forwarded packet bytes.
exhibits.limits: Byte histograms and Hamming distances are diagnostics, not a proof of computational unlinkability.

exhibits.title: Fixed-length packet construction
exhibits.action: Choose path length or an over-limit path and rebuild.
exhibits.outcome: Compare constant header length and filler despite different real hop counts; over-limit paths are rejected.

exhibits.title: Mix replay tag memory
exhibits.action: Send a packet twice or forge a copy before the genuine packet, then clear mix memory.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect duplicate detection from shared-secret-derived replay tags and the consequence of expiring memory.
exhibits.limits: Mix replay memory is modeled in-browser; production systems require bounded epochs and persistence choices.

exhibits.title: Header versus payload tampering
exhibits.action: Flip a header bit and a payload bit, then send both.
exhibits.outcome: The per-hop MAC rejects a changed header; payload corruption reaches the recipient and is detected by structure, not sender authentication.

exhibits.title: Traffic timing correlation
exhibits.action: Choose immediate forwarding or a pool mix and run traffic scenarios.
exhibits.outcome: Compare observer posterior and anonymity-set entropy despite packet-content hiding.

exhibits.title: Mix failure-code reference
exhibits.action: Expand the table of packet rejection codes.
exhibits.outcome: Relate each displayed failure code to a reachable control and real mix-layer result.
exhibits.section: The ways a packet dies here

exhibits.title: Sphinx parameters and group choice
exhibits.action: Expand the implementation-parameter disclosure.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect fixed header and payload sizes and the explanation of why iterated blinding uses ristretto255 rather than X25519 clamped scalars.
exhibits.limits: The implementation makes documented packet-encoding choices and is not a production mix network.
exhibits.section: The parameters this lab runs at

exhibits.title: Distributed Point Function Tree Microscope
exhibits.action: Choose secret point alpha, step levels, and regenerate the two DPF keys.
exhibits.outcome: Shows each key’s tree share and a one-hot point after XOR reconstruction.
exhibits.section: One point, split across two trees

exhibits.title: Two-Server XOR Private Shelf
exhibits.action: Pick one of 65,536 records and fetch it from two full-domain scans.
exhibits.outcome: Reconstructs the selected record from answer shares without sending alpha to either server.
exhibits.limits: Requires two non-colluding servers; there is no answer authentication.

exhibits.title: Server Answer Tampering
exhibits.action: Enable one-server bit flip and fetch again.
exhibits.outcome: Shows corrupted returned record and the outside teaching oracle detects its difference from shelf[alpha].
exhibits.limits: The protocol itself has no verifier for malicious answers.

exhibits.title: Logarithmic Key Size Meter
exhibits.action: Change domain size and compare a serialized DPF key to a full-length Chor XOR query.
exhibits.outcome: Displays key component bytes and the logarithmic versus linear traffic gap.

exhibits.title: Two-Key Collusion Break
exhibits.action: Give one server both DPF keys.
exhibits.outcome: Shows combined evaluations expose the chosen point.

exhibits.title: Start the server
exhibits.action: Create a host key and restart the server with a new key; inspect the resulting fingerprint.
exhibits.outcome: The local client sees a stable identity or changed host key across runs.
exhibits.limits: The server is an in-page model; no network SSH daemon or remote host exists.

exhibits.title: Connect
exhibits.action: Connect under selected StrictHostKeyChecking behavior, accept, reject, verify out of band, forget or reset known_hosts.
exhibits.outcome: The UI shows first-contact prompt, pin creation, repeat acceptance and changed-key warnings.
exhibits.limits: TOFU protects later connections only if the first pin was authentic; the client state is a browser teaching model.

exhibits.title: Host certificate and SSHFP trust
exhibits.action: Create and trust a host CA, sign a host key, or publish an SSHFP record with or without DNSSEC.
exhibits.outcome: The connection policy distinguishes a trusted CA certificate and DNSSEC-authenticated fingerprint from untrusted alternatives.
exhibits.limits: DNSSEC and CA deployment are simulated locally; their trust roots must be authenticated externally in real use.

exhibits.title: Break it (and recover)
exhibits.action: Try MITM after pinning or on first contact, tampered host signature, DNS spoof, rogue CA, and planned or emergency rotation.
exhibits.outcome: The scenario timeline explains which checks reject or accept a host and what recovery steps change the pin or CA trust.
exhibits.limits: Scenarios run in one page and do not model a full OpenSSH deployment or DNSSEC validator.

exhibits.title: The length that is read too early
exhibits.section: The length that is read too early
exhibits.action: Capture a packet, inject a modified ciphertext and compare pre-authentication length handling against a fixed construction.
exhibits.outcome: The packet panel displays differing reactions to malformed length before authentication and the mitigation’s refusal.
exhibits.limits: Packet runs are in-page models; timing and network behavior of a real daemon are not measured.

exhibits.title: The packet that vanished
exhibits.action: Inject IGNORE near NEWKEYS and delete EXT_INFO, then compare late injection and strict key exchange.
exhibits.outcome: The transcript and sequence counters show the prefix-truncation condition and where strict KEX blocks it.
exhibits.limits: A local protocol model, not a live vulnerable SSH server; strict-mode behavior follows implemented scenario assumptions.

exhibits.title: Three trust models
exhibits.action: Compare PKI/TLS, PGP web of trust and SSH/TOFU, then inspect the handshake explanations.
exhibits.outcome: The panels distinguish trust anchors, first-contact behavior and the role of each SSH handshake step.
exhibits.limits: The comparison explains trust models; the implementation remains a focused in-page SSH transport model.

exhibits.title: Scope & provenance
exhibits.action: Inspect the real-world TOFU examples, scope cards, reference links and OpenSSH command crosswalk.
exhibits.outcome: The page maps demo artifacts to practical files and commands and marks the gap between its transport model and a full SSH stack.
exhibits.limits: No actual SSH daemon, negotiation stack or DNSSEC validator is exercised by the page.

exhibits.title: Generate a Fibonacci trace and check AIR constraints
exhibits.action: Generate a trace, check constraints, then tamper a row.
exhibits.outcome: The trace constraint checker identifies a violated transition.
exhibits.limits: Small field and simple recurrence are a learning example.

exhibits.title: Turn a broken constraint into quotient-degree evidence
exhibits.action: Toggle honest and tampered traces, then inspect composition and vanishing quotient.
exhibits.outcome: Displays the nonzero remainder or raised degree caused by a changed trace row.
exhibits.limits: A finite toy interpolation demonstrates the reduction but does not establish a full soundness bound.

exhibits.title: Run a FRI folding sequence
exhibits.action: Choose degree settings and run FRI.
exhibits.outcome: Shows committed layers, folding challenges and low-degree checks.
exhibits.limits: The executed folds and final-code membership are component checks. A complete FRI or end-to-end STARK soundness bound additionally needs proximity, fold-MCA, composition, commitment/hash and Fiat–Shamir/BCS terms that this run does not establish.
exhibits.section: Step 2 — FRI: The Heart of STARKs

exhibits.title: Prove and verify a toy STARK in the browser
exhibits.action: Generate a proof, verify and corrupt a trace.
exhibits.outcome: Displays genuine finite-field and Merkle-based proof checks and a rejection path for altered data.
exhibits.limits: Toy parameters and narrow field do not imply production security strength.
exhibits.section: Step 3 — Prove and Verify in the Browser

exhibits.title: Compare masked openings with a witness-free simulator
exhibits.action: Reveal repeated masked openings and run a distribution experiment.
exhibits.outcome: Fresh masks change off-domain openings while preserving the trace domain; histograms compare with uniform simulator output.
exhibits.limits: A masked-opening distribution is necessary evidence, not a full zero-knowledge proof for entire transcripts.

exhibits.title: Compare transparent STARK and pairing-based SNARK tradeoffs
exhibits.action: Read side-by-side assumptions, setup, post-quantum posture and proof size.
exhibits.outcome: STARK hash/FRI architecture trades larger proofs for transparent setup relative to pairing systems.
exhibits.limits: Representative comparison; proof sizes vary by implementation and parameters.

exhibits.title: Recompute FRI query terms and proof-size costs
exhibits.action: Move blowup and query sliders, then compare capacity-model arithmetic, conditional query-only references, missing theorem terms, authentication bytes and measured proof-size rows.
exhibits.outcome: Recomputes every displayed value while classifying the capacity formula as heuristic, theorem-based references as conditional or limiting, and complete FRI and STARK bounds as unestablished when required inputs are absent.
exhibits.limits: The rate^queries figure is only capacity-model query arithmetic. Unique-radius and Johnson rows are query-only references under stated distance/MCA hypotheses; sampled fixture rejection and representative size rows do not establish universal soundness or production security.

exhibits.title: Relate AIR and recursion to deployed STARK systems
exhibits.action: Read StarkNet, StarkEx, Risc Zero and Polygon Miden system cards.
exhibits.outcome: Connects VM execution traces, AIR, recursive aggregation and proof wrapping to application settings.
exhibits.limits: Context cards, not live deployment verification.

exhibits.title: LSB image embedding and extraction
exhibits.section: Exhibit 2 — LSB Substitution: The Simplest Technique
exhibits.action: Enter a message, optionally select passphrase-based AES-256-GCM encryption, embed it in the cover image, and extract or download the stego PNG.
exhibits.outcome: Displays the altered image, histogram, PSNR, capacity and changed-channel count, then recovers the embedded message or reports a decode error.
exhibits.limits: An educational spatial LSB carrier, not a claim of undetectability; encryption is optional and separate from concealing the message's existence.

exhibits.title: Chi-squared detection of LSB embedding
exhibits.action: Test the original cover and the LSB stego image, or generate a payload-rate detectability curve.
exhibits.outcome: Displays chi-squared statistic, the model's probability-of-embedding value and a threshold verdict for each tested carrier.
exhibits.limits: This specific whole-image histogram test is a heuristic with a chosen threshold; a negative verdict does not establish resistance to other detectors.

exhibits.title: F5-inspired DCT coefficient embedding
exhibits.action: Compute an 8×8 DCT, embed a short message in selected AC coefficient parities, render the inverse transform, and extract from the coefficient stream.
exhibits.outcome: Shows before-and-after coefficient heatmaps, a rendered image, bit capacity status and recovered text from the in-memory DCT state.
exhibits.limits: Raw-image educational DCT workflow, not full F5, JPEG quantization or a proven round-trip through a saved JPEG file.

exhibits.title: Texture-guided versus sequential image embedding
exhibits.action: Compute the Sobel texture map, embed the same message by texture-ranked and sequential placement, then compare the carriers.
exhibits.outcome: Shows residual maps, mean texture and smooth-region fraction at embedding sites, and each carrier's chi-squared verdict.
exhibits.limits: A Sobel-ranked educational simplification inspired by WOW, not WOW or S-UNIWARD; the comparison does not run a machine-learning detector, and either carrier may trigger or evade this chi-squared test.

exhibits.title: Guided Hide, Recover and Detect
exhibits.action: Hide a sample sentence in a picture, compare originals, read it out, run detection and fill the image further.
exhibits.outcome: The introduction reuses the exhibit algorithms and makes the visibility-versus-detectability tradeoff concrete.
exhibits.section: Start here: hide a message in a picture

exhibits.title: Steganography versus Cryptography
exhibits.action: Read the vocabulary, threat distinction and embedding-versus-detection research sequence.
exhibits.outcome: The panel distinguishes hiding message existence from protecting its content and motivates encrypt-then-embed.
exhibits.section: Exhibit 1 — Steganography vs Cryptography: Two Different Goals

exhibits.title: Real-World Steganography Context
exhibits.action: Read printer tracking dots, watermarking, covert network channels, malware and steganalysis examples.
exhibits.outcome: The examples show practical uses and detection contexts for hidden signals.
exhibits.section: Exhibit 6 — Steganography in the Real World

exhibits.title: One-Shot versus Chunked Buffer Footprint
exhibits.action: Change modeled file size, segment size, and available RAM, then run both decrypt traces.
exhibits.outcome: An allocation ledger displays peak footprint and modeled out-of-memory outcome for a retained whole-file buffer versus bounded segment buffers.
exhibits.limits: No large file is read and process RSS is not measured; the two-copy peak assumes this particular one-shot buffer API.

exhibits.title: Chained Segment Authentication
exhibits.action: Switch between a chained Stream Ward construction and independent naive chunks, then inspect sealed segments and byte-level construction.
exhibits.outcome: Real XChaCha20-Poly1305 and SHA-256 bind sequence, prior ciphertext tags, and encrypted FINAL marker in the chained format; the naive split omits those stream guarantees.
exhibits.limits: The public chain state is not a secret and this teaching format has no rekeying, random access, or padding.

exhibits.title: Truncate, Reorder, and Drop
exhibits.action: Apply a byte-preserving truncation, reorder, or drop to the sealed frames and run each real verifier.
exhibits.outcome: The chained verifier aborts on missing final marker or broken tag/order; naive chunks can pass authentication despite a changed application message.
exhibits.limits: A chained verifier can have released an authentic prefix before discovering final truncation; applications must check completion.

exhibits.title: Six Verifier Outcomes
exhibits.action: Run each of three attacks under each of two constructions to fill the scorecard.
exhibits.outcome: Cells are populated from the verifier response and distinguish rejection from silent acceptance of rearranged plaintext.

exhibits.title: Real Operations and Modeled Limits
exhibits.action: Read the implementation and scope disclosures.
exhibits.outcome: The panel identifies actual cipher and hash operations and distinguishes modeled memory, missing rekeying, no random access, and visible segment metadata.
exhibits.section: What this does and does not prove

exhibits.title: Encode a bit in a valid ECDSA signature
exhibits.action: Choose a fictional document and zero or one, then sign using fresh entropy until the actual r field carries that bit.
exhibits.outcome: Shows the genuine P-256 signature, number of attempts, bit decoded from r and acceptance by both noble and native WebCrypto verification.
exhibits.limits: The bit is not encrypted; selection has a 64-attempt cap and can be inconclusive. All keys are local fiction.

exhibits.title: Compare deterministic signature outputs
exhibits.action: Sign the same document twice with RFC 6979 nonce derivation under one key.
exhibits.outcome: Shows byte-identical signatures, closing this particular randomized signer-choice channel.
exhibits.limits: Determinism for a fixed key and message does not exclude channels in message choice, timing, key choice or metadata.

exhibits.title: Test the ordinary signature boundary
exhibits.action: Inspect r and s then alter the signed message while reusing its signature.
exhibits.outcome: Native verification rejects the altered message, and the bit readout is retired as untrusted.
exhibits.limits: The verifier authenticates signed bytes, not the absence of intentionally encoded extra signal.

exhibits.title: Read limitations of the channel
exhibits.section: What the verifier does not check
exhibits.action: Read deterministic signing, coding-rule and deployment boundaries.
exhibits.outcome: Explains why valid signatures can carry an observer-readable symbol and why that does not confer secrecy.
exhibits.limits: No production signing, stealth delivery or hidden recipient system is built.

exhibits.title: Code-KEM key reuse erosion
exhibits.action: Move the public-key reuse slider or choose BIKE, McEliece or HQC reuse presets.
exhibits.outcome: Compare modeled ISD/DOOM margins as a fixed public key accumulates ciphertext targets.
exhibits.limits: Estimates concern the selected ISD/DOOM model and do not cover all structural attacks.
exhibits.section: The erosion, as you reuse one public key

exhibits.title: Syndrome primer
exhibits.action: Toggle error-vector bits, clear the vector or flip one random bit.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect the parity-check syndrome generated by a changed error pattern.

exhibits.title: Hamming-code DOOM scans
exhibits.action: Set target count and run repeated real small-code scans.
exhibits.outcome: Measure guessing work to hit any one of several target syndromes against an expected value.
exhibits.limits: Small-code experiment illustrates scaling, not the attack cost of production code-based KEMs.
exhibits.section: Why more targets make each one cheaper (the √M idea)

exhibits.title: Measured DOOM discount
exhibits.action: Choose maximum target count, trials and work budget, then run or starve the sweep.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect solved fractions, work curve and measured discount across target-set sizes.
exhibits.section: Measure the √M discount on a real code

exhibits.title: Key rotation policy calculator
exhibits.action: Set deployment rate and key lifetime or load a traffic scenario.
exhibits.outcome: See the reuse volume and modeled margin under a proposed rotation interval.
exhibits.limits: The calculator uses sourced parameters and a particular attack-cost model, not a complete security assessment.

exhibits.title: Why key reuse gives DOOM targets
exhibits.action: Read the scheme-by-scheme syndrome harvest explanation.
exhibits.outcome: Distinguish BIKE’s ring-shift head start from HQC’s reduction and McEliece’s lack of ring, and separate an already-budgeted factor from extra reuse.
exhibits.limits: Describes an attack-cost model; it does not assert a practical full key recovery.
exhibits.section: Why it drains: the DOOM lever

exhibits.title: DOOM model misconceptions and known gaps
exhibits.action: Expand the misconceptions and caveats.
exhibits.outcome: Separate modeled multi-instance amortization from actual scheme breakage or structural attacks, and compare idealized and full-ISD slopes.
exhibits.limits: The displayed model cannot certify overall code-KEM security.

exhibits.title: Sourced DOOM parameters and reproduction
exhibits.action: Expand the parameter table and the arithmetic verification note.
exhibits.outcome: Trace each scheme’s single-instance work, code length and crossover back to listed sources and recompute the model formula.
exhibits.limits: The simple square-root discount and full-ISD paper tables have differing slopes; neither includes structural key-recovery paths.

exhibits.title: Syndrome-Decoding Instance
exhibits.action: Flip candidate error bits, compare H·e with the public syndrome, and reveal the planted vector.
exhibits.outcome: Shows parity-check outcomes and whether the candidate has a matching syndrome and allowed weight.
exhibits.limits: The hand-toggle control is a small toy instance; reveal is teaching ground truth.

exhibits.title: Prange and Stern with Perfect Hints
exhibits.action: Choose Prange or Stern, leak support coordinates with a slider, and run one or both solvers.
exhibits.outcome: Runs 15 distinct-seeded attempts per setting, reports recovered verified error, residual length and weight, median work, p10–p90 spread, and run log.
exhibits.section: Pick an algorithm, feed it hints, run it for real
exhibits.limits: The slider reveals informative true support positions; the fault attack cited in prose is not simulated.

exhibits.title: Algorithm and Hint Work Curves
exhibits.action: Move the mirrored hint slider and run attacks at several counts.
exhibits.outcome: Plots modelled Prange/Stern work, polynomial floor, and measured run medians with matching data table.
exhibits.section: Two axes at once: the algorithm and the hints
exhibits.limits: Curves use a modelled elementary-operation ledger; dots come from genuine runs.

exhibits.title: Noisy Weight Hint Model
exhibits.action: Adjust uncertainty left by a block-weight measurement.
exhibits.outcome: Computes a modelled discount in search-exponent bits.
exhibits.section: Approximate hints: soft, noisy side-channel leakage
exhibits.limits: The discount is modelled, not an executed noisy-hint decoder or a measured acquisition channel.

exhibits.title: McEliece and HQC Weight Mechanism
exhibits.action: Run ISD on each small scheme-inspired toy with zero and all support hints.
exhibits.outcome: Compares iterations and hint counts to polynomial search on two deliberately different toy weights.
exhibits.section: The error-weight mechanism, on two toys
exhibits.limits: Toys are not scaled security models; real HQC noise is composite, so the simplified bound is not a cross-scheme security comparison.

exhibits.title: Prange and Stern Work-Factor Formulas
exhibits.action: Open the math disclosure and compare combinatorial search and birthday/collision formulas against modelled work.
exhibits.outcome: Shows the support-hint effect on n and w, the polynomial floor, and the Stern parameter cost model.
exhibits.limits: MMT and BJMM refinements are named, not implemented; formulas apply to this toy model.

exhibits.title: Syndrome Hint Attack Scope and Misreadings
exhibits.action: Read the FAQ and caveats after running the perfect-hint and approximate-hint panels.
exhibits.outcome: Distinguishes a recovered error vector from a decryption forgery or full key recovery, a toy support reveal from a physical fault channel, and modelled noisy-hint curves from executed Prange and Stern decoding.
exhibits.limits: No real HQC or Classic McEliece key recovery, physical acquisition, or noisy-hint decoder is performed.

exhibits.title: Open one branch. Hide the other two.
exhibits.section: Open one branch. Hide the other two.
exhibits.action: Generate new three-commitment Stern rounds, select one of three verifier challenges or derive a Fiat-Shamir challenge from the message.
exhibits.outcome: The UI opens two consistent commitment views, hides the third and reports whether the teaching verifier accepts the opening.
exhibits.limits: A reduced n=12, weight-3 pedagogical round; opening one branch is not the full 219-round signature or a new security proof.

exhibits.title: Cut and choose
exhibits.action: Test a prover with a vector of the right weight but the wrong public syndrome.
exhibits.outcome: The three branch outcomes show which challenge catches it and compute a repeated-round escape illustration.
exhibits.limits: The calculated repetition chance assumes independent rounds in the reduced model; it is not an empirical forgery rate for full Shipovnik.

exhibits.title: Shipovnik sign / verify
exhibits.action: Run the pinned QApp known-answer fixture, sign and verify an edited message through a C-to-WASM worker, then flip one signature byte.
exhibits.outcome: Shows accepted reference signatures, byte size and digest; the modified response-section byte is rejected by the verifier.
exhibits.limits: Compiled pinned reference C in a worker; fixture validity does not imply production safety, and this signature is hundreds of kilobytes.

exhibits.title: A four-leaf Merkle slice
exhibits.action: Edit the message and select a node in the computed four-leaf tree.
exhibits.outcome: The inspector displays selected hash input bytes and Streebog-256 output while the structure map labels where hashes sit in the full scheme.
exhibits.limits: The four-leaf slice illustrates hash wiring; it does not sign or reproduce the full two-layer m_128_20 construction.

exhibits.title: Hypericum sign / verify
exhibits.action: Run the QApp fixture, sign and verify the edited message in a worker, then flip a signature byte.
exhibits.outcome: Reports fixture and fresh signature acceptance, signature size and rejection of the changed signature.
exhibits.limits: Portable reference WASM signing can take many seconds; a valid fixture does not establish hash or parameter security.

exhibits.title: The structures travel. The primitives change.
exhibits.section: The structures travel. The primitives change.
exhibits.action: Compare the two schemes with their NIST structural peers, signature sizes, national-primitive context and pinned sources.
exhibits.outcome: The mirror contrasts hash-based and code-based proof approaches and lists signature byte sizes from the relevant fixtures and FIPS 205.
exhibits.limits: Comparison is a size and structure map, not a security ranking or benchmark of national versus NIST primitives.

exhibits.title: Forge a broadcast as a receiver with a shared MAC key
exhibits.action: Let receiver 2 create a message and HMAC tag using the broadcaster’s shared key.
exhibits.outcome: Receiver 1 accepts the genuine HMAC even though another listener authored it.
exhibits.limits: Shared MAC verification cannot distinguish broadcaster from any other key holder.
exhibits.section: 1 · A shared-key MAC is forgeable by a listener

exhibits.title: Verify a delayed TESLA chain key after dropped disclosures
exhibits.action: Set lost disclosure count and verify K4 against the signed chain anchor.
exhibits.outcome: Ed25519-verified anchor and HMAC-SHA-256 key-chain hashes authenticate delayed keys and release buffered packets.
exhibits.limits: Clocks and radio events are modeled; HMAC and anchor signature operations are real.

exhibits.title: Test a disclosed-key spoofer against receiver clock assumptions
exhibits.action: Change true lag, assumed bound, interval and disclosure delay, then spoof interval two.
exhibits.outcome: A forged packet can have valid HMAC and chain yet be rejected by safe-arrival time; a bound below true lag may admit it.
exhibits.limits: Scheduling and clocks are simulated; the clock-bound guarantee assumes a correct upper lag bound.

exhibits.title: Trade tag and key sizes against airtime and guessing
exhibits.action: Choose tag bits, key bits and bitrate; try 10,000 random tags or forge after disclosure.
exhibits.outcome: Shows calculated airtime, observed guess hits and a valid historical MAC anyone can create once its key is public.
exhibits.limits: Airtime uses entered bitrate; guessing trials are random samples and do not guarantee a hit.

exhibits.title: Relate TESLA model to Galileo OSNMA
exhibits.action: Read OSNMA adaptation, receiver guideline differences and explicit scope notes.
exhibits.outcome: Shows delayed-key disclosure as the shared idea while distinguishing real navigation message formats from the lab model.
exhibits.limits: No OSNMA message parsing, real radio, clock synchronization or deployed receiver.

exhibits.title: Threshold Polynomial Intuition
exhibits.action: Reveal individual points, exactly t, or t−1 on a small polynomial and reroll the secret.
exhibits.outcome: The graph shows that a quorum fixes the constant term while fewer visible shares leave multiple possible curves.
exhibits.section: Exhibit 0 — Why t Points Pin a Secret
exhibits.limits: The graph uses tiny integer coordinates; the live key pipeline operates modulo the P-256 group order.

exhibits.title: Distributed Key Generation
exhibits.action: Choose 3–8 parties and a 2-to-n threshold, compare a trusted-dealer narrative, and run DKG.
exhibits.outcome: Each participant deals Feldman-verifiable shares; summed shares produce a group public key without assembling one full private key.
exhibits.limits: The dealer toggle explains an alternative model; the run action uses the DKG path.

exhibits.title: Encrypt to the Group and Test One Share
exhibits.action: Enter a message, encrypt under the group public key, then attempt solo decryption.
exhibits.outcome: A fresh P-256 shared point derives the AES-GCM key; one participant’s partial gives the wrong key and real tag verification fails.

exhibits.title: Partial Decryption and Chaum–Pedersen Checks
exhibits.action: Generate all partial decryptions, inject a forged point, and verify each public NIZK proof.
exhibits.outcome: The verifier exposes equation checks and rejects a tampered partial before combination.

exhibits.title: Quorum Selection and Threshold Recovery
exhibits.action: Select parties, auto-select a quorum, and attempt recovery below or above threshold.
exhibits.outcome: Valid partials combine with Lagrange weights into a shared point that opens the AES-GCM ciphertext; too few or invalid selected shares are refused.

exhibits.title: Compromised Parties and Parallels
exhibits.action: Move the compromised-party count and read Vault, CloudHSM, FROST, and trusted-third-party parallels.
exhibits.outcome: A live comparison marks when colluding parties meet the configured quorum and relates the structural guarantee to other systems.
exhibits.limits: These named systems are conceptual parallels, not live integrations.

exhibits.title: Encrypted Election Tally and Ballot Proofs
exhibits.action: Choose seven 0/1 or deliberately invalid votes, cast, enable or disable 0-or-1 proof enforcement, sum encrypted ballots, and select authorities to open only the aggregate.
exhibits.outcome: Real P-256 exponential ElGamal, disjunctive proofs, homomorphic addition, and verified threshold partials expose invalid ballot outcomes and bounded tally recovery.
exhibits.limits: Invalid ballot proofs are deliberately simulated; voter eligibility, coercion resistance, and full end-to-end election verification are outside scope.

exhibits.title: Ballot Replay and Vote Receipt Limits
exhibits.action: Replay voter 1’s ballot as voter 2, then reveal a valid voter’s randomness as a receipt.
exhibits.outcome: The voter-bound challenge rejects replay; public equations verify that revealed randomness links a ballot to a specific vote, exposing lack of receipt-freeness.
exhibits.limits: Showing a verifiable receipt is a limitation of this teaching construction, not a property of all voting systems.

exhibits.title: Combine an actual split key byte
exhibits.section: The one real idea you can hold: additive secret sharing
exhibits.action: Reveal server and phone byte shares from a generated ML-DSA-65 key, combine modulo 256 and choose another byte.
exhibits.outcome: Shows neither uniform byte share alone equals the secret, while their sum recovers a real key byte.
exhibits.limits: Both shares and the complete key are controlled in one browser, so this is not independent custody.

exhibits.title: Watch rejection restarts
exhibits.section: Exhibit 1 — Why threshold ML-DSA is hard
exhibits.action: Sign until a sampled illustrative round passes and inspect coordinated restarts.
exhibits.outcome: Displays accepted and rejected rounds, connecting norm checks to repeated multi-party work.
exhibits.limits: Toy numerical trace is illustrative; it does not implement distributed FIPS 204 signing.

exhibits.title: Step through two-party signing shape
exhibits.section: Exhibit 2 — Walk a signing round, one step at a time
exhibits.action: Advance nonce, masked commitment, high bits, challenge, response and accept or restart stages.
exhibits.outcome: Shows actual toy modular values moving among server, phone and channel, separate from the emitted ML-DSA signature.
exhibits.limits: Elides public matrix in w and uses a scalar challenge component; choreography does not create the standard signature.

exhibits.title: Sign and test split-key custody
exhibits.action: Enter a message, sign with both shares or disable the phone, and inspect standard verifier and trust verdicts.
exhibits.outcome: Both parties yield a standard-valid ML-DSA-65 signature after full-key reconstruction; missing phone fails the drop-one test.
exhibits.limits: This path combines shares in one place to sign, so it does not enforce non-reconstruction or perform threshold MPC.

exhibits.title: Measure the local standard path
exhibits.action: Run six iterations comparing standalone signing with reconstruct-then-sign.
exhibits.outcome: Displays measured average wall-clock times and overhead factor for the two local paths.
exhibits.limits: Measured local combine-then-sign path, not a multi-device threshold communication benchmark.

exhibits.title: Run the toy threshold path
exhibits.section: Feel the difference: escrow vs. a real threshold scheme you can run
exhibits.action: Switch to never-combine, run a two-party lattice round and try over-bound or one-unit corrupted phone responses.
exhibits.outcome: Shows secret shares remain separate, genuine rejection sampling and a toy verifier accepting or rejecting the result.
exhibits.limits: Dimension 64 and tiny module rank carry no security; output is not FIPS 204 compatible.

exhibits.title: Compare published threshold schemes
exhibits.action: Read scheme parties, security, signing rounds, standard compatibility and attributed fault-replay research.
exhibits.outcome: Distinguishes published approaches from both local demonstration paths.
exhibits.limits: Table cites research claims; the page does not implement those papers or reproduce the fault experiment.

exhibits.title: Survey threshold signature uses
exhibits.action: Read root CA, blockchain, enterprise and recovery scenarios.
exhibits.outcome: Connects multi-person approval to signature custody use cases.
exhibits.limits: Use cases are explanatory, not deployed integrations.

exhibits.title: Create an RSW time-lock puzzle
exhibits.action: Enter message and work factor, generate primes and a puzzle, then copy public JSON.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect public modulus, base and encrypted payload while the creator retains trapdoor information.
exhibits.limits: Small browser-generated parameters are educational, not calibrated as a real-world delay guarantee.

exhibits.title: Sequential puzzle solving
exhibits.action: Load generated or pasted puzzle JSON, start or stop repeated squaring, try partial-work skip and creator shortcut.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect progress until the AES key and plaintext unlock; creator shortcut uses φ(N) to bypass sequential work.
exhibits.limits: Wall-clock delay depends on the device and implementation; puzzle creation and creator shortcut are intentionally accessible in the same session.

exhibits.title: Security and VDF comparison
exhibits.action: Inspect security explanation, deployment examples and VDF distinction.
exhibits.outcome: Compare a time-lock puzzle’s hidden message with a VDF’s efficiently verifiable delay output.

exhibits.title: Time-lock puzzle applications
exhibits.action: Read scenarios for randomness beacons, sealed bids, commitments, blockchain delays and future messages.
exhibits.outcome: Identify where delayed disclosure or sequential computation may matter and which uses require further protocol assumptions.
exhibits.limits: The page names application scenarios; it does not implement their surrounding protocols.
exhibits.section: Where time-lock puzzles (and VDFs) are used

exhibits.title: Time-lock puzzle versus VDF
exhibits.action: Inspect the separate VDF panel after solving an RSW puzzle.
exhibits.outcome: Compare decrypt-after-work with a VDF’s short publicly checkable proof, which the lab does not produce.
exhibits.limits: This RSW implementation omits a VDF proof; AES-GCM success is only a solver-side check.

exhibits.title: Shared Clock and Scenario Tour
exhibits.action: Drag true time, use expiry moments and skew presets, or step through the guided tour.
exhibits.outcome: Recomputes panel verdicts at the new time and visualizes validity windows on a shared timeline.
exhibits.section: The master clock drives every panel
exhibits.limits: Passage of time and server clocks are simulated numbers; the MACs and signatures use real operations.

exhibits.title: X.509 Certificate Validity
exhibits.action: Advance time through a self-signed Ed25519 certificate’s validity window, run staged verification, and toggle signature tampering.
exhibits.outcome: Distinguishes unchanged signature result from not-yet-valid, valid, and expired time-policy verdicts.
exhibits.limits: Self-signed teaching certificate; no complete certificate-chain or trust-store validation.

exhibits.title: JWT Split-Brain
exhibits.action: Set resource-server skew and leeway, then jump to a point near expiry.
exhibits.outcome: Shows two servers checking identical HS256 token bytes with opposite acceptance verdicts and a true-time comparison.
exhibits.limits: Server clocks are simulated; leeway widens the acceptance window.

exhibits.title: TOTP Window and Replay
exhibits.action: Adjust phone skew and verifier tolerance, submit a code, capture it, and replay with or without used-code tracking.
exhibits.outcome: Shows real HMAC code acceptance, replay detection, and the wider exposure from tolerance or absent one-time-use state.
exhibits.limits: The symmetric ±W band is deliberately looser than the one-step backward recommendation; an intercepted code does not reveal the secret.

exhibits.title: Signed URL Expiry
exhibits.action: Move past expiry and separately roll client or server clock back, then request the file.
exhibits.outcome: Shows the client clock is irrelevant while server rollback can resurrect a genuinely MAC-valid but expired URL.
exhibits.limits: Request serving is simulated locally; only the verifying server clock determines time policy.

exhibits.title: Skewed Replay Caches
exhibits.action: Send a MAC-protected request to server B, move time, set three clock skews, and replay the captured bytes to each.
exhibits.outcome: Shows cache hit, stale rejection, or acceptance by a slow server whose separate cache never saw the original.
exhibits.limits: Server routing, clocks, and caches are local models, not network servers.

exhibits.title: Distributed Token Verdict Matrix
exhibits.action: Adjust clock skew at three nodes while moving the master clock.
exhibits.outcome: Displays per-node Ed25519 token verification and diverging accept/reject decisions with signatures still valid.
exhibits.limits: The nodes and their clock offsets are simulated locally.

exhibits.title: Clock Drift, Signed Time, and Clock Ownership
exhibits.action: Read the closing failure table across honest drift, network time spoofing, and attacker-owned clock.
exhibits.outcome: Relates NTP and Roughtime to distinct trust problems and shows why verification against an attacker-chosen local clock remains unsafe.
exhibits.section: Which of these can better timekeeping fix?
exhibits.limits: NTP and Roughtime are described, not implemented.

exhibits.title: The mechanism, step by step
exhibits.action: Change target and guess and replay the character-by-character comparison.
exhibits.outcome: The exact operation counters show where early exit stops and how many UTF-16 code units each comparator examines.
exhibits.limits: Operation counts are exact for this loop; they are not timing measurements or a proof of engine-level constant time.

exhibits.title: Panel 1 — String Comparison Timing Attack
exhibits.action: Run 10,000 comparisons per mode, inspect prefix-length chart, distribution and table, or toggle the labeled ideal-signal overlay.
exhibits.outcome: The measured browser timings and statistical verdict compare early-exit with uniform-work JS comparisons across known prefix lengths.
exhibits.limits: This calibrates known prefixes and does not recover an unknown secret; coarse timers and noise can obscure leakage, while the overlay is modeled.

exhibits.title: Panel 2 — HMAC Verification Timing Leak
exhibits.action: Enter a message and forged MAC hex, measure prefix timing and inspect the chart and data.
exhibits.outcome: WebCrypto produces the expected HMAC; the page times vulnerable and uniform-work byte comparisons and reports a calibrated prefix slope.
exhibits.limits: Candidates are built using the known expected MAC at five prefix lengths; this is not unknown-MAC recovery, and JavaScript is not guaranteed constant time.

exhibits.title: Panel 3 — RSA Private Key Bit Leakage
exhibits.section: Panel 3 — RSA Private Key Bit Leakage
exhibits.action: Generate a toy RSA key, replay its bit-schedule animation and measure naive square-and-multiply against a ladder with one selected exponent bit forced to zero or one.
exhibits.outcome: The histograms and table show measured timing gaps and the different operation counts; a separate native RSA-PSS mean is a reference.
exhibits.limits: The key uses tiny primes and a chosen bit contrast, not key recovery; the 1024-bit WebCrypto reference differs in algorithm and runtime, and BigInt JS is not guaranteed constant time.

exhibits.title: Panel 4 — Cache-Timing Attack
exhibits.action: Measure repeated hot-array accesses before and after touching a large eviction array, then inspect distributions and the fixed latency diagram.
exhibits.outcome: The browser reports cached-versus-evicted working-set timings, while the L1-to-DRAM figures remain labeled reference values.
exhibits.limits: No AES key extraction or browser cache-line observation occurs; prefetching, scheduling and other effects can affect the measured gap.

exhibits.title: Panel 5 — Defense Patterns and Real-World Impact
exhibits.section: Panel 5 — Defense Patterns and Real-World Impact
exhibits.action: Read the constant-time coding rules, production primitive guidance and historical attack examples.
exhibits.outcome: The panel links secret-dependent branching, memory access and loop count to timing risk and explains why fixed-work JS is only an instructional defense.
exhibits.limits: Managed-runtime execution can vary despite a uniform source-level schedule; production needs vetted native primitives and appropriate system design.

exhibits.title: Measure early-exit and constant-time comparisons
exhibits.action: Measure both comparators and sweep matching-prefix lengths.
exhibits.outcome: Displays wall-clock timing distributions and how an early exit correlates time with matched prefix length.
exhibits.limits: Browser performance.now measurements are noisy and local; constant-time source structure does not prove hardware-level nonleakage.

exhibits.title: Recover a secret from comparator observations
exhibits.action: Generate a short secret, choose ideal or live observations and vulnerable or defended comparator, then launch the attack.
exhibits.outcome: Shows per-position candidate scores and recovery only when the oracle reveals prefix-dependent work.
exhibits.limits: Ideal channel reports exact examined bytes; live channel is a noisy local timer, not a remote attack.
exhibits.section: 3 · Be the attacker — recover the secret from timing

exhibits.title: Run vulnerable and defended comparators over two channels
exhibits.action: Run all four combinations of ideal/live channel and vulnerable/constant-time defense.
exhibits.outcome: Scoreboard separates vulnerability from measurement noise and shows no useful signal from defended comparator.
exhibits.limits: Noisy live runs can vary; a failed bounded attack does not prove a real implementation secure.
exhibits.section: 3 · Be the attacker — recover the secret from timing

exhibits.title: Understand how early rejection leaks prefixes
exhibits.action: Read the comparator timing analogy and attack examples.
exhibits.outcome: A data-dependent rejection time can turn an otherwise hidden comparison into a bytewise oracle.
exhibits.limits: Concept primer; live measurements are in later panels.

exhibits.title: Inspect compiler, hardware and JIT timing hazards
exhibits.action: Read examples of branches, memory access, variable latency and measurement amplification.
exhibits.outcome: A source-level fixed-work loop alone cannot certify machine-level constant time.
exhibits.limits: Historical hardware examples are not reproduced in the browser.

exhibits.title: Review constant-time comparison practices
exhibits.action: Read the checklist and implementation caveats.
exhibits.outcome: Shows branch, memory and loop discipline and use of vetted comparison primitives.
exhibits.limits: JavaScript source pattern is not proof of constant-time machine behavior.

exhibits.title: Step through a TLS 1.3 full handshake
exhibits.action: Use Step, Back, Auto-play, message selection or New session to inspect the message sequence and live transcript-hash chip.
exhibits.outcome: The page runs fresh X25519, Ed25519, HKDF and Finished checks for an educational session, then shows which secrets and checks correspond to each flight.
exhibits.limits: An educational TLS simulation, not an interoperable network stack: both endpoints run in one JavaScript context, certificate parsing is not X.509, and handshake-key badges do not mean each message was record-encrypted.

exhibits.title: Break the current handshake in two ways
exhibits.action: Choose honest, a flipped ECDHE output, or a modified EncryptedExtensions byte and compare the chain, signature and Finished verifier booleans.
exhibits.outcome: The ECDHE mismatch can leave identity checks valid while Finished fails; altering a transcript byte breaks its transcript-bound signature/MAC checks.
exhibits.limits: These are two selectable faults in a single-session model, not exhaustive TLS attack coverage.

exhibits.title: Compare both sides of X25519 ECDHE
exhibits.action: Inspect Alice's and the server's independently computed shared-secret bytes and repeat with New session.
exhibits.outcome: Different private inputs yield matching 32-byte secrets in an honest run; new ephemeral keys change session material.
exhibits.limits: A matching Diffie-Hellman secret alone does not authenticate the peer.

exhibits.title: Test signatures, trust anchor and MITM strategies
exhibits.action: Pick reuse-server-certificate, attacker-key signature or unchanged relay for the current session and inspect the separate client-acceptance and attacker-secret verdicts.
exhibits.outcome: The model runs the chosen strategy against this session's chain and transcript: a forged signature or untrusted chain is rejected, while unchanged relay gains the attacker no key.
exhibits.limits: The chain is a teaching encoding, not X.509; it omits hostname, validity and revocation checking.

exhibits.title: Inspect a live HKDF key schedule
exhibits.action: Read the current session's early, handshake, master and traffic secrets and expand one HKDF derivation to inspect inputs, label, context and output.
exhibits.outcome: The page displays actual derived bytes; a New session keeps the page-lifetime Ed25519 leaf key while changing X25519-derived secrets.
exhibits.limits: The leaf key persists only for the page lifetime and the no-PSK Early Secret is a protocol constant, not an ephemeral secret.

exhibits.title: Inspect and tamper with an AES-GCM application record
exhibits.action: Compare the application plaintext, per-record nonce, authenticated header and resulting ciphertext/tag with the byte-flip verdict.
exhibits.outcome: A first request decrypts back to its plaintext and a one-byte change fails GCM authentication.
exhibits.limits: The application record is sealed for real; handshake messages shown with encryption-layer badges are not separately sealed into records.

exhibits.title: Derive a ticket PSK and test binder admission
exhibits.section: Act B · Resume and bind the ClientHello
exhibits.action: Switch psk_dhe_ke and psk_ke and flip the ticket identity or binder byte before early data admission.
exhibits.outcome: The page shows the PSK and both schedules, distinguishes ticket AEAD failure from binder failure, and withholds early plaintext when either verification fails.
exhibits.limits: The ticket's opaque server contents are a labeled in-memory teaching format, not a prescribed TLS wire format.

exhibits.title: Leak the server's ticket key against recorded sessions
exhibits.section: Act C · Leak the ticket key
exhibits.action: Press Leak the ticket key and compare recorded psk_ke and psk_dhe_ke sessions.
exhibits.outcome: The model opens the ticket and recovers the PSK: recorded 0-RTT data is readable in both modes, while fresh X25519 protects psk_dhe_ke's resumed 1-RTT record.
exhibits.limits: This is a controlled educational compromise of the in-memory server ticket key, not access to a real server.

exhibits.title: Replay a 0-RTT bill payment across two regions
exhibits.section: Act D · Record and replay a 0-RTT bill payment
exhibits.action: Choose a server admission policy, record the ClientHello and encrypted early record, then replay identical bytes to two modeled regions.
exhibits.outcome: The execution logs/counts reveal that valid binder and ticket do not ensure freshness: the broken policy can execute twice, local replay recording can miss a replay in a second region, and shared single-use state changes admission.
exhibits.limits: This is a two-region in-page model with selected policies and one payment action, not a general proof of a deployment's replay safety.

exhibits.title: TLS 1.3 Security Properties
exhibits.action: Read the confidentiality, integrity, authentication and message-flow introduction.
exhibits.outcome: The overview ties separate cryptographic primitives to the handshake channel guarantees.

exhibits.title: Ticket and Resumption PSK Derivation
exhibits.action: Inspect the issued ticket lifetime, age add, nonce, encrypted state and derived resumption PSK.
exhibits.outcome: The panel shows how the full handshake secret and ticket nonce yield the next PSK.
exhibits.limits: The server ticket is a labeled in-memory teaching format, not a deployed server implementation.

exhibits.title: TLS 1.3 versus 1.2 Takeaways
exhibits.action: Compare trips, secrecy, cipher suites, encryption and key schedules.
exhibits.outcome: The table and takeaways separate ephemeral certificate handshakes from PSK-only and early-data guarantees.

exhibits.title: TLS Demo Exactness and Omitted Checks
exhibits.action: Read the faithful calculations, deliberately absent certificate checks, and compressed record handling.
exhibits.outcome: The disclosure distinguishes real X25519, Ed25519, HKDF, Finished and AES-GCM from a non-X.509 chain, missing hostname checks and unsealed handshake records.
exhibits.section: Scope — What This Demo Does and Does Not Model

exhibits.title: Same Text, Different Watermark Key
exhibits.action: Replay three scored runs: marked text under its configured key, byte-identical text under another key, and an unmarked control.
exhibits.outcome: The same token scorer yields evidence for the matching configuration and loses it when only the key changes; input digests let the reader check byte identity.
exhibits.section: The proof — Same text, different key
exhibits.limits: The text and keys are pinned teaching samples, not a detector for commercial products.

exhibits.title: Wrong-Key Null Sweep
exhibits.action: Choose 20–300 random wrong keys and sweep the same marked sample.
exhibits.outcome: A measured score histogram and tail statistics compare the configured key with the wrong-key population and an independence-based spread prediction.
exhibits.limits: The finite sweep is a sample, and the predicted spread rests on independence assumptions.

exhibits.title: One-Bit Key Mutation
exhibits.action: Inspect the same token sequence under the configured key list and a one-bit-changed first key.
exhibits.outcome: The local reference construction’s SHA-256 chain seed changes every layer’s g-values, so the comparison exposes configuration sensitivity.
exhibits.limits: This behavior belongs to the reference construction and is not a general rule for watermarking.

exhibits.title: Cross-Implementation Watermark Reading
exhibits.action: Score the same pinned text and keys with the official reference g-function and the transformers variant.
exhibits.outcome: The table shows that implementation-specific g-value derivation can prevent one faithful variant from detecting the other’s mark.
exhibits.section: The same key, a different implementation

exhibits.title: Keyed Candidate Tournament
exhibits.action: Select a pinned GPT-2 next-token distribution, set 1–30 tournament layers, draw again, or reset.
exhibits.outcome: Literal small brackets or an aggregate large-depth view show keyed candidate selection and the fixed-key distribution shift.
exhibits.limits: Distributions were captured after temperature and top-k; no live language model runs. Distribution preservation is an expectation over random keys at one decoding step, not a fixed-key guarantee.

exhibits.title: Repeated-Context Masking
exhibits.action: Inspect repeated contexts and which scored positions are suppressed in the pinned sample.
exhibits.outcome: The panel illustrates why a repeated context cannot count as independent fresh watermark evidence.
exhibits.section: The rule that stops the watermark repeating itself

exhibits.title: Score Arbitrary Text and Inspect Pipeline
exhibits.action: Paste text or load a committed sample, score it, and open tokenization, masking, per-layer g-values, and exact-null details.
exhibits.outcome: The score card reports mean g and evidence only for the published demo configuration; changing input retires the old verdict.
exhibits.limits: A positive score cannot establish author identity or truth, and a negative score cannot establish human authorship; commercial private configurations are unavailable.

exhibits.title: Detection Strength by Text Length
exhibits.action: Inspect pinned marked and unmarked length curves and recompute the corpus statistics in the browser.
exhibits.outcome: The chart places a 1% false-positive threshold and detection rates beside measured null spread and reveals where longer texts improve separation for this configuration.
exhibits.section: How much text does it take?
exhibits.limits: Thresholds are indexed by token length for the pinned corpus; no universal minimum length is claimed.

exhibits.title: Pinned Context Entropy and Per-Token Evidence
exhibits.action: Compare high, medium, and low-entropy GPT-2 sampling contexts and inspect exact reweighted distributions.
exhibits.outcome: The table relates entropy, effective candidate count, collisions, and each context’s keyed versus plain mean g-value.
exhibits.section: Act III — The watermark needs choices
exhibits.limits: These are fixed contexts and one key; single-context unmarked means need not equal the corpus-level 0.5 null.

exhibits.title: Where the Watermark Failed to Take
exhibits.action: Score the committed watermarked corpus and inspect equally long texts with little or no usable signal.
exhibits.outcome: Repetition loops leave few scored positions, explaining misses even at a fixed 320-token length and a threshold indexed by total tokens.
exhibits.section: Where the watermark failed to take
exhibits.limits: The length-indexed threshold may misjudge a text with few independent scored positions.

exhibits.title: Live Truncation, Deletion, and Replacement Sweep
exhibits.action: Run repeated seeded token attacks over several strengths and inspect curves and individual scores.
exhibits.outcome: Truncation removes trailing evidence; random deletion and vocabulary replacement also disturb context windows, producing measured detector changes.
exhibits.limits: Replacement draws from the original vocabulary; it is not a semantic synonym attack.

exhibits.title: Pinned Translation and Paraphrase Attacks
exhibits.action: Inspect committed model transformations, input and output text, model revisions, and rescored before/after values.
exhibits.outcome: A real offline back-translation and paraphrase capture can move statistical evidence below the configured threshold.
exhibits.limits: Transformations ran offline and are pinned; the browser recomputes scores from their committed outputs, not a live paraphrase model.

exhibits.title: Sign, Tamper, and Strip a Manifest
exhibits.action: Edit text, sign it with a session key, flip an asset byte, strip the manifest, or verify again.
exhibits.outcome: Real ECDSA and SHA-256 validation distinguish a signature/binding failure from absence of verification material.
exhibits.section: Act V — Sign the same text
exhibits.limits: The manifest is C2PA-shaped but lacks conformant JUMBF/COSE packaging, certificate chain, trust list, and signer identity validation.

exhibits.title: Sign and Verify a False Claim
exhibits.action: Edit a plainly false statement or use the shipped claim, sign it, and verify its bytes.
exhibits.outcome: A valid signature and hard binding pass while the truth of the assertion remains unanswered.
exhibits.section: Act VI — A signature can sign a lie
exhibits.limits: The page recognizes only its shipped claim as false; it cannot fact-check edited text.

exhibits.title: Watermark, Signature, and C2PA Comparison
exhibits.action: Switch the mechanism focus and open explanatory rows across three approaches.
exhibits.outcome: A compact demo and eleven-question full table distinguish symmetric-secret detection from public-key verification and the claims each can support.
