exhibits.section: Act VII — What each mechanism actually proves
exhibits.limits: The lab’s published demo keys allow anyone to experiment; this does not imply interoperable third-party detection for private commercial configurations.

exhibits.title: Manifest Stripping versus Text Regeneration
exhibits.action: Rerun a real signing-and-strip path beside the detector score for a pinned rewritten text.
exhibits.outcome: Removing a manifest leaves asset bytes intact but no provenance to verify; rewriting changes text and may remove keyed token-choice evidence.
exhibits.limits: The regeneration half uses a pinned paraphrase; the signing half uses a local session key.

exhibits.title: Corrected Population Prevalence
exhibits.action: Choose a marked fraction, score the committed corpus, and estimate prevalence with an interval.
exhibits.outcome: A calibrated detector’s flagged count is corrected by measured true and false positive rates, with a 95% interval and a growing nested-corpus view.
exhibits.limits: The estimate needs stable calibration rates, enough separation between TPR and FPR, and a representative pinned corpus; it is not an improved individual verdict.

exhibits.title: Calibration and Individual Verdicts
exhibits.action: Inspect calibration versus held-out rates and the false accusations and misses in the same measured corpus.
exhibits.outcome: The table shows how a useful population estimate coexists with weak flags on individual documents.
exhibits.section: What the detector was calibrated to do / The same corpus, one document at a time

exhibits.title: Math, Provenance, and Limits
exhibits.action: Read the exact score equation, limitation list, implementation provenance, pinned data and test vectors, and primary sources.
exhibits.outcome: The reference ties the detector’s binomial-tail argument to repeated-context masking and marks demo simplifications and unsupported claims.
exhibits.section: Reference — Limitations, maths, provenance and sources

exhibits.title: Compare naive group delivery
exhibits.section: The naive corner — why this problem is hard
exhibits.action: Revoke a member under one shared key and compare one-per-recipient wraps.
exhibits.outcome: Counts real AES-GCM wraps and key-reissue cost for two simple designs.
exhibits.limits: Sixteen toy subscribers; reissue and headers are local browser operations.

exhibits.title: Revoke leaves and broadcast
exhibits.section: The subset cover — revoke by clicking
exhibits.action: Click subscribers, choose complete-subtree or subset-difference cover, and broadcast a message.
exhibits.outcome: Shows cover/header sizes, derived wrapping keys and all sixteen actual AES-GCM decryption verdicts.
exhibits.limits: Subscriber keys are local and transparent; sixteen leaves do not establish production performance.

exhibits.title: Inspect one receiver against the cover
exhibits.section: The subset cover — revoke by clicking
exhibits.action: Select a subscriber cell to follow its header scan, subset derivation, key unwrap and payload authentication.
exhibits.outcome: Unrevoked users find a valid covering key, while revoked users cannot derive one and forced wrong-key GCM fails.
exhibits.limits: The UI can inspect every key by design; endpoint compromise is outside the construction.

exhibits.title: Build and identify a pirate decoder
exhibits.action: Copy chosen subscriber keys into a software decoder, run crafted encrypted probes and revoke an accused key.
exhibits.outcome: Displays a binary-search transcript, identified key set and trace-and-revoke loop.
exhibits.limits: Single-traitor guarantee applies to this deterministic tracer model, not an arbitrary stateful pirate.

exhibits.title: Test pooled keys and evasive tracing
exhibits.action: Pool two revoked key sets, inspect a distinguishing probe and run 25 traces under greedy or evasive decoder behavior.
exhibits.outcome: Pooled revoked keys stay excluded; an evasive coalition can induce false accusations in this simple tracer.
exhibits.limits: Full NNL collusion tracing is discussed but not implemented; this binary-search tracer has narrower guarantees.

exhibits.title: Licensed database and AACS examples
exhibits.section: Same math, different building: the licensed database
exhibits.action: Read a scaled licensed-database scenario and AACS device-key history.
exhibits.outcome: Connects stateless recipient revocation and key leakage to deployed media contexts.
exhibits.limits: AACS and 200-institution database are explanatory examples; no deployed infrastructure is contacted.

exhibits.title: X-only ladder on curve or twist
exhibits.action: Enter a Montgomery u coordinate and multiply by seven.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect whether the coordinate is on the intended curve or its twist while the x-only ladder still returns a value.
exhibits.limits: Uses a deliberately small toy field and secret.

exhibits.title: Twist subgroup queries
exhibits.action: Toggle input validation and run five chosen twist-point queries.
exhibits.outcome: With validation disabled, residues of a static secret are combined through CRT and checked against a public point.
exhibits.limits: Requires a chosen-input oracle; no real curve endpoint is attacked.

exhibits.title: Full-coordinate invalid-curve attack
exhibits.action: Toggle full point validation and query small-order points on other curves sharing a parameter.
exhibits.outcome: Observe exact secret residues from small logs and recombination when the service accepts invalid points.
exhibits.section: 3 · Change b and recover the full secret

exhibits.title: On-curve small subgroup and clamping
exhibits.action: Submit an order-four point under raw versus clamped scalar handling.
exhibits.outcome: Compare residue leakage with an identity response after toy cofactor clamping.
exhibits.limits: Toy multiple-of-four clamping is illustrative and distinct from RFC 7748 X25519 clamping.
exhibits.section: 4 · An on-curve point can still be too small

exhibits.title: Public twist orders and RFC vectors
exhibits.action: Inspect public curve/twist order facts and run X25519 RFC 7748 test vectors.
exhibits.outcome: Compare published order factors and computed vector results without querying real systems.
exhibits.section: 5 · Real curves: public facts, no attack

exhibits.title: Sequential Repeated-Squaring Evaluation
exhibits.action: Enter x, set difficulty T from 16 to 16,384, and evaluate.
exhibits.outcome: Shows each chunk’s progress, T sequential modular squarings, output y, and a short proof with measured prover cost.
exhibits.limits: Toy public modulus and a simple prover whose second exponentiation may cost roughly T further group operations.

exhibits.title: Four Worker Dependency Test
exhibits.action: After evaluating, simulate chaining four workers versus starting their slices together.
exhibits.outcome: Computes that chained slices reproduce y after T dependent steps, while shorter parallel slices land on another output.
exhibits.limits: Runs synchronously in one browser thread, with no Web Workers or wall-clock timing; it checks the obvious split strategy, not the full sequentiality assumption.

exhibits.title: Wesolowski Verification and Tampering
exhibits.action: Verify the produced proof, then flip a bit in y or π and verify again.
exhibits.outcome: Checks the transcript-bound challenge and group identity, reports acceptance or rejection and measured verifier operations against evaluation cost.
exhibits.limits: Verification cost is roughly constant in T, but can exceed evaluation for low T; the challenge prime test is probabilistic at 128 bits.

exhibits.title: Time-Lock Puzzle versus VDF
exhibits.action: Inspect the side-by-side property table.
exhibits.outcome: Contrasts shared sequential delay with a VDF’s publicly checkable succinct proof.

exhibits.title: VDF Constructions and Applications
exhibits.action: Read the application examples and compare repeated squaring, Wesolowski, Pietrzak, and group choices.
exhibits.outcome: Identifies where delay is only a component of a larger randomness or fairness protocol and distinguishes proof constructions.
exhibits.limits: The alternative constructions and applications are described, not implemented.

exhibits.title: Factorization Trapdoor Shortcut
exhibits.action: Reveal the isolated trapdoor and recompute y from the toy modulus factors.
exhibits.outcome: Compares shortcut and honest operation counts, showing the same y and whether the shortcut is faster at the chosen T.
exhibits.section: ⚠ Reveal the trapdoor — what the VDF assumes nobody can do
exhibits.limits: Factors ship publicly in this educational bundle; at small T the trapdoor computation can cost more than honest evaluation.

exhibits.title: VDF versus Proof of Work and Time-Lock Puzzle
exhibits.action: Read the opening comparison of sequential work and fast public proof.
exhibits.outcome: Distinguishes a VDF from parallelizable proof of work and a time-lock puzzle whose claimed answer must be recomputed to verify.

exhibits.title: VDF Uses and Surrounding Protocols
exhibits.action: Read examples for randomness beacons, leader election, lotteries, and delayed execution.
exhibits.outcome: Explains that a VDF supplies publicly verifiable delay while fairness and unbiasability require surrounding protocols.

exhibits.title: Deliberately omit and restore the Ed25519 scalar range check
exhibits.action: Switch off the second check, then restore the requirement that S is smaller than L.
exhibits.outcome: The same pinned signatures are recomputed under a single changed acceptance predicate; the hostile S plus L signature can pass only in broken mode.
exhibits.limits: The verifier is educational variable-time BigInt code with public fixtures, not a production cryptographic library.

exhibits.title: Test five published Ed25519 verification examples
exhibits.section: The published tests all pass — either way
exhibits.action: Run the named RFC 8032 vectors under both range-check settings and choose what the green result establishes.
exhibits.outcome: The page counts matching named cases in each setting and later resolves the prediction after the hostile signature is accepted.
exhibits.limits: Passing five positive vectors does not show that malformed or noncanonical signatures reject, much less confer validation.

exhibits.title: Compare genuine, corrupted-message, and S plus L signatures
exhibits.section: The case those tests never asked about
exhibits.action: Inspect the three computed case verdicts and toggle the range requirement.
exhibits.outcome: The genuine signature accepts, ordinary message corruption rejects, and the noncanonical signature changes between rejection and false acceptance while its bytes stay pinned.
exhibits.limits: The Wycheproof case is selected evidence for this failure class, not a full adversarial suite or certification.

exhibits.title: Inspect computed challenge, group equation, and scalar range separately
exhibits.section: Why the forgery satisfies the equation
exhibits.action: Compare live k, group-point encodings, S values and L for canonical and hostile signatures.
exhibits.outcome: Adding L leaves the challenge and group equation unchanged, while the separate S less than L check distinguishes the encodings.
exhibits.limits: The equation is computed for inspection even when the independent range rule requires rejection.

exhibits.title: Construct additional noncanonical signatures from one valid signature
exhibits.section: Forge it yourself — the forgery is not a one-off
exhibits.action: Drag the multiple-of-L slider to encode S plus k times L and reverify each candidate.
exhibits.outcome: The page computes how many 32-byte encodings fit, shows the forged scalar and signature, and contrasts strict and broken verdicts.
exhibits.limits: The family reuses the same public key, message, and R; it is not a new signing key or a general forgery algorithm.

exhibits.title: Mutate a signature byte and identify the failed verifier stage
exhibits.section: Byte surgery — not every rejection means the same thing
exhibits.action: Choose a byte index and replacement value, then restore the original byte.
exhibits.outcome: The mutated signature is reverified and the page names decoding, scalar-range, or group-equation rejection when applicable.
exhibits.limits: The precise rejection depends on the chosen byte and current range mode; not every one-byte change yields a rejection.

exhibits.title: Classify the claims supported by each test result
exhibits.section: What Did the Green Result Prove?
exhibits.action: Match the RFC vectors, hostile acceptance, and restored range rejection to evidence categories; reveal the reference answers.
exhibits.outcome: The exercise scores three matches and explains distinctions among a specification, conformance case, adversarial case, algorithm validation, and module validation.
exhibits.limits: The page issues no NIST algorithm or FIPS 140-3 module validation certificate and makes no application or protocol security claim.

exhibits.title: Cipher: encrypt and decrypt
exhibits.action: Enter text and a repeating keyword, then switch between encryption and decryption.
exhibits.outcome: The transformed text and per-letter input/key/shift/output strip update, with the first tabula-recta cell highlighted.
exhibits.limits: Classical repeating-keyword cipher, not an OTP or a modern stream cipher.

exhibits.title: Break workbench: Kasiski and index of coincidence
exhibits.action: Select a bundled scenario or paste ciphertext, adjust maximum key length, and choose a candidate period.
exhibits.outcome: Repeated substrings and spacings, factor frequencies, and per-period IoC measurements guide a key-length hypothesis or report insufficient evidence.
exhibits.limits: Short text, non-English text, or long sparse columns can make the statistical diagnosis inconclusive; that does not establish secrecy.

exhibits.title: Column frequency solve and candidate decryption
exhibits.action: Run the solver, inspect chi-squared heatmaps for each Caesar column, override shifts, and use Challenge mode to submit a key or request hints.
exhibits.outcome: The transcript, live plaintext preview, confidence diagnostics, candidate key, and decryption update; bundled answers verify exact key and plaintext when available.
exhibits.limits: English quality is a heuristic, not proof; custom ciphertext has no bundled answer for verification.

exhibits.title: Why Vigenere fails: replay
exhibits.action: Spotlight each repeating-key column and toggle mathematical versus historical explanation.
exhibits.outcome: An aligned KEY example shows each column behaving as a Caesar cipher and repeated plaintext at aligned offsets yielding repeated ciphertext.
exhibits.limits: The replay is a fixed illustrative example; the separate workbench analyzes user ciphertext.

exhibits.title: History, Sources and Solver Scope
exhibits.action: Read the Vigenère historical framing, one-time-pad distinction and further-reading links.
exhibits.outcome: The notes limit statistical failure on short text to an inconclusive attack and identify English ranking as a heuristic.

exhibits.title: Compute and publicly verify an ECVRF output
exhibits.action: Enter an input, compute beta and proof, check repeated uniqueness or tamper with beta before verification.
exhibits.outcome: RFC 9381 ECVRF-P256-SHA256-TAI output verifies against the public key and altered values fail.
exhibits.limits: A VRF is keyed and verifiable but does not alone prevent a participant from withholding its output.
exhibits.section: What Is a VRF? The Public-Key Hash

exhibits.title: Evaluate a toy VDF and skip its supposed delay
exhibits.action: Set the squaring count, evaluate, verify Wesolowski proof, and use the lambda shortcut.
exhibits.outcome: The proof checks, but public modulus factors let a single exponentiation reproduce the output quickly.
exhibits.limits: The chosen modulus has public factors and provides no forced delay; browser progress is not adversarial work.
exhibits.section: What Is a VDF? The Time-Lock

exhibits.title: Run a VRF/RANDAO/VDF beacon round
exhibits.action: Choose validator count, delay and a malicious last revealer, then run a full round.
exhibits.outcome: Logs commitments, reveals, optional withholding, VDF evaluation and public proof checks for final randomness.
exhibits.limits: Participant scheduling is simulated; the toy VDF has a public shortcut, so it cannot truly remove last-revealer advantage.

exhibits.title: Compare commit-reveal withholding and delayed prediction
exhibits.action: Read partial-XOR reveal and RANDAO-followed-by-VDF timelines.
exhibits.outcome: A last revealer can choose to withhold once a partial mix is known; an appropriate VDF would delay outcome prediction.
exhibits.limits: The shipped toy VDF has public factors and therefore does not supply the claimed delay.

exhibits.title: Compare deployed randomness services and VRF/VDF properties
exhibits.action: Read deployment cards and property table.
exhibits.outcome: Distinguishes validator selection, request-response randomness, distributed beacon and proposed VDF layers.
exhibits.limits: Read-only context; some cards describe similar families, not the exact ECVRF ciphersuite in Exhibit 1.

exhibits.title: Inspect limits of the featured VRF and VDF constructions
exhibits.action: Read the cryptographic fidelity and post-quantum notes.
exhibits.outcome: P-256 VRF and RSA-style unknown-order VDF assumptions are vulnerable to Shor; the toy instance also reveals factors.
exhibits.limits: Explanatory caveat, not a quantum attack simulation.

exhibits.title: Shamir, Feldman, and Pedersen Decision Guide
exhibits.action: Compare the dealer trust, verification, and hiding requirements for three sharing protocols.
exhibits.outcome: The guide maps a trusted dealer to plain Shamir, public-share verification to Feldman, and hidden commitments to Pedersen with its independent-generator assumption.

exhibits.title: Secret, Threshold, and Dealer Controls
exhibits.action: Set a secret, t, n, reproducible seed, advanced internals, and a cheating dealer or target party.
exhibits.outcome: Changed inputs retire previous results and drive every subsequent share and commitment experiment; invalid secret input is shown as a fallback.
exhibits.limits: Deterministic mode is for replay, not secrecy.

exhibits.title: Shares as Polynomial Points
exhibits.action: Adjust the controls and cheating dealer while inspecting the curve illustration.
exhibits.outcome: A small-number drawing locates the secret at x=0 and shows a tampered party point moved off the honest polynomial.
exhibits.section: The picture: shares are points on a curve
exhibits.limits: The drawing is illustrative; protocol arithmetic uses a 2048-bit safe-prime subgroup.

exhibits.title: Break Plain Shamir
exhibits.action: Choose one of four parties for tampering and toggle a cheating dealer.
exhibits.outcome: The share table and two-share reconstruction show that an unverified bad share can corrupt the secret without an advance warning.
exhibits.limits: This introductory step fixes a two-share reconstruction to make the failure visible; shared lab controls affect later VSS runs.

exhibits.title: Feldman Share Verification
exhibits.action: Run Feldman with honest or altered share, open the check decomposition and homomorphism panels, and inspect or copy coefficients and commitments.
exhibits.outcome: A per-party equation compares g raised to the received share with the product of coefficient commitments, rejecting the altered party.
exhibits.limits: C₀ = g^s exposes guesses and small secrets; the panel does not claim commitment hiding.

exhibits.title: Blinded Pedersen Verification and Equivocation
exhibits.action: Run Pedersen with a cheating dealer, inspect blinded share pairs and changing commitments, and open the equivocation explanation.
exhibits.outcome: The verifier checks g^s·h^r against public commitments and catches altered shares while blinded commitments conceal the secret.
exhibits.limits: This demo derives h deterministically from g; a known discrete log between them defeats binding, so it is not a production setup.

exhibits.title: Feldman versus Pedersen Side by Side
exhibits.action: Run both protocols using the same secret polynomial and threshold and inspect verification and property rows.
exhibits.outcome: The table contrasts commitment forms, hiding, binding, setup assumptions, share size, and use cases.
exhibits.limits: Comparison uses honest shares regardless of cheating toggle to isolate construction differences.

exhibits.title: Threat Model and Crypto Parameters
exhibits.action: Read attacker capabilities, protected and unprotected properties, group parameters, and randomness rules.
exhibits.outcome: The disclosures place share verification and secrecy against availability and side-channel limits and explain secure randomness and the generator caveat.

exhibits.title: Build and certify a keyring
exhibits.action: Generate a fresh browser keyring, add signed certifications, inspect signed payloads and revoke keys or certifications.
exhibits.outcome: Shows genuine WebCrypto signatures and verifies them before the trust graph can count an edge.
exhibits.limits: Keys share one browser session; IDs are deliberately truncated to eight bytes and are not OpenPGP fingerprints or packets.

exhibits.title: Set trust policy
exhibits.action: Assign each identity full, marginal or no owner trust and adjust marginal quorum and depth.
exhibits.outcome: Changes the personal introducer policy used in the next validity computation.
exhibits.limits: Owner trust is a personal policy judgment, distinct from a cryptographic certification.

exhibits.title: Compute and trace trust paths
exhibits.action: Recompute key validity and select graph nodes to trace introducers and verified certifications.
exhibits.outcome: Reports valid and invalid keys under current threshold and depth policy, with traceable trust paths.
exhibits.limits: Models GnuPG-style trust logic, not OpenPGP packet encoding or a production keyserver.

exhibits.title: Mutate trust and attack the model
exhibits.action: Run forged certification, orphan, over-trusted introducer, depth cap and 50-signature flooding scenarios.
exhibits.outcome: Forged signatures are rejected, while policy changes alter validity and a signature flood adds operational work without trustworthy paths.
exhibits.limits: Fifty local signatures model an operational concern; timings are browser-specific and not an SKS reproduction.

exhibits.title: Compare Web of Trust and PKI
exhibits.action: Read decentralized introducer policy beside hierarchical CA validation and trust vocabulary.
exhibits.outcome: Highlights who vouches for identity and who chooses the trust anchor.
exhibits.limits: Comparison does not run a real CA chain or OpenPGP client.

exhibits.title: Read deployment and failure context
exhibits.action: Read usage stories and operational pitfalls of key discovery and social trust.
exhibits.outcome: Places the model beside real-world trust management examples.
exhibits.limits: Narrative examples are not live integrations; production key management needs a vetted OpenPGP implementation.

exhibits.title: Passkey registration teaching flow
exhibits.action: Create a credential for the selected relying party and inspect the registration fields.
exhibits.outcome: See a public key enrolled while the private key remains with the authenticator model.
exhibits.limits: The in-page teaching engine models an authenticator; the separate live passkey panel invokes actual browser WebAuthn.

exhibits.title: Passkey assertion verification
exhibits.action: Authenticate and inspect challenge, origin, rpIdHash, flags, signature and counter checks.
exhibits.outcome: See verifier acceptance of a fresh assertion under registered credential data.

exhibits.title: Phishing, replay and wrong RP
exhibits.action: Run phishing, replay, wrong relying party and cloned-authenticator scenarios against the teaching verifier.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect the failing check for each attempted login and a valid baseline control.
exhibits.limits: Counter-based clone detection is limited, especially with authenticators that do not increment a per-credential counter.
exhibits.section: Break it (and watch each attack fail)

exhibits.title: Assertion field tampering
exhibits.action: Flip a signature byte, forge an origin or alter signCount in authenticatorData.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect signature or policy check failures on mutated assertions.
exhibits.section: Try tampering with a good assertion

exhibits.title: Real browser passkey experiment
exhibits.action: Use browser WebAuthn to register and authenticate a passkey on the page’s relying party.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect results from navigator.credentials rather than the classroom model.
exhibits.limits: Requires a secure origin and an available browser authenticator; no external identity service is part of the teaching flow.
exhibits.section: Try it with a real passkey

exhibits.title: What a passkey assertion signs
exhibits.action: Inspect the authenticator-to-server diagram and its signed fields.
exhibits.outcome: Trace challenge, origin, RP ID hash, flags and counter through the assertion to public-key checks at the relying party.
exhibits.limits: Diagram simplifies the browser serialization; the separate live panel shows real WebAuthn bytes.

exhibits.title: Discoverable credential and user verification
exhibits.action: Run discoverable login, missing-UV and missing-UP scenarios against a registered teaching credential.
exhibits.outcome: Compare verifier checks when the authenticator selects by RP ID and when user-presence or biometric/PIN flags are absent.
exhibits.limits: Flags and authenticator selection are modeled in the teaching engine; the real browser ceremony is separate.

exhibits.title: Passwords versus passkeys
exhibits.action: Read the phishing-resistance cards and expand the properties table.
exhibits.outcome: Compare shared-secret password login with origin-bound public-key assertions and server credential storage.

exhibits.title: Teaching verifier versus full WebAuthn relying party
exhibits.action: Inspect the six production-gap cards and their demo-versus-production columns.
exhibits.outcome: Distinguish checks modeled in the teaching verifier, discoverable/UV extensions, and requirements surfaced by the real browser ceremony.
exhibits.limits: The scope cards are explanatory; they do not themselves execute the missing production controls.
exhibits.section: What this teaching demo does not show

exhibits.title: RC4 Key Scheduling and Keystream
exhibits.action: Enter an inspection key, step or scrub 256 key-schedule states and initial keystream output bytes.
exhibits.outcome: Shows the permutation, swap indices, and emitted bytes from the actual RC4 state.
exhibits.limits: Inspection key belongs only to this panel and is unrelated to the later recovery target.

exhibits.title: Published RC4 Vector Check
exhibits.action: Inspect the table of expected RFC 6229 bytes and locally computed keystream bytes across keys and offsets.
exhibits.outcome: Shows exact match or difference for each row and a summary verdict.
exhibits.limits: Vector agreement tests implementation correctness, not RC4 security.

exhibits.title: RC4 Second-Byte Bias
exhibits.action: Choose sample count, measure independently keyed RC4 output and a control, then find a conditioned key and replay two output rounds.
exhibits.outcome: Shows zero-byte counts, confidence intervals and histogram, and exposes the state condition behind the distinguishing bias.
exhibits.section: The cipher on its own: the second byte leans toward zero
exhibits.limits: This is a distinguishing measurement, not the cited broadcast or TLS plaintext-recovery attacks.

exhibits.title: WEP Protected-Body Construction
exhibits.action: Set 40- or 104-bit shared key, three-byte IV, Key ID and message, then inspect encryption and receiver verification.
exhibits.outcome: Displays IV-prepended per-packet key, CRC-32 ICV, clear header, encrypted body and recomputed receiver ICV.
exhibits.limits: Models the protected body only; MAC header, outer frame check and radio are absent, and a matching CRC does not authenticate the sender.

exhibits.title: IV Collision and Crib Drag
exhibits.action: Generate synthetic packets until two share an IV, XOR their ciphertexts, then move an assumed plaintext crib across the result.
exhibits.outcome: Shows collision counts, C1⊕C2=P1⊕P2 and candidate sibling bytes under the chosen assumption.
exhibits.limits: XOR alone does not identify either plaintext; ground-truth reveal is outside the attacker path.

exhibits.title: CRC-32 Packet Modification
exhibits.action: Change an assumed same-length payload field, compute XOR mask and affine CRC correction, and compare uncorrected control with corrected packet.
exhibits.outcome: The uncorrected bit flip fails the ICV; the repaired altered packet reaches the same receiver and passes its ICV check.
exhibits.section: Change a message the receiver will still accept
exhibits.limits: Same-length edits only; ICV acceptance alone does not imply an application accepts the packet or that the attacker guessed its plaintext correctly.

exhibits.title: PTW Shared-Key Recovery
exhibits.action: Choose packet count, generate local distinct-IV capture bytes, and run the bounded PTW worker; inspect votes and optional ground-truth reveal.
exhibits.outcome: Reports validated key candidate or scoped non-result, sample and candidate counts, and separate controller confirmation against the hidden 104-bit key.
exhibits.limits: Synthetic local ARP-profile traffic, 20 held-out validation packets, 200,000 candidate or 30-second cap; no key within budget is not evidence of security.

exhibits.title: PTW Votes on Running Key Sums
exhibits.action: Inspect the attack’s vote tables and the public-IV estimator equations.
exhibits.outcome: Shows how candidate running sums yield secret bytes by differences, with strong-byte cases and candidate validation instead of assuming each vote is a key byte.
exhibits.limits: Vote leaders are evidence, not probabilities; strong-byte sums can remain equidistributed even with more packets.

exhibits.title: Explain the role of post-quantum key agreement and shared secrets
exhibits.action: Read the introduction and expand the glossary before starting the exchanges.
exhibits.outcome: It separates the attacker model, public keys, ciphertext, agreed secret, and authentication without treating PQC as a stronger lock.
exhibits.limits: This introduction explains a threat model; it does not run a quantum attack or establish the security of ML-KEM.

exhibits.title: Run a classical X25519 exchange between two parties
exhibits.section: Two people agree on a secret, in the open
exhibits.action: Run the classical panel again with fresh private and public values.
exhibits.outcome: Rae and Dev calculate matching 32-byte secrets independently and the UI shows the two public values that crossed the wire.
exhibits.limits: No quantum computation or present-day break of X25519 occurs; the shared secret is not an encrypted conversation.

exhibits.title: Run ML-KEM-768 encapsulation and decapsulation
exhibits.section: The same thing, on a different hard problem
exhibits.action: Run the post-quantum panel again with a fresh keypair and sealed box.
exhibits.outcome: The page compares the encapsulator and decapsulator secrets and lists the public key and ciphertext transmitted.
exhibits.limits: The ciphertext generates a shared secret; it does not contain Dev’s message, and this bare exchange does not authenticate the key owner.

exhibits.title: Measure and compare the exchange bytes
exhibits.section: Bigger, on a different problem — and that is the whole list
exhibits.action: Compare to-scale bars, per-object sizes, total wire bytes, and the quotient from the two live exchanges.
exhibits.outcome: The UI computes the ratio from emitted byte arrays while keeping the locally held 32-byte secret out of wire totals.
exhibits.limits: The ratio describes these key-agreement messages, not a whole TLS connection, speed, or a security-strength ranking.

exhibits.title: Change one ciphertext byte and inspect implicit rejection
exhibits.action: Predict an outcome, change one byte of the ML-KEM sealed box, compare both secrets and the error status, then restore it.
exhibits.outcome: Decapsulation returns a well-formed, different secret without reporting a failure; the prediction is graded against the measured run.
exhibits.limits: The panel does not perform the later authentication or key-confirmation step that a real protocol needs to detect divergent keys.

exhibits.title: Demonstrate the missing authentication of a bare key exchange
exhibits.action: Predict the result and choose whether Rae or an impostor handed Dev the public key.
exhibits.outcome: Dev and the actual owner agree on a secret even with the impostor key, while the intended Rae does not share it and the exchange reports no warning.
exhibits.limits: The same authentication gap applies to the bare X25519 demonstration; signed keys or transcript binding are outside this panel.

exhibits.title: Illustrate delayed decryption of a recorded classical session
exhibits.action: Follow the record, wait, and possible future reading frames and the long-lived-secret disclosure.
exhibits.outcome: The illustration reuses the measured public-value byte total from panel 1 and explains why a future break could expose previously recorded traffic.
exhibits.limits: No traffic is captured, no future quantum machine is simulated, and no arrival date is predicted.

exhibits.title: Identify what the live demonstrations establish
exhibits.section: What is real here, and what this does not prove
exhibits.action: Open the implementation and verification disclosure after the demonstrations.
exhibits.outcome: The page distinguishes real browser cryptography and checked primitive vectors from unshown quantum attacks, unproved security, and omitted ML-KEM internals.
exhibits.limits: This is a teaching demo with tab-local keys, not production cryptography or proof that ML-KEM is secure.

exhibits.title: Rerun seven cipher known-answer tests
exhibits.action: Rerun published block-cipher test vectors for all seven algorithms.
exhibits.outcome: Displays pass/fail per implementation against known plaintext, key and ciphertext values.
exhibits.limits: Passing finite vectors confirms those examples, not every implementation or security property.

exhibits.title: Encrypt and decrypt with Camellia and compare AES-CBC
exhibits.action: Enter text and key, select ECB or CBC, encrypt/decrypt and run AES-CBC comparison.
exhibits.outcome: Displays Camellia ciphertext and round structure plus distinct AES-CBC output for the same inputs.
exhibits.limits: ECB and CBC examples are confidentiality-only and require appropriate key, IV and authentication handling.

exhibits.title: Encrypt with ARIA and inspect substitution and diffusion
exhibits.action: Encrypt/decrypt, apply an S-box, and apply the diffusion transform twice.
exhibits.outcome: Displays ciphertext, inverse behavior and ARIA internal transformation properties.
exhibits.limits: Block-cipher output alone provides no message authentication.

exhibits.title: Encrypt with SM4 and replay the 32-round trace
exhibits.action: Encrypt/decrypt a block and replay the round animation.
exhibits.outcome: Shows per-round state changes and final ciphertext.
exhibits.limits: Round animation is explanatory; security is not measured from one trace.

exhibits.title: Encrypt and decrypt with Kuznyechik
exhibits.action: Set key and plaintext and run encryption/decryption.
exhibits.outcome: Displays encrypted bytes and recovered plaintext.
exhibits.limits: Single-cipher demonstrations do not provide authentication or justify selecting a deployment mode.

exhibits.title: Encrypt and decrypt with Kalyna
exhibits.action: Set key and plaintext and run encryption/decryption.
exhibits.outcome: Displays ciphertext and recovered plaintext.
exhibits.limits: The demo is not a complete authenticated encryption protocol.

exhibits.title: Encrypt and decrypt with BelT
exhibits.action: Set key and plaintext and run encryption/decryption.
exhibits.outcome: Displays ciphertext and round-trip plaintext.
exhibits.limits: The block primitive does not by itself authenticate data.

exhibits.title: Encrypt and decrypt with SEED
exhibits.action: Set key, IV and plaintext and run SEED-CBC encryption/decryption.
exhibits.outcome: Displays ciphertext and recovered text.
exhibits.limits: CBC needs an unpredictable IV and separate authentication for secure use.

exhibits.title: Flip an input bit across seven block ciphers
exhibits.action: Choose a cipher and bit flip, run or randomize the key and block.
exhibits.outcome: Counts differing ciphertext bits and visualizes a single-sample avalanche result.
exhibits.limits: One bit-flip sample is not a statistical test or security guarantee.

exhibits.title: Compare repeated blocks and an encrypted image
exhibits.action: Encrypt identical blocks under ECB and CBC and encrypt the provided picture.
exhibits.outcome: ECB repeats ciphertext patterns while CBC with its IV obscures repeated plaintext blocks in these samples.
exhibits.limits: CBC without authentication remains malleable; the image view demonstrates pattern leakage, not complete mode security.
exhibits.section: Exhibit 9 — Why Mode Matters: ECB vs CBC

exhibits.title: Inspect seven-cipher comparison and selection flow
exhibits.action: Read the comparison table and decision tree.
exhibits.outcome: Maps key sizes, rounds and regional standards for the seven implemented ciphers.
exhibits.limits: Static comparison is educational context; choosing a cipher also depends on standards, implementation and protocol needs.

exhibits.title: Hash Properties with Live SHA-256
exhibits.action: Type text and watch SHA-256 digest, byte count, fixed output size, and a neighboring input change.
exhibits.outcome: The introduction demonstrates deterministic output and visible avalanche while explaining one-way and collision-resistance goals.
exhibits.section: Start here — what is a cryptographic hash?
exhibits.limits: A visual avalanche example does not prove resistance to collisions or preimages.

exhibits.title: SM3 Hash and Selectable Avalanche Edit
exhibits.action: Enter text or hex, compare live SM3 and SHA-256 digests, select a character to flip, and inspect the changed output.
exhibits.outcome: Changed nibbles and bit diffusion make a narrow-pipe Merkle–Damgård construction tangible.

exhibits.title: Streebog 256/512 Hash
exhibits.action: Choose text or hex and 256- or 512-bit output, then inspect digest and one-character avalanche.
exhibits.outcome: The output shows the Russian standard’s distinct digest sizes and explains its wide-pipe and S-box design.

exhibits.title: Kupyna 256/512 Hash
exhibits.action: Choose input encoding and 256- or 512-bit digest and inspect the live output and avalanche comparison.
exhibits.outcome: The explanation traces wide-pipe chaining and its output transformation rather than treating Kupyna as a sponge.

exhibits.title: Seven Live Digests and Reference Anchors
exhibits.action: Enter one text or hex message to compute SHA-256, SHA-3, SM3, Streebog, Kupyna, Bash, and LSH side by side.
exhibits.outcome: The panel distinguishes SHA-3 and Bash sponges from chaining constructions and compares seven one-edit avalanche outcomes.
exhibits.section: Exhibit 4 — SHA-256 and SHA-3 as Reference Anchors
exhibits.limits: The Bash sponge and LSH implementation are local code with separate vector provenance and limitations.

exhibits.title: Known-Answer Verification
exhibits.action: Inspect load-time test results and source provenance for the digest implementations.
exhibits.outcome: The table reports live vector agreement, while Bash Annex A checks and independent versus Crypto++ LSH checks are counted separately.
exhibits.limits: Cross-implementation agreement is distinguished from independent standard vectors; vector matches do not prove full security.

exhibits.title: Real SHA-256 and SM3 Length Extension
exhibits.action: Select SHA-256 or SM3, change the server secret, public message, append suffix, and secret-length guess, then run the forgery or wrong-length control.
exhibits.outcome: A resumable compression implementation forges the naive H(secret‖message) tag when the length matches and compares it byte for byte to the server recomputation.
exhibits.section: Exhibit 5 — Break it: length extension, for real
exhibits.limits: This attacks a deliberately naive secret-prefix tag, not HMAC.

exhibits.title: Length-Extension Resistance Lineup
exhibits.action: Try analogous tag continuation against SHA-3, Bash, Kupyna, LSH, Streebog, and HMAC and inspect state bits withheld and countermeasure columns.
exhibits.outcome: The table differentiates sponge/wide-pipe nonexposure from explicit finalization and HMAC, and shows where naive continuation cannot match.
exhibits.section: The same attack against the constructions that resist it
exhibits.limits: Failure of this attack does not establish that Bash(secret‖message) is an authenticating MAC.

exhibits.title: Truncated Digest Collision Search
exhibits.action: Choose an algorithm and 8–32 bit truncation width, run a birthday search, or impose a 50-hash budget.
exhibits.outcome: A pair of distinct inputs is rehashed to confirm matching truncated prefixes while full digests remain distinct, with attempts and expected work shown.
exhibits.section: Collision resistance, at a width you can actually attack
exhibits.limits: This only collides short prefixes; it does not break full digests.

exhibits.title: National Standards Comparison and Decision Tree
exhibits.action: Compare seven algorithm columns by origin, output size, construction, standardization, deployment fit, and editorial trust notes.
exhibits.outcome: The guide separates factual properties and observed vector evidence from the author’s trust opinions and ecosystem caveats.
exhibits.section: Exhibit 5 — Six-Way Comparison and Decision Tree
exhibits.limits: Trust grades are explicitly editorial opinion; the displayed table actually has seven algorithm columns.

exhibits.title: Tamper the signed prekey signature
exhibits.action: Flip the SPK signature byte or substitute an attacker-signed SPK while Bob's identity key remains in the bundle.
exhibits.outcome: XEdDSA verification fails and the X3DH handshake aborts before deriving a shared secret or sending a message.

exhibits.title: Replace the whole prekey bundle
exhibits.action: Offer a different identity key and its correctly signed prekey, then compare the offered fingerprint with a previously trusted Bob fingerprint.
exhibits.outcome: The signature can remain valid while the identity pin mismatches. The deliberately unpinned continuation lets the attacker derive the same session key and decrypt the first message.
exhibits.limits: The trusted fingerprint is a teaching fixture; real users must authenticate identities independently. The unpinned continuation demonstrates the failure and is not a secure protocol path.

exhibits.title: Drop the optional one-time prekey
exhibits.action: Toggle off Bob's one-time prekey and examine the DH set and status strip.
exhibits.outcome: The fourth DH term is omitted, while Alice and Bob can still derive a matching shared secret.
exhibits.limits: This teaching contrast does not constitute a forward-secrecy proof.

exhibits.title: Corrupt Alice's ephemeral key on the wire
exhibits.action: Flip a byte of the transmitted EK_A public key and follow Bob's derivation and initial-message decryption.
exhibits.outcome: The independently computed secrets diverge and AES-GCM authentication fails at Bob.
exhibits.limits: The initial-message demonstration omits X3DH's identity-key associated data, explicitly disclosed in src/ui.ts:628.

exhibits.title: Signed Prekey Bundle and Identity Pin
exhibits.action: Inspect Bob’s published key bundle, XEdDSA signed prekey and offered-versus-trusted identity fingerprint.
exhibits.outcome: The verifier authenticates the prekey under an offered identity; an independently established pin is needed to know the identity belongs to Bob.
exhibits.section: Panel 1: Key Registry — offered prekey bundle

exhibits.title: Alice Initiates Asynchronously
exhibits.action: Advance to Alice’s fresh identity and ephemeral keys and the fetched public prekey bundle while Bob is offline.
exhibits.outcome: The panel shows which public fields Alice receives before computing the first-session DH terms.

exhibits.title: X3DH Diffie-Hellman Terms and Commutativity
exhibits.action: Toggle Alice and Bob views, compare DH2’s two computations, regenerate keys and inspect DH1 through DH4.
exhibits.outcome: With matching keys, both endpoints derive identical 32-byte leg outputs; an absent OPK drops DH4.

exhibits.title: Concatenated DH Material to Session Key
exhibits.action: Inspect F and the computed DH blocks entering HKDF-SHA-256 and compare Alice and Bob session keys.
exhibits.outcome: The output shows byte equality or a highlighted difference when tampered inputs change a DH term.

exhibits.title: Initial AES-GCM Message and Ratchet Handoff
exhibits.action: Inspect transmitted public fields, IV and ciphertext and Bob’s decryption outcome.
exhibits.outcome: The panel shows the derived SK protecting the first message before Double Ratchet handoff.
exhibits.limits: The demo omits the spec’s identity-associated data, weakening context binding.

exhibits.title: Understand the proof families
exhibits.section: What even is a SNARK or a STARK?
exhibits.action: Follow definitions and suggested reading order for succinct arguments and transparent proofs.
exhibits.outcome: Introduces proof, verifier, zero knowledge, succinctness and setup vocabulary.
exhibits.limits: Primer is conceptual and does not implement a full SNARK or STARK.

exhibits.title: Compare systems by dimension
exhibits.action: Select comparison dimensions using tabs or keyboard and inspect winner and explanation.
exhibits.outcome: Contrasts setup, proof size, verification and assumptions across SNARK/STARK families.
exhibits.limits: Values and winners are explanatory approximations, not measurements of two production proof systems here.

exhibits.title: Draw relative proof bytes
exhibits.action: Move a circuit-size slider and inspect dot-scaled proof bytes and gas projections.
exhibits.outcome: Shows how the modeled size curves diverge and how visual dots are truncated for display.
exhibits.limits: Formula-driven illustrative sizes, not generated proof artifacts or live blockchain gas measurement.

exhibits.title: Run a zero-knowledge identification
exhibits.action: Choose toy or safe group, interactive or Fiat-Shamir mode, honest or forged prover, and step commit, challenge, response and verify.
exhibits.outcome: Checks Schnorr equations using browser BigInt and random/hash challenge generation.
exhibits.limits: Schnorr is not a SNARK or STARK; toy composite-order group leaks information from its public key.

exhibits.title: Extract weak-group secrets
exhibits.action: Run Pohlig-Hellman on the selected public key or setup parameter in toy versus safe group.
exhibits.outcome: Demonstrates information recoverable from a weak group before any transcript is observed.
exhibits.limits: The small composite-order group is deliberately weak; safe-group demonstration is bounded and not a security proof.

exhibits.title: Forge a commitment with retained setup trapdoor
exhibits.action: Choose destroy or keep tau, run a ceremony, commit and attempt a false opening.
exhibits.outcome: Verifier rejects an ordinary guess but accepts a back-solved opening when trapdoor remains.
exhibits.limits: This Pedersen analogy models a setup failure; it is not a deployed SNARK ceremony.

exhibits.title: Score a use case
exhibits.action: Answer use-case questions and optionally share the result via URL.
exhibits.outcome: Shows a scored recommendation balance between proof families.
exhibits.limits: A teaching heuristic, not a production architecture review.

exhibits.title: Survey implementations and history
exhibits.action: Read named systems, milestones and common properties of proof families.
exhibits.outcome: Connects the interactive comparisons to particular implementations and chronology.
exhibits.limits: Examples and timeline are curated context; no named external system is run in the page.

exhibits.title: Ali Baba cave repeated challenge
exhibits.action: Run one or ten rounds with an honest or bluffing prover.
exhibits.outcome: Compare the probability that a bluffer answers independent verifier challenges across rounds.

exhibits.title: Graph three-coloring commitments
exhibits.action: Run a graph-coloring proof, challenge an edge, tamper an opening or repeat rounds.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect local edge-color checks and the effect of tampered commitments.

exhibits.title: Commitment brute force and transcript extraction
exhibits.action: Brute-force weak commitment nonces or feed accepted rounds to a transcript extractor.
exhibits.outcome: Compare a small nonce search with stronger randomness and inspect what repeated revealing transcripts expose.
exhibits.limits: The tiny nonce variant is deliberately weak; it does not generalize to adequately randomized commitments.

exhibits.title: Schnorr identification and nonce leak
exhibits.action: Run or step a Schnorr identification transcript, simulate cheating and reveal nonce r.
exhibits.outcome: Check the verifier equation and recover the witness when an honest prover’s nonce leaks.
exhibits.limits: Uses a small teaching group; the cheat run may have no valid witness to recover.

exhibits.title: Hash commit and reveal
exhibits.action: Submit two bids, reveal nonces and bids, then attempt to change a committed bid.
exhibits.outcome: The verifier recomputes SHA-256 commitments and detects changed openings.

exhibits.title: Non-interactive Fiat–Shamir proof
exhibits.action: Generate a proof, tamper with its message and compare verification; export transcript.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect how message-derived challenge changes and when the verifier equation fails.
exhibits.limits: The toy challenge domain has 50 values; different messages can collide and the demo explicitly reports that boundary.

exhibits.title: zk-SNARK intuition pipeline
exhibits.action: Generate a toy proof, alter its public input, and compare the verifier result.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect a checked polynomial relation and SHA-256 digest; the proof envelope contains the private witness, making this a visible teaching model.
exhibits.limits: The toy envelope exposes its witness and does not implement a zero-knowledge proof or a SNARK cryptosystem.

exhibits.title: Okamoto and Guillou–Quisquater
exhibits.action: Run Okamoto and GQ proofs, rewind answers and test a public-data-only cheater.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect verifier equations, witness extraction under alternate challenges and empirical cheating acceptance.

exhibits.title: Transcript comparison workbench
exhibits.action: Load or paste two prior proof transcripts and compare their public fields.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect differences and replayable public transcript records across exhibit types.

exhibits.title: Sum-check and a bounded GKR layer walk
exhibits.section: Sum-check and a GKR layer walk
exhibits.action: Run or step the sum-check prover and verifier over an explicit prime-field polynomial, replay malformed or dishonest transcripts, then reuse the checked primitive to walk a fixed two-layer circuit from outputs to public inputs.
exhibits.outcome: Inspect every round polynomial, degree and recurrence check, post-message challenge and direct final evaluation; then inspect two wiring-identity reductions, line checks and the verifier's terminal multilinear-extension evaluation.
exhibits.limits: The page executes an interactive proof, not zero knowledge or a SNARK. The fixed two-layer adaptation enumerates six gates and omits GKR's uniformity machinery, sublinear verifier and general theorem; seeded challenges are replay controls and do not satisfy the displayed soundness premise.

exhibits.title: Ordered Security Policy and Selector Narrowing
exhibits.action: Run concrete Telnet, DNS and ICMP flows through the ordered SPD and compare each first-match disposition with the independently selected route.
exhibits.outcome: Shows DISCARD, BYPASS and PROTECT outcomes beside routing, then computes the traffic-selector intersection installed for the Child SA.
exhibits.limits: Uses fixed IPv4 TEST-NET flows and an in-browser policy model rather than a kernel SPD or routing table.

exhibits.title: Four-Message PSK IKEv2 Handshake
exhibits.action: Run fresh or fixed evidence to encode IKE_SA_INIT, compute X25519 and the IKE key schedule, authenticate both identities, and seal and open both IKE_AUTH messages.
exhibits.outcome: Displays the exact four-message transcript, shared secret, SKEYSEED, PSK AUTH, IKE AAD and independently verified identities and transcript bindings.
exhibits.limits: The bounded profile supports one PSK, one transform proposal and no certificate, EAP, NAT-traversal, MOBIKE or interoperable socket layer.

exhibits.title: Two Directional Child Security Associations
exhibits.action: Inspect the receiver-selected SPI, AES key and salt for each simplex direction after initial Child KEYMAT derivation.
exhibits.outcome: Shows that initiator-to-responder and responder-to-initiator traffic use distinct 20-byte KEYMAT slices and inbound SA identifiers.
exhibits.limits: The first Child SA has no fresh DH exchange and the lesson models one selector pair and one transform suite.

exhibits.title: Transport Echo, Tunnel Fallback, and Protected Deletion
exhibits.action: Request tunnel or transport mode, vary the responder echo and local fallback policy, and rerun the negotiation.
exhibits.outcome: Establishes transport only when USE_TRANSPORT_MODE is echoed, otherwise executes tunnel fallback or a protected paired-SPI Child-SA deletion.
exhibits.limits: Mode negotiation is confined to the declared IKEv2 teaching profile and does not install operating-system policy.

exhibits.title: Authenticated ESP Packet and IPv4 Boundaries
exhibits.action: Protect an actual IPv4 fixture in the negotiated mode, inspect every ESP field, then authenticate, decrypt and reconstruct the packet.
exhibits.outcome: Displays clear SPI, sequence and explicit IV, exact AAD, nonce, ciphertext, encrypted trailer and 16-byte tag while contrasting transport and tunnel packet boundaries.
exhibits.limits: The sequence-derived explicit IV is this profile's uniqueness construction, not a universal negotiated ESP rule.

exhibits.title: ESP Replay-Window Receiver State Machine
exhibits.action: Submit reordered, duplicate, too-old, modified-ahead, later-valid and unknown-SPI packets to controlled receiver states.
exhibits.outcome: Shows SAD lookup, pure replay precheck, AES-GCM authentication and replay-state commit in order, including that an invalid tag cannot advance the window.
exhibits.limits: Uses a 64-packet non-ESN window and synthetic in-browser packets; it does not measure network timing or loss.

exhibits.title: Child-SA Rekey, Overlap, and Retirement
exhibits.action: Derive fresh Child-SA keys and SPIs, accept old and new generations during overlap, try old key material under the new SPI, then delete and retire the old pair.
exhibits.outcome: Shows fresh keys, salts, counters and replay windows, authentication failure for wrong-generation keying, protected paired-SPI deletion and refusal after retirement.
exhibits.limits: This is Child-SA rekey without a fresh DH transform; it does not implement IKE-SA rekey or production lifecycle coordination.
